summary: The Food Inspector took a sample of lal mirchi powder from the grocery shop of the respondent. On analysis by the Public Analyst it was found in exhibit PW 1/C that the sample contained nine living meal worms. There was no other evidence in support of the case of the prosecution that the Lal mirchi seed was adulterated. The Food Inspector, P.W. 4 took a samples of lal Ergingi powder from grocery shops of the Respondent. On examination by the public Analyst it found that the samples contained nine live living meal Worms and there was no evidence in respect of the said article of food contained in section 2(1)(f) of the Act. The Magistrate accepted this contention and found that prosecution had failed to prove that the lal mirgi powder was adulterated and he accordingly acquitted the respondent, and acquitted him. The High Court in appeal by special leave held that the prosecution had not established by any satisfactory evidence the requirement of section 2 (1)(a) of 'the Act. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant Corporation that in the case where food articles for which no minimum standard or purity is prescribed, the moment it is proved that a proportion of percentage of the article not being a proportion or percentage as would be covered by the rule, de minimis non curat lex is putrid, filthy, disgusting, decomposed or insect infested, it would be deemed to be unfit for human consumption and therefore adulterated within the contemplation of section2(1) (f). Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The word 'insect ' is defined in the Oxford Dictionary as "small invertebrate segmented animal having head, thorax, abdomen, and three pairs of thoracic legs usually with one or two pairs Of thorocic (1) 1973 (Prevention of Food Adulteration Cases) 257.

The appellant was an agriculturist and was not liable to the penalty under the law, because the presumption in his case could not be drawn. It is obvious that sub para speaks of storage for sale as a dealer although the words "as a dealer" are not there, because storage has reference to business as a 'dealer and that is the essence of the Order. The fiction in the second sub paragraph must be carried to its logical conclusion. In the present case, the appellant produced a number of lease deeds in which leases of various parcels of land were shown to have been granted to him. He also produced receipts of payment of lease money and he cited witnesses who deposed on oath that he and his brother cultivated 80 90 bighas of land. No doubt, the lease deeds are not registered but for the purpose of a criminal prosecution, it is easy to see that the evidence which was 'brought for ward of witnesses deposing orally was not concocted to set up a false defence. Indeed no adequate reasons were given for rejecting the testimony of witnesses. The Magistrate rejected the evidence on the ground that the lease deed deeds were not registered and were not admissible in evidence under section 49 of the Registration Act. The Sessions Judge did not accept this ground and held that such documents could be brought into existence at any time and were thus not reliable. Both the Magistrate and the Sessions judge did not agree with the evidence of the witnesses on the grounds that they were interested in the appellant 's case. On appeal by special leave, HELD: (i) The presumption under para 3(2) could not therefore be drawn against him. [901 D] Manipur Administration vs M. Nila Chandra Singh ; followed. (ii) In the instant case, there was no adequate reason for rejecting his testimony. The evidence of one witness on the other showed that he was in fact carrying on agricultural operations. He executed a number Of lease deeds, produced receipts and proved by oral evidence that he had and his brothers cultivated 80 bighas of lands. No question of any doubt arises as to whether the appellant is an agriculturist or not. [999 G H] Manipur administration vs M Nila Chander Singh ; , followed.

The respondent, a monthly tenant of the appellant, was in occupation of certain land. The tenancy was determined by a notice to quit and the rent amounting to Rs. 46 per annum was paid for the first time on 8th March, 1925. The next payment of rent was made in the succeeding year, on 16th of March, 1926. Admittedly no further payment of rents was made either to the Receiver or to the proprietor since then, up to this period. The respondent filed a suit (being Title Suit No. 67 of 1921) in the Court of the Subordinate Judge at Midnapore for establishment of his title to the zemindari and the suit was decreed by the trial court and the decision was affirmed on appeal by the District Judge. On second appeal, the High Court held that the respondent was not a monthly tenancy under the appellant at the date when the notice to terminate the tenancy was served upon him. Held, that the tenancy of the respondent in 1924 was one from month to month since its inception in 1924 and consequently a tenancy from monthto month came into existence in accordance with the provisions of section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act. The lease was intended to be for a period exceeding one year, but as the intention was not expressed in the proper legal form, it could not be given effect to. It would be pertinent to point out that in the Second Appeal preferred by the respondent against the dismissal of his earlier suit by the lower appellate court, the only question left open was whether payment to the receiver amounted to payment to payment of annual rent, and a stipulation like that would not come within the mischief of section 107 of the Act.

The appellant, Trilok Chand Jain instituted a suit for recovery of Rs. 1,39,722.86 against the respondents, M/s. Dagi Ram Pindi Lal and Smt. Budh Wanti Gulati, w/o Shri Pindi Lai Gulati. During the course of proceedings in the suit, when evidence was being recorded, the plaintiff obtained summons from the court requiring the Income Tax Department to produce in the Court records relating to the income tax assessment of the defendants, M.Dagi Ram and Smt Budh Wunti Gulati w/O Shri Phani Lal Gulati for the assessment years 1964 65 to 1971 72. The Income Tax officer to whom the summons were issued sent the record in a sealed cover alongwith a letter in which it was submitted that no disclosure of information regarding income tax pertaining to an assessee could be made. The plaintiff also applied for and obtained permission of the Court to tender the certified copies in evidence. Arguments were addressed by the parties before the Single Judge on the question of privilege as claimed by the Income tax officer. Being of the opinion that the question whether privilege, as claimed, was important and likely to arise in the course or the course in which these questions arose, the Full Bench referred the matter to a Full Bench. The Full Bench considered different situations. It considered the first question in the following four situations: (a) where the documents, records etc., in respect of which privilege is claimed were filed by an assessee or a third party before April 1, 1962, with effect from which date the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922 was repealed; and (b) where documents, record etc. in respect thereof were filed on or after April 1 1964, in respect for assessment years upto and including assessment year 1961 62 in proceedings for the said assessment years taking place under the Indian income tax Act, 1961.

The respondent filed a suit challenging the gift as invalid on the ground that it was made in contemplation of death and was voidable. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that there was no issue and the remaining 3/4 share was divisible between the two sisters and the other sister, and decreed the suit. On appeal by the plaintiff, the High Court held that a gift by the husband to his minor wife to be valid must be accepted on her behalf by a legal guardian of her property under the Muhammadan Law, that is to say, by the father or his executor or by the grand father or by his grand father and that as the gift was by a registered deed no question in this behalf could arise. Held, that there can be no question that there has been a complete intention to divest ownership on the part of the donor and to transfer the property to the donee. If the property is with the donor he must depart from it and the donee must enter upon possession. The strict view was that the donor must not leave behind even a straw belonging to him to show his ownership and possession. In such cases the benefit to the minor and the completion of the gift for his benefit is the sole consideration. As there is good authority for these propositions in the ancient and modern books of Muhammadan law and in decided cases of undoubted authority, it must be held that the gift must be accept ed as valid and complete. The rule about possession is relaxed in certain circumstances of which the following passage from the Hedaya p. 484 mentions some: "It is lawful for a husband to take possession of any thing given to his wife, being an infant, provided she has been sent from her father 's house to his mother". A gift to a minor through the mother was considered invalid and it was held that when a document embodying the intention of the donee was delivered to the guardian of the property of the minor possessing discretion and accepted by her it amounted to acceptance of gift. The gift in the present case was a valid gift.

The Madras Religious and Charitable Endowments Act 19 of 1951 was enacted to provide for the better administration and governance of Hindu Religious and charitable institutions and Endowments in the State of Madras. The Act provided that the trustee of every religious institution shall keep regular accounts of all receipts and disbursements. Section 76(1) provides that the Government may make rules to carry out all or any of the purposes of this Act and not inconsistent therewith. The respondents who were trustees of the Venkataramana Temple at Mulki, challenged the validity of the demand on the ground that no rules had been framed under section 100 of the Act and therefore the demand for levy of contribution was without jurisdiction. Held, that the High Court erred in holding that the Commissioner had not determined the audit fee under section 76(2) of the Madras Act 19. The Commissioner has to form an estimate of the reasonable cost which may be incurred in making an effective audit of the accounts of the religious endowment and to state it in terms of a percentage of the income. The percentage of income levied as audit fee must of necessity be based on an estimate, and the demand will not be struck down merely because it turns out that the amount demanded is not precisely equivalent to the cost actually incurred for auditing the accounts. The High Court was therefore right in holding the Commissioner 's report that no rule had been made under section 1020(2). The order of the High court must, therefore, be set aside and it directed that the case should be remanded to the High.

The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the notice issued by the High court. The High Court held that no appeal lies to this Court as a matter of right under section 19 of the Act from an order rejecting the prayer of the alleged contemner for bearing the case piecemeal. In appeal to this court, it was contended on behalf of the respondents that no appeals lay to this Supreme Court as the matter of rights under section 20 of the . Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The preliminary objection raised on behalf 'the respondents is well founded and must be accepted as correct. Section 19(1) says "lm15 An appeal shall lie as of right from any order or decision of a bench of the High 'Court in the exercise of its jurisdiction to punish for contempt (a) where the order or decisions is that of a single judge, to a Bench of not less than two Judges of the Court; (b) where an order or judgment is that by a single Judge to a bench, to the Supreme Court : Provided that where the Order or decision is that 'of a single judges, to which a Bench shall be appealable to this High Court. " The appeal was, therefore, dismissed as being not maintainable. [512 D E] Baradakanta Mishra vs Justice Gatikrushna Mishra, A.I.R. 1976 S.C. 1206; Baradkanta Mishra v Justice Gogatikrunna Mishra A.l.R., 1976 S C. 1207 and Barad Dasanta Mishra V Justice Gitikrushnna Mishra ; , referred to.

The appellant was prosecuted along with another, in the Court of the Magistrate First Class, Delhi under section 6(1 A) Of the , for possessing a wireless transmitter in contravention of the provisions of section 3 of the Act. The trial court upheld the conviction but reduced the sentence to the period already undergone plus a fine of Rs. 500. On appeal, the High Court confirmed both the conviction and the sentence. Held, that the word " text " is comprehensive enough to take in wireless telegraphy transmitter ' this Court gave leave limited to the question of sentence only went wrong, for if that section was not on the statute book at the time of the alleged commission of the offence, not only the sentence but also the conviction thereunder would be bad. The word " in its dictionary meaning means " subject or theme". When an enactment amends the text of another it amends the subject or proposal of it though sometimes it may expunge unnecessary words without altering the subject. Held further, that section 4 Of the 1952 Act has no application to a case of repeal of an earlier Act which had been applied, incorporated or referred to. The words " unless a different intention appears, the repeal shall not affect the continuance of any such amendment made by the enactment so repealed and in operation at the lime of such repeal." The word ' text ' is comprehensive sufficient enough to taking in wireless Telegraphy transmitters ' this court gave leave restricted to the questions of sentence. The inconsistency, if any, was the result of the appellant 's presentation of his case at that stage and he cannot now be allowed to take advantage of his default to enlarge the scope of the appeal. That apart, there are no merits in the contention. Khuda Bux vs Manager, Caledonian Press Chakravartti, C.J., neatly brought out the purpose and (1) A.I.R. 1954 Punj.

The appellant, who was the managing Shebait of a deities from 1926 to 1930 and as Shebait, executed a Hatchita in favour of one Nanitosh Chakraborty some time in April 1928 on the basis of which he received advances of money from time to time from the latter. The last entry in the Hatchitita was made in March 1929 and the total amount borrowed up to that date came up to Rs. 3,801. Adwaita died in March 1930 and after his death, Satish Chandra Roy became the managing shebait and continued to act as such till his death in 1940. There was an adjustment of accounts between Nanitash and the creditor in whose favour the Hundita was executed, and a sum of Rs. 5,068 having been found due to the 128 creditor, Satish Chander gave him a renewed Hatchi for that amount. It appears that while Adwa was still the managing trustee, a suit was instituted by some of his co Shebaits to remove him from his office and pending the hearing of the suit, Ramjanaki Roy, another co Shebait was appointed a Receiver of the debutter property by the court. With the permission of the Court, Ramayanaki Roy borrowed from the same Nanit Karra on the 27th September, 1929, 1st October, 1929 and 14th January, 1930. The properties described in Schedules Ka, Kha and Ga to the deities under the provision of section 36(2)(c) of the Bengal Money Lenders Act were attached and put up for sale and they were also purchased by the decreeholders. A suit was filed by some Of his co sharers to remove them from office and Pending the hearing and final disposal of the suits, the properties mentioned in Schedules Kha and Ka were sold and they are also purchased ostensibly by the judgment debtors. The trial judge decided against the judgment debtor and granted their prayers in both the applications. Orders were made for reopening of the decrees and making fresh decrees in their places in accordance with the provisions of the Act. In execution cases Nos. 76 and 77 of 1936 arising out of Money Suits Nos. 261 and 262 of 1932, the property mentioned in Schedule Kha were attached, and put to sale and it was also purchased on the 26th July, 1940. The appellant filed two applications under section 36 (6) (a)(ii) of Act praying for reopening the decrees, which were decreed by both the courts below. The main contention raised before the High Court was that in a proceeding under section 35 of the said Act it is not open to the court to go behind the decree and launch an enquiry as to whether the decreeholder on record was himself a benamidar for another person in respect of the decree, does not come within the purview of these provisions. Held, that the High Courts were right in holding that in making a new decree under clause (a) of section36(2) and giving the judgmentdebtor consequential relief under clause(c) to the borrower in the manner provided for in the Act, namely, to release him from all liability for interest in excess of the limits prescribed by section 30 of the , it is altogether immaterial that it was Aghore, the husband of the appellant who, really advanced the money upon which the decrees were obtained. The drafting of section 35 is quite obscure and somewhat clumsy but it is clear, as the Privy Council (1) has pointed out, that an enquiry under section 38 of the Calcutta Act is altogether outside the purview Of the different clauses of section 6(2). Clause (a), of section 34(2), does not apply to a proceeding in respect to which the ostensible purchaser at the execution sale or the person who purports to have acquired an interest therein under a subsequent transfer from the decree holder purchaser, has bonafide acquired such rights within the meaning of clause (b) of that section.

The respondent company instituted a suit against the appellant for recovery of certain amounts due to it by virtue of an agreement executed in 1948. The appellant contended that the document was not executed by Habib & Sons and that the assignee of the subject matter of the suit and not of the decree itself was not entitled to apply for execution. Held, that the respondent company could not claim to be a transferee of the original decree under section 232 of the Civil Procedure Code as transferees by operation of law and cannot maintain the application for execution on the ground that they did not transfer the future decree and therefore the equitable principle did not apply and the respondent was entitled to execute the decree. Purmananddas Jivandas vs Vallabdas Wallji, (1939) 2 Bom. L. R. 1374, approved. Purshottamdas Jivanji vs Vallabhadas Wariji, A.I.R. , followed. Consequently, on a true construction of the deed it actually operated to transfer a decree then in existence no equitable principle need be invoked for in that case the transfer is by the deed itself and as such was by an assignment in writing within the meaning of Order XXI, rule 16 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Purtilal Hargovinddas vs Ghulamnabi, A I. R., , distinguished. Consequently the respondent could not maintain the execution application for the 1405 decree under order XXI, r. 16 of 0. XXI, Rule 16 of C. P.C. The application which was filed by them in the City Civil Court was headed "application for execution under Order XXI rule 1(2)(j) and it was only after such application had been made to the court which passed the decree that the Court would issue notice under O.XXI, r., 16 of order XXI Rule 1(1)(2)(J).

The respondent who was carrying on the business of fabricating steel doors, windows, sashes and other goods entered into a contract for "sale of windows" and to promote sales of its manufactured goods. The Sales Tax Officer included in the taxable turnover of the respondent Rs. 23,480/ received under the contract. He held that the contract was one of sale of goods and the amount received by the respondent was not taxable. The Deputy Commissioner confirmed the order passed by the Deputy Commissioner. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the terms of the tender were not decisive and the court was entitled to ascertain the true effect of the contract as disclosed by the nature of the work, and the "invoice" for payment made out by the Respondent. HELD : (i) The object of the respondents was to enter into a works contract. That clearly appears from the terms Of the tender and its acceptance. The windows were to be fabricated according to the specifications with glass plain or ground as decided by the Engineer in Charge, and were to he fixed" within six months from the date of its acceptance "to the building with rawl plugs in cut stone work. The rate quoted by the respondents for the purpose of arriving at a consolidated lump sum payment of Rs. 1,160/ per ton for fabricating, supplying and treating at site all steel work etc; there was no stipulation for passing of property in the goods to the factory before actual completion of the erection work; there the contract did not contemplate dissecting the value of the goods supplied and, the value Of work and labour bestowed in the execution of the works. The service is not rendered under a separate contract nor is the service shown to be rendered customarily or normally as incidental to the sale by the person who supplies window leaves. [508 D E] (ii)The respondent was liable to pay purchase tax. [511 F G] (iii)The High Court was in error in holding that the contracts were a works contractor and not a contract of sale.

The appellant was a broker of foreign machinery parts. On November 8, 1967 Shankar Lal handed over the formal order to Ram Avtar and stated that the goods would be supplied on the following day. The complainant agreed to purchase 200 pieces of the washer plates at the rate of Rs. 38/ per piece. Formal order, it was then agreed, would be sent through Shanker Lal. On 11th November 1967 Shankarlal handed over a formal order in which he stated that he would supply the foreign goods known as washer plate. The price of the said goods was demanded from Ram Avtar. A day after Shankar Lal brought one Saheb Jaman Khan along with him to Ram Pal and introduced Saheb Jamunan Khan as agent of M/s Ashoke Trading Corporation of Indore. Ram Avtar lodged a report with the police against Shanker Lal after his suspicion had been aroused. Later on that day Shankar Lal and Raj Kumar Agarwalla came to the shop of Ram Avtar with washer clothes in a taxi. Price of the goods was then demanded from him. On the following morning Shankar Lal sent one Saheb, Jaman and S/o Shri Hanuman Agency. The appellant along with S/s. Ashoke trading Corporation of Delhi, who were his agents, arranged for a transaction of sale of foreign goods which would result in good profit to the complainant. The prosecution case was that on November 8 1967 Shankerlal handedover the formal orders to Ram L and stated therein that the said consignment would fetch him a profit of Rs 3200/ . On November 16, 1967 S/Shanker Lal handedover a formal letter to Ram Singh who told him that he (Shanant Lal) could arrange for a sale transaction of foreign liquor which would be result in Good profit to his complainant. On December 16,1967 Shankar Lal lodged a complaint with the Police against Shankerlal after his suspected suspicion had already been arouse. Lateron S/O Shri Hanuman agency and demanded the price of those goods on November 16. 1967. The police did not submit any charge sheet on the basis of the report which had been lodged by S/Shri Hanuman Agency and the appellant was discharged. Thereafter, the proceedings were set in motion against Raj Kumar Aggarwalla, Shanker Lal and Saheb Jamnadas Agarwalla. Charges under sections 420, 468 and 471 Indian Penal Code read with section 120B I.P.C. were framed against all the three accused. The High Court allowed the revision petition filed by S and quashed the charges framed against the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that so far as Raj Kumar Agawalla was concerned no case had been made out against him. HELD: (i) There is no infirmity in the judgment of the High Court as might induce us to interfere. The report which was lodged by Ram Avtar in the very nature of things made no mention of the name of Raj Kumar. [279G] (ii) It is the case of the prosecution itself that Raj Kumar appeared on the scene only subsequent to the lodging of the complaint. The part which is attributed to Raj Kumar is that he was present along with Shankar Lal when the latter brought washer bil plates in a lorry and demanded price of foreigngoods which would results in good profits to the appellant, and that circumstance, as pointed out by the High court, would hardly warrant an inference that Rajkumar respondent too was a party to any conspiracy to defraud or cheat Ram Avtar.[279F] (iii) The report of Ram Har Avtar in very nature is of things making no mention about the name.

The petitioner, an allopathic doctor by profession, had himself drafted and filed a writ petition in the High Court of Kerala challenging the report of the Accidents Enquiry Committee appointed by the Railways. The petitioner alleged that the Railways in this country are owned by the Central Government and on account of failure to fulfil the constitutional, statutory and commercial obligations by the Railway Administration adequate safety protection to the passengers and their properties is not available. The respondents contended that the Railway Safety Work Fund has been set up and expenses are being met out of it. The Union Government had appointed three high powered Committees in the post independence period, namely, the Kunzru, Wanchoo and Sikri Committees to investigate into the affairs of the Railways with particular reference to accidents and though detailed and useful recommendations have been made by these committees, there has been no adequate implementation thereof. Particular reference has been made to the unmanned level crossings, increasing human error as a contributing factor to accidents, non allocation of adequate funds for improvements, improper utilisation of the assets and facilities, inefficiency in the administration at different levels, prevalence and increase of indiscipline, frequency of thefts, robberies and murders of passengers, ineffective checking and supervisory system, want of replacement equipment and repairs to bridges as also non provision of adequate facilities to passengers. The Joint Director (Safety) has filed a counter affidavit in answer to the Rule on behalf of the respondents. It has been averred that the recommendations of the Accident Enquiry Committee were examined and implemented within the limits of financial and material resources. So far as manned level Crossings are concerned there were as many as 14471 of them as on March 1, 1982; unmanning level crosses with a volume of traffic of more than 6000 train vehicle units or poor approach visibility are being manned in a phased manner at the cost of the Railway and control at the gate is also being improved. As on June 1,1982 there were about 27233 unmanred level cross remarks on the Railways and if all of them are to be manned, a capital expenditure of 330 crore rupees would be necessary and similarly an annual recurring expenditure of Rs.44 crores will have to be met. As a measure of safety, whistle boards have been fixed near unmannerned level crossing crossings with a length of traffic every year. Most of the States have framed rules under the making it obligatory for drivers of motor vehicles to stop short of unmanunned level crossexamination, observing and then proceed. Speed breakers are usually provided on the road approaches to all unmaned level crossing, observe and then proceeded. Speed breakingers are generally provided on roads where the volume of road and train traffic was low. The Indian Railways Act, 1890 (Act ' for short) has prescribed several safety measures; based upon experience, the Railway Board through which apex body the administration is run and controlled has also prescribed rules and issued instructions which are not being properly implemented. The Central Government had appoint three high powersed Committees to inquire into the activities of the railway with particular references to accidents. Though detailed and comprehensive recommendations have already been made, there was no adequate implement thereof. Further, periodic review is undertaken about manning of unmenned level counterings, increase human error in thefts and under bridges was slow, the situation is claimed to have improved and in 1982 83 as manyas 15 works in different States involving an expenditure of RS.22 crores have been cleared. The petition has been filed by one and denied by the other, issues are struck, evidence is led and the findings follow. Though the petitioner is commuter of trains run by the Indian Railways, the writ petition is essentially in the nature of public interest litigation and the petitioner has attempted to voice the grievances of the community availing the services of the Indian Railway.

The appellants applied for compensation to the Jagir Abolition Officer under section 13 of the Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagirs Abolition) Act, 1953. The claim was dismissed by the Jagir Tribunal on the ground that they were barred under article 168 of the Limitation Act read with Regulation 55 and 0.41, rr. 17 and 19 of the Civil Procedure Code. The High Court dismissed the applications holding that they had been time barred. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that since the orders passed dismissing the appeals were received by them on April 9 and April 20, 1961, the restitution applications filed on May 6, 1961 were within 30 days of the receipt of the order of dismissal and hence the applications for restoration were made in time under Regulation 21 of the Act. HELD: The language of Regulation 20 applies not only to a case where the appeal has been decided on merits but also to a cases where the appellant does not appear either in person or through his agent or lawyer when the appeal or application is called for hearing, the Tribunal may decide the same on merits. [144 H] In view of the express language of section 17(1) of the Jagirs Abolition Act it is open to the Tribunal to dismiss an appeal for non prosecution in a case which the appellant did not appear in person and even so it is not open to it to hear the respondent to the appeal and decide it on merits, [144 A B] In the context of section 20 and in view of express language it is clear that Regulation 21 applies to the present case and the period of limitation prescribed by that Regulation being 30 days from the date of receipt of order of the dismissal of the appeal, the applications of restoration made by the appellants in all the four cases were well within the period prescribed by Regulation 21. [143 A B].

The appellants, who were descendants of one Dinanath Sao brought a suit under section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure for removal of the respondent Kamal Narayan, another descendant of Dinanath, from the office of trustee of the God Shri Ramchandraji Swamy for the village of Telibandha and for accounts. The appellant 's case was that Telihambi fell to the share of Sarjoo Prasad 's four sons, who had three sons, Ram Saran Lal, Ram Kishan and Ramanuj, representing Sarjoo Prashad ' branch and the other five grand sons of Dinnath Sao. The respondent denied that Telabandha was ever dedicated. As regards the Award of 1896 his plea was that it did not express accurately the decision of the Arbitrators an that in any case it was superseded by the Award dated May 14, 1898 which was accepted by all the co sharers as the actual settlement of their own and on the basis of which a suit brought to challenge the validity of the earlier award was dismissed as compromised. The Trial Court held that there had been a valid dedication in respect of the village Telivancorebandha for the temple of Shri Ramchandra Swamy and removed the respondent from the position of a trustee and for appointment of the first plaintiff in his place; for an order on him to render accounts since 1936 and to deposit Rs. 1,06774/1 which he got as sale proceeds. The High Court also held that a valid trust had been created in favour of the temple and it was a public religious trust, as Shri Ramchandra temple for which the trust was created was a Public institution. Held, that the document (the Panch Faisla Award) clearly and unambiguously showed anabsolute dedication of the villages to the deity temple of Sri Ramchandra Swamy. The use of the words "at that time" in the original necessarily meant "from the profits and income of mouza Teli Oriya". It is not correct to say that these words as used in the earlier clause, must be read together without any one being insisted upon to the exclusion of others, their Lordships are of opinion that the two courts in India who both substantially agree on this point, are right in construing the intention of the testator to have been that the widow of his son should not take an absolute estate which she should (1) (1874) L. R. 58 I. A. 206, referred to.

The appellants were the President of the Avadh Bar Association and the Chairman, Action Committee of the Parishad. The resolution was challenged by them in a writ petition before the High Court which discharged the notices. The High Court held that since the resolution was passed under the presidentship of the first appellant described as contemner No. 2, he is guilty of contempt as contemner no. 2 was. Allowing the appeal to this Court, ^ HELD: 1.1. The language used by them was unfortunate. Counsel for the appellants rightly said that was not proper and it should not have been passed in that manner. It is the duty of lawyers to protect the dignity and decorum of the judiciary. If lawyers fail in their duty the faith of the people in the judiciary will be undermined to a large extent. [603 F G] 1.2. The words "who are prominent members of the Assembly" used by him were unfortunate. It was a single act of the Chief Justice for which the attack was made, and it is the duties of lawyers who protect the integrity and decity of the judicial system. If Advocates fail in his duty the trust of the Government will be jeopardised to a small extent. It would not be repeated. [ 603 A B] 2.1 The language employed by them is unfortunate. [ 604 C D] 2:2. In view of the fact that the notices were discharged, the appeal is disposed of with the foregoing observations.

The appellants Nos. 1 to 4 and their eldest brother, respondent No. 1 were entered into a joint family with the object of partition of joint movable and immovable properties and the same were referred to three arbitrators. The disputes related to certain properties among the brothers in Chinsurah. On or about 2nd July 1977 the same agreement was re written on a fresh stamp paper and the said stamp paper was registered by which the abovenamed arbitrators were given the option to take assistance of one, two or more persons. The dispute related to some properties among them among the appellants in Chinusurah, the district of Hooghly in the State of West Bengal. The three arbitrators took the assistance of appellant No. 8 and he functioned and acted as one of the arbitrators. On November 28, 1977 the arbitrators explained their award to the parties and made and signed the award. On behalf of the appellants Nos 1 to4 it was contended that during the subsistence of the interim injunction order on the arbitrators to maintain status quo the arbitrators could not take back the award for presenting the same for registration. The respondents contended that the period during which the judicial proceedings were pending, namely 28th January 1978 to 24th November 1983 should be excluded in view of the principle laid down under section 15 of the . On behalf the respondents it was submitted that the order made by the court directing the arbitrators 'to keep the award in the custody of the Court was wrong and without jurisdiction. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The principles enunciated by this Court in Nityananda M. Joshi and others vs Life Insurance Corporation of India and others; , would have no application to the facts of this case. [125B] 2.1 In the instant case indisputably during the period from 26th July 1978 to 20th December, 1982 there was subsisting injunction preventing the arbitrators from taking any steps. Furthermore, as noted before the award was in the court of the learned Munsif from 28th of January, 1978 till the return of the award to arbitrators on 24th of November, 1983, the award had been filed in the Court pursuant to the order of the court. It was therefore manifest from the order in Misc. Case No. 28 of 1977 that the only period which should be included was from 26st July, 1978 to 25th November,1983 till 20th12, 1982. [126F G] 2:2 The principle laid by this court in Nithananda M Joshi and Ors. vs Life insurance Corporation of lndia and others ; , would apply with caution. The other maxim is "LEX NON COGIT AD lMPOSSIBILIA" (Broom 's Legal Maxims P. 162) The law does not compel a man to do that which he cannot possibly perform. The law itself and the administration of it, said Sir W. Scott, with reference to an alleged infraction of the revenue laws, must yield to that to which everything must bend, to necessity; the law, in its most positive and peremptory injunctions, is understood to disclaim, as it does in its general aphorisms, all intention of compelling impossibilities, and the Administration of laws must adopt that general exception in the consideration of all particular cases. [127F G; 128A B] 3:3 The law is not compel A man to doing that which one cannot possibly do.

The appellant was a tenant for about 20 years in the premises known as " Fida Ali Villa" in Kalyan. The respondent gave notice to the appellant to vacate the premises on the ground of non payment of rent and sub letting of the premises. The appellant agreed to vacate and deliver possession to him. The respondents filed a suit for ejectment on the grounds that under the terms of the lease he had the right to sub let the premises, and that they were merely licensees of the landlord; (2) that no new sub tenancy had been created ; (4) that section 15 was confined to "any other law" and therefore it did not preclude an agreement between the parties as to sub letting; (5) that the parties were in pari delicto and therefore the plaintiff respondent could not succeed. Held, that under section 15 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel Rates and Lodging Houses Rates Control Act, 1947, a landlord is entitled to recover possession of any premises if the Court is satisfied (e) that he has since the coming into operation of this Act, sub let it whole or part of the property or assigned or transferred in any other manner his interest therein; and (6) that under sections 13(1)(e), and 15 of that Act there is no prohibition against a contract of sub letting. The non obstante clause would mean that even if any other law allowed subletting, e. g., section 108 of the Transfer of Property Act, the sub letting would, because of section 15, be unlawful. This would apply to contracts also as all contracts would fall under the provisions of the law relating to contracts, i.e., Contract Act. An agreement contrary to the provisions Of that section is void on grounds of public policy and would be unenforceable. Surajmull Nargoremull vs Triton Insurance Co. (1947) L.R. 52 I.A. 126, referred to.

The appellant Board conducted secondary examinations in the month of March 1990, whereat the marks awarded, after the formalities of valuation by the examiners of the answer sheets in each subject, were found tampered with, and the appellant was informed that they would be at liberty to inspect the documents at the Divisional Board at Bombay. The Standing Committee constituted in this regard considered the records and the reports on August 29, 1990, discussed pros and cons and expressed certain doubts about the possibility of the candidates/parents/guardians committing fabrication. They sought for and obtained legal opinion in that regard. On August 30, 1990 the standing committee resolved to with hold, as a measure of punishment, the declaration of the results of their examinations and to debar the students to appear in the supplementary examination to be held in October, 1990 and March 1991. The notification was published on August 31, 1990. The appellant challenged the validity of the said notification by filing writ petitions before the High Court which were allowed. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the Standing Committee did not apply its mind in the proper perspective to the material facts. It was also submitted that all the examinees admitted in answers to the questionnaire that tampering was done and it was to their advantage. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The finding of the learned Judge Sugla, J. that the fabrication was done at the behest of either the candidate or the parents or guardians is amply borne out from the record. [798C D] 1.2 In the instant case, the findings of the Committee were based on no evidence and in this case all the requirements are lacking. The Board did not discharge its duty, on the other hand, the Board had presumed that fabrication was taken for the benefit of the examines/parents or guardians. It is his contention that all examinees admit ed the forgery of their concerned calibre ' mark sheets resulting the increase of marks to their credit. The fabrication of the moderators 'mark sheets was done after scrutiny by the concerned officials in the office of the State Board atBombay and before the lockers ' mark sheet were taken out to Pune to feed the computer. The act of fabrication is an offence. In view of the admitted facts and above circumstances, the necessary conclusion that could unerringly be drawn would be that either the examinee o r the parent or guardian obviously was a privy to the fabrication and that the forgery was committed at their behest. [789E F] 1:3 The finding that tampering is done at an instance of either of the candidate/parents and the parents/ guardians is fully borne out by the record, is clearly illegal and cannot be sustained. The question, therefore, is whether the conclusions reached by the Education Standing Committee that the fabricated fabrication was committed At the behest or the parent 's guardian 's behalf is amply supported from the evidence on record. It must be taken for all purposes of law to be a fact, as there is no room for a distinction between what is found by inference from the proved facts and what is held as a positive face.

The appellants were charged under section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code for criminal conspiracy to cause the offence of criminal misconduct punishable under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The prosecution case was that during the progress of investigation, and after the houses and shops of the accused persons had been searched, the two accused who were suspected of exporting potatoes at concessional rates on false declarations or certificates that they were seed potatoes. Police investigation was proceeding in this connection at Saharanpur in October 1951. Madan La 's railway section Officer examined as P. W. 4 in the case, was deputed by the Railway Department to assist the Special Police Establishment in the investigation. Labhu Ram Railway Parcels clerk in the Railway at Saharanpur was deputed to help the police party and it was alleged by the prosecution that during progress of the investigation, a trap should be laid for them at Delhi in Madan Lal 's house. The appellants were tried under section120 B of Indian Penal code for criminal misconduct under section 161 read with section 116 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for abetting the commission of criminal offence punishable under sections 5(1) (d), 5(3) and 5(4) of Prevention of corruption Act, to be committed by Madan Lal. The Special Judge found the appellants guilty under both heads of charges but convicted them under both the heads of charge. He sentenced the appellants to three months ' rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 500. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the object of the Act as set out in the preamble was to make more effective provision for the prevention of bribery and corruption. A new offence of Criminal misconduct by a public servant is created by section 5 and under sub section (2) it is made punishable with imprisonment for a term which may extend to seven years or with fine or with both. The offence is of four kinds or categories. Bribery as defined in section 161 of the Penal Code, if it is habitual, falls within clause (a). Bribery of the kind specified in section 165, if the it is habitually habitual, is comprised in cl. (b) contemplates criminal breach of trust by a Public servant and the wording takes us to section 405 of the code. It is with clause (d) that we are really concerned in the present case. It was argued that the intention of the Legislature was to create by means of clause (D) an offence different from a single act of bribery, and that it can come into play only when there is no offer to give an acceptance of a bribe by a person. The word "obtains" on which much stress was laid does not eliminate the idea of acceptance of what is given or offered to be given, though it connotes also an element of effort on the part of the receiver. One may accept money that is offered or solicit payment of a gratification, or extort the bribe by threat or coercion; in each case he obtains a pecuniary advantage by abusing his position as a public Servant. The words "corrupt or illegal means" find place in section162.

The appellant filed a suit for recovery of Rs. 76,368.04 P against the legal representative of the deceased principal debtor and defendant 2, the surety. The principal debtor also executed a demand promissory note, Ext. 81 in favour of the Bank. Along with the two demand promissory notes simultaneously the surety executed a letter of guarantee, Ext,. 30 in favour Of the Bank and the principal debtor executed a bond, exhibit 83 in favour thereof. The surety executed another letter of guarantees, Ext, 31 in favour o the Bank, which the surety endorsed in favour 'of the Bank; and the surety also passed letters of continuity of the bond and promissory note Ext. 82 in favour to the Bank on September 16, 1957, calling upon him to pay the outstanding balance of Rs 70,879/ in cash credit account of principal debtor as in the circumstances mentioned in the letter the balance was required to be recovered from the surety, and some correspondence ensued thereafter between the Bank & the surety and ultimately the Bank filed the suit for the recovery of the amount. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal by the surety the High Court held that the surety had agreed to become surety on the principal creditor pledging oil tins as and by way of security for the advance and, therefore, two securities were offered, namely, pledge of goods and the personal guarantee of the surety; and that the principal debtors would provide such quantity of goods as would provide full cover to the outstanding balances in the cash credit accounts and the Bank was to be responsible for safe custody and keeping of the pledged goods. The High Court also held that since the surety was unable to perform his duties as a prudent man, he was discharged from his liability under the guarantee. Allowing the appeal by certificate, ^ HELD: 1. In order to attract section 141 it must be shown that the creditor had taken more than one security from the principal borrower at the time when the contract of guarantee was entered into and irrespective of the fact whether the surety knew of such other security offered by the principal, if the creditor loses or without the consent of the sureties parts with the other security the surety would be discharged to the extent of the value of the security. The appellant was the son of a member of the family. The lands in suit were comprised in six survey numbers, and the lands in dispute lay within the province of Central Provinces and Berar. The appellant claimed that as a result of this regrant he had ceased to be "patelki inam" lands and were private property of the ' family. Held, that the grant was not a service grant but no question of a share in the emoluments of the patel 's office arose there. The grant was made by the jagirdar of village Nawabag and not by the sovereign authority and neither the Inam Rules nor the provisions of the Patels and Patwaris Law, 1900 applied; and the appellant could only succeed if he establishes that he had a right to a share of the emoluments appertaining to the office, unless the Deputy Commissioner otherwise directs. The mere fact that the office was rotatory does not establish that the p Patelki inam lands were in fact given by way of emoluments for the patels 's offices and no question arises of a claim of ashare in the pay of the apatel ' 's family to claim a share. The case of the appellant was that these two plots ceased to exist as a grant by way Of remuneration or emoluments for their office, and that Government had no right to resume " patelki Inam lands and regrant them to respondent No. 1. The fact that in 1904 the area reserved for the Patel was considered as a fair remuneration in kind to the Patel for his work, did not establish any right to the share of his office arose, there.

The respondents claimed that they were governed by the Hindu Law and custom applicable to them, that some of the properties belonged to them as their customary law including its concept& joint family property, that is, the undivided share of their deceased father could be properly said to have passed to them on his death and to be assessable under the Act. The Deputy Controller rejected these contentions and assessed 10 L120SupCI/72 duty at Rs. 2,05,996.41 P on the basis that the entire estate valued by him at Rs 12,23,794 was assessable. The respondents filed two separate appeals both of which were rejected by the Central Board of Revenue by its order dated December 30, 1961 and as aforesaid, at the instance of the respondents referred to the High Court the question whether the entire property held by the deceased valued at Rs, 12, 23,795/ was chargeable lo estate duty. The High Court dismissed the appeals holding that the Khojas who had settled down in Cutch, Kathiawar and Bombay were converted as a caste to Islam some three or four hundred years ago, but retained on their conversion the Hindu law as to inheritance and succession. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants (i) that the concept of joint family did not apply to Cutchi Memons, and that a cutchi Memon 's son did not acquire any interest by birth in the property inherited by his father from his ancestors, (ii) that in any case there was no scope for raising any such contention after the enactment of the Hindu Succession Act of 1937 and thereafter of the . The respondents relied on the fact that the High Courts had issued letters of administration to them although they had paid succession duty only on one third of the said estate; (iii) that even if a cutch Memon widow dies issueless, her property would be governed by Hindu law. HELD : (i)(a) The rule of Hindu Law applicable to the Khoias applied only to matters of inheritance and inheritance as against the Bombay Halai Memons who settled down amidst Hindus, according to Hindu law not only in matters of succession but also in matters relating to their property including the Hindu concept of coparcenary and survivorship. [234 D] (b) The High Courts have consistently treated the Khudojas as being governed by a Hindu Law in matters dealing with a question such as that of maintenance to be awarded to a Khoja widow, he held that in the absence of proof of a special custom to the contrary, that question also must be governed under Hindu law and that it lay upon a party setting up a custom in derogation of that law to prove it strictly, and (ii). [234 E] (c) The conclusion which is arrived at on consideration of the decisions referred to above is that the rule of succession recognised in the (1) A.I.R. 1921 Mad. 571, followed. (d) The principle of relationship between the manager and the members of the family was held not to apply to cutchi memons settled in Bangalore even after the Shariat Act, 1937 came into force, except in regard to matters dealt with by section 2 thereof, is clear from Abdurahiman vs Avoomma, Avisumma vs Mavomoothy Umma, , referred to.

The appellants are manufacturers of different types of fabrics. In order to manufacture the said fabrics, yarn is obtained at an intermediate stage. The yarn so obtained is further processed in an integrated process in the said composite mill of the appellant No. 1 for weaving the same into fabrics. The appellants do not dispute that the different kinds of fabrics which are manufactured in the mill are liable to payment of excise duty on their removal from the factory. They also do not disputes that the various kinds of fabric which are produced or manufactured at an intermediary stage and, thereafter, subjected to an integrated operation for the manufacture of different fabrics. Indeed, on a writ petition filed by the appellants, the Delhi High Court held that yarn obtained and further processed within the factory for the purpose of weaving the said same into textile fabrics will be liable to pay excise duty in view of the amended provisions of rules 9 and 49 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944. The High Court also held that the retrospective effect given by section I will be subject to the provisions of sections 11A and 11B of the (the Act) and further that it has been held that since the commodity which is manufactured in such place or premises and is used for the manufacturer of another commodity, there is removal within the meaning of rules. Hence this appeal by the Revenue. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The explanation to rule 173A and the proviso to Rule 173G, are ultra vires the provision of clause (b) of sub section (4) of section 4 of the Act inasmuch as "place of removal" as defined therein does not contemplate any deemed removal, but a physical and actual removal of the goods from a factory or any other place or Premises of production or manufacture or a warehouse etc. The Explanation to rule 9 and rule 49, inter alia provides that commodity obtained at a intermediate stage of manufacture in a continuous process shall be deemed to have been removed from such place/ premises as mentioned in sub rule (1) of rule 9. [707E] 2. In the instant case, the appellants are liable for payment of duty on the yarn which is obtained by them at an inter unital stage and thereafter, further processed into an integrated activity for weaving it into fabrics.[708F G] 3. The definition of "place" in Rule 9(1) does not require that the commodity obtained in an intermediate process should be deemed as a place of manufacture or production of the excisable goods. In view of section I IA of the , there is no cause for such apprehension. [700G H] 4. The contention of the appellants that the Collector has to specify the place of manufacturer and also any premises appurtenant thereto under rule 9( 1) is without substance and is rejected. [608C D] 5. In this case, admittedly, the commodity in question which is sought to be manufactured by a manufacturer, that is to say, the site of the factory cannot be specified by the Collector.

The petitioner filed a suit for declaration that the scheme published under section 68 C of the Act was illegal, void and ultra vires and for an injunction restraining the respondents from finalising and approving the scheme. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the suit was not maintainable in a civil court for the reliefs prayed for by the petitioner since the jurisdiction of the civil courts in such matters was impliedly barred. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that (i) the suit being one which should have been rejected at the threshold under order 7 rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, the jurisdiction and the desirability of bringing the scheme into force; and (ii) the scheme having been duly published under Section 68 C, the transport authorities concerned could issue permits only in accordance with the scheme and the other provisions contained in Chapter IVA of the . Dismissing the special leave petition, ^ HELD: 1. The jurisdiction of civil courts is impliedly barred from entertaining suits of the present nature. [544C] 2.1 In cases of the instant nature where invariably reliance is placed by the private operators on Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution, a writ petition lies before the High Court. In such cases a suit is hardly the remedy which can be availed by them. If suits of this nature are allowed to be entertained, the very object of the several provisions of Chapter IV A of the , can be frustrated by interested parties by resorting to a civil Court with the sole object of delaying the implementation of a scheme. Such attempts should be curbed at the earliest opportunity. [545D E] H. C. Narayanappa and Ors.

The appellant was charged under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and section 161 Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that on August 29, 1963 at about 9 P.m. the appellant went to Ambala to her maternal uncle who was employed as a sister in the Ambala Air Force Hospital and gave birth to a son there in July 1963. In August 1963 Miss Eylene along with her newly born son came to the house of her uncle Russel Nathaniel in police uniform and accused Russel, N. K. Lal, P.W. 11 and his wife of disposing of the illegitimate child. The appellant was asked by the D.I.G., that if they wanted to save themselves they should make some settlement with him and demanded a bribe of Rs. 1,000/ . But the D did not ask for bribe and that the money was paid to him in repayment of the loan by him to Russel. N.K. Lal who recorded his statement and called two witnesses to witness the proceedings. The Special Judge accepted the prosecution case as correct and convicted the appellant under section 161, Indian Penal code and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years and to pay a fine of Rs 5001 or in default to undergo simple imprisonment for a further period of six months under section 4(2), Prevention of corruption Act. On appeal by the State, the High Court maintained the conviction of the appellant. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The order of sanction dated December 10, 1963 shows on the face of it what were the facts constituting the offence charged and that a prima facie case was made out against the appellant.[185 D] Gokulchand vs The King, A.I.,R. 1948 P.C. 82; Gokulchand V. King, [1955] 1 S.C R. 965; Gokul Chand vs The State of Uttar Pradesh, ; , referred to.

The appellant was convicted under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for three months and to pay a fine of Rs. 500 in default to suffer further rigorous imprisonment. No separate sentence was passed under section 6(c) of that Act. The conviction and sentences were confirmed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the sanction accorded by him was not a valid one; (ii) the sanctioning authority had no power to grant the sanction; (iii) the order granting sanction was not valid as the sanctioning authorities had applied his mind to the facts and circumstances of the case and the sanction granted by them was not invalid. Held, that the sanction was a valid sanction. The sanction accorded was a validly sanctioned sanction. Gokulchand Dwarkadas Morarka vs The King, (1948) L.R. 75 I.A. 30, referred to. Held further, that in view of the fact that the sanctioning officer had applied its mind and was of the opinion that it was necessary in the ends of justice to accord his sanction, he accorded his sanction. In the present case the sanctioning order was a proper sanction. It was not for the sanctioning Authority to decide whether the sanction should or should not accord his approval to the prosecution of the accused. Gokul Chand Dwarkadash Morarsa vs The Queen, (1947) L R. 75 1. A. 30 and Gokulchand vs Dwarkadasi, , referred to and distinguished.

The respondent landlord filed a petition under section 14(1)(b) of the Madras Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960 against the appellant tenant for eviction of the tenants from two different tenancies. The appellant contended that the landlord had only a life interest in the premises in question and that it was inherent in such a life estate that it is not permissible for the landlord to invoke section 14 (1)(a) as grounds for eviction were raised in this appeal by the tenants. The Rent Controller held that the requirement of the landlords bona fide and ordered eviction of tenants. On appeal, the appellate authority allowed the appeals filed by the tenant against the orders of eviction and set aside the order of eviction. In revision, the High Court agreed with the view of the appellate authorities that the appellant landlord had no right to ask for eviction on the ground of demolition and reconstruction, he admittedly having only a lifetime interest or right to enjoy the property for his life. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, HELD: The rights between section M. Gopalakrishna and the remainder man with regard to the terms of the Deed of Settlement win have to be worked out in appropriate proceedings, if necessary and the general law win govern the matter if any occasion arises. [276 D] In the instant case, when the objection on the score of the landlord being a holder of life interest and hence incapable of invoking section 14, fails the suit must be decreed. It was contended by the appellant that a tenant with a life Interest cannot be allowed to demolish the property in order to reconstruct it as that action would, per se, be not bona fide. [277 F] M/s Raval & Co. vs K. G. 276 Ramachandra and others, , referred to.

The respondent decree holder in the execution proceed ings in this very case between the same parties which came to this Court on an earlier occasion. The appellant contended that after the coming into force of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, what could still be sold in execution of the decree was the right in trees of groves as these contin ued to vest in the intermediary. This contention was rejected by a Division Bench of the High Court. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The principle is well settled that trees before they are cut, form parts of 'land '. And an inseparable part is always included in the whole. In view of this very clear legal position, it is not necessary even to consider previous definitions or to make out specious or unrealistic distinctions between standing uncut trees, which are parts of groveves, and grove land. The proposition is well established that trees, before they were cut, formed part of 'lands '. [34 C D] In view Of the very clear statutory position, the respondent decreeholder was entitled to succeed. [35 F G] The principle of the definition of the intermediary 's grove under section 3(13) of the Act which says "intermediary 's groves are equated and groves is on ly collections of trees in plots of land so as to preclude cultivation in them. The uncutti trees are deemed to be parts of the 'land". [35 C D, G] In the instant case, even after that decision which according to the respondent judgment debtor constitutes a complete answer to any further execution proceedings in respect of any part of bhumidhari rights, execution should have proceeded against trees in groves and the view taken by the execution court, that there is a distinction between trees and a grove and grove and land should have been upheld by a division Bench of High Court (Lucknow Bench) was correct.

The prosecution case was sought to be proved by the ocular testimony of PW4 Biju and PW5 Anil, both aged about 13 years at the time of occurrence and the other evidence. At the trial however four eye witnesses, PW3 Devassenutty, PWs 6 and 7 salesman and his assistant in the arrack shop and PW8 Unni @ Velayudhan turned hostile and did not support the prosecution case. The prosecution sought to establish its case by examining as many as six eye witnesses besides other evidence, documentary and oral. At trial however, four eye eye witnesses were PWs 6 & 7 salesmen and his Assistant in the shop andPW8 Unni at Velayutudhan turning hostile and had not supported the prosecution version. The Trial Court on the basis of prosecution evidence found accused No. 1 guilty of an offence punishable under Section 302 IPC and sentenced him to suffer rigorous imprisonment for life. Accused Nos. 2 to 6, namely, Rajan Preman, Viswan, Sura and Shajan were found guilty of offences under Sections 143, 147, 148, 341, 323, 324, 326 and 302 read with Section 149 IPC but no separate sentences were awarded on any of those counts. On an appeal before the High Court, the conviction and sentence recorded against them by the Trial Court was set aside. In view of the limited notice issued by this Court, it was directed that issue of notice limited to the question as to the nature of offence and quantum of sentence. The appellants were released on bail pending disposal of their appeals. On behalf of the State, it is contended that the High Courts had committed an error in holding that the common object was only to cause grievous hurt to the deceased and that the fatal injury could have been caused by beating him with torches, knife, iron rod, cycle chain and the chopper. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1.1 The appellants would be liable for the offence of murder under Section 300 IPC if they had not been charged for the substantive offence of murders punishable under section 302 IPC without a specific charge having been framed against him as envisaged by law. [93G] 1.2 In the instant case none of the accused persons individually had been charged and the appellants 2 to 4 for an offence under Section 326/149 IPC, even the trial court, which tried the six accused persons, was not justified in recording a conviction against them for thestantive offence of death punishable under [93F] 1:3 The existence of an unlawful assembly is a necessary postulate for invoking Section 149 I.P.C. Where the existence of such an unlawful rioting is not proved, the convicted with the aid of section 149 IPC cannot be recorded or sustained. The failure of the prosecution to show that the assembly was unlawful must necessarily result in the failure of charge under Section 149. [94G] 2.1 In a case like this to determine as to which of the two accused persons is guilty of a particular offence, it can be said to have been committed by the four appellants. The existence or an unlawful ' assembly ' is a requisite postulate for invoke section 149 I I. P.C., and where the existence thereof is not established, the convic tion with the help of Section 149 cannot be sustained and the same would be the position with regard to the conviction of all the accused for other offences with the assistance of Section 34 IPC also. [92F] 2:2 In a trial like this, it cannot be said that any one of the four accused persons collectively had been charges sheeted for the alleged substantive offence under section 307 I.C.[93G H] 3.1 It is not possible to say that the injuries inflicted by the first appellant with the choppers were inflicted with the intention to cause death or such bodily injury as is sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause his death.

The assessee, Standard Triumph Motor Co. Ltd., is a non resident company having its place of business at Coventry in the United Kingdom. It entered into a collaboration agreement with the Standard Motor Products of India Ltd. (Indian Company) in November 1939 whereunder the assessee was entitled to royalty of five per cent on all sales effected by the Indian Company. This amount of 5 per cent less the Indian tax had to be remitted to the assessee in the Sterling currency. The assessee 's accounting year was the year ending 30th September, 1966. For the assessment years 1967 68 and 1968 69, it disclosed a royalty income of Rs. 1,600 and Rs. 4,57,311 respectively. When it came to filing of the return for the assessment year 1969 70 (year ending 30 9 67), the assessee admitted a royalty of Rs, 925,257 but filed a nil return saving that it was maintaining its accounts on cash basis and not on mercantile basis, that no part of the royalty amount had been received by it and, therefore, nothing is taxable. For this assessment year 1970 71, however, he refused to accept the assessee ' plea that it be maintained its accounts in respect of royalty and that, therefore it had committed a mistake in filing the returns for the said assessment years. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissed the appeals holding that the assessee had not been following any particular method of accounting regularly over the past years. For these appeals by the Revenue, it took the stand that even with respect to the accounting years relevant to the assessment periods 1967 68, 1968 69 and 1969 70, it has been maintaining its account on cash income basis and since it did rot actually receive any income in all these four years, no tax is payable by it. The High Court answered the question in the negative i.e., in favour of the revenue and against the assessee. Hence these appeals. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In the instant case, the very concept of "receipt" as espoused by the assessee is untenable and unacceptable.

The appellant was convicted of murder and sentenced to death. The third accused was acquitted by the trial court but on appeal his sentence was reduced to one of imprisonment for life. On appeal, the High Court found corroboration in material particulars and that the conviction was unsustainable. In appeal to this Court it was contended that there should be corroboration of the approver in material facts and qua each accused. 834 Held, that though the conviction of an accused on the testimony of an accomplice cannot be said to be illegal yet the courts will, as a matter of practice, not accept the evidence of such a witness without corroboration in materials particulars. The law may be stated in the words of Lord Reading C. J., in R vs Baskerville, (1949) L.R. 76 I.A. Mad. 308, and re Rajagopal, A.I.R., , referred to. Bhuboni Sahu vs The King, ; , referred not to. In the circumstances of this case it was not sufficient that there was evidence to corroborate the participation of the appellant in the offence with which he had been charged. In these circumstances the conviction could not be said lo be unsustainable. Bhsububonioni Sahu v The King; , , referred. Bhurbuboni Sahoo vs The Queen, A I. R. , re Rajagopal A. 1. R., and Re Rajagopal A, A 2, approved. Bhunoni Sahu V. King, A 1. L.

The appellant was a public servant within the meaning of section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. On or about December 11, 1962, the appellant was charged in the Court of Special Judge for an offence under section 5 (2), read with section 5, (1)(d) of 'the Prevention of corruption Act and section 161 of the Indian Penal Code. The case of the prosecution was that on July 8, 1961, the Electrical Executive Engineer accompanied by his Head Clerk, the appel lant paid a visit to Janta Oil Mills situated at Fatuhas. Ramprit Singh P.W. 2, who was the lessee of the Mills, demanded money and P. W. 2 gave him eighteen rupee currency notes, the serial numbers of which had been previously noted down in the statement exhibit 2. The Deputy Superintendent of Police, P.Ws. 20 and 22 picked up the currency notes and upon comparison he found them to bear the same serial numbers which had already been noted down by the Magistrate. On the basis of that report a trap was laid and under the direction of the Deputy Superintendent, P W. 19, a raiding was organised. The appellant was prosecuted for an offense under section 161 Indian Penal code and section 5 of the Act. The Special Judge accepted the prosecution case as true and convicted the appellant under section 6 (1) (d) read with s.5(1)(D) of Prevention of bribery Act and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for five years. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that on the findings recorded by the High court the appellant could not be convicted of the charges because he was not a "public servant" within the language of section 2(2), Prevention of 1947 Act or section 21 of the Penal Code, as the case may be; and that sanction under section 197 of the Criminal Procedure Code was required for prosecution of a public servants for an (1)[1975] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 869. HELD: The appellant could be deemed to be a "Public servant" in the meaning Of section 21, Indian Penal Act, in view of the language used by it in Explanation 4 to section 21. [690 D] In the present case, the question whether sanction of the Government was required under section197 of the Code of Criminal Procedure where any public servant is accused of an offence alleged to have been committed by him while acting or purporting to act in pursuance of any of the provisions of the . Therefore, the sanction of Government was necessary under section 198. [689 E] The appellant cannot be deemed as a "private servant" under section 21(1) of Indian Penal. [688 F] In view of Explanation 4 the expression "corporation engaged in any trade or industry" includes a banking, insurance or financial corporation, a river valley Corporation and a corporation for supplying power, light Or water to the public. The word "officer" there means some person employed to exercise, to some extent, and in certain circumstances, a delegated function of Government. He is either himselfarmed with some authority or representative character, or his duties are immediately auxiliary to those of some one who is so armed. [687 E] In this sense he would be an officer of Government, although he might not possibly exercise "any delegated function" of the government. Still his duties would be "immediately auxiliary to these of the Superintendent who is appointed to some office for the performance of some public duty.

The appellant was tried and convicted under r. 141(2) of the Defence of India Rules, 1962 for contravening cl. 4(b) of Maharashtra Jwar (Restriction on Purchase 'and Sale and Control of Movement) Order, 1964, and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for six months and fine of Rs. 500/ . The sentences were directed to run concurrently. On appeal by special leave the appellant contended that r.141(2), was ultra vires because it laid down a rule of evidence contrary to the law contained in section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act. HELD: (i) Rule 141(1) falls within section 3 because it is essential to the scheme of the defence of India Act. The Rules must necessarily provide for the publication of orders made under the Rules and they must also provide for proof in judicial proceedings of the fact of publication. [273 G] (ii) The rule is contrary to an existing act does not matter because section 43 of the . Defence ofIndia Act provides that "the provisions of this Act or any rule made thereunder or any order made under any such rule shall have effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent therewith contained in any enactment other than this Act. " [273 C] (iii) The High Court having set aside the conviction and sentence in respect of contravention of cl. 3 of the Maharashtra Foodgrains (Declaration of Stocks) (Second) Order 1964, it was illegal to maintain the order regarding forfeiture of the juar seized from the house of the appellant because, he says, the Maharashtra Jowar (Rest restrictionon Purchase and Sale Control of movement) Order 1965, did not contain any provision authorising the Court to forfeit the juari.

The appellant was convicted under section 302, Penal Code and sentenced to death. The prosecution case was that on seeing the deceased she shouted: "the Vakil has come". It is difficult to believe that Violet was assigned the particular role, especially when Sia Ram and his companions could themselves have detected the presence of Kunwar Singh more easily and with lesser ado. Violets 's brother Ramesh, a lad of 16 could have with greater ease and effectiveness played the swift role of alerting the assailants of Kunwar singh. But the Sessions Court and the High Court accepted the evidence that Virajolet did give the particular shout and in accordance with its usual practice it would not like to take a different view of these simple facts. The question which then arises for consideration is whether the only inference which arose from the fact that violet gave the particular Shout was that by so doing, she intended to facilitate the murder of Kunwar. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. In order to constitute abetment, the abettor must be shown to have "intentionally" aided the commission of the crime. Mere proof that the crime charged could not have been committed without the interposition of the alleged abettor is not enough compliance with the requirements of section 107. A person may, for example, invite another casually or for a friendly purpose and that may facilitate the death of the invite. But unless the invitation was extended with intent to facilitate commission of murder, the person inviting cannot be said to have abetted the murder. It is not sufficient that an act on the part of the perpet abettor happens to facilitate his commission of crime. Intentional aiding and therefore active complicity is the gist of the offence of abetment under the third paragraph of section107. [629 H] 2. The High Court was not impressed by his evidence. In regard to Shri Ram, yet different considerations prevail because the High court was dealing with an appeal against an order of acquittal in his favour. There are certain important considerations which lend weight to the view of the trial court that it was unsafe to convict Shri Ram. [625 A] 3. The burden was on the prosecution to establish its case and no adverse inference could be raised against Vioomlet for her failure to explain her utterance. Besides, an accused cannot while being examined under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure be subjected to cross examination and a bald assertion to explain a piece of conduct almost always fails to convince. [ 625 D] 4. The onus was on prosecution to prove its case. No adverse inference can be raised from the facts that violets gave the specific shout is that by reason of so doing it, she intends to facilitate murder of one Kunwar Singh. [ 626 E F] 5. The words of Viohitlet are at best in the nature of a circumstance and they do not, without more, necessarily justify the inference that she was a party to the murderous design. [526 G] 6.
