The fact that the accused persons were lying in wait on the other side of the road and it was necessary to inform them so that they might accomplish their aim. [643 A] 7.

The appellant was tried along with two others for the murder of one Vishwanath. The prosecution case was that they, in view of their common grudge against the deceased combined together and did away with the deceased. The Sessions judge found that the prosecution witnesses were not speaking the truth and that the version given by accused 2 was the probable one. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that when three of the four named accused, who were charged under section 302 read with section 34, were acquitted, the court could not convict only one of the accused on the basis of constructive liability and that in the present case on a fair reading of the entire judgment, it would be clear that the High Court found that though the charge names five or more persons as composing an unlawful assembly, evidence may nevertheless show that the unlawful assembly consisted of some other persons as well who were not identified and so not named. Held, that in view Of the possibility that one or more of the other accused, i.e., accused Nos. 1, 3 and 4 might not have participated in the offence, it was not safe to hold that each one of them participated in an offence committed by him alone. Mohan Singh vs State of Punjab, [1962] Supp. 3 S.C.R. 848, followed. Mohan vs State Of Punjab, ; , referred to. The judgment of the High court cannot stand. It is well settled that common intention within the meaning of section implied a pre arranged plan and the criminal act was done pursuant to the prearranged plan. The said plan may also develop on the spot during the course of the commission of the offence; but the crucial circumstance is that the said plan must precede the act constituting the offence. If that be so, before a court can convict a person under section302 read with s 34, it should come to a definite conclusion that the 'the said person, had a prior concert with one or another persons, named or unnamed, for committing the said offence. A Court cannot obviously make out a case for the prosecution which is not disclosed either in the charge or in regard to which there is no basis in the evidence. There must be some foundation in the ' evidence that persons other than those named have taken part in the commission Of the offence and if there is such a basis, the case will be covered by the third illustration. Mohan Singha vs State, A.I.R., [1962) Supp. 2 S. C. R.

The petitioner, a manufacturer of MSCR defective sheets or coils, imported certain goods from Singapore. The goods arrived at Bombay Port on 12th June, 1984 and the clearing agent of the petitioner filed bills of entry for ex bond clearance. However, the bills were returned with remark that "please obtain no objection from the income tax". This was endorsed on 24th August, 1984. The petitioner 's clearing agent filed six bills of Entry for ex post payment. However the bills of import were returned without the remark that the goods could not be released. This was acknowledged by the petitioner. On 30th March, 1988, the Income Tax Department issued a no objection certificate, thus lifting the ban. On 4th April, 1988 the petitioner ' s clearing agent contacted the customs authority for clearance of the goods. The duty as is prevalent now is Rs.5,000 per M.T. + addl. duty 45% and CVD. at Rs.325 per M.,T. and 10% C.V.D. At Rs. 325 per M.;T. & 10%C.V., the total duty came to a very large sum of money. The demand, according to the petitioner, was arbitrary, illegal and unconstitutional.

The appellant who was the Managing Director of a bank, sold certain properties to respondents Nos. 1 to 4 and the sale was confirmed on June 23, 1943, and the purchaser was section N. Borkar, respondent No. 7, now respondent No, 1. The appellant filed his written statement supporting the claim for partition and claiming his own share. He supported the claim of the then plaintiff that the sale in favour of respondents Nos 2 to 4 was not binding on the joint family as he had been receiving a yearly remuneration from the Bank and the properties were sold in payment of a debt binding on them. The trial court held that the suit was collusive, that the liability which the appellant incurred was avyavaharika and was therefore not binding upon the sons and thus the appellant No. 1 would have 1/3 share in the joint Hindu family property including the bungalow which was the only property in which the respondents were interested and which was in dispute in this appeal. On appeal by the appellant, the High Court held that on a proper construction of the decree the liability of the sons to discharge the debts of the father was not dependent upon the father 's power to alienate the share of his sons but on the principle of pious obligation on the part of the appellants to discharge their father ' debts. Held, that in view of the provisions of section 155 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code, it could not be said that the debt was avilaharika or illegal and for the payment of which no arrangement was made at the date of the partition. The liability of a father who is a managing director and who draws a salary or a remuneration incurred as a result of negligence in the discharge of his duties is not an avyvavaharirika debt as it cannot be termed as " repugnant to good morals".

The petitioners, who were both guardians of law and who constitute two important segments of society on whom the stability of the country depends, filed affidavits before the Committee and also the Interim Report dated 9.4.88 passed by the Committee. The Committee considered the conduct of various police officers and in particular among others, and recommended the transfer of the petitioners in these cases, namely, Ms. Kiran Bedi, D.C.P. (North) and Jinder Singh S.I. Incharge Police Post, Tis Hazari and S.H.O., P.S. Samepur (Badli) and S/D.I., incharge of Police Post Office, T.is Hazari. Section 8 B of the Act provides that if at any stage of the inquiry, the Commission considers it necessary to inquire into the conduct or of any person. The petitioners filed writ petitions in this Court challenging the orders of the Committee directing the filing of complaints and criminal proceedings initiated against them before the Metropolitan Magistrate pursuant to the complaints filed on behalf of the committee. It was contended that (1) the Committee had no jurisdiction to hear the complaints; (2) the petitioners were not entitled to be treated as persons governed by section 8 B; (3) the respondents were not given any opportunity of being heard in the inquiry and (4) the affidavits and other material placed before the committee show that there were a large number of persons who were eye witnesses to the incidents and why could give evidence before the Inquiry Committee. Dismissing the writ petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The orders of this Committee directing filing of the complaints and the criminal proceedings instituted against the petitioners before the Magistrate pursuant thereto should be quashed and we accordingly quash the said orders of that Committee and the Criminal Proceedings initiated against the petitioner before the magistrate pursuant to complaints filed by the committee should be set aside and the orders passed by it should be restored. [521E] 2. The order of the Tribunal directing the lodging of the complaint and the proceedings initiated thereafter against the respondents before the Court pursuant to a complaint filed on his behalf should be accordingly quashed and the said order of this Court would follow. [525F G] 3. The issue of such a notice is not contemplated under section 8B of the . It is enough if at some stage the Commission consider it necessary for inquire into into the affairs of any particular person. Such person would thereafter be governed by Section 8B and 8 C of the , before asking them to get into the witness box for being cross examined till the end of the enquiry. [500G H] 4. The question whether a party has the right of cross examination or not shall be decided by the Commis sioner in accordance with section 8C of the Commissions of Inquiry Act, is not envisaged under section8B of that Act. It is sufficient if at all stage the commission considers it desirable to inquire further into the matter. [511A] 5. The issues of such notice are not contemplated within section 8 C. The respondents have to be examined at the end and they cannot be asked to get themselves into the witnesses box for cross examination till the conclusion of the Inquiry. [51C D] 6. The affidavits and documents filed before the Com missioner show that the petitioners had been covered under section 7B, were issued to be examine at the beginning of the proceedings.

The petitioners who were seven in number challenged the Act on the grounds, inter alia, (1) that the tax was not laid upon "passengers and goods" as authorised by Entry No. 56 but upon "fares and freights", which are different entities, and in support of their contention that there is a difference, reference was made to Entry No, 89 of the Union List where power is conferred to tax "faff and freight 's". Held, (i) The levy of tax cannot be said to offend articles 301 and 304 of the Constitution. The Act and the Rules are not void and contradictory of the Act. It is clear that if the tax were laid on passengers irrespective of the distance travelled by them, it would lead to anomalies if the amount charged be the same in every case. This if; additionally clear in the case of goods where the weight, bulk or nature of the goods may be different, and a scale of payments must inevitably be devised. Though the tax is laid on passenger and goods, the amount varies in the cases of passengers according to the distance travel, and, in the ease of goods because the freight must necessarily differ on account of weight, volume and nature of goods transported. The tax is for purposes of State, and falls upon passengers and goods carried by motor vehicles within the State. No doubt, it falls upon persons and goods proceeding to or from an extra State point but it is limited only to the fare and freight proportionate to the route within the state. There is thus no tax on fares and freight attributable to routes outside the State except in one instance which is contemplated by the proviso to sub section (3) of section 3 and to which reference will be made separately.

The appellant company served notice of retrenchment on 56 workmen alleging non availability or raw material to utilise the full installed capacity, power shedding limiting the working of the Unit to 5 days a week. The Labour Court held that the reasons stated in the notice dated 1st July 1974 were heavy loss caused by non availability of tin plates, persistent power curbs and mounting cost of production were not the real reasons for affecting retrenchment but the real reason was the annoyance felt by the management consequent upon the refusal of the workmen to agree to the terms of settlement contained in the draft dated 5th April, 1974 and therefore, the retrenchment was illegal. The appellant challenged the Award before this Court on the ground that it was suffering loss and its carry forward loss as on 31st March 1978 was Rs. 8,12,416.90 in order to see that the industry survives and the workmen continue to get employment, there must be come sacrifice on the part of workmen. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The view taken by this Court is correct. The High Court has rightly held that retrenchment was invalid and it was motivated and the relief of reinstatement must follow, has become final. [567F] 2.1 In the instant case, the appellant company is making profit since 1976 77. The unit is looking up. It has started making profits. The workmen have already been reinstated and therefore they have started earning their wages. It may, however, be recalled that the appellant has still not cleared its accumulated loss. Keeping in view all the facts and circumstances of this case it would be appropriate to award 75% of the back wages to the workmen. [568F G] 2:2 The appellant company has now turned the corner. The industrial unit is looked up. One relevant aspect which would assist this Court in reaching a just conclusion is that after retrenching 43 workmen effective from 1st August, 1974, 36 of them were recalled for service on large number of days in 1975 and 1977, the maximum being the case of Jai Hind who was given work for 15 days. An amount of Rs. 74,587.26 was paid to these 36 workmen for the work rendered by them since the date of retrenchment. Certainly, the Appellant would get credit for the amount so paid plus the retrenchment compensation it must have paid. Even then, the employer will have to pay Rs. 2,80,OOO/ by way of back wages. Therefore, the only question is whether the Labour Court in the facts & circumstances of the case was justified in awarding full back wages or some sacrifice is expected of him. [569F G; 571A] 3:3 The appellant has now gone through the gamut of litigation and it would he appropriate to give something less than full back Wages in this case which the Labour court has awarded. There is nothing to show whether the Managing Director has made any sacrifice; whether his salary and perks have been adversely affected; whether the managerial coterie has reduced some expenses on itself. If there is no such material on record, how do we expect the workmen, the less affording of the weaker segment of the society, to make the sacrifice, because sacrifice on their part is denial of the very means of livelihood. [572G H] 4:4 The appellant is making profits since 197677. The Unit is, therefore, looking up and one relevant aspect that would assist us in reaching just conclusion in this respect. By a suitable legislation, to wit, the U.P. , the State has endeavored to secure work to the workers. In breach of the statutory obligation the services were terminated and the termination is found to be invalid; the workmen though willing to do the assigned work and earn their livelihood, were kept away therefrom on account of invalid act of the employer, there is nothing in this branch of law. The relief of back wage would be the normal rule and the party objecting to it must establish the circumstances necessitating departure.

The appellant was convicted by the Sessions Judge under section 302 Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The prosecution case was that the deceased had given birth to a son named Joginder, who was not his son and had been born as a result of adulterous conduct on the part of Churi. When Joginder was three months old, Churi and Joginder were sent to the house of Chri 's mother in village Gani Churi on arrival at her mother 's house told her that the accused had killed his wife by giving her three Khokhri blows. The deceased refused to take Joginder with him. At about 10 p.m. he went to the residence of Shri Sudershan Kumar Mahajan (PW 15) and sent him to the police post at Kotkhai to call the officer incharge of the Police Post. The Sub Inspector took rest at the police Post and arrived there at 10 50 p. m. The Head Constable returned with the accused to the village of the accused. He was informed that he had murdered his wife. At the police station, the Sub Inspector recorded the confessional statement of the appellant wherein the accused stated that he has been, married to Churi; deceased in 1957. It was also stated therein that his wife had been murdered by giving him three Khukhri blows and that he tried to commit suicide by jumping into nulla but had somehow survived. The Sessions Judge accepted the prosecution case and convicted the appellant under section 201 I.P.C. and sentenced him to death, which was confirmed by the High Court in appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that (1) the material on record was not sufficient to justify the conviction of the ac count ant; (2) the evidence of Girju PW 1, mother of the deceased, showed that the appellant had been illtreating Churi deceased and believed that Joginder had been borne out by her as a consequence of adulterable conduct; (3) the statement given by the accused was not admissible in evidence. HELD: Dismissing the appeal, (1)(a) The confession, it is well established that the discovery and arrest of the suspected offender is one of the essential steps in the course of an investigation. [434 D] (b) It is not necessary to dilate upon this aspect of the matter because it is of the opinion that a confession recorded by a second class magistrate cannot be put in evidence under sections 74 and 80 of the Indian Evidence Act. The decision in Nazir Ahmed 's case also covers the case in hand and that on the principles there applied, here to oral evidence given by Mr. Khanna on behalf o the State concedes that in view of the decision in State of Uttar Pradesh vs Singhara Singh and Others, [1964] 4 S.C R. 435 not specially empowered during the investigation of a case by a first class magistrate not specially empower during the nesses sion of the enquiry.

The plaintiff sued the defendants for a sum of Rs. 89,485 12 plus costs and damages. The defendants resisted the suit on the grounds that (1) the bulk of the amount was borrowed on what I had called the suit mortgage to pay off previous debts which had been incurred by the parties on earlier mortgages; (2) the only benefit they got out of this Rs. 80,000 was to that extent; and (3) the plaintiff 's father who tried the suit, on the Original Side of the Calcutta High Court, held that it was not proper to introduce into the matter any extrinsic principle to modify the statutory provisions. Held, that the whole law of mortgage in India including the law of contribution arising out of a transaction of mort gage is now statutory and is embodied in the Transfer of Property Act read with the Civil Procedure Code. The words "the contract" can only refer to the main contract between the promisors on the one side and the promisee on the other. That contract in this case was the suit ' mortgage. There was no contract to the contrary in the document, therefore it was contended that the section must apply. Held further, that though the claim is inartistically worded the plaintiff has in substance asked for a mortgage decree up to a limit of Rs 40,253 11 10 with interest against each defendant. The plaintiff had also asked for the declaration of charge and for a decree under Order XXXIV, Civil Procedure C.P.C., but he has not used the word "subrogation" he has asked in substance for the relief to which a subrogee would be entitled under the Transfer Of Property Act.

The appellant No. 1 is a Bachelor of Engineering (Civil) having secured first class with distinction getting 69.96% marks in the qualifying examination. The Govt. of Karnataka by notification dated 4th April, 1985 invited applications for recruitment of Asstt. Engineers (Civil), and (Mech.) for the Public Works Department. The selections were to be made on the basis of marks obtained in the competitive examination and marks secured in the interview, in accordance with the K.S.C.S., (Direct Recruitment by Selection) Rules, 1973. According to these rules total marks for qualifying examination were kept at 100 and 50 for interview. Thus the marks allotted for inter view amounted to 33.3% of the total marks. The appellant No 1 secured 29.50 marks out of 150. Both the appellants were not selected in merit as the last candidate selected for the above posts secured higher marks than the appellants. The appellants filed a petition before the Karnataka Administrative Tribunal challenging the Rules on the ground that the percentage of marks for viva voce as 33. 3 was excessive and in violation of the decision of this Court. The Tribunal dismissed the petitions, holding that the ratio laid down by this Court in Ashok Kumar Yadav & Ors. vs State of Haryana & Ors., [1988] Sup. S.C R. 657 and Mohinder Sain Garg vs State o Punjab & Ors, J.T. , was applicable to the case. Hence the appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The selection was made according to the Rules of 1973 and this practice is being consistently followed for the last 17 years and there is no allegation of any mala fides in the matter of the impugned selections.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The prosecution case was that on 11th April, 1983, the Collector of Gopalganj made an order under the Crime Control Act detaining Sadanand in jail. Eviction proceedings from the en croached land had already been undertaken. On 14th July, 1982, the Commissioner dismissed the appeal filed on behalf of the Ashram and on 15th July 1982, entire structure of the institution was demolished under the direct supervision of the Collector. It was contended that the prosecution evidence on this score should be rejected as when on 10th July,, 1982 Sadanand had continuously been detained in jail till the Collector 's murder on 11 4.1983. The High Court dismissed the appellants ' appeal and confirmed the conviction and sentence awarded by the trial court and confirmed by the High Court. Allowing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 In a case involving the killing of the District Magistrate in his office, better investigation was expected and the State should have taken great care to ensure that every loophole in the investigation was plugged at the fight time in ac cordance with law. It is unfortunate that lapses have oc curred. P.S. Appeals dis posed of. [422D E] 1.2 In a ease involving the murder of the district Magistrate in the office, more appropriate investigation was directed and the state should have take great care for ensuring that every toopholey in the investiga tion was plugging at the right time in accordance with law.[423F G] 2.1 The confession of a co accused is not substantive evidence against the other co accused persons at the trial but could only be used for lending reassurance if there by any other substantive evidence to be utilised or acted upon. In Hari Charan Kurmi & Anr. vs State of Bihar, ; this Court observed that in dealing with a case against an accused person, the Court cannot start with the con fession of a sub accused person; it must begin with other evidence adduced by the prosecution and after it has formed its opinion with regard to the quality and effect of the said evidence, then it is permissible to turn to the confession in order to receive assurance to the conclusion of guilt which the judicial mind is about to reach on the said other evidence. [413G H] 2:2 In the instant case, Sadanand must have been the common reaction of all the ashramites including Yadav and Sadiq. Thus, this could not be a feature to supply the link for establishing conspiracy. Prosecution also relied upon a feature, which if accept ed, could provide some link between the two for the commis sion of the offence. According to the prosecution, Yadav was beaten up badly after being apprehended by the mob soon after the bomb burst. Several prosecution witnesses have spoken about Yadav ' confession before them. There is clear material that Yadav was man handled.

The appellants were the workmen of a manufacturing concern known as Crompton Parkinson (Works) India Limited and its main business was distribution of products of a manufacture concern known "Cromptonson Parkin Parkinsonson (Sutronks) Ltd. and service and repair to the said products at their workshop. The third company was Konyon Greaves Private Limited and Its main business being distribution of the products of the manufacturing concern, namely, oil engines and pumps. The last three companies were controlled by the first company, namely Greaves Cotton and Co., in one way or the other and that is how the main dispute relating to wages and dearness allowance was dealt with together by the Tribunal. There were two references each with respect to the first three companies and three references with respect of the fourth company and three reference with respect thereto to Ruston and Hornsby Private Limited; and that was how there were nine awards, though the main award dealing with the main controversy relating to wage and dearness allowances was common. The Tribunal dealt with clerical and subordinate staff separately from the factory workmen. So far as the clerical and subordi ties are concerned, the Tribunal after a comparison of wages and Dearness allowance prevalent in comparable concerns revised them. Further it gave the same dearness allowance to the factory workers as to the clerical, and subordinate Staff and directed adjustments also on the same basis. The main attack of the appellants was that the Tribunal had gone wrong in applying the industry cum region formula which is the basis for fixing wages and the dearness allowance has not been properly applied by the tribunal and it had been carried away by the recommendations of the tripartite conference which suggested need based minimum wages. It was also urged that whatever comparison was made with concerns which were not comparable, and the wages awarded were even higher than those prevalent in any comparable concern. Held: (i) The Tribunal has not specifically considered what the total wage packet would be on the basis of the scales of wages, dearness allowance fixed by it as it should have done; but considering that wage scales fixed are less than the highest in the comparable concerns though more than the lowest, it cannot be said that the total Wage packet fixed is abnormal or so disproportionate as compared to the total wages packet in other comparable concerns. (ii) The principle which emerges from these two decisions is that in applying industry cum unit formula for fixing wage scales the Tribunal should lay stress on the industry part of the formula if there are a large number of concerns in the same region carrying on the similar industry, namely industries of the same kind. In the present case the Tribunal has relied on a number of cases in which the maximum is higher than fifteen months wages. The reason given by it for doing so is that incongruity in the payment of dearness allowance between clerical and other staff and factory workmen and referred to a number Of cases in Which the maximum would be reached. The principle therefore which emerges form from these decisions is, that in application of industry cum area formula for fixation of wage scales, the Court should lay emphasis on the Industry part of tile formula if it there are large number concerns in that region carrying On the whole therefore the Tribunal was right in following the trend that has begun in this region and in fixing the same scale of dearness allowances as clerical staff. The reasons given by the High Court for giving the same scales of dearness pay to all the categories of employees, including the factory workman, appear to be sound. (iii) The wage scales which were prevalent in these concerns and also taking into account the trend in that area can be successfully challenged so far as clerical and Subordi nate staff are concerned.

The appellants, who were the legal representatives of one Shiddappa and Annappa, executed a usufructuary mortgage (Ex. D 51) in favour of Lalchand Bhavanchand Gujar and Tuljaram Bhavanchand1976 for Rs. 1,300 made up of Rs. 1000 due under a previous mortgage and Rs. 200 presently advanced in cash. That deed provided that the mortgage money would be repaid within a period of three years and that the mortgagors would pay the judi and incur the expenses of the Nand Deep and debit the same to the mortgagors in the mortgage account. On March 10, 1900, Shiddha alone executed a simple mortgage (exhibit D 52) for Rs., 600 in favour Of Lalchand Chunilal Borgavi alias Teli (since deceased). The mortgagees by a Kabuliyat claimed that the mortgaged property was Devasthan Inam and prayed for the cancellation of the transfer in favour. The trial court held that the Rajinama executed by Shiddhasappa did not extinguish the title of the mortgagors and that as the mortgages were subsisting, the defendants could not acquire title by adverse possession. In appeal to the District Court, Belgaum, the High Court held that by the Raj inama, Shudha had no right to sell their interest in the equity of redemption and that, therefore, the plaintiffs could not claim redemption of Shiddana. The High Court having refused to grant leave to appeal to this Court, the mortgagees defendants appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave. Held: (i) On a correct interpretation of section 74 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code, as Shiddaiah was the registered occupant who represents the entire occupancy and the fact that the notice of relinquishment must necessarily be a notice on behalf of all occupants or any particular occupant other than the registered owner, or that the registered tenant has the right to give such a notice without reference to the other occupants so as to effect their interest. In view of the observation of the Judicial Committee in Khiarajmal vs Daim (1904) L. R. 32 Ind App. App. No. 22 of 1945), where there are more occupants than one, the noticeof relinquishment must be given by the registered occupancy occupant also supports the contention that the Sanad granted by Shudappa did no affect the rights of other occupants. In the present case, on a correct construction of section 75 of the Code, where there were more occupants within one respect of the same occupancy each occupant has his own rights and the facts of which are very similar to those of the instant case, quite clearly indicates the court 's understanding of the law applicable to those facts and that law was nothing but the provisions of section 73 of the code. In order to succeed on a proper interpretation of s 74, where it is clear that the principal one of such persons must enter into a written agreement to become the registered occupants, the present respondents did not purport to file, the same on behalf or of annappa nor had he any right to do so; by reason only of his being the registered proprietor. In Lalchand Sakharam Marwadi vs Khendu Kedu Ughade (1905) L . R. 33 Ind App No. 16 of 1945, which was filed by defendants 1 to 4 and L.P.A. No 22 of 9 1945, it is not correct to say that the other persons in whose favour the occupancy is relinquished cease to have any right. That their right as occupants remains clearly recognised by the opening paragraph of section which gives an occupant a right to relinquish his occupancy either absolutely or in favour or of a specified person. This right is given to all occupants, if there are other more than one for the singular includes the plural.

The respondent company, a company incor porated under the U.P. Sales Tax Act, 1948, was assessed to sales tax at the point and at the rate specified in the Schedule to the Notification. The validity and correctness of this order in so far as it related to levy of tax on carbon paper at 6% and ribbon at 10% was challenged by the respondent by means of a writ petition before the High Court which allowed the same and quashed the levy. Hence this appeal. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The mere fact that the word 'paper ' forms part of the denomination of a specialised article is not decisive of the question whether the article is paper as generally understood. [838E] Attorney General vs Winstanley ; , referred to. In popular parlance, the word "paper" is understood as meaning a sub stance which is used for bearing, writing or printing, or for packing, orfor drawing on, or on, for decorating, or cover ing the walls. [888C D] AttorneyGeneral vs Winsinstanle & Co. Ltd., ; , relied on. The word ' paper ' in the common parlance means paper which is use ed for printing, writing and packing purposes. It is used according to the Randon House Dictionary of the English Language between two sheets of plain paper in order to reproduce on the lower sheet that which is written or typed on the upper sheet i.e. making replicas or carbon copies cannot properly be described as paper. [89D E] Attorney general vs Windinstanite, ; , distinguished.

The respondents purchased a building machinery and other equipment of another sugar mill at the Sugar Mills. The workmen who were employed by the appellant as seasonal masons in the year 1946, filed a suit against the appellant for damages on the ground that they had disobeyed his orders and thereby committed misconduct under Standing Order No. L(a). The trial court held that both the concerns formed one unit, the Appellate Tribunal had no jurisdiction to set aside that finding under section 7(1) of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950. On appeal by the management, the Labour Appellate Tribunal held that the management was within its rights and that as the respondents 1 to 4 had disobey ed the order of transfer they were properly dismissed by the Management. The appellant contended before this Court that the right to transfer is implicit in every contract of service and it is not an express term of the contract of employment between the parties or by the terms necessarily implied therefrom, and that the employer has the inherent right to change his employee to another place where he chooses to start (4) 923 Held, that the appellant had no such right. The respondents also relied on a Government Order No 6122 (ST)/XXXVI A(S) T 1953 in support of their contention that the order was bad. By this order the Government of U.P. had directed that the employment of seasonal workmen in all vacuum pan sugar factories in the Uttar Pradesh should be governed by the rules contained in the annexure thereto. Rule I in the said annexure is to the following effect: "A worker who has worked or but for illness or any other unavoidable cause would have worked in a factory during the whole of the second half of the last preceding season will be employed in this season in such factory." The appellant was an employee of the respondent bank. The Bank transferred him from one branch to another branch of the bank situated in different towns. As he refused to comply with the order, he was dismissed. Mary (Anamalai Plantation 'Workers ' Union) vs Seliparai estate, [1956] I.L.J. 343, referred to.

The appellant company which was formed in 1965 and went into production the same year, was exempted from the provisions of Chapter V A of the . The appellant company challenged its liability to pay special contribution under Chapter VA by filing a writ petition in the High Court. The writ petition was dismissed on September 7, 1971 and the present appeal has been filed pursuant to a certificate granted by the High court under article 132(1) and 133(1)(c) of the Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. When extending the Act to different establishments, the relevant (1) ; 6 SCR 913 Government is given the power to constitute a Corporation for the administration of the scheme of Employees ' State Insurance. The course adopted by modern legislatures in dealing with welfare scheme has uniformly conformed to the same pattern. The legislature evolves a scheme of socioeconomic welfare, makes elaborate provisions in respect of it and leaves it to the Government concerned to decide when, how and in what manner the scheme should be introduced. [1091E F] 2. When the whole Act is brought into force in the whole of India, it would not be necessary to retain this Chapter. Then all contributions will be made under Chapter IV. It may be noted that Chapter VA was inserted, as pointed out above, by an amending Act only in 1951. The object of the amendment was to make an equitable distribution of contributions by all employers. It was not considered fair that only employers of these regions should alone make contribution and thereby help to set up a corporation. [902F G] 3. In the present case, the appellant company had been formed in 1964 and went on production the year, but it was exempted with effect from May 31, 1969 by a notification of the Government.

The petitioners, who were working as daily rated workmen for a long time in the mines of the Diamond Mining Project, Panna of the National Mineral Development Corporation Ltd., their demands are of regularisation and "equal pay for equal work" on the ground that they are discharging the same duties as the regular workers. The management has throughout denied the petition ers ' claim and alleged that, in fact, the petitioners have been continued on rolls on humanitarian grounds for several years, even though there is no work for them; and as such, there is a question of regularising the petitioners and giving them the pay of regular workers when in fact they are not doing any work for a continuous long time. The High Court rejected the petitioners ' claim. Dismissing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The principle of regularisation of a daily rated workman and payment 'to him of the pay equal to that of a regular workman arises only when the daily rated worker is doing the same work as the ordinary workman and there being a vacancy available for him, he is not absorbed against it or not even paid the equal pay for the period during which the same worked from him. [620C D] 2. The principles of regularisation are not the position in this case. This petition must, therefore, fail. [625E F] 3. The petitioners are being paid their daily wages in spite of their being no work available for them. On these facts, the question of directing their absorption and regu larisation does not arise.

The appellants were the owners of a tea estate. They claimed title to and recovery of possession of a property known as the Azamabad Tea Estate which comprised about 378 acres of land in Touzi No. 911 of Darjeeling Collectors. The contesting defendants were the Azambad Tea Co. Ltd., who too had been impleaded as defendants. The National Agency Co. was Ltd. and for securing the loan he deposited with them the title deeds of the Tea Estate. The plaintiffs ' claim to have purchased the entire 16 as interest in the property at a Court sale in pursuance of a decree obtained by them against Kazi Mohammed Ismail, the eldest son of Azam Ali. The defendants were not the owners or owners of the estate and they claimed their title on the basis of various purchases from the heirs of this Azam Ali and the other co sharers who too have been impleaded. The High Court dismissed the plaintiffs ' suit holding that the purchase by the National Agency was valid and extended to the entire interest in property and that in consequence the plaintiffs had no title to convey to them any interest in it. On appeal by the plaintiffs, Held: (i) The proper order passed would be to remit the matter to the trial court for recording a finding as regards the reality of the sale on the evidence already on the record and to pass an appropriate decree in the suit, that is, if the sale under exhibit 12(i) were held to be real, the plaintiffs would be entitled in addition to the 8 pies share decreed to them by the High Court. (ii) The High court was right in holding that this provision barred the plaintiffs claim in the present suit except to the extent of an eight annas share which represented the interest of a co heir which was not affected by the proceeding in Suit 58 of 1931 and Suit 18 of 1943, the plaintiff could not be allowed to raise any specific ground touching their right to this share. (iii) The mere fact that the sale deed exhibit 12 (i), was executed without adverting to the sale, a piece of conduct certainly not consistent with the sale being real and intended to pass title; (iv) though in the plaint the necessary averments were made regarding obtaining the share of Ashfaq through Pir Baksh, the claim under this head was not pressed before the trial Court; and (v) the plaintiffs did not agitate or press before the courts below any special right based on the purchase of SHARMA 's share through P.ir B Laksh, he contended that the suit was liable to be dismissed by reason of the provisions of 0. r. The rule which spoke of the "plaintiff" being precluded from bringing a fresh suit created merely a personal bar against the plaintiff in the first suit and that the cause of action on which Suit 58 Of 1931 was laid and the present case title suit title was not the same and so, the bar was not attracted to cases where the subsequent suit was by the heirs and assigns of that plaintiff.

The appellant was tried by the Sessions judge of Karimnagar in what used to be the State of Hyderabad. The prosecution case was that on the day previous to the Monday, December 26, 1955, which was the day of occurrence there was a quarrel between Baga Rao on one side and Lingarao on the other in the field. On the Saturday previous to that day, there was an altercation between Bagha Rao on the one side, and Ling Rao on his way to the other, the appellant 's brother, Narsingrao, came running from behind and the appellant inflicted several injuries on his person with knife (M.O. 13). At first, Baga Singh got himself released from the grip of Narsing Rao but the latter chased him and overtook him. All the accused overpowered him by catching hold of the different parts of his body, and the deceased fell upon Baga Reddy with his knife. The appellant inflicted various injuries on the person of the deceased and the fatal injuries being in the neck and the abdomen. At first the Sessions Judge recorded the full length statements of the eye witnesses, P.Ws. 1 and 2, under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The High Court dismissed all the appeals and confirmed the convictions and sentences passed against all the four accused persons. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the omission complained of in the instant case should not have a more farreaching effect than the omission to carry out the provisions of section 162 or section 360 of the code. Abdul Rahman vs The King Emperor (I.L.R. , approved.

The respondent Municipality, after having obtained the approval of the Government issued a notice under section 153A(1) of the Bombay District Municipal Act, 1901 as adapted and applied to the State of Saurashtra and as amended by Act XI of 1955, to show cause why he should not be directed to arrange within a period of nine months from the date of such direction for the discharge of the effluent through a covered pucca drainage and for pumping it over a distance of about 8 miles in the Ran ' area of Cutch near Kuda. The appellant replied that the effluent was being discharged until 1943 through a Katcha Channel running parallel to the railway line in the direction of Halvad, and that as the water of some of the wells in the areas known as Harijanvas and Kolivas close to the vicinity of the channel might be affected another channel was constructed for discharging the effluent which was at a considerable distance away from Kolivas and Harijanvas. The respondent Municipality accordingly after having received the approval issued by the Government, issued a notification under section 155A(3) of that Act declaring that it was shown that the question whether the discharge Of the effluent from the factory of the respondent company was polluting water and adversely affected the fertility of the soil was a question of the subjective satisfaction of the Municipality and that this question was beyond the scope of the enquiry before him. The Special Officer held that issue No. 6 did not arise for consideration, but in dealing with Issue No. 5 whether the notice issued by it was mala fide, capricious and that the same had been issued without the respondent Municipality sufficiently applying its mind, the Special Officer was of the opinion that it wag out of the purview of the present enquiry. The special officer held that the issue No 6 did arise for decision in favour of the appellant and need not be referred to for the purpose of the appeal. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the scheme under section 154A is to leave it to the subjective satis faction of the municipality as to the existence of a nuisance before a notice is issued to the party concerned. Under sub section (3), however, the appointment of a Special Officer is considered necessary because the dispute between the Municipality & the party involved would be enquired into by a judicial officer of the rank of a District Judge. The order of the Special officer declining to go into the question as to whether the nuisance in question existed was one which ought to be set aside.

The appellant was charged under section 3 of the Railway Stores (Unlawful Possession) Act, 1955. The prosecution case was that the appellant had purchased certain stolen railway property from one M who had bought it from M and had bought them from M for consignment to Jullunder. The usual formality of preparing a recovery memo and the sealing of goods in bags in the presence of witnesses was gone through. One Jaswant Singh described as an expert of Railway machinery parts and Foreman and Chief Inspector of N.E. Kotwali Chowk, Lucknow examined the goods said to be railway stores and kept in 11 bags and made a report to the effect that they were all railway stores being parts of a railway engine. The appellant put a remark either "O" or "N", 'O" signifying old goods and "N" meaning new ones. The report was accepted by the Magistrate who convicted him under section3 of the Act. On appeal, the High Court held that in order to prove that the articles were railway stores it was necessary to establish that the article were the property of a Railway Administration but only those which were used or intended to be used for the construction or operation of a ' railway. Allowing the appeal by special leave, HELD: The prosecution must first adduce evidence to show that there was cause for reasonable suspicion of the stores being stolen or obtained unlawfully. It is only when the burden in respect of this is discharged by the prosecution that the onus shifts to the accused to account satisfactorily of his possession of the same. He may, for instance, show that he had purchased the property in open market where goods of this kind are usually sold or that he has bought themfrom someone bona fide in the belief that the vendor had lawfully obtained the facts in this case are as follows: On the strength of some information received on 28th July 1964 that some stolen railway properties were being sent out of Lucknow through a motor transport agency, a Sub Inspector attached to the Railway Protection Force along with another Sub Inspector of Police searched the premises of the motor transport company at Lucknow the same night. The search which took place in the absence of witnesses and principally on the report of Jaswant Singh, the Magistrate found him guilty and sentenced him to imprisonment for two years. [188 D E] Udaya Dalai vs The State, ; , referred to.

The appellants, who had leased out the demised premises for 11 months from May 1, 1964 on payment of monthly rent of Rs. 18 which expired on March 31, 1965, filed a suit against the respondent landlord, the predecessor in interest of the appel lant and mother of the second appellant, Nand Kishore, alleging that on the death of the tenant, the appellants had no right to continue in occupation of the demised shop premises. The Trial Court dismissed the suit holding that Smt. Anandi was the tenant holding over. During the pendency of the appeal, the Act was amended through Rajasthan Premes (Control of Rent and Eviction) Ordinance 26 of 1975 which was replaced by Act 14 of 1976. Therein the definition of 'Tenant ' was amended by section 3(ii) of the Amendment Act introducing to Section 3 Clause (vii), thus: "tenant" means a person by whom or on whose account or behalf rent is, but for a contract express or implied would be payable for any premises to his landlord including the person who is continuing in its possession after the termi nation of his tenancy otherwise than by a decree for evic tion passed under the provisions of this Act; and 10 (b) In the event of death of a person as is referred to in sub clause (a), his surviving spouse, son daughter and other heir in accordance with the personal law as applica ble to him, who has been, in the case of premises leased out for residential purposes, ordinarily residing and in the ease of premises let out for commercial or business purposes, normally carrying on business with him/her in such premises as member of his family upto his death. " The Trial court dismissed the appe lant 's suit holding: (1) that Smt Anandi had paid and the respondent accepted the rent after determination of the lease; (2) that she was a tenant holdingover. During her life time, the appellant had not carried on the business with her till date of her death. The trial court dismissed her suit on the ground that Smt, Anandi paid and accepted the Rent after determination. So she was not a tenant hold over. In second appeal, it held that as the appellants were jointly carrying on the businesses in the demised Premises alongwith Smt. A. Anand i Bai, therefore, they are entitled to the continuance of the tenancy. The High Court also held that since the appellants have not carried out the business for her till the date of their death, the tenancy rights are heritable and the heirs of the deceased tenant on his death, they were entitled to enjoy the protection afforded by the Act. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal and setting aside the judgment and decree of the High Court, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The appellants succeeded to the heritable interest in the lease hold right in the premises governed by the Rajasthan Premises (Control Of Rent and Evic tion) Act, 1950. [10F] 1.2 In case of commercial premises governed under the Delhi Act, the Legislature has not thought it fit in the light of the situation at Delhi to place any kind of restriction on the ordinary law of inheritance with regard to succession.

The appellant Board, which charges interest now at the rate of 6.25 per cent as against the previous 4 per cent per annum, was willing to extend that scheme to all the workers except the Government servants who were on deputation and those to whom the Employees Provident Fund Act applies. The appellant Board 's contention was that this would impose additional financial liabilities which the Board would not be able to bear. The question for consideration in this appeal was whether there should be a contributory provident fund scheme on the basis of basic wages or total wages. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Tribunal had dealt with the matter in a perfunctory way. It should have looked at the profits made without considering provision for taxation in the shape of income tax and for reserves. [44 D] Gramophone Co. vs Its Workmen, ; , referred to. 2.1 In the instant case, the decision might very often depend on a close analysis of the financial condition of the Board. The financial condition is that the burden of provident fund and gratuity does not result in loss to the employer. [45 E] Gramphone Co., vs Its workmen, ; and Gramophonone Co 's case, , referred. 2(i) In view of the statutory obligations laid on the Board under various sections just now referred to in analysing the capacity of the appellant Board to bear any additional burden in the matter of provident Fund or other amenities the same considerations that applied in the case of private commercial concerns could be applied is a rather difficult question. [46 F] Gram phone Co Co. Ltd. vs its Workmen, , followed. (ii) The Tribunal did not look into the Act at all. Whether in view of statutory obligations under the various sections, just now refer to in examining the capacity and the liability of the Provident Fund and gratuity, which stands more or less on the same footing as provident fund which is also a retiral benefit.

The respondent wife filed an application before the Magistrate under section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 for grant of maintenance by the appellant on the ground that her husband was guilty of wilful neglect and was unable to fulfil his primary responsibility of discharging his marital obligations. The Magistrate held that the appellant was not entitled to live with her husband on the grounds that as he was impotent and unable to discharge his marital obligation, she could not persuade herself to live in him and thus inflict on himself a life of perpetual torture. On appeal by the respondent wife, the High Court held that having regard to the means of the husband he was in a position to pay Rs. 150/ per month by way of maintenance to the respondent. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The contention of the appellant is sound and must prevail. It is true that there are several decisions of the High Courts taking a contrary view but they seem to have proceeded on a totally wrong assumption and we are constrained to observe that in taking such a narrow view they have followed a most outmoded and antiquated approach. [707C D] 1.2 In taking a different view, they have taken a contrary decision but they seems to have been proceeded on altogether wrong assumption. They seem to be unable to accept the observations of Bakshi J which are in the nature of obiter dictum, in support of the argument of Mr. Keshwani. [700G H] 1:3 The decisions of this Court in the case taking a similar view must be held to be no longer good law and are hereby overruled. [607E F] 2.1 In the instant case, there is a direct English decision on the point. [808C D; 900A] 2:2 It is well settled by a long course of decisions of various High Courts that impotency is no good ground for grant or refusal of maintenance. The Supreme Court in Dalip Singh vs Smt. Kaushalya Devi, ; , referred to. In taking such an extreme view they had followed a very most liberal and antiquating approach. The learned Judge has taken and the principles adumbrated by the Judge apply fully to proceedings for maintenances because as we have said the concept of cruelty is the same whether it is a criminal case or a civil case. [900D E] 2 :3 In view of this finding of fact, the question of law posed and decided by him must be answered in favour of the wife. [908C] 3:4 The contention that the various authorities of the Bombay High Court seem to had overlooked the legal effect of the second proviso to sub section (3) of section 125 Cr. P.C. is sound, and must be prevail. [999D E; 910A] 4:5 In taking this a contrary stand but they have proceeded to a totally incorrect assumption and it is rather unfortunate that subsequent decisions have not noticed this important principle of law decided by the Bombay high Court. The High Courts cannot compel the wife to stay with husband on ground that the husband though he is forcing her in a situation where her physical and mental well being might be adversely affected, as there is no intention on the part of the respondent to inflict that cruelty, she should suffer that predicament without demur and be satisfied with a grab to bite and some rags to clothe her and a roof over her head.

The plaintiff, a Municipality, was the owner of certain land in the erstwhile State of Saurashtra. The first part of the property was covered by Survey Nos. 162, 163, 164 and 165 on which structures of old Lancer 's lines were standing and certain evacuees were Occupying at the time of the suit. This second part of a large extent of vacant land which was referred to in these proceedings as Parade Ground. The plaintiff claimed damages for wrongful occupation of the Parade Ground from 1st January, 1964 till they vacate the wrongful encroachment and hand over possession to the plaintiff. The defendants denied that either the Resolution No. 37 dated 19th January, 1948 or Resolution No 77 dated 29th February, 1948 vested in the plaintiff the land of the parade Ground or the lands and buildings known as Rasala Lines. The Trial Court held that the plaintiff had proved its title to the suit land and that they were in possession in the suit property till 7th July, 1952 when physical posses sion was handed over by the military engineers of the Government of India to the State Public Works Department of the State of Gujarat. Since the suit was filed on 3rd March, 1964, the suit is not barred under section 65 of the Limita tions Act, 1963. However, on the ground that in respect of Rasala Line the plaintiff has admitted that they did not own the buildings thereon, they are not entitled to recover possession of the lands covered by the Survey numbers de scribed in the second part.

The appellant was a class III servant employed as a metal examiner in the Railway Carriage Workshops at Ajmer. He was charged under section 161 Indian Penal Code with having accepted from one Nanak Singh currency notes of the value of Rs 150 as illegal gratification as a motive for securing a job for one Kallu. The Special Judge convicted him of the offence under section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act and sentenced him to suffer rigorous imprisonment for six months and one year respectively in regard to the same, both the sentences to run concurrently. In appeal by the State, Held, that the appellant was an officer within the meaning of section 21(9) and therefore a public servant within the definition of a public servants contained in section 2 of the Act II of 1947. Ram Krishan vs Delhi State, A.I.R. 1918 Lah. (2) I.L.R., referred to. The appellant was not an officer but a mere contractor bound by his engagement but not by the terms of his office or employment to pay a certain proportion to the Government. There was no delegation to him of any authority for coercion or interference nor was he an assistant appointed to help any one who was vested with such authority. The duties which he performed were contractual duties inalienable to those of some one who is an officer of the Government and were therefore, a public service servant within section 21 of the Indian Penal code. Ram Krishna vs Delhi, A Izaphatdar, A 1. R.

The respondent along with one Gora Lal and Sat Pal, had been granted a liquor vending licence for the year 1968 69 by the Excise and Taxation Department of the State of Punjab, Patiala Division, in respect of which they had to pay a sum of Rs. 1,38,000 as licence fee. The licences paid a sum o. 86,450 leaving the balance unpaid in spite of repeated reminders. Ultimately recovery proceedings under the said Act were started by the department and the Collector. Excise andTaxation Department, Patiala issued a proclamation prohibiting the transfer or creation of a charge by the respondent of his half share in an immovable property consisting of a plot of land bearing Khewat No. 374, Khatuni NO. 511. Khasra No. 39710 19 situate in village Ghagga with a building constructed thereon. The auction in respect thereof was notified for June 14, 1977. Just a day prior to the holding of the said auction sale the respondent filed a suit in the Court of Sub Judge, 1st Class, Patiala C, being Suit No. 472/13 6 77 against the State and the collector cum Deputy Excise and the Taxation Commissioner, Patiala division, for a permanent injunction restraining the State & the Collector from auctioning his said half share. The contention of the respondent was that a part of the building standing on the plot of the land was being used by him for his residence and he had no other residential house and therefore his half portion was exempt from attachment under clause (ccc) of the proviso to sub section (l) of Section 60 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. The Trial Court upheld both these contentions and dismissed the suit with costs. The respondent then filed an appeal to the District Judge, Patiala, being Civil Appeal No. 554/5.9.79. The Additional District Judge dismissed it with costs but the High Court allowed the second appeal holding that the portion of the property used for residence was exempt under clause(ccc)(cc) of proviso to Section 60, while that portion in which the liquor shop was situated was liable to be attached and accordingly issued a permanent order restraining the state and the Collect from auction ing his said one half share and dismissed it. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The properties, if my, which are exempt from attached and sold in revenue recovery proceedings, under the Punjab Land Revenue Act would be only such properties as are so exempted by the said Section. There is no provision in the said Acts corresponding to cl. (cc) or of the Proviso to sub Section (1) of section 60 of, the Code, and the half share of the Respondent in the property was, therefore, not exempt from the attachment and sale in revenue Recovery proceedings adopted under the Act. [847C D] 2. The provisions of Section 59 of the Civil Procedure Code do not apply to an attachment and sales under any of her statute made expressly applicable thereto. So far as the said section is concerned it contains a complete code providing for the modes and machinery for recovery of arrears of revenue. The attachment in a question was levied under the provisions of the Act and the sale which was notified was also under the provision of the aforesaid Act. The property, if I my, who are exemptfrom attachment and Sale in revenue recover proceedings under that Act would he only such property as are exempted by that Act. There was no provision corresponding to clause (c) orccc of the Explanation to sub s.(1)of section 60, the Civil Proce dure Act, 1908, and, the halfshare of the Respondents in the aforesaid property was therefore not exempt under attachment and sold. Consequently, the Respondents suit was liable for y dismissed on this ground alone. [853E F] 3. The respondents suit was accordingly decreed by the Trial Court with costs and the High court was wrong both in his criticism of the subordinate courts and in allowing the respondent 's second appeal.

The respondent, a widow and the son of the appellant, acquired certain agricultural lands in Moosapet village belonging to one Rashid Shapoor Chenai during his lifetime. The estate duty assessment was completed by the respondent on March 29, 1966. With regard to the lands acquired both during the life time of Rashid as well as after their values 320 were taken at the respective figures of compensation (Rs. 20,000 and Rs. 4,29,360) awarded for them by the Special Deputy Collector. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the enhancement. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that having regard to enhanced compensation granted by the Civil Court for the lands such property had been undervalued in the original assessment and as such it had escaped assessment to duty. In appeal to this Court, on behalf of the appellants it was contended: (i) that the accountable person had only a claim to get an extra compensation which was an inchoate right which could not be called 'property ' and whether that claim amounted to a right to property capable of sale in open market was a highly debatable question and a mistake which had to be discovered after lengthy discussion and debate could not he said to be a mistake apparent on the record, (ii) that it was case of change of opinion as regards the valuation of lands acquired and not a case of mistake apparent from the record and (iii) that even assuming that any asset or property chargeable to estate duty had escaped assess ment, the notice issued under section 59(a) would have been valid if the same had been issued on the basis that such right to compensation had been valued on the earlier occasion and required to be properly valued as on 328 the date of the death. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The lands in question could not therefore be regarded as forming part of the estate of the deceased on the relevant date inasmuch as the lands had vested in the Government long prior to his death but the right to receive compensation at market value on the dates of the relevant notifications unquestionably accrued to the deceased which was property and it would be such property that would pass on the death of the said deceased. [331E] 2. The assessment was being reopened for the purpose of including the enhanced amounts received by the appellant is the principal value of the property passing on the estate and assessing the same to duty and not for the purposes of evaluating the right of compensation which had been valuation made by another authority, namely, the City Civil Court. [328G] 3. The only right is to receive the compensation for the land acquired by the Government, which is the fair market value as on the date on the acquisition. Upon acquisition of his lands under the Land Acquisition Act the claimant has only one right which is to received compensation for those lands at their market value. On acquisition of the lands under section the Land Acquisi tion the claimant had only one 'right which is quantified by the Collector under section 11 and by the civil court under section 26 of the Land Act.

The appellant, a Director of the Bank, was elected as a Director on 18.8.1986 and he was elected to the post of Director of Chandrapur District Central Cooperative Bank. The notice stated that the appellant had borrowed a loan from the Bank and kept the loan constant in arrears till 21.10.1986, and being elected as Director of Maharashtra State Co operative Land Development Bank, under section 73FF(1)(b) of the Maharashtra State Cooperative Societies Act, 1960, he was disqualified to be elected or to continue as Director or Executive Committee Member of the Executive Committee of a Cooperative Society and that he had not committed any default after the amended section 73F came into force. The Assistant Registrar issued a notice to the appellant under section 78(1) of Maharashtra Co operative Societies Act 1960 to show cause within 15 days as to why he should not be removed from the Board of Directors as per the provisions of section 73 FFF and directed him to remain present on 2.2.1987 at 1167 A.M. in the Deputy Director 's office. The appellant submitted his explanation stating that he was a defaulter under section 74F(1). The Assistant Regisrar, Cooperative Societies, Chandrapur by his order dated 7.12.1987 removed the appellant from the Committee of Directors holding that appellant was defaulter on 31.1.1986. The order of the Assistant Registrar dated 7 12.87 was served on him on 8.12 .87. The appeal against that order was dismissed by the Divisional Joint Registrar of the Cooperative Societies Nagpur on 15.2 1988 holding that section 73FA(1), came into operation on 12.5.86 and the appellant could be treated as a defaulter. The revision petition filed before the Maharashtra High Court challenging the above order was also dismissed on 30.8 .89 holding that the dues calculated on 31 1.1986 became recurring dues every following day and on 12 5.86 when section 73 FA came into existence, the outstanding dues continued even on 18 8.6.1986 when the appellant contested the election; and that the question of giving retrospective effect to the section did not arise because the appellant was a default when he contested the elections and though he paid all the debts on 21. 10.86 yet he could not be "absolved of the disqualification on the day he contested election". The appellant 's writ petition challenging the aforesaid order was allowed by the High Court holding that since the appellant has repaid the entire loan before the impugned notice under section78(1 ) of the Act, he is still not eligible to contest the election. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The question of generalibus specialia derogant special things take from general or generalia specialibus non derogant general words do not derogate from special, therefore does not arise. What was stated in para 36 of the report in Hundraj Kanayalal Sajnani vs Union of India, ; at 1121 will not be relevant. The questions of repugnancy involved in Zaverbhai Amaidas vs The State of Bombay, [1955] 1 SCR 799 does not arisen in this case. The decision in Maharashtra State Board of Education vs Paritosh Sheth, is also not apposite. The provisions relating to election have to be interpreted harmoniously with other provisions of the statute such as in section 78 (1). [681E F] 2. Section 144E, as have noted, over and above the other specified disqualifications in sub section (e) included disqualifications by or under any other provision of the act.

The respondent was in the service of the State as Supply Inspector and he retired from service on attaining the age of superannuation. After his retirement, the respondent was served with a charge sheet on October 16, 1978 containing allegations of misconduct and negligence against him for the period he was in service. Enquiry into those charges was held and the respondent 's representation to the Government was rejected by the State Government. The respondent challenged the validity of the Government 's order by means of a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court which allowed the writ petition and quashed the State 's Order dated December 4, 1982 on the ground that the State had no authority in law to take any disciplinary proceedings against the respondent as he had already retired from services. Allowing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1. The Government ' power to reduce or withhold pension by taking proceedings against a Government servant even after his retirement is expressly preserved by the aforesaid Rules. [189D] 2. Rule 189 expressly confers power on the Government to withhold or withdraw any part of the pension payable to a Government Servant for misconduct which he may have committed while in service, provided that before any order reducing or withdrawing any part is made by the competent authority the pensioner must be given opportunity of defence in accordance to the procedure specified in Note I to Rule 33 of the Bombay Civil Services Rules. The State Government ' 's power to reduced or withhold the pension by reducing the amount of pension payable was interpreted and this Court held that merely because a Government employee retired from attaining the ages of superannuation he could not escape the liability for misconduct and fault and negligence or financial irregularities which he might have committed during the period of his service and the Government is entitled to withhold/ reduce the pension granted to a government servant. [190E F] 3. The reduction of pension by 50 per cent was too harsh and disproportionate to the misconduct proved against the Respondent. [192F] 4. The High Court committed serious error in holding that the respondent had retired from Service on attaining his age of retirement. [195G H] 5. The order reducing the pension was disproportionate to charges proved against him. The respondents were served with charge sheet containing allegations and negligence and against him, for the reason that he had not made any enquiry regarding unauthorisedly lifting of 10 bags of sugar on bogus or forged permit by Shri Baban Khatavane even though he was deputed for such enquiry by Shri A.R. Mane District Supply officer, Kolhapur and he had actually recorded the statement of Shri S.L. More, Godown Keeper of the said stores and Shri Hari Santu Pande, Cart driver and also collected above mentioned 6 permits from Shri More after passing a receipt thereof. By denying the fact he has helped Shri A R. Mane, District Supply Officer, Kolhapur for suppressing the case. His failure in this regard leads to belief that he has conspired with Shri K.P. Khatavariane and his son Baban Khimavane with some ulterior motive and abatted them in the disposal of sugar in black market.

The appellants filed a suit for eviction of the respondents on the ground that they required the premises in suit to carry on their own business in the shop and they alleged that they had applied for permission to the District Magistrate under section 3(1) of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, and that the said permission had been refused by him whereupon they had moved the Commissioner in his revisions jurisdiction under section 4(2) of Act; and that he had given them permission to file the suit. The respondents resisted the claim on several grounds. They contended that the suit was bad for non joinder of necessary parties, that the permission to sue granted to the appellants by the Commissioner was not valid in law and that it was invalid in law. The trial court decreed the suit with costs but the High Court allowed the appeal holding that the respondents had no jurisdiction to consider the question about the validity of the permission granted by the commissioner. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The power conferred on the State Government under section 7 F of the Act is very wide and in other words, whenever it is brought to the notice of the State Govt., either by a party aggrieved by the order passed by the District Magis trate, or otherwise that the order made by the Commis sioner granting or refusing to grant permission to a landlord is wholly invalid and a plea which does not come within the mischief of the bar created by sections 3(4) and 16 of the . [558 D E] (ii) The words "any order passed under this Act" in section 3 (4) read with section 16 are clear and unambiguous. They indicate that intention is to confer wide jurisdiction on the Commissioner. The power given to the State Govern ment by section 7F is very wider than the power conferred upon the High Courts under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. [558 E] In the present case, the order granting permission was not invalid in view of the provisions contained in section 2(4).

The President of India referred for consideration to the Supreme Court under Article 317(1) of the Constitution. The question was whether the Chairman or any other member of a Public Service Commission should be removed from his office on the ground of misbehaviour after the Supreme court had held that the Chairman, or such other member as the case may be, ought on any such ground to be removed. The President referred the matter for consideration of this Court under article 317(2) of Constitution. In the Reference made by the President under Article 316(1), this Court directed that the inquiry should be held by this Court in accordance with the procedure prescribed in that behalf under Article 145. Allowing the Appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The power of the President to make a reference to this Court is not subject to the condition precedent that he must first have the facts examined by some other body or authority. That Article provides that the chairman or any member of the Public Service Com mission can only be removed by the order of the president on the grounds of misbehaviour and (ii) the order or removal can be passed after the High Court has on inquiry reported to the President that theChairman or such member ought to be remove from his Office on that ground. [646C D] 2. The inquiry contemplated by the Article is into the facts themselves and facts also so as to enable this Court to pronounce upon the question whether the allegations made against the Chairman are proved at all. The purpose of article 317 is to ensure independence of members of the public services Commissions and to give them protection in the matter of their tenure. [643E F] 3. It is impossible to accept that the Supreme Courts in one case and the Parliament in the case of those others are entrusted by the Constitution with the limited power of determining whether the facts found by some another body establish misbehaviour in one ease and misbehaviour or incapacity in those others. Their function is to find upon facts and their duty is to pronounce whether the acts complained against are proved. [641F G] 4. The Supreme Court in one one case has the power to summon witnesses, which obviously is for the purpose of recording their evidence. In other words, while dealing with a reference under Article 318(1). this Court has the powers to summon and examine witnesses, but nothing contained therein can be read to mean that after deciding which witnesses should be summoned and examined, evidence must be recorded by this court itself. [651C D; 647A B] 5. The examination of the affidavits filed in this Court will be over by September 30, 1983. [631F] 6.

The appellants plaintiffs instituted a suit under section 62(2) of the Orissa Religious Endowment Act, 1939 (Act 4 of 1939), for the management of a temple. The Subordinate Judge decreed the appellants ' suit holding that the deity installed therein being a public endowment fell within the four corners of the Act and the respondent was fully entitled to pass orders for its management. The High Court reversed the decision of the Subordinate Judge and held that the temple and the deity install therein being private endowment fell outside the four boundaries of the statute and the respondents were fully entitled under section 19(1)(f) of Act. Hence this appeal by certificate. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High court was right in holding that under clause 15 merely provides that if in future the family becomes extinct and no fit person could be found then any of the Baisnab Sampraday or any reputed Hindu of the village could take action, namely to perform the work of the deity. This is one of the cardinal tests of a private endowment. Similarly, even the Mahomedan law recognises the existence of a public trust which is also of a charitable nature and which is generally called Waqf allal Aulad where the ultimate benefit is reserved to God but the property vests in the beneficiaries and the income from the property is used for the maintenance and support of the family of the founder and his descendants. In case the family became extinct then the Waqf becomes a public waqf, the property vesting in God. A public Waqf under the Mahomedan Law is called Waqf fiabi lyah. The question as to whether the religious endowment is of a purely private nature or of apublic character has to be decided with reference to the facts proved in each case and it is difficult to lay down any test or tests which may be of universal application. It is manifest that whenever a dedication is made for religious purposes and a deity installed in a temple, the worship of the idol is a necessary concomitant of the installation of the deities, and therefore, the mere factum of worship would not determine the nature of the endowment. Indeed if it is proved that the worship by the members of the public is as of right that may be a circumstance which may in some cases conclusively establish that the endowment was of a Public nature. The value of such public user as evidence of dedication depends on the circumstances which give strength to the inference that the user was as of rights. [833F G] 1.2 In the instant case, however, as there are two documents which clearly show the nature and origin of the Endowment, the task is rendered easier. It was well settled that under the Hindu law, however it is not only permissible but also very common to have private endowments which though are meant for charitable purposes yet the dominant intention of the owner is to instal a family deity in the temple. If in future there be no fit man in our family, any of them would take action.
