The appellant Bank entered into certain contracts and executed an irrevocable power of attorney in favour of the appellant on July 13, 1946. The power of Attorney recited: "Whereas we are working as contractors to the Government in its various departments and have entered into various contracts and will in future enter into other contracts and whereas an agreement dated 13 7 1946 has been made between us and the Bharat Bank Ltd., in pursuance of which the attorneys had agreed to finance contracts and to advance moneys to Malhotra against his bills for supplies under the contracts. " The appellant was also authorised to sue for, recover and receive the monies due in connection with the contracts with the approval of MaLhotra, to conduct and defend proceedings in consultation with him and to take steps in his name and on his behalf. Malhotra promised and declared that "all powers hereby granted are and shall be irrevocable as long as any claims of the attorney 's against us whether for principle, interest, costs, charges or otherwise remain outstanding and unpaid. " Intimation of the power of the Attorney was given by the appellant to the military authorities for payment. Before the appellant received the payment, the amount due under the bill was attached by Takhatmal in execution of a money decree obtained by him against Malhotra. The appellant contended that the power Of attorney dated July 13. 1946 coupled with the endorsement on the bill dated July 19, 1948 amounted to an equitable assignment of the monies payable under the Bill in favour and that Takhat Mal had no right to attach it. Held, that there was an agreement between the lender and the borrower that the debt owing to the lender would be paid out of a specific fund of the borrower in the hands of the Government authorities. The loan was to be advanced by the Bank against Malhotra 's bills for supply under the contract. The contention that the document was a pay order was revocable mandate, was not correct. There could be a valid equitable assignment and there could be no valid equitable assignor. Palmer vs Carey ; , referred to.

The assessee was the manager of a Tea Estate under the managing agency of M/s. Gillanders Arbuthnot & Co. Ltd., The said company had a Provident Fund scheme for its employees. But that provident fund was not a recognised one. The Income tax Officer assessed this amount as the assessee 's income from other sources. That order was confirmed in appeal by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. But on further appeal to the Tribunal, the High Court answered that question in the negative and in favour of the assessee. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The meaning of section 17(3)(ii) is plain and unambiguous. Hence there is no need to call into aid any rule of construction as was sought to be done by the High court. [436 E] (2) The receipt of Rs. 27,948/ by the assessee in the relevant accounting year cannot be considered as salary though undoubtedly that is an income. Section 17 has nothing to do either with deductions or with exemptions. It is merely a provision defining the expression "salary". As the income in question is not salary and the same cannot be said to be either interest on the securities; income from house pro perty; profits and gains of business or profession or capital gains. it has to be considered "income from other source" and brought to tax under section 56. [441 G H] (3) The expression "profits in lieu of salary" is plain & unambiguous.

The Bihar and the Madhya Pradesh Acts which impose a total ban on the slaughter of cows of all ages and calves of buffaloes, male and female, are not enforceable by any court of law but nevertheless they are fundamental in the governance of the country and it is the duty of the State to give effect to them. The Act does not contravene article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution as it discriminates against the beef butchers. The Bihar and Madhya Pradesh Act makes no distinction between she buffaloes, bulls and bullocks which are useful as milch or breeding animals and those which are not and indiscriminately prohibits slaughter of her buffaloes, breeding bulls and working bullocks (cattle and buffalo) which are essential for milch cattle or breeding or draught animals and they are not confined to the animal. The impugned Acts impose a maximum ban on her slaughter of all categories of animals mentioned in the last part of article 48 of the constitution and is therefore void. The petitioners challenged the validity of the Act on the grounds, inter alia, (1) that the impugned Acts were violative of article 19 (1)(f) of 'the Constitution as they infringed the fundamental rights under article 19 of the petitioners who are butchers, tanners, gut merchants, curers and cattle dealers to carry on their respective trades; (2) that a total prohibition of the slaughter was not in the interests of the general public and that being, therefore void no question could arise, even in Bihar, of any total prohibition against the slaughter Of all animals belonging to the species of bovine cattle which includes buffaloes (male or female adults or calves) and (3) that there was a total bar on the slaughtering of cows. Held, that the Act is constitutionally valid in so far as it prohibits the slaughter by her buffaloes ( bullocks, bulls, bullocks and buffaloes) which were useful as rains and buffalo and not to the slaughter without prescribing any test or requirement as to their age or usefulness. The provisions of the impugned Act are not ultra vires article 19 and must be struck down. The State of Bombay vs R. M. Shesondas, ([1952] S.C.R. 759), referred to.

The respondent, a 'workman ' was dismissed from service by the appellant company on the ground that he had been receiving a basic salary of Rs. 30 per month in July 1936 and that after 1949, he was not in any way concerned with the preparation of summaries and annual statements of accounts of the consumers department. The respondent submitted his explanation on December 3, 1955, in which he said that the charge was vague and that he was asked to explain why certain double adjustments had been made in the accounts of 1954 relating to the consumers ' department of the Company, the allegation being that a sum of Rs 1,05894 7 which represented the amount of bills of the Central Railway had been deducted twice in the account. The appellant contended that the Standing Orders did not apply to him because he was an employee within the meaning of the Standing Order and therefore his case was not governed by the Standing orders; Held, that the respondent was not an 'employee ' as defined for the purpose of the Act and the mere fact of employment in the office, Mains Department Stores, Power House or Receiving Station of the company was not enough to make a person so employed an ' employee ' within the definition of the 'workman " as defined in the Standing order. The words " whose names and ticket numbers are included in the departmental muster musters " occurring in Standing Order No. 2(a) should be read as " whose name and ticket number, if any, are included In the depart mental musters ".

The appellant, a company owned and managed by it, was started in the year 1961 and it went into production in the years 1964 65. No profit was earned at least right up to the year 1967 68. The workmen claimed bonus at the minimum rate prescribed under the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 on the plea that this Project was a separate establishment in respect of which separate balance sheets and profit and loss accounts were maintained, so that no bonus was payable until either this Project itself earned profits or from the sixth accounting year following the year 1964 65 when this Project went into the production. The Tribunal held that alloy Steel Project could not be treated as a separate Establishment because under the Act a company is itself an establishment. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The Tribunal committed an obvious error in ignoring the fact that separate balance sheet and profit & loss accounts are maintained for each unit and the consolidated accounts are prepared only for the purpose of complying with the requirements of the companies Act. [631 F] (ii) The proviso to section 3 will apply to establishments consisting of different departments, undertakings or branches which are owned controlled or managed by a person or body other than a Government company or a corporation. Obviously, therefore, an establishment in a public sector hag to be owned, controlled or run by a persons other than companies. This is further clarified by the provisions of sub section (3) of section 1 which lays down the applicability of the Act. The proviso applies even to new departments, Undertakings or branches set up by existing establishments. Consequently, even if alloy steel Project was treated as an establishment newly set up for purposes of section 16(1), the exemption claimed would be fully justified. [643 G] (iii) The provisions of section 3 cannot be resorted to at all when the Act itself is inapplicable in view of the provision contained in section 1, sub section It is quite clear that the Tribunal went entirely wrong in holding that simply because alloy iron Project was set up bonus was paid to the employees of all the units on the basis of consolidated profits of all such units. The only exception has been in the case of workmen of the Head Office where no separate profit and losses was worked out and the bonus was given on the principle of consolidated Profits of all of the units belonging to Hindustan Steel Ltd. That, of course, was fully justified because the Head office was working for all the Units, though as a single unit. It was in the accounts of the head Office that the entire paid up capital was credited and advances were made by the Head Officer to various units out of this capital or out of loans taken by the head office.

The appellant State issued a notification under the . The cess was payable by every person carrying on any specified industry and every local authority and is calculated on the basis of water consumed by such person or local authority as the case may be for any of the purposes specified in column I of Schedule II to the Act, at such rate not exceeding the rates specified in the corresponding entry in column II thereof as the Central Government may by notification in the Official Gazette from time to time specify. The cess is payable by a person carrying out any specified industries and every such local authority is calculated upon the basis on water consumed for such person. The Cess Act provides for levy of cess on water used by persons carrying on certain industries and by the local authorities with a view to augment the resources of the Central Board and the State Boards constituted for the prevention and control of water pollution. Section 3 of the Cess Act which may be termed as the charging section states that there shall be levied and collected a cess for the purposes of and utilisation thereunder. The appellant challenged the vires of the cess on the ground that it was not an enactment to regulate and control pollution but a fiscal measure to raise revenue for augmenting the resources. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In order to bring an industry within any of these entries in Schedule I it has to be seen what is the end product produced by that industry. Sugar cane is not a vegetable though it may be an agricultural product. If the botanic meaning of vegetable as referring to any and every kind of plant life is to be given then some of the indus tries listed in Schedule 1 like Paper Industry and Textile Industry and even chemical industry which are covered by other entries could also be brought within Entry 15. The word 'vegetable ' has been defined in many ways. In the World Book it is defined as follows: "In the usual sense, the word vegetable is applied to those plants whose leaves, stalks, roots or tubers are used for food, such as lettuce,paragus, cabbage, beet and turnip. It also includes several plants whose fruits are the edible portions, as peas, beans, melons and tomatoes. " In the world Book it was defined as: "Plant, esp. herbaceous plant, used for culi nary purposes or for feeding cattle, e.g. cabbages, potato, turnipan, bean, dandelion, etc., also the edible part of such a plant, as prepared for market or the table. Vegetables and fruits are some times loosely distinguished by the used need of cooking the former or the use of man, while the latter may be eaten raw; but the distinc tion often fails, as in the case of quinces, barberries, and other vegetable. 23, "vegetables" is defined to mean: "a general term used as an adjective in refer ring to any kind of Plant life or plant product, viz. 'vetgetable matter". The edible portions of many plants considered aS vegetables are in a botonical sense, fruits. The common distinc tial between fruits and vegetables is often indefinite and confusing, since it is based generally on how the plant or plant part is used rather than on what it This Court in State of West Bengal & Ors. vs Washi Ahmed etc.

The respondent, an Advocate filed an application before the Rent Controller seeking eviction of the appellant from the premises in question on the ground that he required the premises for carrying on his profession as an advocate. The application was contested by the appellant who was carrying on the business of manufacturing art jewellery in the premises. The respondent contended that the practice of the profession of an Advocate was not business within the meaning of section 10(3) (a)(iii) and, therefore, the respondent could not seek the eviction of his tenant on the grounds of his requirement unless it was for the purpose of carrying on a business. The Rent Controller rejected the application holding that the word 'business ' in section 10 (3) used the expression "business" only and not the expression 'profession '. The Appellate Authority confirmed the order of eviction against the appellant. In revision, the High Court held that the respondent bona fide required the building for the purposes of carrying out his profession. Dismissing the appeal to this Court, HELD: 1.1 The expression business occurring in section 2(a)(ii) is used in a wide sense so as to include the practice ' of the professions of an advocate.[14F] 1.2 In a broad sense it is taken to mean everything that occupies the time attention and labour of men for the pur pose of livlihood or profit '. [14G] 1:3 The expression 'business" occurring in Section 10( 3)(a)(i) is not used in wide sense but is confined to activities of a commercial nature. It is obvious that the meaning must be gleaned from the context in which it occurs and not in the context of other statutes or in a manner alien to the context.

The respondent filed a suit against the appellant for recovery of Rs. 4,11,367.92 with interest and costs. The appellant contended that it was money lent under an agreement that it would be paid on demand and therefore the limitation would commence from the date of demand and the suit was filed within three years from the demand. Held, that the respondent had to pay the amount before the limitation could start from the time of demand. The period during which the appellant made entries in the pass book showed that there were advances which were in the nature of deposit and were not covered by the award. The respondent 's case was that the money lent was advanced under an arrangement that it had to be put on a footing of financial stability by giving the appellant the use of the money by way of deposit. The transaction was between the appellant and the respondent and the appellant. The contract was between them and the amount was paid with the appellant in order to enable them to have financial accommodation without immediate worry of repayment. The payment was not a case of loan. The relationship between the parties, the surrounding circumstances at the time when the transaction, the pecuniary position of the appellant were all overwhelming features to recognats the oral as well as the documentary evidence of the respondent that the amount in question was deposited with the respondent. The award would have evidentiary value to show as to how the parties treated and understood their financial dealings. It is also significant that when the respondent demanded money by a letter dated 27 April 1953 (exhibit 7) totally denied the claim. The statement of account of the plaintiff would have shown how they treated the transaction. Ram Ratan Gupta, the author of the letter. The roznamcha entry was proved by Gopi Kishan Saraugi a munim of the defendant and the evidence in the cross examination of Gopi Kishan Kishan Saraigi spoke of the proper maintenance and keeping of books of account and that it is not possible to arrange the presence of the writer of the entry.

The petitioner was detained by an order passed by the Additional Secretary to the Government of India, Ministry of Finance, Department of Revenue, dated February 28, 1986 made in exercise of powers vested under section 3(1) of the COFEPOSA. The petitioner challenged the said order on the ground that the period of parole had to be excluded in recoking the period from 15th May, 1986 till February 22, 1987 should not be added to the period for detention speci fied in the impugned order under section 2(1). The writ petition was dismissed by a Single Judge of this Court. In the appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that (1) the period during which the detenu had already surrendered in respect of the criminal charge against him should not he added to his period of detention specii fied; and (2) the order of preventive detention could only be justified against a person in detention if the detaining authority was satisfied that his release from detention was imminent and the order was necessary for putting him back in jail. Dismissing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The fact that the detenu is in jail custody does not take away the jurisdiction of the detaining au thority in making an order of detention. What is necessary in a case of that type is to satisfy the court when detention is challenged on that ground that tho detaining authority is aware of the fact that he was already in custody and yet he was satisfied, that his preventive detention was necessary. [848C D] 2. The facts of the present case indicate that the petitioner was in jail for at the most one day. Charge sheet had not been submitted against him in the criminal case and he had been remanded to judicial custody on the 27th February, 1986 with the direction to be produced before the Metropolitan Magistrate on the 28th of February,1986. [850E F] 3. The order of deten tion is dated 28th February 1986. It was addressed to the detenu at his residential address at Delhi and not to the jail authorities for service on the detenu. From the facts and circumstances emerging in this case it is clear that the fact remains that only one contention had been raised. There is absolutely no basis for the alle gation in paragraph 2 of the writ peti tion that if the Court had indicated to Mr. Jethmalani in course of arguments that the submission on this limited point did not find favour with the Court he would have proceeded to argue the other points. That certainly was an unusual expectation. It is open to Mr, Jethmalani to make full submission on all as pects arising in the writ Petition. That having not been done, it was improper on the part of Mr. Chatterjee to raise these allegations in paragraph 4(iv) of his counter affidavit. [853F H] 4. The law laid down by this Court in Vijay Kumar vs State of Jammu & Kashmir, ; and Rameshwar Shaw vs District Magistrate, Etah, , referred to. In view of the positive case of the respondents that there was no summons and the detenu has been orally directed to attend the office by the authorities concerned, it would not be proper to hold that summons under section 108 of the Customs Act was in existence. Once the summons is not in existence, there is no foundation in the submission that there is prejudice to the detenue on account of the authority 's withholding the summons. [852G H] 5.

The petitioners were not satisfied with the reply received by them. They, therefore filed a writ petition in this Court for the issue of a writ in the nature of mandamus to the Union of India to direct it to pay to the petitioners same salary and allowances and other benefits as are being paid to the regular and permanent employees of the Union Government in the corresponding cadres and to direct the Union to regularise the service of the casual labour who had been in continuous service for more than six months. The respondents contended that since the petitioners belong to the category of casual labourers and are not being regularly employed, they are not entitled to the same privileges which the regular employees are enjoying. It was further contended that the State cannot deny at least the minimum pay in the pay scales of regularly employed workmen even though the Government may not be compelled to extend all the benefits enjoyed by regularly recruited employees. Dismissing the writ petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The petitioners have not been regularly recruited but many of them have been engaged as casual labourers for nearly ten years. They are rendering the same kind of service which is being rendered by the regular employee doing the same type of work. Clause (2) of Article 38 of the Constitution of India which contains one of the Directive Principles of State Policy provides that "the State shall, in particular, strive to minimise the inequalities in income, and endeavour to eliminate inequalities in status, facilities and opportunities, not only amongst individuals but also amongst groups of people residing in different areas or engaged in different vacations." Even though the above Directive Principle may not have been enforceable as such by virtue of Article 37 of the constitution of India, it may be relied upon by the petitioners to show that in the instant case they have been subjected to hostile discrimination. It is against this background that we say that non regularisation of temporary employees or casual labour for a long period is not a wise policy. [608C D] 2. The Government cannot take advantage of its dominant position, and compel any worker to work even as a casual labourer on starving wages. It may be that the casual labourers has agreed to work on such low wages. That he has done because he has no other choice. It would be poverty that has driven him to that State. The government should be a model employer. [ 608D E] 3. On the facts and in the circumstances of this case, the classification of employees into regularly recruited employee and casual employees for the purpose of paying less than the minimum wages payable to employees in the respective cadres is not tenable. [ 609E F] 4. The contention that since they belong to category of causal labourers and were not being regular employed, it was for this reason that managements and the Government agencies in particular should not allow workers to remain as casual labour or temporary employees for an unreasonably long period of time, where is any justification to keep persons as casual labourer for years as is being done in the Postal and Telegraphs Department. [06F] 5. The State cannot take benefit of its monopoly position, compel any employee to work at even as casual Labourer on starveving wages, it might be that he has driven himself to that state. The Govern ment cannot take assistance of its intervene and compel anyone to work in even as the casual labourer is a socialist republic. [1001F] 6.

The assessee, a public notice under section 22(1) of the Income tax Act, issued by the Income Tax Officer on 27 2 1950, required every person whose total income during the previous year exceeded the maximum amount which was not chargeable to income tax to furnish within such period not being less than sixty days as might be specified in the notice. The assessee did not make a return of his income and the Income 'tax Officer included the sum of Rs. 59,026 in the total income of the assessee and assessed him on it for the assessment year 1945 46. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected his contentions but the Tribunal on being moved by him raised two questions of law under section 66(1), which were: (i) Whether the notice issued under section 34 of the Act by the Incometax Officer on 28 2 1950 after the assessee had filed a voluntary return was valid in law? and (ii) Whether, in view of the provisions of section 22 (1) Of the Act, the assessment completed on February 26, 1951 was invalid. Held, that the notice under s. 34(1)(a) of Income tax was not invalid as it was served within the time prescribed by section 34(3), and the consequent assessment equally so. The notice under S.23(2) was therefore valid and the consequential assessment also so. Commissioner of Agricultural Income tax vs Sultan Ali Gharami, , followed. Held further, that in view Of the provisions contained in section 22 of the Indian Income tax (omitting the parts not relevant to the case, the notice could be treated as a return filed under section 24(1).

The petitioners, who are the principal office bearers of a nationalised bank, challenged the circular dated 23.8.1982 (Annexure A) issued by the Joint Secretary to the Government of India, Ministry of Finance, Department of Economic Affairs, (Banking Division), New Delhi, on the ground that it was contrary to the mandate of the Banking Companies (Acquisi tion and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1970 and the Natio nalised Banks (Management and Miscellaneous Provisions) Scheme 1980. The petitioners contended that the circular was contrary tO the mandate contained in Clause 3 of the Nationalised Banks ( Management and Miscellaneous provisions) Scheme, 1980, and that the Nitio nal Banks (management and Miscellaneous provi sions) Scheme was ultra vires Section 9 of the Act unless the said clause was so read as to be in harmony with the Section, and when so read, the said Clause does not justify or support the impugned circu lar. The respondents contended that there was no justification whatsoever to issue any such circular for the very object of the Neti tions of the Non Compa ny Act, 1971, which postulates both election and nomination of members of the Board of Directors and the choice between the two modes of appointment is left to the Central Government; and that there is no justification whatever whatsoever to issued any such Circular for the said very object. The Central Govern ment contended that Clause 3 was vaguely drafted and when read without regard to the legislative intent, as disclosed by the Act, is capable of a contrary interpretation, as is now sought to be put upon it by the Central Govern ments, and, that interpretation is, in our view, wrong, and in any case, out of harmony with tho principle enshrined in Articles 19(1)(c) and 43A of the Consti tution of India. The Additional Solicitor General also contended that appointment by election was not the only mode of representative appointment but nomination is perfectly valid and more effective from the point of view of the true institutional interest, particularly with reference to management efficiency. In the light of these rival contentions, it was con cerned that there has been no justification for restricting the choice to the office bearers or the Associations of the Association of Officers. Allowing the petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The object of Section 9 is to nationalise the banks in order to, as stated in the preamble to the Act. control the heights of the economy and to meet progressively, and serve better, the needs of development of the nation in conformi ty with the national policy and objectives. The mode of election or nomination must, therefore, be such as would be ideally suitable and appropriate to the banking industry and the inden ticity of the mode is generally a matter for decision by the central Government. [857E F] 2.1 The object underlying the Act is to promote the growth of a "management culture". It is with this object in view that the Act has envisaged a truly representative Board of directors chosen by election where election is feasible or by nomination where that mode is more appropriate. But the legislature has left it to the central Govern ment to specify by a scheme the manner in which the election or nominations is to be conduct ed, bearing in mind the true character and objective of the banking Industry and its distinguishing features as a highly sensitive commercial enterprise. Neither the election nor the nomination should be conducted in a manner unmindful of the distinctiveness of the Indian banking industry.

The respondent was imposed penalties under section 271(1)(c) read with section 274(2) of the Income tax Act, 1961 for concealment of certain income and furnishing inaccurate particulars. The assessee preferred appeals to the Appellate Tribunal and made an interim prayer for stay of collection of the penalties imposed. The Tribunal declined to grant any stay holding that it had no power to grant such a prayer. The High Court in appeal held that the power to stay was incidental to and implicit in the appellate jurisdiction created by section 64. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) By the provisions of the Act or the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal Rules, 1963 powers have not been expressly conferred upon the Appellate Assistant Commissioner to stay proceedings relating to the recovery of penalty or tax due from an assessee. At the same time it is significant that under section 220(6), power of stay by treating the assessee as not being in default during the pendency of an appeal has been given to the Income 'tax Officer only when an appeal had been presented under section 246 which would be to the appellate Assistant Commissioner and not to the Tribunal. [69 D E] (2) The powers which have been conferred by section 254 on the Appellate Tribunals with widest possible amplitude must carry with them by necessary implication all powers and duties incidental and necessary to make the exercise of those powers, fully effective. In the instant case, when section 220 confers appellate jurisdiction, it impliedly grants the power of doing all such acts, or employing such means as are essentially necessary to its execution and that the statutory power carries with it the duty in proper cases to make such orders for staying proceedings as will prevent the appeal if successful from being rendered nugatory.

The respondent was appointed a constable in U. P. Police Force on December 1, 1945, he was promoted to the rank of Head Constable and posted as Station Officer at Sidholi. On February 27, 1953, he made an application to the Superintendent of Police recommending his transfer to some other station. The Superintendent of police, who conducted the trial, examined many witnesses and found that seven out of the nine charges had been established. Thereafter, he issued a notice to the respondent calling upon him to show cause why he should not be dismissed from the police force. On March 20, 1954, the respondent submitted his explanation on November 29, 1952. The respondent submitted an explanation on September 12, 1953. The District Magistrate rejected the explanation and dismissed the respondent from service with effect from the said date. The appeal preferred by the respondent to the Deputy Inspector General of Police was dismissed by his order dated June 2, 1954. Thereafter the respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court for quashing the orders of dismissal. The High Court held that the enquiry was only a further step in respect of the misconduct of the respondent in regard whereto the magisterial inquiry was held at an earlier stage and therefore it fell within the express terms of para 489(2) of the Police Regulations. Held, that the departmental enquiry was not only a second step in the matter of misconduct of respondent in relation whereof he had been charged with committing cognizable offences and therefore the Superintendent Of Police had no jurisdiction to proceed with a departmental trial without complying with the provisions of sub paragraph (1) of para 486 of the police Regulations.

The appellant, a highly qualified ophthalmic surgeon feeling aggrieved by the promotion of respondents 4 to 24, who were promoted on different dates to supertime grade II, sought redress of his grievance praying for a mandamus that he may be deemed to have been promoted from February 18, 1971 failing which more out of frustration and less by any justification he seeks quashing of the promotion. The Union of India has framed Central Government Health Scheme and in implementation thereof has set up various institutions for medical relief and medical education. A Central Health Service became a necessity for effectively implementing the scheme. With a view to constituting the service, Central Health Services Rules 1963 were amended by Central Health services (Amendment) Rules 1966. Rule 7A(1) provided for absorption of departmental candidates holding posts in supertime Grade I and super time grade II respectively of reorganised Service under the 1966 Rules. The Rules envisaged categorisation of personnel manning the Service into five different categories, to wit, category 'A ' supertime scale Rs. 1600 2000, category `B ' super time scale Rs 1600, category II including General Duty Officers Grade I, and category IV comprising General Duty officers grade II. On account of various imponderables the service could not be constituted and 1963 Rules were amended in 1966 by Central Government. The appellant contended that as these 28 posts were in Specialists ' grade and the strength of Specialists Grade posts was reduced by 28, whenever any post out of these 28 vacancies added to super time Grade II was required to be filled in it can only be filled by promotion from amongst those originally belonging to specialists ' Grade I. The respondent contended that the 19 unspecified Specialists " posts" were meant only for promoting category 'C ' clinical Specialists to super Time grade II and that as such these 28 appointments were in contravention of Rule 8(3) of the Rules and, therefore, invalid. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the 29 posts were meant merely for promoting group 'C clinical Specialities to super lime grade II; that the 20 unspecified specialists " grade posts" and that the strength was reduced from 28, when any post in super time cadre II was created at Willingdon Hospital from amongst unspecified persons. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The 19 uns specified Specialists" posts were intended only for promotion category 'D ' and not in any other manner and particularly not by transfer. [10E] 2.1 The last limb of the argument is that the19 unspecified "specialists" post must be filled In from amongst these persons who may be promoted from "General Duty Officers grade I because General Duty Officer Grade I are also promotable to superjunct grade II because General duty officers grade I are only promoable to Supertime grade 11. There is, therefore no substance in the contention that all 28 posts must be made in by promotion amongst those who might belong to Specialists ` grade only. [11F G] 2:2 The appellant was not qualified for being promoted to any supertime post in the speciality in which each one of them was promoted. The answer was that there is a common seniority list of persons belonging to super scribed specialists, posts were converted into "specialist" posts and that promotion of the aforesaid four respondents should be set aside.

The Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953 was enacted to bring about an agrarian re ordering so pivotal to the progress of our rural economy. Haryana, happily a granary of our country is one of the States where land reform laws are likely to generate great changes by banishing big concentration of Natur 's bounty in a few feudal hands, creating an enthusiastic sense of distributive justice and exploiting the productive potential of land by the possessive passion of the landless many. So strategic is land reform that special constitutional concern has been shown for this programme. The scheme of the Act with which we are concerned is fairly simple and somewhat scientific, although its language, what with frequent amendments dovetailed from time to time, has made for ambiguity, obscurity, marginal inconsistency and a rich crop of litigation. Indeed, the conflict of opinion at the High Court level and the bone of contention before us arise from this drafting deficiency Legal Preface: A thumb nail sketch of the Punjab Act is a prefatory necessity. The defines 'small land owner ' as section 2(2) having in mind the optimum ownership in the given conditions. 'Permissible area 'section 2(3)] is a cognate concept limiting the maximum permissible extent a person may hold, and so long as he does not have any excess, he is a small landholder. He can evict the tenants from his holding and be in actual enjoyment as provided by the Act. If, however, he has lands beyond the permissible area, he becomes a large land owner and has to cough up the excess. However, he was given the option to choose there best area he desires to keep, called 'reserved area ' [section 2 (4)] and then he must make available to the State such excess as surplus area. The creation of a surplus pool or reservoir is vital to the success of the statutory project since, by distribution of such lands, rehabilitation of ejected tenants and landless persons is to be "accomplished". Maximisation of the surplus pool and suppression of evasion by large holders are of profound legislative concern. Even if a person is a big holder, it is quite on the cards that, by inheritance or other operation of law, or by voluntary transfer he may acquire lands in excess of the permissible limit. The law takes care to see that such excess is also made available for re settlement of ejectees and their ilk. In short, the legislative mandate is that every agricultural holder in the State shall hold no more than the permissible permissible area and the surplus in the hands of large holders, whether acquired by voluntary transactions or involuntary operation of laws will go to feed the surplus Pool. A careful study of the history of the legislation and the provocation for and frequency of amendments thereto, suggests an unspoken criticism about judicial approach which we will refer to later. Suffice it to say that the law is interpreted a radical agrarian measure; its basic goals are to cut down large holdings and distribute lands to various landless people according to a design and to foster, according to legislative policy, an agrarian community of peasant proprietors. De hoarding and hide outs are essential to make the twin objects successful and so sections 10A and 19B among others, have been written into the Act; and this modus operandi is that if the constitutionally envisioned socio economic revolution is not to be a paper tiger, agrarian laws have to be meaningfully enacted, interpreted and executed and the court is not the anti hero in the drama of limping land reform. [630 H] Amar Singh vs State of Haryana & Ors., ; , followed.

The appellants, who were the descendants of one Amarshah, filed a suit for possession of property in dispute on the ground that the Zamindari was impartible and that the decision of the Compensation Officer regarding Malguzari lands which vested in consequence of the enactment of the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals Alienated Lands) Act 1 of 1951 had become binding and conclusive against the appellants. The suit was decreed by the Trial Court but on appeal the High Court confirmed the decree passed by the trial court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the right to determine inheritance is not a mere life interest but a right to decide the question of succession, and that in any event the decision or order of the compensation officer became final and conclusive and could not be reopened in a suit filed more than six years after that date. HELD : (i) The right to determining inheritance is a creature of statute and it cannot be said that the legislature intended that the rule of primogeniture should apply only to cases where there are several heirs of the same class who would be entitled to succeed to the property if it were partible under the general Hindu law. [334 C] (ii) The question whether a person is entitled to claim compensation or not depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. [333 D E] (iii) The decision of Governor in 1950 declaring Dayaram to be the successor on the death of Amarshih was erroneous because it was based on an assumption that the Government had the right under section 14 of Act 1 Of 1951 to determine the succession, which was not done by the Code of Civil Procedure. [332 G] (iv) The order of compensation Officer became final, and conclusive could not therefore be reopened.

The respondent landlord terminated the tenancy of the appellants on the ground that the appellant was in arrears of rent for more than six months. The appellant filed a suit for recovery of possession of a portion of the ground floor of a building on the grounds, inter alia, that the respondent bonafide required possession of the premises in suit and that they were not ready and willing to pay the rent. The trial court held that the contractual rent was excessive and excessive and therefore the tenant could raise a dispute as to standard rent. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the dispute concerning standard rent is one which must have been raised before service of the notice and since there was admittedly no dispute in regard to standard tenancy or permitted increases at the date of service of notice under section 12(2) of the Act, the second condition in section 12 (3)(a) that there was no dispute regarding the amount of standard rent was fulfilled. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The provisions contained in sections 12 (1) and 12 (4) of Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 deal with orders which may be passed by the Court during the pendency of the application disputing the rent and also with orders passed consequent upon dispute as regards standard rent or permitted increase. It is only when an application disputing rent is made within the time contemplated by Explanation I to section 12 of the Bombay Rents. Hotel and House Rates (Control) Act, that such a right can be implied from the Explanation. The provisions in section 11(3) deal with order which may have been passed consequent on dispute as well as as on rent. It does not contemplate such a fight. [632 D E] In the instant case the respondent landlord gave a notice to the tenant on 18 April, 1955 demanding arrears of arrears of standard and also terminating the tenancy. The notice was received by the appellant on 21 April,1955. The suit for ejectment was filed on 15 March, 1956 on the basis that the tenant made no payment within the period of one month of the service of that notice. [625 E] Ambalal vs Badaldas, ; , followed.

The respondent company was a company incorporated in what was then British India having a capital of Rs. 3,600 divided into 360,000 shares of Rs 10 each. The Aluminium Limited, a company registered under the provisions of the Indian Companies Act, 1913, held 359,790 shares in the chargeable accounting periods ending on December 31, 1939 and December 31,, 1943, and December31, 1943, respectively and December 30, 1942, and January 31, 1943. In exercise of the power given to it by article 105 of the articles of association of the respondent company appointed three permanent directors on the board of directors of the Company. Two of these directors thereupon retired and only one, namely, Mr. L. G. Bash who continued to be a director of the company nominated by the Aluminium Ltd., Mr.L. G . Bash and continued to remain a director. The respondent company therefore filed a petition under section 21 of the Excess Profits Tax Act, 1940, read with section 66(1) of the Act for the issue of a writ of certiorari quashing the order of the Income tax Officer on the ground that it was not a company as contemplated by section 2 (21) of that Act. The High Court held that in view of the powers conferred by article 102 of the Constitution, the controlling interest remained vested in the Aluminium Limited and was at no time vested in Mr. K. L G. Kashgow Expanded Metal Co., Ltd. vs Commissioners of Inland Revenue ([1946] 14 I.T.R. (Suppl.) 7; New Shorrock Spinning and Manufacturing Co. Ltd. v Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay ([1945] 14 1.T R. ( suppl.), approved.

The respondent was serving as an Accountant Grade II in the Electricity Department of the former State of Hydabad. On 1st October, 1957, he opted to the Service under the Board and ceased to be an employee of the Government with effect from that date. In 1960, the Board framed Recruitment and Promo tions Regulations in exercise of its powers conferred on it under section 79(c) of the Electricity (Supply.) Act, 1948. The respondent opted to continue in the Government service or to opt to the Board. On 21st November 1972, the respondent opted for the Service. In the year 1960, he was allotted to the new State of Mysore with effectfrom 1st November 1956. The post which he held came to be equated with that of I Division Clerk in the former state of Mysore. On 30th December 1966, some persons junior to him were promoted on their having passed the S.A.S. examination while promotion was denied to the respondent as he had not passed the examination. The Respondent made several representations one such representation being on 24th December 1970 and 21st Nov., 1972. On 31st November, 1972, he filed a writ petition before the High Court on 13th February 1973. The Single Judge who heard the petition dismissed it and the respondent preferred an appeal to a Bench of the Karnataka High Court which held that the writ petition could not be thrown out on the ground of inordinate delay and laches on the part of the respondent and also on the view that in view of the later Resolution of the Board dated 5th January, 1970, it was no longer open to the Respondent to rely on the Resolution dated 19th May, 1969. The Division Bench of tile High Court held that in the circumstances of the case the relief to the respond ent should not be denied on the grounds of delay and limitation. On appeal by special leave, it is contended for the appellant that the court was in error in construing the relevant provisions of the Regulations and the Resolutions and holding that the respondent is exempted from passing the S .A. examination before qualifying for the promotion. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Resolution dated 5.1.1970 cannot be understood as altering the position existing "as before". This reasoning is erroneous for, as pointed out by the earlier Resolution was not intended to cover the case of allottees and merely because the allottees were excluded from the operation of the resolution the inference that the allottees are exempt ed from passing of the examination is not justified. [502 D E] 2. The resolution dated 5 1 1970 cannot be interpreted as altering a position existing 'as before" which was passed by the Board in pursuance of certain proceedings of the Govern ment referred to in the Resolution itself. Paragraph 2 of the Resolution provides that unless in the Recruitment Rules relating to the service concerned Depart mental Examination had been incorporated and prescribed unless it is clearly specified for what purpose the tests are prescribed viz., whether for increments or promotions, the passing of Departmental tests cannot be legally insist ed upon for grant of increments or for according promotion to higher posts. The three Government orders make it clear that the relaxation of the rule relating to passing of tho S. A.S., test is only as regards services where the rules do not specifically require the passing passing of examination and the language test. These G.O.s do not apply in the present case as the Regulations framed by the Electricity Board under section79(c), specifi cally prescribe the passing or the S,A.T. test. test is prescribed in Chapter V of Annexure 2. [511 E F] 3. The High Court found that the later resolution did not affect the earlier Resolu tion on the plea that the subsequent Resolution did not make any reference to the earlier resolution and that there was no reference to tho allottees at all. Relying on the words "the passing of S.As. Examination for promotion to the cadre of Accounts Superintendents as before be insisted".

The petitioner 's son was taken in police custody on 1.12.1987 by respondent No.6, Sarat Chandra Barik, Assistant Sub Inspector of Police, outpost under Police Station Bisra, Distt. Sundergarh in Orissa. The allegation made is that it was a case of custodial death since Suman Behera died as a result of multiple injuries inflicted to him while he was in police service and thereafter his dead body was thrown on the railway track. The petitioner came to know that the dead body of her son was found on the Railway track near a bridge at some distance from the Jaraikela railway station. There were multiple injuries on the body of Suman Behra when it was found and obviously his death was unnatural, caused by those injuries. The respondents filed a petition under Article 32 of the Constitution for determining the claim of compensation to the petitioner, the mother of the deceased for contravention of the fundamental right guaranteed under Article 21 of the constitution. The State of Orissa and its police officers including Sarat Chander Barik and Constable No.127, Chhabil Kujur of Police Outpost Jeraikela, Police Station, Bisra were impleaded as respondents in this petition. The defence of the respondents is that Suman Behara managed to escape from police custody at about 3 a.m. on the night between 1st and 2nd December, 1987 and it was likely that he was run over by a passing train after he had escaped from police possession. In short, on this basis the allegation of custodial deaths was denied and consequently the respondents responsibility for unnatural death of Suman Sehera. The Additional Solicitor General contended that the evidence adduced during the inquiry does not support the defence of respondents and there is no reason to reject the finding of the District Judge that Suman be died in police detention as a consequence of injuries inflicted on him while his son was in Police custody at the Police Out Post Jerai severely. Allowing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The liability of the State for payment of compensation in an action based on tort is confined to the sphere of liability in tort which is distinct from the State 's liability for contravention under Article 20 of the Constitu tion. It may have recourse against those officers" (pp.513 14) (emphasis supplied) [658E] 2. The Court is not helpless and the wide powers given to this Court by Article 32, which itself is a fundamental right, imposes a constitutional obligation on this Court to forge such new tools, which may be necessary for doing complete justice and enforcing the fundamental rights guaranteed in the Constitution, which enable the award of monetary compensation in appropriate cases, where that is the only mode of redress available. The power available to this court under Article 142 is also an enabling provision in this behalf. [659F] 3. The right available to the Supreme Court under Article 136 is a remedy available in public law and is based on the strict liability for violation of the basic and indefeasible rights of the citizen.

The two prisoners have been sentenced to death for an offence under section 302 Indian Penal Code and the petitions filed by them to the President of India for commutation of the sentence are reported to have been rejected by the President recently. Before considering the merits of the application, it would like to observe that the constitutional right to freedom of speech and expression conferred by article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution is not an absolute right nor indeed does it confer any right on the Press, to have an unrestricted access to means of information through the medium of an interview of the two prisoners who are sentenced to imprisonment for life. No such right can be claimed by the Press unless in the first instance, the person sought to be interviewed is willing to be selected. The existence of a free Press does not imply or spell out any legal obligation on the citizens to supply information to the Press. The press is entitled to exercise its freedom of freedom of expression by publishing a matter which does not invade the rights of other citizens and which does neither violate the sovereignty and integrity of India, the security of the State, public order decency and morality. But in the instant case, the right claimed by her is not the right to express any particular view or opinion but the right of the petitioner to form an opinion on merits and in accordance with the jail regulations. The question for determination was whether the two detenus are ready and willing to interview the prisoners right since the President has rejected the petitions for commutation. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The constitutional right claimed is not a absolute right but indeed does not confer any rights on the press, to which have an unfettered access to mean of information. [1186C] 2. Rule 549(4) of Chapter XXXII of the Manual for the Superintendence and Management of Jails, which is applicable to Delhi, provides that every prisoner under a sentence of death shall be allowed such interviews and other communications with his relatives, friends and legal advisers as the Superintendent thinks reasonable. [1108C] 3. The right claimed in the petition is not that they can always and without good reasons be denied the opportunity to interview a condemned prisoner. If in any given case there are weighty reasons for doing so, which we expect will always be recorded in writing, the interview may appropriately be refused. But no such consideration has been pressed upon us and therefore it does not see any reason why newspapermen who can broadly and we suppose without great fear of contradiction, be termed as friends of the society be denied a right of an interviews under clause (4) Of rule 549. [1086E F] 4. The petitioner has been asking for permission to interview two prisoners, namely Billa and Ranga, today. The interviews may be allowed at 4 O 'Clock in the evening. The representatives agree that all of them will interview the detenus jointly and for not more than one hour on the whole. There will be no order as to costs. [1008G] 5. Rule 559A also provides that all reasonable indulgence should be allowed to a condemned detenu in the matter of interviews with relatives, relatives friends, friends, legal adviser and approved religious ministers. Surprisingly, but we do not propose to dwell on that issue, this rule provides for a search of the person who wants to interview A prisoner. [The Court cannot overlook that the petitioner has not been asking either for permission or permission to be heard at the hearing of the petitions. The petition is directed to allow the petitioner in interview the two convicts Billa as also Ranga and the other prisoners, because there is under section 161(2) of Criminal Procedure Code.

The respondent mortgaged a tea garden to the appellant Bank. On January 19, 1950, the Bank applied for the appointment of a Receiver. The District Judge directed that the Bank should nominate a Receiver in terms of clause 12 of the mortgage deed. The appellant filed an appeal against that order but it was dismissed on June 29, 1970. In the meantime, the respondent moved an application asking for damages from the Receiver on the ground that the fire had occurred due to his negligence. The Subordinate Judge decreed the suit on May 31, 1956 but he allowed the respondent 's cross objections and enhanced the damages to Rs. 4,525. He directed that in case the Receiver should furnish the requisite security within the time allowed to him, the amount should be recovered from the security of Rs. 50,000. The High Court dismissed the appeal on June 30, 1970 holding that the surety bond was executed both by the Receiver and the appellant in favour of the respondent as he was neither the successor nor the assign of the District Judge; and that under the terms of the bond, the appellant is not answerable for the loss caused to the tea garden by fire. Allowing the appeal to this Court, ^ HELD: The surety bond is a part of the proceedings pending before the District judge and on the transfer of the suit the entire proceedings including the bond stood validly transferred to the court of the Subordinate Judge. [360 F] Under section 150 of the Code of Civil Procedure, save as otherwise provided, where the business of any Court is transferred to any other Court, the transferee Court has the same powers and is entitled to perform the same duties as those respectively conferred and imposed by the Code upon the transferor court. The surety bonds are a part and parcel of the proceeding pending before him and on transfer of his entire proceedings, including the surety bonds.

The appellants who were dealers in food grains supplied to the Regional Food Controller diverse quantities of wheat in compliance with the provisions of the U.P. wheat Procurement (Levy) Order, 1959. The Sales Tax Officer levied tax under the U .P. Sales Tax Act on the aggregate price of the price of wheat by the appellants, rejecting the contention raised by the appellant that the wheat supplied was not sold by them to the Controller and in appeal the Assistant Commissioner (Judicial) Sales Tax held that the turnover resulting from supplies of wheat was not taxable since there was no "sale" within the meaning of the Act. The order was confirmed by the Additional Judge (Revisions) Sales tax. The High Court answered both the questions in the affirmative. In appeal to this Court, HELD: Under section 21 of the , a dealer is obliged to sell to the State Government fifty per cent of the wheat purchased by him every day beginning with the date of commencement of the Order and thereafter fifty per centum of the quantity of wheat procured or purchased by it every day commencing with the day of commencement. The levy order takes no account of the volition of the licensed dealers and until the State Govern directs otherwise, of the Controller or the authorised officer. Food grains Dealers Licensing Order 1959 to deliver the quantities of sugarcane specified in the Order. The State Government is directed by the Order to pay for the wheat supply supplied at the controlled rate. The source of the obligations to deliver specified quantities of the goods and to pay them is not in any contract but in the statutory order. [666 F H] M/s New India Sugar Mills Ltd. vs Commissioner of Sales Tax, Bihar, ; , followed.

The appellant was in jail from November 12, 1985 onwards awaiting trial on a charge of murder. He was due for release from prison on June 23, 1986. On that day, however, an order for his detention was made under the provisions of the Gujarat Prevention of Anti Social Activities Act, 1985. The mandate of article 22(4) of the Constitution is that no law providing for preventive detention shall authorise the detention of a person for a longer period than three months unless the Advisory Board has reported within the period of three months that there is in its opinion sufficient cause for such detention. Section 10 stipulates that in every case where a detention order has been made under section 11, the State Government shall, within three weeks from the date of detention of the person under the order, place before the Advisory board the grounds on which the order has be made, the representation, if any, made by the detenu and the report, ifany, of the authorised offi cer. What is important for the purposes of this case is that section 11 stipulates that no Act providing for detention shall authorize the detention Of a person who for a shorter period than 3 months unless an Advisory Board consisting of persons who are or have been qualified to be appointed as Judges of a High Court has reported before the expiration of the said period of 3 months that it is in the opinion sufficient Cause for such deten tion. Section 11 stipulates the procedure to be followed by the Advisory Boards. What was important for purposes of the case is whether a law may be made providing for successive orders for detention in a manner as to render the protection of article 19(4). The period of two weeks stipulated by section 11 expired on July 14, 1986 and the appellant was entitled to be released on July 8, 1986 as no reference had been made to the Advisory Committee within the said time. On August 7, 1986, an earlier order of detention was passed on the same facts on the ground that there has been a contravention of the constitutional protection afforded by article 22 (4) and therefore, the appellant is entitled to get set at liberty. He did not dispute that under section 15(2) of Act, the expiry or revocation of an earlier detention order shall not bar the making of a subsequent detention order under the Act against the same person, subject to the proviso that if there were no fresh facts, the maximum period for which a person may be detained shall not extend beyond the expiry of 207 a period of 12 months from the day of detention under the earlier detention Order. He also contended that this provision, if to be sustained, as constitutionally valid must be read down so that it does not offend the mandate of Article 22( 4) of tho Constitution that no right providing for Preventive deten tion shall authorise detention of any person for longer period exceeding three months without the intervention of an independent body with persons on it of judicial qualifications of a high order. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The procedural requirements are the only safeguards available to a detenu since the court is not expected to go behind the subjective satisfaction of the detaining authority. [209E] 2.

The petitioner, a father of the respondent, filed an application for setting aside the award and sought the judgment in terms of the award under section 17 of the (hereinafter called 'the Act '). A notice consequent upon the filing of the Award was issued to the petitioner. The petitioner filed his objections to the application but did not file any application within the prescribed limitation of 30 days. The trial Judge rejected the objections filed beyond the period of limitation and for reasons that (1) the notice was already given to the party concerned about the filing, and (2) the time for making an application to set aside the Award had expired and no such application was made. The High Court dismissed the revision application holding that the First Appeal and Civil Revision Application were withdrawn in pursuance of an agreement reached between the parties on or about 14th August, 1978. Dismissing the Special Leave Petition, ^ HELD: 1. In view of the facts and circumstances of the case, it is clear that the conduct of the parties that there was an arbitration agreement and by signing the award it could be said that the parties had agreed to refer the dispute in writing to the arbitration of the named arbitrator. This agreement was done twice, firstly by signing an endorsement below the award, and secondly by entering into an agreement in the form of a letter dated 14th 8 1978 (Exhibit 40). In that view of this matter, it cannot be said to be a proper arbitration agreement in terms Of section 2(a) of the Act. [530G H] Prasun Roy vs The Calcutta Metropolitan Development Authority and another, A.I.R. 1988 S.C. 205; referred to. 2. In the light of the fact that the proceedings under the Act are conducted and without an exception challenged in Courts, has made lawyers laugh and legal philosophers weep. This Court further observed that experience shows and law reports hear ample testimony that the proceeding under the act have become highly technical accompanied by unending prolixity, at every stage providing a legal trap to the unwary. With respect, we could not agree more in the facts of this case. [540A B] 3.

The respondent filed a suit against the appellants for partition of the Searsole Raj Estate. The suit was decreed by the trial court and a final decree for sale was made in favour of the respondent. On appeal, the High Court held that the attachment was not valid because it was made under Order XXI, rule 57, as amended by the Calcutta High Court. Held, that the order of January 30, 1937, was a final order which brought the Execution Case No. 118 of 1936 to an and the attachment continued, not because there was a pend ing execution proceeding but because a special order was made thereunder. The respondent had not received the notice referred to in clause (a) of sub section (1) of section 28, sub section(1), since section 28 sub section, sub s.(1) is concerned only with assignment of debts" and the question as to whether the assignment was such as to establish a debtor and creditor relation between the assignee and the debtor so as to bring the case within the purview of the Act. The words "all the rights of any assignee or holder for value" in section 2(22) of the , make it plain that an assignee of a mortgage debt is within the sub section since section 29, sub sections (1), (ii) and (iii) are not concerned with assignment or distribution of debts. Promode Kumar Roy vs Nikhil Bhusan Mukhopadhya, A.I.R. 1937 Cal. 971, referred to.

The appellant was the Karta of a joint family consisting of himself and his four sons. The appellant was his concubine since 1945 until his death on February 22, 1949. By two registered deeds purporting to be sale deeds dated April 15, 1946, (Exbts. A 1 and A 2), he transferred certain properties belonging to the joint family. In 1947 after the execution of exhibit A 1 & A 2 there was a disruption of the joint Hindu family and a severance of the Joint status between the appellant and his sons. In 1954, his widow and sons instituted O.S. No. 12 of 1954 against the appellant for recovery of possession of the properties alleging that the documents dated April 14, 1946 were executed without consideration or for immoral purposes, and were void. The trial court dis missed the appellant 's suit holding that the transfers were made by Venkatacharyulu in favour of the appellant in view of past illicit cohabitation 45 with her, such past cohabitation was the motive and not the consideration for the transfers under exhibit A I and A2. Held, that the gifts were invalid as they were made in consideration of past cohabitations, having regard to section 2(d) of the . The gift was without consideration by way of gift and as such was not bit by section 6(h). Balo vs Parbati, (1940) All. 370, referred to. Held further, that on a proper construction of exhibit D 1 & 2, it is clear that the past cohabit ment was the foundation for the gift under exhibit 186. The transfers were without consideration and were by way Of gifts. The gifts were not hit by section 2 (d) by reason of the fact that they were motivated by a desire to compensate the concubines for her past services. In the present case, the appellant had no power to make a gift of the undivided interest in the coparcenary properties to his concurbubine. The respondents contended that assuming that the transfer was made in the consideration of previous promise, she was competent to alienate for value his undivided interest and not her properties. Held also, further, (i) that the appellant was not entitled to make any gift of his divided interest in a coparcenary property to his coffinine.

The appellant filed a suit against the respondent for a declaration that he was entitled to prefer an appeal under section 116 A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The suit was dismissed by the trial court but on appeal the High Court held that the appeal presented to them by the respondent was within time if computed after making deductions permitted by section 12 of the Limitation Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the words "different from" urged by the appellant were accepted and this requirement would be satisfied only if the First Schedule made provision for an identical appeal as that under the special law, still it was submitted by the respond ent that even this was satisfied in this case; (ii) the construction of the words 'difference from ' urged by him were accepted, and this require ment would be con sidered only if a period of limitation different from the period prescribed therefor by the first schedule. HELD: (i)(a) The word "for the purpose of determining any period of Limitation" in article 156(2) of the Constitution is not restricted to cases where the Act prescribes a period for such an appeal, but also the circumstances under which the delay can be excused indicating thereby that the general provisions of the . [143 E] (b) The words "for determining any periods of limitation prescribed for any suit, appeal or application by any special or local law" in the first limb of sub section (2) Of section 29 are not wide enough to include a suit, appeals or applications under a special or general law which is of a type for which no period of time limitation is prescribed in the First schedule. [144 G] (c) The expression "dispute" used in article 157(1)(a), does not mean that the Act should be construed as a whole and the words are capable of being understood by their plain grammatical meaning. In order to deal with the second ground given by the High Courts under section 29(2), sub section 2 of section 29 is concerned only with proceedings of this kind, that is, proceedings under special or other local law for which a period Of limitation is provided in the Act. [143 H] (d) The first limb is not attracted to an appeal against an order of acquittal under the said section. [145 E] State of U.P. vs Smt. Kaushaliya etc., A.I.R. , followed.

The appellant, a person providing transport service in the District of Mathura challenged the validity of the Order dated May 22, 1986 passed by the District Magis trate declaring Plot Nos. 701 and 703 in the Town Area, Baldev (Mathura) as a bus stand/halting place of Baldev, where the stage carriages were directed to stand for the purpose of allowing the passengers of Baldev to get into and to get down from the stage carriage routes in a writ petition, Civil Miscellaneous Writ Petition No. 501 of 1986 filed before the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution of India challenging the said order. The High Court was of the opinion that section 76 of the Act conferred wide powers on the District Magistrate 'to fix the places for the bus stand orhalting places ' and that it could not be construed as an order fixing the area as a Bus stand. It further held that since the impugned order did not specifically state that the bus operators could allow the passengers to get up and pick up the passengers, it could cannot be construed that as an arbi triction fixing the areas as a vehicle stand. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave against the said decision of the High court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Section 76 of U.P. Motor Vehicles Rules, 1940 which authorises the District Commis sioner to specify places within the limits of any municipality notified area, town area or cantonment or within such other limits as he may define where alone public service vehicles or any specified class or classes of public services vehicles and/or goods may stand indefinite or for such period as may be specified or public serv ices may stop for a longer time than is necessary for the taking up and setting down of passengers. [718C D] T.P Ibrahim vs Regional Transport Authority, Tanjore, ; , followed. T. P. Ibrahim vs District Magi trate, T.B. Ibrahim & Ors., ; , referred to. 2. The Town Area Committee can derive any assistance from this rule. It only authorises the State Government to exercise the powers under section 76 which is confined to the question of determination of parking places and halting places which are not the same as bus stands which can only be notified by the Regional Transport Author ity as held by this Court in T.V. Ibrahim 's case. [18D E] 3. The District Magistra trate had passed the impugned Order in question with the object of establishing a bus Stand in the area in question. That appears to be so from the order passed by tho District Magistrate and the letter dated 10.10.1986 written by the Executive Officer of Baldev Town Area committee, Baldev to the President of the Union requiring the bus operator to stop their buses at the bus stands and to start from there and permit the passengers t get out of their buses upto and to be got out of his buses at that bus stand. [ 718E F] 4. The order passed under that provision was open to revision under section 64A by the State Transport Authority. The appeal is accordingly allowed. There shall, however, be no order as to costs.

The appellants were prosecuted under section 3(1) of the , and section 7, read with section 8 of the . The trial court convicted all the accused ' but on appeal the Additional Sessions Judge set aside the conviction. In revision to the High Court it was contended that (i) there was no attempt on the part of the appellants to commit the offence of export; (ii) there had been an attempt on their part to commit export paddy to Delhi, and so there was an attempt to commit an offence of sale; and (iii) there were no provisions in the Act which made a preparation to commit any offence punishable. HELD: (i)(a) The appellants should not have been convicted under section 7 of the for these reasons it is clear that the appellants should have been warned that they had no licence to carry the paddy and they may have changed their mind at any place between Samalkha Barrier and the Delhi Punjab boundary and not have proceeded further in their journey. [666 D] (b) The preparation consists in devising or arranging the means or measures necessary for the commission of the offence. On the other hand an attempt is to commit a crime, he must be shown first to have had an intention to commit that the offence, and secondly to have done an act which constitutes the actus reus of a criminal attempt. The sufficiency of the actuus reous is a question of law which has led to difficulty because of the necessity of distinguishing between acts which are merely preparatory to the commission. [667 E F] (c) There was no provision in the , which makes a preparation for committing an offence punishable, and it follows therefore that the appellant should not be convicted under s 7 of 'the . For these reasons there is no substance in this argument.

The Sassoons executed in favour of the appellant company, a sum of Rs. 27,94,504, Mulraj and Company Ltd., and Rajputana Textile (Agencies) Ltd., for the year 1943 45 and the net consideration was Rs. 75,77693, Chidambaram Mulraj & Co. Ltd., which received from them on such transfers was taken by them to the "Capital Reserve Account". The Income tax Officer and the Excess Profits Tax Officer included in the assessable income of the Sassoon Rs. 28,51,934 made up of Rs, 25,61,692 in respect of the Managing Agency of the E. D. Sassoon United Mills Ltd., a sum Of Rs. 2,37,602 and also included in its assessable income tax assessments of the said Sassoors for the assessment year 1944 45 and chargeable accounting period 1st January, 1943 to the 31st December, 1943, the original income tax and excese profits tax assessments for the years 1943 45, to the 30th November, 1943. The Income Tax Officer and Excess Profits tax Appellate Tribunal accepted the contention of the transferees that the Sassoonons had not earned any part of the managing Agency commission which had been paid by the companies to the transferees and were not liable to tax in respect Of the same. The High Court on reference held against the appellant. Held, that the shares in this income which accrued to the Sas Soons on the completion of a definite period of service and at stated periods, that it was a condition precedent to the recovery of any wages or salary in respect thereof that the service or duty should be completely performed, that such remuneration constituted a debt only at the end of each such period of services and that no remuneration or commission was payable to the Managing Agent for broken periods. The mere ownership of the agency cannot as a matter of law be treated as the source of income, as explained above, any term in the Managing agency Agreement between the principal and the agent entitling only the assignee to receive the year 's remuneration and negativing to the assignor any direct recourse to his quondam principal for his share of the income, cannot have the effect of denying to the assigningor a substantial right to a share in the remuneration, if otherwise he has a vested right thereto. It is not correct to say that by virtue of this clause the service of the assignee subsequent to the date of assignment can be tacked on to the service for the entire year which earns the remuneration and the negativingto the assignee any direct resort to his own share of income.

The appellant was a resident of the Lucknow. He had two sons, Badri and Kirpa Shanker. The deceased and his wife were residing with their father. It is said that Sunderpatti developed illicit intimacy with Sahoo; but there were incessant quarrels between them. On August 12, 1963, at about 6 p.m. the appellant brought her buck and after some wordy altercation between them they slept in the only room of their house. The only other inmate of the house was the appellant 's second son, Kirpa Shankar, a lad of about 8 years. On the morning of August 13, 1963 Sunderpatti was found with serious injuries in the room of the appellant and his two sons. The appellant brought his buck, and after sometime he came back to the verandah of the House he heard some gurgling sound and saw his father going out of the said house at about six a.m., on that day soliloquying that he had finished Sunderpatti and thereby finished the daily quarrels. This Court in a series of decisions has reiterated the following well settled rule of "circumstantial evidence". The circumstances from which the conclusion of guilt is to be drawn should be in the first instance fully established. All the facts so established should be consistent only with the hypothesis of the guilt of the accused and the circumstances should be of a conclusive nature and tendency that they should be such as to exclude other hypotheses but the one proposed to be proved. "All the facts, so established, should be inconsistent only with, the hypothesis or of the innocence of theaccused and the circumstance should be so consistent only in the hypothesis that they are proved.
