The probative value of an admission or a confession does not depend upon its communication to another, though just like any other piece of evidence, it can be admitted in evidence only on proof. This proof in the case of oral admission or confession can be offered only by witnesses who heard the admission or the confession, as the case may be. The following illustration pertaining to a written confession brings out the said idea: A kills B; enters in his diary that he has killed him, puts it in his drawer and absconds. When he places his act on record, he does not communicate to another; indeed he does have any intention of communicating it to a third party. Even so, at the trial the said statement of the respondent can certainly be proved as a confession made by him. If that be so in the ease of a statement in writing there cannot be any difference in principle in the matter of an oral statement. Both must stand on the same footing. This aspect of the doctrine of confession received some treatment from wellknown authors on evidence, like Taylor, Best and Phipson. In "A Treatise on the Law of Evidence" by Taylor, 11th Edn., Vol. I, p. 262, referred to.

The appellant was working as Divisional Manager at Delhi. The general insurance business was nationalised and its management was taken over by the Central Government under General Insurance (Emergency Provisions) Ordinance, 1971 replaced by Act 57 of 1972. Under the Act, the services of the appellant and others stood transferred and vested with the custodian. Under section 16(1), in Chapter V provides that if the Central Govt. is of the opinion that for the more efficient carrying on of General Insurance business, it is necessary to do so, it may by notification frame one or more schemes providing for all or any of the following matters; (e) the rationalisation or revision of pay scales and other terms and conditions of service of officers and other employees wherever necessary. Pursuant thereto, the central Govt. framed the New India Assurance Co. Ltd. Merger Scheme, 1973 with effect from December 31, 1973. The appellant submitted his reply on December 7, 1974. While dropping the proceeding, the appellant was served with termination order dated April 17, 1975 issued by the respondent. The appel lant challenged it in a writ petition in Delhi High Court which was dismissed by a learned Single Judge on November 11, 1983 and was confirmed by the Division Bench in Letter Patent Appeal No.351/1984 dated April 23, 1984. In the appeal to this Court, on behalf of the respondent it was contended that Rule 5 is ultra vires of Article 14 of the Constitution; that Rule 9 of the Rules of Delhi Transport Corporation Service Regulation gives naked power to terminate the services and that Rule 10 does not become arbitrary; that the rule was capable of two constructions; that since Rule 9 in D.T.C. 's case Rule 5 provides guidelines, the Board of Directors have to take a decision, whether the need to continue the employee 's service subsists which would be based on the relevant material; and that the post which the employee is occupying may continue and would be put to an end by giving one month 's notice or pay in lieu thereof. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1.1 The Board of Management did not abolish the post but put an end to the service of the appel lateant. Obviously due to loss of confidence as his honesty and integrity became suspicious and his continuance in service was felt inexpedient and not in the interest of the business of the respondents. But Rule 8 was available for taking action for misconduct but was not availed. Therefore, the impugned order terminating the services is illegal. [226F G] 1.2 The Board did not abolishing the post, but put a end to it to the appellant.

The Collector of Mayurbhanj issued a notice to the successful bidder for establishing 70 outstill shops for 1970 71. Ajodhya Prasad Shah gave the highest bid for a group of seven shops, in one lot, for Rs. 34,000/ per month. His bid was accepted and his name was entered in the prescribed register, and the entry was signed by the successful bidders and the Collector. Ajendra Prasad Shah made an application to the Excise Commissioner for depositing Rs. 68,000 for the month of April but the Superintendent did not pass the deposit challan. Ajadesh Ranjan Kumar filed a writ petition (O.I.C. No. 329 of 1970) in the High Court with the allegation that the Collector was not acting according to law as the State Government had issued instructions to him not to issue the licenses, and that the State Gov ernment had no power to interfere with the auction held by the Collector after it had "become final in appeal and revision", and prayed for a direction that in the mean time he made arrangements for establishing his shops and incurred an expenditure of about Rs. 1,50,000. He also filed a petition ( O.I .C.No. 329/70) on April 13, 1970. The Collector issued a fresh notice to Ajodhya Prashad Shah who gave the lowest bid for the group of 7 shops, and after hearing the parties passed an order dated August 19, 1970 for re auctioning the license and declared that rule 103(1) of the Board 's Excise Rules was ultra vires the Act. The High Court held that section 6(a) did not authorise the exercise of "such absolute and naked power in determining the sum of money" as was sought to be done by the order dated 8th February, 1971, and declared Rule 103(I) of Board ' Excise Rules as ultra vires. It further held that the amended section 29(2)(b) had not been made retrospective in operation, the effect of section 6 was that thereby the Legis lature had directed the State to disregard the decision given by this Court in Ajodhya Pra sad 's case (I.L.R. [1954] S.C R. 969), and held that as the petitioner was the highest bidder on February 20, 1970 and his names were entered in a bid register and the entries were signed, the petition was entitled to the grant of the exclusive privilege under section 22 by virtue of section 29 (2)(a) of Amending Ordinance No. 17 of 1970. Allowing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The power to accept or reject a tender without assigning any reason cannot be said to be arbitrary as section 29 provides for re instate ment and it has expressly been provided in section 29 that it shall be exercised in the interest of the Excise Revenue" (ii) by the specified authority, and (iii) under such control as may be specified.

The appellant was charged with having entered into crimi nal conspiracy with an approver. The prosecution case was that the deceased and his wife were friends and that the appellant had a son who was of fair skin and wore khaki shorts and a white shirt, Mohan Lal Boob, an agriculturist gave evidence that on 27th December 1967 he was watering the crops. The High Court found that there was corroboration of the evidence which connected accused No. 2 not only with the offence of theft but also with murder. Allowing the appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) There was no corroboration of actual participation in the murder and the theft formed the same transaction and were committed by the same persons. The fact that there were civil and criminal proceedings between him and the appellant and the deceased was seen alive in the company of accused No 2 and Dinkar is not to be lost sight of. Accused No. 3 gave several articles to a person called Takalkar. One of the utensils was found to have a name thereon scraped off. There was also a piece of hand writing with the signature of accused 2 at the foot of it and that was the list of the articles sold to Gadekar. The recovery of the chain which Narendra wore was identified by Dr. Nanavati was not challenged in cross examination. It is obvious that silver lump could not be identified. At this stage it is to be noticed as to whether there was evidence to connect accused No 3 with murder and in regard to accused No, 3. [621 D] (2) The circumstantial evidence did not support the prosecution case because it was put to Dinkar in cross examine that it was Dinkar alone who killed Narendra. Therefore, the medical evidence as to the skull and the bone is not of importance in view of the death of Narendra. [625 E F] Lachi Ram vs State of Punjab ; , followed. (3) The fact of recovery of chain which the deceased had been identified by the doctor did not affect the prosecution version.

The appellant was the Karta of a Hindu undivided family. The Town Planning Scheme, Surat No. 8 (Umarwada) was declared by the Government under section 22 of the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954. On July 4, 1967 a draft scheme was published which included among other lands an area admeasuring 1,37,961 sq. meters of which appellant as Karta of Hindu undivided Family was the lessee. The appellant claimed compensation for deprivation of his right in the land at Rs. 50 per sq. by his order made on November 4, 1971. Not satisfied with the decision of the Town Planning Officer the appellant preferred an appeal before the Board of Appeal. Before the Board the appellant reduced his claim to Rs. 950 p. per sq.; but the Board awarded compensation to the appellant at the rate of Rs. 2.40 p. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appeal was not maintainable as the Act did not provide an appeal from a decision of Town Planning officer on matters dealt with by him in his order dated November 4 1971. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that in case the Board 's decision in the appellant 's case was appealable either under clause (viii) or clause (xiii) of section 32(1). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Act contains the necessary provisions for estimating the compensation payable to an owner of land who has not been given a reconstituted plot. Under section 64(1)(f), the amount by which the total value of the plots included in the final scheme shall be liable to contribution to the costs of a town planning scheme in accordance with the provisions contained in section 65; and under section 67, the amount of such excess shall be deducted in arriving at the costs. [92 D E] 2. The expression "person interested" as defined in section 3 of the Land Acquisition Act means all persons claiming an interest in compensation to be made on account of the acquisition of land under that Act. The sense in which the expression 'injurious affection ' is used in section 23(1) of the Act is the generally accepted meaning of that expression and it would be more helpful for appreciating the contentions raised on behalf. [93 F] 3. Under the Land Acquisi tion Act, compensation payable is determined on the basis of "market value" of the land on the date of the notification under section 4(1), which is the guiding rule in respect of all lands covered by the scheme. The word 'person interested ' as defined by section 3 has to find out the market value of each of the original plots at the date on which the declaration of intention to make a scheme. [94 F H] 4. Under clause (xiv) the Town planning Officer is required to estimate the compensation to he paid to the owner of any property or right injuriously affected by the making of a Town planning scheme In accordance with section 64, the 'owner of each plot included in his final scheme estimated on the assumption that the scheme has been completed would exceed the market price of the same plot when taken into account without the improvements. Under cl.

The appellant, who was a foster son of the testator, made a will on October 4, 1927, appointing his brother Seetharama Iyer a guardian of his minor daughters as well as of his foster son. He left the management of his properties to his brother and provided that as soon as his minor daughter attained majority he should give to them per head one veli nanja land and one vela of punja land in vattam No. 149 in village Nagampadi 976 and further provided that the said Seetharams should deliver possession of the remaining properties to him immediately after he attained majority. It was also provided in the will that Seetharamma should pay to the minor daughters the income from the properties devised to them after the death of the legatee. The appellant, therefore, filed a suit for partition of land according to quality but was not prepared to accept the right of selection claimed by the daughters. The trial court upheld the contention of the daughters and decreed the suit. On appeal the High Court held that the English rule of benevolent construction that a legatee has a right to choose in such circumstances applies to India also and has further held that on the construction of the will in this case the right to select was in the legatees and not in Seetharamas or in the legateees. Held, that where it is not possible to say on the interpretation of a will that the testator himself indicated the selection or appointed a third person to make the selection but still intended to make a gift which could be made certain by selection made by the legatee, the English Rule of construction that in such cases the testator intended the legatee to select should be applied in India also, and the decision in Narayanasami Gramani 's case was that the testatrix 's own selection could be spelt out of the Will and once that was so no question of any selection by the legate &rose.

The appellant, a co bhumidar of the plots in dispute, was the widow of one Syed Laek Husain and defendants No. 1 and 2 were her husband 's cousins. The plaintiff 's case was that she went to the village from time to time and got her share. In her statement before the trial court she had clearly stated that the defendants, Mohd. Bashir and Mohd. Rasheed used to manage the properties which were joint and used to give her share and assured her that her share would be properly looked after and protected by them. The appellant further alleged in her statement that during the consolidation proceedings, separate plots were carved out and she was never informed about any proceedings by the defendants and was under the Impression that her shares were being properly looked upon. It was only three years before the suit that the plaintiff came to know that her name had been deleted from the khewat and the entire property was mutated in the consolidation of holding proceedings in the name of the defendants. The allegation of the appellant that the respondents had committed fraud was stoutly denied. The trial court decreed the suit for joint possession in respect of plot Nos. 201 and 274 only. As regards plot No. 93, 94 and 106, the dismissal of the plaintiff ' s suit by the trial Court was upheld. In second appeal, the District Judge held that on the admitted facts even after the abolition of zamindari, the position was that in 1357 Fasli the appellant 's name was clearly recorded as a co sharer with the defendants; that in 1362 Fasli the plots were entered exclusively in the names of Mohd. Shah Mohammad and Mohd., Rasheed and that there was no order of any authority or court to show the circumstances under which the plaintiff had 's names was suddenly deleted, nor were there any judicial proceedings under which his name was wrongly deleted nor were they there any Judicial proceedings under the name or of the respondent as a sub sharers.

The petitioner, a Deputy Prime Minister of India, was appointed as the Chief Minister of the State. The oath of office of his new assignment was administered to him by the incumbent signed as Prime Minister and all other ministers sign as Ministers. He further indi cates that describing Shri Devi Lal as Deputy Prime Ministers is descriptive only and for all purposes he is a Minister and there is no 3 constitutional sanction for the post of Deputy Prime Minis ter as such. Relying on a bench decision of this Court in Virji Ram Sutaria vs Nathalal Premji Bhavadia & Ors., , this Court held that the prescribed oath should be divided into two parts, one which is descriptive and the other which contains the sub stantial part. Allowing the writ petition, HELD: 1. The essential requirement of Article 173 read with Form VII A was that the person taking the oath or making the affirmation would bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution and uphold the sovereignty and integrity of India. [312C] Virjiram Ram Sutari vs Natulal Premnani & Ors. , referred to. 2. The words which precede this portion are merely descriptive of the person and of his nomination as a candidate. " In view of the clear statement made by the Attorney General that Respondent No. 1 is just a Minister like other members of the Council of Ministers though he has been described as Deputy Chief Prime Minister but the description of him as Deputy Ministers does not confer on him any powers of the Prime Minister, along with his other submis sions, this Court think the first contention raised by the petitioner has no force. [412E F] 3.

The appellant, a carding and spinning department of the Carnatic Mills stopped work some at 4 p.m., some at 5 p. m. The stoppage ended at 8 p.M. in both the departments. By 10 p. M. the strike ended completely. The apparent cause for the strike was that the management of the Mills had expressed its inability to comply with the request of the workers to declare the forenoon of the 1st November, 1948 as a holiday for solar eclipse. On the 3rd November, the strike ending completely. was held and the workers were not entitled to annual holidays with pay under section 49 B (1) of the Factories Act. The appellant contended that on a proper construction of section 49B(1) 29 222 of the , the management was right in its decision that the continuity of service was broken by the interruption caused by the illegal strike and that as a consequence the workers who participated in such strike were not enti tled to annual leave with pay. Held, that the conclusion reached by the adjudicator was clearly right and the conclusion could be avoided that the workers 'were acting in concert. That being so, the action of the appellant on the night of 1st Nov., 1948, fell within the definition of the expression "strike" as given in section 2(q) of . Held, further, that in view of the facts and circumstances detailed in the adjudicators ' award this contention cannot be seriously considered. The decision of the Labour Appellate Tribunal on this point is set aside.

The appellant, a producer of cinematograph films, filed a complaint alleging that the fascinating title was misleadingly foul and beguiled the guileless into degeneracy. The Magistrate after examining some witnesses took cognizance of the offence and issued notice to the accused. Thereupon, the producer moved the High Court under section 482 Cr. P.C. on the score that the criminal proceeding was an abuse of the judicial process and engineered by ulterior considerations and that no prosecution could be legally sustained in the circumstances of the case, the film having been duly certified for public show by the Board of Censors, the public exhibition circulation or distribution or the production of the film even if it be obscene, lascivious or tending to deprave or corrupt public morals, cannot be an offence. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that once a certificate sanctioning public exhibition of a film has been granted by the competent authority under the (for short, the Act), there is a justification for its display thereafter and by virtue of the antidotal provisions in section 79 of the Penal Code, the Public exhibition, circulation or distributed distribution or distribution of the production or the Production of the films even if that it be objectionable, lambascivous or ting to depraves or corrupt persons morals cannot be said to be an abuse offence. Dismissing the appeal by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The prosecution is unsustainable because section 79 is exculpatory when read with section 5A of the Act and the certificate issued thereunder. [517E] 2. Section 79 makes an offence a non offence. When ? Only when the offending act is actually justified by law or is bona fide believed by mistake of fact to be so justified, the weapon of section 79 demolishes the prosecution. What is merely certified as suitable for show by a law may not go the length of holding that it is justified by Law. Such niceties need not deter us once we grasp the sweep of the . Indeed, the Penal code is general, the special. The scheme of the latter is deliberately drawn up to meet the explosively expanding cinema menace if it were not strictly policed. No doubt, the cinema is a great instrument for public good if geared to social ends and can be a public curse if directed to anti social objectives. The freedom of expression, the right to be equally treated and the guarantee of fair hearing before heavy investments in films are destroyed belong to Indian citizens under the Constitution. But all freedom is a promise, not a menace and, therefore, is subject to socially necessary restraints permitted by the Constitution.[517G H; 516A B] K. A. Abbas. Maybe, art cannot be imprisoned by the bureaucrat and aesthetics can be robbed of the glory and grace and free expression of the human spirit if governmental palate is to prescribe the permit for exhibition of artistic production in any department, more so in cinema pictures. So it is that a special legislation viz. the Act of 1952 sets up a Board of Film Censorors of high calibre and expertise, provides hearings, appeals and ultimate judicial review, pre censorship and conditional exhibitions and wealth of other policing strategies. [ 516D E] K A.A.

The petitioner, a Government Pleader for the Patna District, was appointed as an Advocate in Bihar State. During the currency of his term a plurality of nine Assistant Government Pleaders was appointed and one of them was put in charge of a bunch of land acquisition cases. The petitioner challenged the power of Government to appoint any other lawyer except under him and never by excluding him. He went to the extent of writing to Government: "I am, therefore unable to comply with your instruction in allowing any Assistant Government Pleader to work in this case". I shall myself conduct this case and have enough time for it." The petitioner was asked to make over those briefs to the new nominee. Thereupon, the petitioner challenged his power of government, like any other litigant, to appoint a suitable lawyer except by him and not by excluding himself. He also went to a extent of submitting to Government that in future he would not be given such cases. Chagrined by this loss of income and mayhem to his monopoly he rushed to the High Court for the universal panacea of a writ. The chemistry of Article 226 was governed by severe rules, and the High Courts declined to dispense the magic remedy. So he has sought special leave from this Court but Article 136 has its own conditions and limitations. In utter nudity, his case is a claim of monopoly of all government cases in the Patna district including lucrative land acquisition litigation as part of the professional 'estate ' of a Government pleader. The prospective cash value of this heavy crop of cases is estimated by him to be around one lakh of rupees and this secret is perhaps at the back of this lawyer 's litigation. Sri Govindan Nair, appearing for him, has argued that his client 's claim as the sole representative of Government in courts is not a legal cover for seeking lucre but for vindicating the inviolability of the high public office of Government Pleader by politicking men in the Secretariat or by practitioners of favouritism dressed in 'little brief authority ', a deeper issue in which the Bar has a stake and the Bench must also be concerned. The State of Bihar, through its Secretary, Ministry of Law & Justice, Government of Bihar (the petitioner) was requested to make available to him briefs for the purpose of enabling him to represent ' Government in all civil cases. During currency of this term a Bench of nine Assistants was appointed, and one thereof was put In charge of the bunch of Land acquisition cases, the Bar had a stake, and he went to that extent. The fabric of facts, on which the grievance in law rests, may be appreciated first. The Petitioner was requested by Government Pleader (the Petitioner) to make up those brief sen to the newly added nominee. Thereafter, the Petitioner challenged the powers of Government, like, any other person, to appointment any other counsel except under himself and never through excluding him, and never even by excluding the petitioner. He then went to this Court under Article 136. The High Court declined to interfere with the order of the High court. In appeal to this court it was contended on behalf of the Petitioner: (1) that his clients ' claim as a sole representative in courts are not a valid cover for seek lucred but for statistical purposes; (2) that the Government Pleader, Madras is only an agent of the Government, that his duties are only to the Government who are his principles and that he owes no duty to the public at all and that for reason he would be the holder of a Public office. Dismissing the special leave petition, ^ HELD: 1(a) The petitioner is not entitled to any relief under Article 32 of the Constitution.

The appellants held 570 out of a total issue of 800 shares of the Navjivan Mills Ltd., Kalol, a public limited company. The shareholders had to pay Rs. 100 for each new share. The Mills as the holder of 5,000 shares became entitled to receive 1,6662 shares of that company at the rate of Rs. 50 per share. On receiving the circular letter, the Directors of the Mills passed the following resolution: "Resolved that the company having a holding of 5.,000 ordinary shares in the capital of the Bank of India Ltd. having now received an intimation from the said Bank that this company is entitled to get 1,676662 more ordinary shares on payment of Rs 50 as capital and Rs.50 as premium per each share and it was considered proper to invest in the said issue of the said bank the funds of this company to the extent of 66 shares only and to distribute the right of this Company to the remaining 1,600 shares of which the issue amongst the shareholders of this concern was to be distributed among its 800 share holders. The appellants agreed to the allotment of these shares and ultimately transferred them to a private company Jesinghbai Investment Co. Ltd., which was the holder. The Income tax Officer assessed the income of the seven appellants on the footing that the release by the Mills amounted to distribution of "dividend" within the meaning of section 2(6A) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 and had escaped tax. The order of the Income tax officer reassessing the income was confirmed in appeal by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and by the Tribunal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the High Court was not justified having regard to the form of the question which expressly related to the distribution of the right to apply for the shares of Bank ofIndia being dividend within the extended meaning of that expression in section 2 (6A), and (2) the distribution by the company amounted to a distribution of dividend within section 2.(6A). HELD: (i) The High Court had rightly held that the distribution amounted to "docividend", and the value of the rights released in favour of the shareholders though taxable under section 12 of the Act, had escaped assessment. [588 D] (ii) The scheme of the provisions of the Companies Act is that the shares should be distributed amongst the share holders of the company. When the Legislature by section 2, 6A, sought to define the expression "deductend" it added to the normal meaning of the expression several other categories of receipts which may not otherwise be included therein. By the definition in section 1(6 A), "d coparcener" means dividend as normally understood and includes in its connotation several other receipts set out in the definition. The Tribunal had referred the question whether the distribution was of dividend. [589 E] (iii) The resolution did not purport to distribute any dividend. It took the form, of distribution of a right which had a monetary value. But by the form sanctioning the distribution, the true character of the resolution could not be altered.

The appellant filed an election petition under section 81 of the Representation of People Act, 1951 for short). The returned candidate as well as all other candidates who lost the election were impleaded as parties. In the election petition charges of corrupt practice and irregularities in the conduct of election were made. The returned candidates contested the petition. After going through the pleadings of the parties, the Court ascertained the points on which parties were at variance and framed appropriate issues. The election petition reached the stage of recording evidence. It appears an application was filed by the appellant seeking permission to produce and examine witnesses whose names were set out in the application. It was averred in the petition that the names of the witnesses whom he desires to produce are already mentioned in the appropriate paragraphs of the election Petition and that the petitioner would keep the witnesses present. The Court considered the points raised by the returned candidate and framed an order on November 29, 1982 upholding the objection raised by him that the purpose for which the witnesses were offered is not mentioned in his list and therefore the election petitioner could not be permitted to examine more witnesses whose name had not been mentioned in that list. A further observation was made by the Court that the election Petitioner could not he allowed to examine only more witnesses who had not already been mentioned. The High Court held that except Bahre son of Sher Singh no other witness could be examined and that as soon as the evidence of the afore said witness was recorded, the court would proceed to record the evidence on behalf of the returned candidates; and thereafter the matter will be set down for hearing oral arguments of the learned counsel of either side. It is this order which was questioned in this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The obligation to supply the list of witnesses within the time prescribed under sub rule (1) of Rule 1 of Order XVI is in respect of witnesses to procure whose attendance the party needs the assistance of the Court. When a summons is issued by the court for procuring the presence of a witness, it has certain consequences in law. If the summons is served and the person served fails to comply with the same, certain consequences would ensue as provided in Rule 10 of Order XVII. [532C D] 2. The scheme is that after the Court framed issues which give notice to the parties what facts they have to prove for succeeding in the matter which notice would enable the parties to determine what evidence oral and documentary it would like to lead, the party should file a list of witness with the gist of evidence of each witness in the court within the period prescribed by sub rule(1).

The appellant, a double M.A. and holding a Doctorate applied in response to an advertisement that appeared in Hindi Daily Bhirgu A Chetna and Dainik Jagran on May 18, 1980 for the post of Principal. Pursuant to this decision of the Selection Committee, the Manager of the College issued an appointment order dated April 7, 1981 to the appellant informing him that the Committee of Management had appointed the appellant as Principal on one year probation in the scale of 550 1200 at initial pay alongwith DA admissible under the rules. The appellant was required to present himself before the Manager and take over charge within 10 days of the receipt of the order failing which the appointment would be void. On receipt of this letter, the appellant wrote to the Manager that as permitted by him he has assumed charge of the post and he has convened an urgent meeting of the staff to be held on the same day after college hours in the teachers ' room. The State Government was contemplating to bring about a radical change in the mode method and power of appointment of teaching staff in non government aided schools and accordingly Secretary to the Government of U.P. Education Department issued an order dated 4th April, 1981 communicated by a radiogram to the various authorities. It reads as under: "From Secretary to Government of Uttar Pradesh Education/ Department G.O. No. 1701/l5 7 FI 1 (27)/81 dated 1st April 1981 Stop all fresh selections and appointments of Principals Headmasters and teachers including recruitment by promotion in all non government secondary schools except minority institutions pending further orders(.) District Inspectors to ensure non drawal of pay of teachers appointed after his date(.) Detailed instructions follow(.)" Pursuant to the receipt, the District Inspector of Schools, Ballia had sent a copy of it to the College. There was some dispute between the parties as to whether this copy of the radiograms was received by the Management of the college but there is a letter dated May 1, 1981 addressed by the District Superintendent of Schools to the manager of the institution. The letter further shows that on April 8, 1981 the Institution had received the order that the power of appoint of Principal has been withdrawn or suspended and therefore the appointment of the appellant would be by a body not authorised to make the appointment and hence ineffective though it may not be invalid. In view of the finding that sub section (4) of Section 9 did confer power on the State Government to make, modify or rescind any regulation as also make such other order consistent with the provisions of the Act, the second contention of Mr. Sanghi was equally bound to fail. It is therefore necessary to turn to the alternative contention based on sub sec.(10) of section 16 E. The marginal note of Section 16 E reads: "Procedure for selection of teachers and head of institutions. Sub sec. 4 of Section 8 confers power on Director of Education to cause inspection of recognised institution to be made from time to time and sub clause 2 to sub sec.

The respondent, a textile mill, sold by the Delhi Cloth & General Mills Co. Ltd., to manufacturers of tyres, who use it for the purpose of impregnating it with rubber, fell under entry 18 of the Schedule of the Rajasthan Sales Tax Act, 1954. The petitioners contended that they were exempt from sales tax and accepted the case of the petitioners that they had manufactured "a textile" and also that it serves as part of raw material for what ultimately went into the manufacture of a fabric. After indicating the manner in which and the substance out of which "rayon tyre cord fabric" is made and its composition, the petition sets out item 22 of the first schedule of the Central Excises and Salt Act, 1941 as the applicable entry covering the goods manufactured by the petitioners. This item was omitted in 1973, which reads: "18. All cotton fabrics, rayon or artificial silk fabrics, woollen fabrics, sugar and tobacco, as defined in the Additional Duties of Excise (Goods of Special Importance) Act, 1957". The Sales Tax officer rejected the petitioners ' objections to sales tax on "ray on tyre cord fabrics" manufactured by it. Thereafter, notices under the proviso to section 12(1) were issued for the years 1965 to 1969 with a view to reopening the assessments on the ground that the sales of these goods had wrongly escaped assessment. The petitioner challenged the order and provisional assessment dated 21st November 1971, which was dismissed by the Commercial Tax officer. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent that (1) the goods now sought to be taxed were not the "end product" but the "tyre cord fabric". Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (i) The High Court was right in not interfering with the decisions of the taxing authorities at this stage. [501 D] (ii) The question whether the tyre cord cloth is the end product or not in the final manufacture of an other fabric was quite irrelevant. It was a question which appertains to the knowledge of technical aspects of textile weaving and production to determine at what stage threads or cords forming warps and wefts really amount to a "fabric". [502 F] (iii) The essential question to determine is the stage at which the goods under consideration become a 'textile fabric". The meaning of the term "fextiles", given in the Oxford English Dictionary is: "A product of skilled workmanship". The first example of such a product is: (a) " manufactured material; now only a 'Textile fabrics". [ 502 A] (iv) The word "feel" has a wide meaning. Its first meaning given in Webster Oxford English dictionary is: 'A product is, "An edifice, a building." The fourth example of the First meaning is: `textiles". There fore, the essential question is to determine the stage when the goods are sought to he taxed. [ 502 B] (v) The test to be determined by the Tax authorities themselves is whether the product under consideration constitutes a fabric entitled to exemption.

The appellant company was engaged in construction of coal. The management held domestic enquiry into the incident and found him guilty of committing theft. He was dismissed from service. The dispute arising therefrom was referred under Section 10(1)(c) of the . The Labour Court registered the case as refer ence case No. 4 of 1988 and issued notice to the parties. The parties entered appearance and filed their respective pleadings. When the matter was thus pending consideration, the respondent seems to have written to the Government stating that it would be difficult for him to attend the Labour Court since he has been residing at Hajipur and it would he convenient for him if the case is transferred to Labour Court Patna. That application was made without intimation to the management. The Government howev er, has acceded to the request of the respondent and without opportunity to the Management transferred the case to Labour court Patna. The Notification issued in that regard reads as follows: "NOTIFICATION Patna dated 8th August 1988 S.O. In exercise of powers conferred by sub section (1) of Section 33 B of the , the Governor of Bihar after careful consideration of the application of the petitioner Shri Shivajee Prasad Sinha wherein he has prayed for the transfer of adjudication proceedings to Patna keeping in view to the difficulties expressed by him to attending the labour court, Dhanbad regu larly due to his residence at Hajapur is pleased to withdraw the proceeding shown in Annexure 'A ' pending before Labour Court, Dhanbad and transfer the said proceeding to the Labour court, Patna for speedy disposal from the stage at which the case was transferred. " The management moved the High Court by way of writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution to have the Notification quashed. The High Court did not agree and summarily dismissed the writ petition with an observation that since no prejudice is being caused to the petitioner and no allegation of mala fide has been made against the presiding officer, Patna, it would not amount to giving reasons as required by Section 33B of the Act. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The power to transfer pending case under section 33 B is not a mere administrative but quasi judicial power and the appropriate Government cannot transfer a case on the basis of allegations of one party without giving reasonable opportunity to other party to represent its point of view. This was also the view recognised by the Madras High Court in Management of Sri Rani Lakshmi Ginning and Weaving Mills Ltd. vs State of Madras, [1961] II LLJ 122, that the power to transfers pending case is not an administrative or quasi judicial powers and the Government cannot transferred a case to another Labour Court without it except of course where the very object of transfer would be frustrated if notice was given to the party affected. [295E F] 2. The expression "may" in sub section(1) Of Section 33 A only makes it discretionary in so far as the appropriate Govern ment taking a decision as to whether the power conferred thereunder has to be exercised or not. But when once a decision is taken to transfer a pending case then the requirement of giving reasons becomes mandatory. The authority is under legal obligation to record reasons in support of its decision. Reasons would be life of the decision. Failure to give reasons or giving reasons not germane would be fatal to the decision.[295F G] 3. In the instant case, the State has withdrawn the pending refe rence from the Labour Courts, Dhanbad & transferred it to another labour court at the distant District of Patna on the representation of the workman, without getting it verified from the management and the State in fairness ought to have got it verified by giving an opportunity to manage which is a party to the pending reference.

The appellant, a manager of the Hotel Imperial, New Delhi, was dismissed by the Industrial Tribunal on the ground that it did not specify how many of the 480 workers of thirty different categories working in the hotel were involved in the dispute. The appellant contended that the reference was incompetent as the union could not be made a party to the reference under the , and (2) the reference in this form was incompetent. Held, that the appeal must fail. The fact that more than three years have passed since the reference is made, does not make the reference incompetent merely because it is mentioned therein that the workmen will be represented by such and such union in the present dispute. State of Madras vs C. P. Sarathy, [1953] S.C.R. 334, followed. State Of Madras vs M. C.P. Sarthy, [1954] S,.C. R. 334 and State of Bombay vs B. N. Sinha, [1960] 1 S. C R. 869, referred to. Held further that the attack on the grounds of vagueness also fails. There is no force in this appeal and it is hereby dismissed with costs. The question whether the reference made by the Tribunal was incompetent merely for the sake of convenience so that the tribunal may know to whom it should give notice when proceeding to deal with the reference. Held also, further, that there is no substance in the contention that the references were bad simply because in the order of reference the words " as represented by the Hotel Workers ' Union, Katra Shahanshahi, Chandni Chowk, Delhi " have been added.

The appellant, a bushings and bearings imported by the appellant were assessed to duty under the Customs Tariff Act, 1975. The appellant claimed that the exemption notification No. 281 Cus/76 granting part exemption from payment of customs duty in respect of the rod bushes and camshaft bushes imported by it was not applicable to the parts, which were covered by Heading 84.06. The Assistant Collector and the Collector of Customs (Judicial) overruled the contention of the appellant that the bushits and bearions are the same and as the bearings come under the Heading No. 84.63 and not under Heading 84,06 they are not entitled to the benefit of exemption under the said Notification. The Customs Excise and Gold (Control) Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal of the Appellant and affirmed the orders of the Customs authorities. According to the Appellate Tribunal, the busihs and bearances are thesame and as borneings have been provided for under Heading No 84.04, they are parts of the engines referred to in Heading No, 84.07 and not a few parts thereof. The Notification also mentions the 'parts thereof '. In the absence of any clear and unambiguous provision that exemption will be granted in respect Of parts of engines, which must be all the parts constituting the engine or engines, it is difficult to uphold the contention that they are part of the internal combustion piston engines falling under Heading Nos. 8406.06 and 84. The Appellate Tribunal was influenced by the fact that the functions of the bushs and borneings are the identical. It may be that two articles have the same functions but nonetheless, they arc distinct and separate. As the functions and functions of bushions are those which of the bear ings, sometimes bushins are also called bearings, as pointed out by the Appellate Assistant Collector, it was difficult to accept the contention made on behalf of the respondents that as Heading No . 8406 does not mention 'part ' of such engines. Non mention of 'part" in Heading 8406 has given rise to a controversy between the parties. It is also contended that even assuming that Heading No., 84.05 also contemplates parts of engine, such parts must be parts of tile engines mentioned under Heading NO. 8404 and not as a few part thereof. In other words, his contention is that Heading 8407 will apply when an internal combustion Piston engine in imported in a knocked down condition. Lastly it is contended that the bushes and bear ingings are not identical articles but they are distinct and independent, yet there is no material for holding that the highways which have been imported by appellant, are parts parts of their engines referred under Heading 83.06, are excluded from the benefit. of the Notification. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The notification has been inartistically drafted. It does not provide that it must be All the parts of an engine or engine. It simply provides 'parting thereof ' [225F] 2.

The appellants and their counsel were not present when the suit was filed. The respondents filed a written statement taking the plea that they were entitled to be in enjoyment of the Dargah for a period of 27 days in all in the months of February, March, June, July, October & November each year and that the said 27 days shall be Febru ary 1 to 6, June 1 to June 1, June 2 to June 6, and October 1 to 8th for the first plaintiff and that they are entitled to the relief of possession of the said right to be In management of the Wakf. The Trial Court decreed the suit and in the operative part held that the plaintiffs were entitled only to manage the Dargah and to bein enjoyment of Hundial income during the said period. The High Court took the view that the Courts below proceeded upon an erro neous assumption as if it was the duty of the defendants to prove by what hostile assertions of title and possession ouster had been established. It further held that even if really the rights of Fathima Bee had become barred by her not exercising the rights, the plaintiffs themselves can have no independent right to claim. The appellants and counsel for the respondents contended that they was not arguing that the aforesaid judgment and decree were res judicata or binding on the parties. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 There is no controversy now as regards the period of 28 days falling to the share of the plaintiffs and on the question that females are also entitled in the right and management of Dargah according to Muslim Law. Thus the only controversy now left to be determined is whether the High Court was right in holding that the rights had become bar by ouster and as such the plaintiffs who were also claiming through Fathiman Bee had lost their right by ouster? It would first be necessary to make it clear as to what is the impact of the decree dated 11.8.1910 passed in Civil Suit No. 116 of 1909, so far as the present litigation is concerned. A perusal of the Judgment goes to show that there was no dispute now as regard the period and females are equally entitled in this right and the management of Wakf according to Hindu Law. [526E F] P. It is well settled that where one co heir pleads adverse possession against another co heir then it is not enough to show any one out of them is in sole posses sion and enjoyment of profits of the properties. The possession of one co sharer is considered in law, as possession of all the co heirs. Thus it is a settled rule of law as between co heirs there must be evidence of open assertion of hostile title coupled with exclusive possession and enjoyment by one of them to the knowledge of the other so as to construe ouster. [525F G] P .

The first respondent was a gangman in the employ of the Central Railway. The Government of India introduced a scheme of grant of compensatory (city) allowance and house rent allowance at rates specified in their memorandum No. E47 CPC/14 dated 1st December 1947. As a result of this scheme certain railway employees stationed at specified headquarters were eligible for the allowance aforesaid at certain specified rates. The first respondent put in his claim before the Authority for Rs. 290 on the ground that the house rent was not "wages" within the meaning of section 2(vi) of the Act and that therefore the house Rent Allowance claimed by him came within the purview of the definition of "wages ' contained in the Act. Held, that the rules which constitute the terms of the contract between the employer and the employee contemplate that an employee posted at one 173 1352 of the specified places would be entitled to house rent allowances; but that as soon as he is offered Government quarters for his accommodation he ceases to be so entitled, whether he actually occupies or does not occupy the quarters offered to him. The rules distinctly provide that the allowance will not be ad raissible to those who occupy government quarters or to those to whom such quarters have been offered but who have refused to take advantage of the offer. Once an employee of the description given above has been offered suitable house accommodation and he has refused it, he ceases lo be entitled under section 23(1) of . Held, further, that in view of the provisions of sections 7 and 11 of the , the rules framed by the Government governing the grant of house rent Allowance do not make it unconditional and absolute in terms. The house rent in the first instance is not admissible to all the employees of a particular class.

The detenu was one Indru 's Ramchand Bharvani; while in Writ Petition 435 of 1980, the detenu was alleged to have smuggled diamonds and precious stones in partnership under the style of "M/s. Gems Impex Corporation". 35, New Marine Lines Bombay, since 1971. On November 16, 1979, the Customs Officers raided the residential premises of the son Indru" and seized two cameras and three wrist watches worth about Rs. 55 lakhs and also some jewellery and Rs. 1,40,000 in Indian currency and two gold sovereign coins. On the following day, the customs officers raided the residence of the detenu and seized certain diamonds worth about rupees 55 lakhs. The detenus were arrested on November 23, 1979 and interrogated during interrogation. During interrogation, the detenus claimed that they had purchased the gems and other articles seized from them and gave the names of four persons from whom these gems had been acquired. Both the father and the son were arrested and were produced before a Magistrate. They were released on heavy bail subject to the condition that they would attend daily before the Customs officers and cooperate in the investigation. The detention order was authenticated by the Under Secretary to the State Government. On February 18, 1980, an order of detention purporting to have been made under section 3(1) of the (for short COFEPOSA) by the State Govt. was served on the detenus alongwith the order of Detention on February 16, 1980. This order was attested by the under Secretary to State Government and the grounds of detention were also served on them along with the order. On March 25, 1980 the detenu also made a representation to the Central Government which, according to the information furnished at the Bar by Mr. Phadke appearing for respondent 1, was declined. The Central Government advised the State Gov ernment to furnish the detenus with the material relied upon by the detaining authority in the grounds for detention. On April 3, 1980 copies were received by the detenus on March 25 and March 24, 1980 respectively. On May 3,1980, the wife of the detenue addressed a letter to the first respondent (Under Secretary to Government of Maharashtra), requesting him to furnish them with the materials relied upon in the ground of detention. The detenu also sent a petition through the Central Govt., complaining of the non supply of copies of the necessary documents. They also made an application to the detaining au thority that their request for revocation had been rejected. On July 3, 1981, the Central Govern ment wrote to the detenus that their requests for revocation of the detention had been refused. The State Government informed the detenu that the copies had been declined in exercise of its jurisdiction under COFEPOSA. This was followed by a writ petition filed in this Court. In the counter affidavit filed on behalf of the first respondents it was contended that the grounds contained only the substance of the statements, while the detenu had asked for copies of all the documents. It was further submitted that there was no evidence of smuggling in this case at all and the detaining authori ty committed illegality inasmuch as it relied on presumption under section 123 of the Customs Act. The use of this presumption was not available to the Detaining Authority in the exercise of his jurisdiction under the COFEPOSA. Dismissing the writ petition, ^ HELD: 1. There is merit in the submission that the supply of the copies given by Mr Phadkar, it may be recalled, is that the Collector had said that the supplies of the earlier statements which were entirely in favour of the detenus and the full texts of which have been with held, could not, by any reckoning, expose those persons to any alarm or danger at the hands of the agents or partis of the petitioners. [352F G] Khudiram Das vs The State of West Bengal & Ors., ; , followed. 2.

The Gujarat High Court in its order referred to SS 258, 410 and 423 of the Code and came to the conclusion that the scheme of Chapter XXXI of the Criminal Procedure as disclosed by these sections and particularly by section 419 is against the maintainability of a joint appeal by the State against an order acquitting several accused persons tried jointly. The High Court also recorded the main judgment only in Criminal Appeal No. 60 of 1965. The question which arose for determination was whether several accused person jointly tried have been acquitted by the trial court, the state can prefer one appeal against the acquittal of all them. The appellant contended that r. 6 in Chapter XXVI of the Bombay High Court Appellate Side Rules (which are applicable to the proceedings in Gujarat High Courts) was inconsistent with Chapter XXXI and of the code of Criminal Procedure with the result that a joint appeals by several accused were not maintainable under section 419 of the Cr. P.C. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: The power to frame this rule is specifically conferred on the High Court by section 554(2)(c) Cr.P.C., and r.6 does not seem to be inconsistent with any provisions of the said Code. Holding this rule to be valid, in agreement with the decision of the Full Bench, the competency of a Joint appeal by several persons convicted at one trial must be upheld. [879 H] Mahadeolal Ranodia vs The Administrator General of West Bengal, ; , referred to. In the instant case, on the construction of this section it is clear that section 417 which provides for an appeal in a case of acquittal empowers the State Government to direct the public prosecutor in any case to present an appeal from an order of acquittal. This section does not appear to be consistent with any provision of the Act. The contrary view taken by the High court on the interpretation of this s is clearly unacceptable. Section 417 which provided for an Appeal in a ease of acquittal empowered by the same judgment, but if an appeal by persons jointly tried and convicted is competent, then on principle it is difficult to negative the maintainability or of a separate appeal by tho State against a common order acquitting some persons acquitted in a criminal case.

The appellant was a firm carrying on business in India and in the former Federated Malaya States and it was assessed under the Indian Income tax Act, 1918. The family which consisted of Meyyappa Chettiar and his two brothers carried on money lending business in British India and it had been assessed under section 25(3) of the 1922 Act. In the course of assessment for the year 1939 40 it was claimed by M that having regard to the severance of joint family status, the income from April 13, 1938 to June 2, 1938 was not liable to be taxed by reason of the provisions of section 25 (3). The Income tax Officer rejected the contention and rejected the claim. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner also held that the assessee was entitled to relief under section 26(3), but rejected the contentions of the assessee. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the income derived by the assessee from the foreign business was in relation to a business and therefore the assessment of the income must be treated as an assessment of his business, and that the interest on securities formed part of the assesee 's business income for the purpose of the exemption from tax under section 24(3). HELD: (i) The High Court was in error in holding that the foreign income of the foreign firm was not charged under the provisions Of the 1918 Act. [908 D] (ii) The assessee received the entire profits of the Indian business in the British India, and the entire income was assessed to income tax in the hands of the assesses under the 1918 act. [09 E F] Commissioner of Income tax, Madras vs section V.R.M Palaniappa Chettiar and Others, , followed. (iii) The exemption under section25(3)(a) is general. It is not correct to say that because tax was payable by the assesse on the profits rec eived from a business in a foreign territory such assessment is an assessment for computation of the total income. [ 909 A B] Commissioner Of Income tax Madras vs Section V. R.M. Palanippa Chettiar, , applied. (iv) The words "on which" in section 25 of the Act cannot be interpreted as meaning "with reference to which" and that in order to claim and avail the benefit under section 5(4), the tax clearly should be charged on the business as such under the 1922 act. In other words, the tax under the 1920 Act was charged upon the assessee in respect of his activity styled foreign business and in relation thereto it must therefore be taken upon the facts found by the appellate Tribunal in this case that the Indian income received by the joint family could not have been charged under section 3 Of the 1922 Income tax.

The respondent entered into a contract with the Public Works Department of the Government of Gujarat on September 6, 1965 for manufacture and supply of kiln burnt bricks to the said department. The Deputy Commissioner of Sales Tax held that the supplies of bricks were sales. At the instance of the assessee, the Tribunal referred the following question of law to the High Court: "Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case the transaction envisaged by the contract entered into by the applicant with the public Works Department for the manufacture and sale of kiln burning bricks to a department and the supply of bricks to it in terms of their running Bill No. XI dated 28th October 1967 is a sale or a works contract ? The High Court answered the question in favour of the respondent holding that the transaction was a works Contract. In coming to this conclusion, the High court held as follows: (1) The contract in this case is a contract of sale and not a works contracts; (2) The question will depend upon the intention of the parties executing the contract; (3) Whether a particular transaction is a 'a works contract ' depends upon the true construction of all the terms and conditions of the document when there is one. The question would depend on the intention to execute the contract. As it has been observed in Chandra Bhan Gosain vs The State of orissa and others, , this Court observed as follows in State of Gujarat vs Variety Body Builders (I) which we have just delivered there is no standard formula by which one can distinguish a contract for sale from contract for work and labour; and (4) The High court was wrong in holding to the contrary. [162 G H] Chandra Bhan Bas Gosain, ; , followed.

The petitioner, an assessee under the Income tax Act and Wealth Tax Act during the assessment year 1976 77 was assessed to income tax for the assessment years 1976 77 and 1977 78. The petitioner challenged the validity of the Proclamation of Emergency issued by the President of India on 26th June 1975 in exercise of his powers conferred by sub clause (a) of clause (2) of Article 352 of the Constitution on the ground that it had ceased to be in operation on 4th February, 1972 and therefore all Acts passed by the House of the People during the extended period including the Finance Act 1976 were ultra vires the Constitution. The contentions raised before this Court were: (i) The Proclamation of emergency issued by President of the India was either ultra vires or had ceased not to be effective in operation at the expiration of two months from the date on which each of them was issued as the resolutions of the Houses of Parliament approving each of the two Proclamations of Emergency; and (ii) The proclamation of Emergency dated 3rd December, 1971 had ceased in operation by 26th August 1975 because the resolutions passed by both Houses of the Parliament approving the two Proclamation of Proclimations of emergency as required by clause (1) of article 352 were in force and therefore Parliament was entitled to extend the period of the House for a period not exceeding one year at a time. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1(i) It is seen that any public notification issued under Article 364(1) has to be published in the official Gazette as provided by Article 366(19) of the constitution. The provisions of Article 118(1), (2), (3) and (4) show that the procedure prescribed for the purpose of passing the law or the resolutions in the Houses is not followed. [436C D] 2(i). The two Pro visions of Emergency were kept in force by virtue of the resolutions dated 26th March, 1977 passed by Parliament until they were duly revoked by the two Houses of parliament. Since the two proclamions of Emergency had been approved by the resolutions which were issued by both the Houses, it amounts to proof of the said resolutions. [441E F] 2.(i). It is not correct to say that the two provisions of article 118(2), and (3), show that they are mandatory. The two provisions show that there is a distinction between the two clauses in the two parts. The first clause deals with the second clause deals only with the third clause relating to the third one relating to third clause which deals with third clause. Clause (5) deals with three clauses relating to fourth clause relating, namely, clause (6), clause (7), clause 8 and clause 9. Clause 9 deals with two clauses relating, viz., clause (8), clause 9 and clause 10.

The appellant filed an application in the District Court for a declaration that the said premises were private property and for an order setting aside the said decision. The application was subsequently converted into a suit by an order of the High Court. He was therefore entitled to contend at the time of the leave application that the property in dispute was of the value of not less than Rs. 20,000/ . Held, that the appellant 's case was accepted by the Trial Court but was rejected by the High court and the High Courts were right in holding that the properties in question constituted a temple. The High Court was therefore wrong in proceeding on the assumption. The subject matter of the dispute had to be ascertained with reference to the claim made by the plaintiff in his plaint and since according to the plaint, the property was the private property of the said family capable of alienation, the High 'Court ought to have valued the property accordingly though according to it the respondents the property belonged to the Thoguluva Thirumalayyan, and therefore the property could not be said to be a temple as defined by Madras Act 19 of 1951. The appellant 'S case was that in execution of the decree in Suit No. 650 of 1882 passed against the said Kuppaiyan the property had been sold by public auction and purchased by Thogallappa Thirumalaya Thirumalayanayyan. The case of the respondents was accepted and the trial court held that the premises constituted a Temple within the meaning of Madras Act 1 of 1927.

The appellant, a subordinate staff of the respondent company, was employed as clerks and 131 belonged to the subordinate staff. The respondents claimed that they should be given cash allowance in lieu of the tiffin arrangements at present made by the appellant. The Tribunal granted the first claim and directed that the clerical staff should be paid As. /8/ per day and the subordinate Staff as also in regard to the lowest grade clerks, the Tribunal thought it unnecessary to make any such direction. That is how the latter claim has been partially allowed. It was against this award that the appellant came to this Court by special leave. Held, that the question posed by the respondents ' demand must be considered. The fact that the re employed persons have made an affidavit supporting the practice adopted by the appel lant can have no material bearing in dealing with the point; in the very nature of things, the said re employed person are bound to support the appellant and the result is, the appeal fails and is dismissed with costs. Chandi Charan Banerjee vs The State of West Bengal, ; , referred to. In the instant case, the question raised by the respond ents was not one of fact but was one of law and it was not obligatory on the part of the appellant to make a provision for the taqin of its employees. Chandili Charan Banerjee 's case, [1959] S.C.R. 869, referred to and distinguished. The facts that the respondents felt that the policy adopted by them in re employing the retired personnel was not based solely on humanitarian grounds, were irrelevant and they could not be blamed on that account; but there were some other factors in relation to this problem of re employment which cannot be ignored. Chandhi Charan Banerjee & Co. vs The Union of India, [1960] 1 S.R .

The respondent, an employee of the East India Railway and was a subscriber to the State Railway Provident Fund. He applied for and obtained an order for attachment of the money lying with the Reserve Bank. The cheques were attached and under orders of the executing court the cheques were encashed and the amount realised was deposited in the executing Court. The Union of India applied to the High Court of Calcutta in revision. The High Court confirmed the order passed by the executing judge. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The money in the hands of the Reserve bank had ceased to be provident fund money and was liable to be attached. It was somewhat faintly suggested that the Union of india had no interest in maintaining an application for removal of attachment. But the Union had no right in maintaining the application for removing of attachment, but the Union was a trustee for the subscriber of the amount. When the amount lying with Reserve Bank as the agent of the Railway Administration was attached the Union has clearly an interest to maintain the application. [32 D] (ii) The High court was in error in holding that the money in question had ceased lo be provident Fund money and it was liable for attachment under the law and that the attachment was "illegal and without jurisdiction". [33 F G] (iii) The Union Government was a Trustee for the subscribers of the fund. When, the amount remained under the control of the railway Administration as the Provident Fund money, it was exempt from attachment. Clause (b) of r. 1413(1), which provides that a compulsory deposit in any Government or Railway Provident fund shall not in any way be capable of being assigned or charged and shall not be liable to attachment under any decree or order of any Civil, Revenue or Criminal Court in respect of any debt or liability incurred by the subscriber or depositor, and neither the Official Assignee nor any receiver appointed under the Provincial Insolvency Act, 1920, shall be entitled to, or have any claim on any such compulsory deposit.

The appellant, a workman of the respondent company, was dismissed from service by an order dated September 2, 1970. The appellant challenged the said order before the Labour Court under section 33(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 on the ground that it was not bona fide and that the action being a simple termination without a sting, the process and consequence of a disciplinary action were not attracted. The Labour Court held that the punishment was illegal and that even in a case like the present the requirement of bona fides was essential and if the termination of service was a colourable exercise of the power or as a result of victimisation or unfair labour practice, the industrial tribunal would have the jurisdiction to intervene and set aside such termination. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that even where a management had the power to terminate the services of its employee without reasons but with notice pay only, the colourable exercise Of that power invalidated it, and the (1)[1972] 3 section C. R. 822, followed. Held:(i) The Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1970 was not ultra vires the provisions of the Act. It was a case where the management sought to make out, that his denial of leaking out office secrets was an after thought pleaded only in the rejoinder and therefore liable to be discredited. (ii) Even if the loss of confidence was exalted as a ground but the special circumstances of the case exonerated bad faith in discharge simpliciter. The Management had not dis closed the grounds oil which this suspicion arose in 1968. Further after 1968, the appellant was given two extra increments in addition to his normal increments, as stated earlier, in appreciation of his hard work. It could not be argued that the loss was ex facie by way of dismissal. (iii) Even assuming that the management wanted to cover up the inability to establish by an enquiry, illegitimately but ingeniously passes an innocent looking order of termination simpliciter, such action is bad and is liable to he set aside. (iv) The loss of interest was not a disguise or cloak for dismissing the employee and the ground given that he was a cantankerous person undesirable to be retained was good. The management had not discharged the grounds on which this inference could be drawn. (v) Even in a ease like the instant, the requirement that the employer should disclose to the Court the grounds of his impugned action so that the same may be tested judicially. In the present case, this has not been done. There is only the ipse dixit of the employer that he had been suspecting since 1968 that the appellant 's employee was divulging secrets relating to his business.

The petitioners, who were the State of U.P., and the Lions Club of Pottery Town, filed a writ petition in this Court alleging that the victims of this medical mishap be given expert rehabilitatory treatment and appro priate compensation; that the Government did conduct a thorough investigation as to the conditions which rendered a medical misadventure of such a scale possible and evolve proper guide lines which will prevent recurrence of such tragedies; and that appropriate legal action be instituted against them. The petitioners also alleged that the State would act in a manner prejudicial to the interests of the victims, and that the appropriate legal provi sions be instituted for the tragedy was concerned, it was submitted on behalf of the respondents that persuant to the results of the inquiries conducted by the Deputy Director (Eye Treatment) and the Sub Divisional Magistrate, appropriate follow up action is contemplated by the Government against persons concerned and that, indeed, a criminal case has been regis tered against Dr. R.M. Sahay and his team and also against officers of the Government who, according to allegations committed serious breaches of duty in sanctioning permission for the conduct of the 'eye camp ' without ensuring a strict compliance with the conditions prescribed in the guidelines prescribed by the government in that behalf and in not effectively dis charging the duties enjoined upon them to over see the satisfactory and safe functioning of the camp. Disposing of the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The Revised guidelines dated 9.2.1988, with the suggested modifications, can be held to be satisfactory. [249F] 2.1 In a case where the plaintiff developed meningitis as a result of some infection in the apparatus used in the operation it was held that there must have been some negli gence by the hospital staff for which the hospital authority was responsible. The State Government, in the wake of reports of mishaps in 'Eye Camps ' constituted a Committee under the Chairmanship of the Union Health Minister with six State Health Ministers and four experts as members to re examine and update the existing guidelines or evolve fresh ones. As a result, of the deliberations of the said Committee and pursuant to its recommendations, the guidelines for conduct of eye camps earlier issued have been updated and revised. 1988, is filed before the Court. The Indian Medical Council, after its impleadment in these proceedings also constituted a sub committee with Dr. A.S. Mittal and the recommendation of the Sub Committee of the Indian Medical council may be consid ered by the Union Government for incorporation in their Revised Guidelines dated 9th February, 1988. [250F H] 2:2 The guidelines issued by the Central Government on 9.3.1988 arrived at after a careful study of all aspects of the problem are quite comprehensive. However, it venture to suggest that some points made in the Report and Recommendation of the expert sub committee of the U. P. State Government may be considered by the union Government for incorporated in their revised guidelines dated September 9, 1988, [250G H] 3:3 The prescriptions re ferred to by the said sub committee are these: "Staff: The operations in the camp should only be performed by qualified, experienced Oph thalmic Surgeons registered with Medical Council of India or any State Medical Council.

The petitioner, a registered society under the Societies Registration Act, 1951, was elected as a member of the Assam Rashtrabhasha Prachar Samiti. The Society had its own constitution known as Bidhan which is also regis tered with the Registrar of Societies Assam at Gauhati. It was established in Madras City in the name of Dakshin Bharat Hindi Prachar Samchar Samiti with its head office at Gauhati, and it was registered under the Indian Registration Act. In 1948, the petitioner No. 1, a Registered Society, had a membership of about 164 22,000 persons scattered all over the States and Union Territories of North Eastern part of India. The Samiti has district committees under its control. The Board also consists of two affiliated bodies namely Manipur Hindi Pra charchar Sabha, Imphal and the Asom Rashtraba Prachar Parishad. This Samiti has a sole constitution known by which the petitioner Society had a sole consti tution known as the Assam Munici pal Samitia Samiti, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Manipur Tripura and Arunachal Pradesh as provided in Article 351 of the Constitution of India, and also production and publica tion of prescribed text books in Hindi for Primary Schools, High School, Higher Secondary schools and the Colleges upto the degree standard. The petitioner No 1, who is a registered Society under the with its registered office at Hedayatpur, Gauhati, challenged the action taken by the respondent State Government under the Asam Rashtra bhasha Samitian Samiti (Taking over of Management and Control) Act, 1984 on the ground that it was an Act enacted by the Legislative Assembly of Assam and received the assent of the Governor of Assam. The petition was contested by the petitioner contending that as this amendment was passed from this date the Chief Minister ceased to be the Ex officio President and since then according to the petitioner he had nothing to do with the Samiti or its ideals and who were not even the members of the Samiti have been nominated as the members under the Bidhan (constitution of the Society) and they are supposed to run the affairs of the society whereas those who have contributed their heart and soul for the ideals of the Samiti ay Sabha. The respondent State filed an affidavit in which it was stated that the Board from the very inception had acquired assets and properties and the assets and the properties at the time of filing of the petition were stated to be: 1. Buildings Rs.70,64,000.00 2. Printing Press with Machines Rs.15,00,000; 3. Furniture Fixture Rs.3,00,,000. 10.00. 5. Typewriting Schools including Rs. 60,000 and furnitures 7. Iron Safe Rs. 30,00000.00 8. Bank deposits Rs. 3,43,000 10.50.00 11.

The appellants, who were the sons of one Ram Kishori Lal, died during pen. The respondents filed a suit for declaration that a deed of gift dated March 10, 1940, executed by Sumitra Devi in favour of her daughter Kamala Devi was void and inoperative beyond the lifetime of Sumitra Devi and was not binding on them. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court affirmed the decree of the trial court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the proper finding should have been that Sumitra Devi made a "sankalpa" of the gift of four houses at Asansol, which was accepted by Nand Lal on behalf of his minor daughter in law and that such a gift was again confirmed at the Gowna ceremony. Held: (i) The High Court was right in holding that there was antenuptial agreement by Sumitra ' that she would give four houses to the respondents as her share on partition. (ii) The evidence showed that Sumitra had made a written "samalpa " of the gifts of the four houses in question at Asisol and that it was accepted on behalf by his minor son in law, and that the gift was later confirmed at Gownta ceremony. (iii) The finding of the final court of fact as correct, the gift being of a reasonable portion of the estate of the deceased husband 's daughter was binding on the reversioners. (iv) The findings of the courts below were based on no evidence and they could not be relied upon by the High Courts in dealing with oral evidence as to the verbal gift made at the time of the marriage.

The appellant, who was the only candidate in the election to the Baghapurana Constituency (District Faridkot) filed an election petition against the respondent alleging that he was guilty of committing corrupt practices, detailed in the petition. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the allegations of corrupt practices indulged in by the respondent have been clearly proved and that the allegation of corrupt practice indulged in had been clearly established.
