Allowing the appeal to this Court, ^ HELD: 1.1 In view of the very narrow margin of votes (123) between Tej Singh and Avtar Singh, a strong presumption and possibility that the votes polled in favour of section Tej Singh will be deemed to have been cast in his favour, the appellant has proved beyond reasonable doubt that Tej Singh had actually paid for the posters which were printed at his instance and Rup Lal was not collected with the printing of the posters. [419D E] 2.1 The High court was right in holding that Tej singh had actually received the posters and circulated them to the voters so as to make them believe that one of the candidates, viz., Ruplal, had withdrawn and any vote given to him would be considered as a vote given for Ruplar. [416E F] 2:2 In view Of the very limited margin of vote (123), between Tej singh and Avtar singh, a great presumption and probability that the voters polled in his favor would have gone to the appellant (Avtar Singh) and, therefore, the result of the election would have been materially altered.

The appellant, a Forest Minister in the Council of Ministers headed by Shri Bhajan Lal, was personally keen on giving him an office of profit. In order to achieve this objective, he got an Ordinance promulgated by the Governor. The Ordinance provided that the constitution of a Forest Development Board would be constituted with a view to appointing the said Devinder Sharma as its Chairman. It was further alleged that after having failed to threaten and demoralise the appellant through indirect means the respondent, Bhajan Lal called him to his official residence on July 26, 1983 through the Acting Chief Conservator of Forests and criminally intimidated him to withdraw the writ petition. Thereafter, the appellant filed an application for contempt against the respondent in the High Court complaining of interference by the respondent with the due course of judicial proceedings. The application was admitted and a rule nisi was issued upon the respondent. The respondent appeared in the rule and opposed the same by filing an affidavit denying all the allegations made against him by the appellant. The Single Judge of the High court took the view that there were circumstances to indicate that it was not a fit case in which the Court should exercise its jurisdiction under the Act. In appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 An appeal will lie under section 19(1) of the Act only when the High 'Court makes an order or decision in exercise of its jurisdiction to punish for contempt.

The respondents, who were the daughter and grand sons of the original plaintiff, filed a suit against the present defendants for possession on the ground that the lease had determined by forfeiture for non payment of rent. The trial court dismissed the suit but granted relief against forfeiture. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the amendment made in 1929 to section 111(g) of the Act embodies a principle of justice, equity and good conscience and notwithstanding section 2 of the , that principle was applicable in this case and there could be no forfeiture unless notice in writing to the lessee of his intention to determine the lease by the lessor bad been given. Held, that the rule laid down in section 111 (g) is not a rule of law but a statutory recognition of a principle which equity and justice are not such a variable commodity, that they change and stand altered on a particular date on the mandate of the legislature and that to leases made between 1882 and 1930 the principle of equity applicable is the one contained in sub section (g), as it stood before 1929. The law in India and England on this subject is not the same and it cannot be said that this sub section enacts or enunciates any general principle of Equity. F] Foa vs Beari, A.I.R. 1929 Bom. 1021, referred to. Held further, that when the Act was so express to provide a wide discretion, meaning no doubt, to prevent one man from forfeiting what in fair dealing belongs to some one else by taking advantage of a breach from which he is not obsessed and irreparably damaged, it is not advisable to lay down any rigid rules for guiding that discretion. The rule laid by the Master of Rolls in the present case is not applicable to leases executed prior to 1929 or even prior to the coming into force of the . In view of this the High Court was right in holding that the provisions of section 111 of the Transfer of Property Act were not applicable and the suit must fail.

The appellant, a retired Judge of the M.P. High Court, was dismissed from service by the Management on the ground that while fomenting the strike without giving 14 days ' prior notice as also the acts on the part of the respondents amounted to serious mis conduct under the certified Standing Orders applicable to the quarries. The appellant challenged the award in a writ petition before the High Court which confirmed the dismissal order and dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended that the learned Arbitrator had misconstrued the Standing Order No. 17 and that no second opportunity was required to be given to the respondents and that in the alternative the interference with the punishment of dismissal in respect of the appellant was erroneous while another writ petition (Misc. Petition No. 129 of 1970) was filed by the respondents against the punishments that were awarded to each one of them, the High court by its judgment dated 27th July 1972 confirmed the award of the Arbitrator by dismissing both the writ petitions. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The real question that arises in these appeals is, does the certified standing order No.17 provides for second opportunity being given to a workman to show cause against the proposed punishment of dismiss ment after he has been found guilty or the opportunity spoken of is the opportunity to meet the charges in the domestic inquiry ? In this connection it will be pertinent to mention that the concerned S.O. was framed and came into force on March 1, 1946 and was duly certified on October 16, 1954 under the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946 i.e. prior to the enunciation of the law by Courts regarding observance of the principles of natural justice such as issuance of a charge sheet, holding of an inquiry, opportunity to lead evidence etc. and it is well known that after the pronouncement of these principles it merely contains a bald provision for `giving the accused an opportunity to offer any explanation '. In other words, different stages in domestic enquiry were never in the contemplation of the framers of the S.0. That being the position it would be difficult to attribute any intention to the framers thereof to provide for a second opportunity to be offered to the delinquent of showing cause against tho proposed punishment. The latter part of para 3 merely casts a unilateral obligation on concerned authority or the officer to give due consideration to the gravity of the misconduct and the previous record of the delinquent in awarding the maximum punishment. It is true that the Arbitrator has taken the view that the opportunity spoke of by para 3 does not refer to the opportunity which to meet charges but refers to the further opportunity being afforded to the accused to show his explanation. [371C D] 2. The question obviously depends upon the proper construction to be placed on said S.S.O No. 16. It may be stated that the certified S. O. 16 enlists several acts or omissions that constitute 'mis conduct ' and striking work either singly or with other workers without giving 15 days previous notice, inciting whilst on the premises and worker to strike work and indulging in a Gherao, which would amount to an `act subversive of discipline or efficiency ' are obviously included therein. [372E F] 3.

The appellant, who was the owner of certain lands in Malabar to which the provisions of the Madras Preserva tion or Private Forests Act 1949 were applicable on the 11th day of April, 1955 or which was unsurveyed on that date. The High Court took the view that the benefit of section 7D would apply only to persons whose occupa tion of the private forests or unsurv erable lands had a lawful origin and not to persons in unlawful occupation based on trespass or forcible and unlawful entry. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. For a proper understanding of the scope and intendment of section7D, it is necessary to examine the setting and the context in which the said section occurs in the Act. This will require a conjoint study of the provisions con tained in section 7A to 7C and Sections 8 and 9 of the Act which immediately precede and succeed Section 7D. Those sections are in the following terms: "7A. Certain persons occupying land for not less than ten years to be deemed tenants notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in any law, or in any contract, custom or usage, or In any judgment, decree or order of court, any person who is in occupation of the land of another at the commencement of the Kerala Land Reforms (Amendment) Act 1969, shall be deemed to be a tenant. " 114 On a careful scrutiny of the aforesaid provisions, it becomes abundantly clear that the intention of the legisla ture was to grant protection only to those persons whose posses sion had a valid origin in the sense that they had either bona fide believed the lands to be Government 's lands of which they could later seek assignment or had taken the lands on lease from persons whom they bona fide believing to be competent to grant such leases or had come into possession with the intention o attorning to the lawful owners or on the basis of arrangements like varam etc. which were only in the nature of licences and fell short of a leasehold right. It was not within the contemplation of the Legisla tion to confer the benefit Of protection on persons who had wilfully trespassed upon lands belonging to others and whose occupation was unlawful in its origin. The expression "in occupation" occurring in section 2D must be construed as meaning "in lawful occupation". [114F H] 2. For proper understanding, of the amplitude and intendment underlying section 7 D, it would be necessary to examining the setting, and the background in which it occurs in this Act. [114G H] 3. The intention of ture is to grant relief only to person whose posssion had an lawful origin in his sense that he had either mala fide believed them to be government 's land of which he could later obtain assignment or has taken the land on lease by persons who have wilfully trespass ed upon lands belong ing to others. [115A] 4. The appellant was not entitled to the protection of section 2(c) of the Land Reforms Act, 1964. [116B] 5. The question whether an amount of Rs.50,000 should be deposited by the respondents in the trial court within a period of three months from today, whereupon the appellant will be at liberty to withdraw the said amount from Court without furnishing any security. Subject to the aforesaid observation and direction, the appeal and the Special Leave Petitions are dismissed.

The appellant was found in possession of the goods on 21 4 1967. He was also found to contain cigarette lighters of "Imco Triplex Junior". The five boxes containing flints had the words "Dubai" and "Made in Austria". Each of the six boxes were tightly packed with a locked connecting door fixed in the passage to the sub divided part. This portion was again sub divided with a lock and the keys produced by the appellant. Subsequently, the seized articles were made over to the Inspector of Central Excise and Customs, Marine and Prevention Division, Bombay on 24 4 1967 under section 110 of the . The value of 7200 cigarette was stated as Rs. 14,400/ and of 250 tins of flints as Rs 15,000/ on which customs duty of Rs. 15,840/ and Rs 10,500/ respectively was alleged to be payable. In the complaint filed on 30 5 1968 by the Assistant Collector of Central excise, Marine & Prevention Division Bombay it was alleged that the cigarettelighters and flints were imported into India without an import licence and in contravention of provisions of Government of India, Ministry of Commerce & Industry, Import Control order No. 17/55 dated 7 12 1955 issued under section 3(2) of the Imports & Export (Control) Act, 1947 which was to be deemed to be an order passed under section 11 of the Act. The appellant denied having been in possession and of the offending goods although he had admitted the production of keys from his possession He alleged that he had kept the goods there. The Assistant Collector held that the cigarettes lighters and Flints were not imported into the country without payment of duty. On appeal, the High Court convicted him under section 135(1)(ii) of 'the Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) even if the goods with which we are concerned here were not seized under the Act as provided by section 111 of the , it is contended on his behalf that the presumption contained in section 123 of the Bombay Act, corresponding to section 128(A) of . Or any other provision of law would place the onus of proving innocent possession of these goods upon the appellant; (ii) even assuming that the appellant was deemed to have been in Possession with full knowledge of what the goods actually were, the Court could not go further and assume them to be smuggled or imported into it from another country of their assumed origin after a time when the restrictions on their import had been imposed. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i). The appellant 's conduct, including his untruthful denial of his possession, indicated consciousness of their smuggled character or means rea. In any case, there was some evidence to enable the Courts to come to the conclusion that the goods must have been known to the appellant to be imported even if he was not a party to a fraudulent evasion of duty; and (iii) even though the appellant is deemed to he in possession with full know knowledge of the incriminating nature of their contents. Otherwise, why should he, at first, have refused to produce the key he had ? [541 D] Gian Chand & ors. vs State of Punjab ; , referred to. (ii). The admissibility and sufficiency of (1) [1962] Supp. 1 S.C.R.

The appellants filed a preliminary objection to the effect that the suit was not maintainable by reason of section 4(2) of the Rewa State Companies Act, 1935. The trial court held that the other members of the Association were not entitled to participate in the profits made on the sale of 284 bales of the Gwalior cloth and that as Nagar Mal had rendered accounts with regard to all other transactions, the suit for accounts must fail. Held, that the preliminary objection must succeed. It was a claim by some members of an illegal association against another member on the footing that the association should be treated as legal in order to give rise to a liability to render accounts in respect of the transac tions of the association. Such a claim is clearly negatived by section 4 (2) Of the Indian Companies Act and not by any greater favour to one party to an illegal transaction than to his companions, if proceedings are instituted by one member of an unlawful partnership against another in respect Of the partnership transactions, it is competent for A to require B to hand back the money if B has not already parted with it and the illegal purpose has not been carried out. The analogy does not really apply. For the reasons given above, the preliminary objections must succeed and must be upheld. Surajmull Nargoremull vs Triton Insurance Company Ltd., (1924) L.R. 52 I.A. 126, referred to. Surajmalull Narkoremull V. Tritton Insurance Co., Ltd., ([1951] S.C.R., 98), distinguished.

The respondents, who were accused in the two complaints, moved the High Court under section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure or quashing of the order taking cognizance against them. The High Court quashed the proceedings against the respondents on the ground that an investigation by the police was in progress in relation to the same offence and that as an investigation was in connection with the same offences the learned Magistrate would be required to stay the proceedings on the complaint and call for a report in the matter from the police; and that the learned Magis trate acted without jurisdiction in taking cognizance of the offence and ordering issue of process against the accused. The State filed appeals before this Court contending that the High Courts were wrong in quashing the proceedings. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Section 210(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code is much wider section 56 of the . [465G] 1.2 In order that the prohibition is attracted the same act must constitute an offence under more than one Act. In other words, the test is that taking the allegations and the complaint as they are without adding or subtracting anything, if no offence is made out then the High court will be justified in quashing proceedings in exercise of its powers under section482 of the present Code. [465C] 1:3 The expression "any act or omission which constitutes any offence under this Act" in section 56 merely imports the idea tat the same acts or omission might constitute an offences under another law and could be tried under such other law or laws also. [466D E] 1 :4 In the instant case, even if the jurisdictional police purported to register a case for an alleged offence against the Act, section 210(I) would not be attracted having regard to the position that cognizance of such an offence can only be taken on the complaints of the officer mentioned in that section.

The petitioner, who was a surety for a non bailable offence either as undertrial or as convict, who had appealed or sought special leave, applied to the Court under section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, for bail in his favour "to the satisfaction of the Chief Judicial Magistrate". The direction of this Court did not spell out the details of the bail and so the magistrate ordered that a surety hl a sum of Rs. 10,000/ be produced which, in actual impact, was a double denial of the Bail benefit. For one thing the miserable mason. the petitioner before us could not afford to procure that huge sum or manage a surety of sufficient prosperity. Affluents do not befriend indigents. For another, the magistrate made an odd order refusing to accept the suretyship of the petitioner 's brother because he and his assets were in another district. If mason and millionaire were treated alike, egregious inegality is an increditability. Likewise geographic allergy at the judicial level makes mockery of equal protection of the laws within the territory of India. India is one and not a conglomeration of districts, untouchably apart. When this Court 's order for release was thus frustrated by magisterial intransigence the prisoner moved this Court again to modify the original order "to that extent that petitioner be released on furnishing surety to the tune of Rs 2,000 or on executing a personal bond or pass any other order or direction as this Hon 'ble Court may deem fit and proper". From this factual matrix three legal issues arise (1) Can the court under the Code enlarge, on his own bond without sureties, a person undergoing incarceration for a Non bailable offence neither as undertrial nor convict who has appealed or seeking special leave ? (2) If the Court decides to grant bail with sureties, what criteria should guide it in quantifying the amount of bail and (3) Is it within the power of the court to reject a surety because he or his estate is situate in a different district or State ? This formulation turns the focus on an aspect of liberty bearing on bail jurisprudence. The victims when suretyship is insisted on or heavy sums are demanded by way of bail or local bailors alone are presona grata, may well be the weaker segments of society like the proletariat, the linguistic and other minorities and distant denizens from the far corners or our country with its vast diversity. In fact the grant of bail can be stultified or made unconsciously inconvenient and expensive if the court is powerless to dispense with surety or to receive an Indian bailor across the district borders as good or the sum is so excessive that to procure a wealthy surety may be both exasperating and expensive. The problem is plainly one of the human rights, especially freedom vis a vis the lowly. This poignant import of the problem persuaded the Chamber Judge to invite the Supreme Court Bar Association and the Citizens for Democracy to assist the Court in decoding the Code and its provisions regarding bail. The Kerala State Bar Federation was permitted to intervene and counsel for the parties also made submissions. Disposing of the petition, HELD: 1.1 The law in its majestic equality, forbids the rich as well as poor to sleep under bridges, to beg in the streets and to steal bread, lampooned Anatole France. The reality of this caricature of equal justice under the law, whereby the poor are priced out of their liberty in the market is the grievance of the petitioners. His criminal appeal pends in this Court and he has obtained an order for bail. He stays in jail for one reason only because he is poor.

The assessee, a newly established undertaking, had advanced Rs. 3,21,460 to another concern, the Bombay Fine Worsted Manufacturers ' Castle Mills and claimed under section 15C of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, exemption from tax in respect of 6% of the capital employed in the undertaking as a newlyestablished undertaking and sought to include in the computation of the Capital so employed Rs. 2,21.460 advanced to 'Castle '. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that there were two undertakings, one of which was an industrial undertaking conducted in the name of Eldee Velvet and Silk Mills called for the sake of brevity 'Eldee ' as a new concern and sought exemption from taxation in respect thereof. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected the assessee 's claim holding that the income from 'C 'astle" had not been computed and included in the assessment of the assessee. On appeal by the assessee, the Tribunal modified the assessment and directed in clusion of the amount advanced to the new concern in the calculation of capital invested for the purpose of 429 section 15 C. The High Court refused to require the Tribunal to state the case on the view that a question of law does not arise out of the order of the Tribunal. Held, that the refusal of the Income tax officer to state a case for the opinion of the High Court on the question of fact is not conclusive and the High court was in error in holding that a particular question of facts did not arise. The jurisdiction of the Appellate Assistant Commission under section 66(2) of the Act to require a Tribunal to refer it, if the Appellate Tribunal has refused to state its case on a question which of law arises out of an order of Tribunal is not decisive.

The Minister concerned, who heard the parties and made a speaking order on February 18, 1975 affirming the earlier seniority list. The writ petition was thereafter amended by a fresh petition. In the amended petition it was contended that the allegations made in the amended writ petition do not disclose any personal animus on the part of the Minister concerned and as such the High Court was in error in directing that the Minister be impleaded as a party. Allowing the appeal, HELD: The direction for impleading of the Secretary as a Party was given by the High court with a view to apprise the Minister of the allegations contained in the petition and thus to afford him an opportunity of controverting those allegations, if he so deemed proper. Taking the totality of the facts and circumstances of the case, it is not possible to interfere with the order of the High Courts adding the Minister as a respondent to the writ petition. [97 H] The direction of the high Court in so far as it directed that the Secretary be impleaded was set aside. [98 C D] In the instant case, the High COurt was in its opinion in error. It is essentially for the Minister alone concerned to decide in the light of the allegation made in a petition as to whether he should or should not file an affidavit. The other part of it order whereby the Minister con cerned was directed to file his personal affidavit is set aside and the appeal shall stand disposed of accordingly. [99 D E] In view of the fact that the High Curt came to the conclusion that the Government was a necessary or proper party, this Court should not interfere in the matter.

The respondent was a tenant of the appellant. An application was made by the Cantonment Executive Officer, Ambala, for realisation of a sum of Rs. 64950 from the respondent under section 259 of the Act on the ground that the amount was due as arrears of rent on the basis of a lease in favour of the respondent. The Magistrate held that he had jurisdiction and issued warrants for attachment of the movable property of the Respondent on June 13, 1961. Thereupon the respondent went in revision to the Sessions Judge contending that the magistrate had no jurisdiction to realise the arrears of rents due under a lease 343 under section 260 of the . The Sessions Judge accepted the view of the Magistrate and held that rent under a leases could not be recovered under section 258 of the , and made a reference to the High Court under section 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The High Court, on appeal by special leave, took the view that rent was not claimable by the Board under the Act or the Rules but only under the lease in respect of the leased property. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the Magistrate acting under section259 of the Cantonment Act acts as a persona designata and therefore his order is not revisable under sections 435/439 of the Criminal Procedure Code; (2) the words "rent on land and buildings" which appear between the words 'any tax ' and 'any other money ' occurring in section 259 must be claimable under the , as it stood after amendment by Act II of 1954. HELD: (i) The provisions of section 259 cannot be utilised for realisation Of arrears of Rent on land or buildings only if such rent is recoverable by a Board or a Military Estates Officer under the Punjab Municipal Act, 1911. [344 C] (ii) Section 259 provides that in the event of non compliance with the terms of any notice, order or requisition issued to any person under this Act, or any rule or bye law made thereunder requiring such person to execute any work or to do any act, it shall be lawful for the Board, whether or not the person in default is liable to punishment for such default or has been prosecuted or sentenced to any punishment therefor after giving notice in writing to such person, to take such action or such steps as may be necessary for the completion of the act or work required to be done or executed by him. [345 D] (iii) The section does not bar the right of the Board as an owner or holder of land and building to take action for recovery of rent thereof by suit under the general law of the land. Further, by providing for recovery by suit or by application rent of the kind it makes no claimable or recoverable by either of the two authorities specified therein. [346 E] (iv) The words " rents on land" and buildings ' in section 260 must be claimed as a restricted meaning that word itself would be rendered otiose because there is no provision whatsoever in the Act which expressly made rent claimable nor recoverable by both the authorities specified in the section. [347 G] (v) Section 258 does not debar the Board from recovering rent of its land and premises on lease. In the present case, the Magistrate had the power to recover rent due to the appellant in the manner provided for in the s. The section did not bar a right of appeal under the special law of rent of their land and property by suit for such rents are entirely outside the section and the right to recover it is ultimately traceable to the Act inasmuch as this liability has arisen by reason of the exercise of a power exercised or performance of duty by the board under express provisions of the statute and the Rules.

The appellant who was employed as a section salesman in the respondent company, was terminated from service on 12th July 1973 on the ground that he was on an unauthorised absence since 13th January, 1973 and shall be deemed to have left the company 's service of his own account. The Labour Court held that the appel lant was not a "workman" and that, therefore, the reference was incompetent. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that (i) the definition of "workman ' under the Industrial Disputes Act as it stood in the year 1973 when the appellant 's services were terminated; (ii) the Labour Court had given findings in favour of the appe lant on the question whether the termination itself was illegal. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The finding of the Tribunal that the appellant was not an "workman", is correct and it is borne out by the document produced before the Labour court. [475C D] Burmah Shell Oil Storage and Distribution Company vs Burmah South Management and Staff; , ; D.S. Nagraj vs Labour Officer, Kamal & Ors., 1973 F.J. (42) P. 440, J.M. Dechane Distributor vs State 476 of Kerala and others, [1974 11 LLJ 9, referred to. 2. The appellant was employed to do canvassing and promote sales for the company. The duties involve the suggesting of ways and means to improve the sales, a study of the type or status of the public to whom the product has to reach and a study in the market condition. He was also required to suggest about the publicity in markets and melas, advertise ments including the need for posters, holders and cinema slides. These duties do require the imaginative and creative mind which could not be termed as either manual, skilled, unskilled or clerical in nature. The supervising work of other local salesmen was part of his work considered by the Tribunal as only incidental to his main work of canvassing and promotion in the area of his operation. Such a person cannot be termed "workman". [476E F] Burmahs Shell Oil storage and Distribution Co. vs Burma Shram & Ors.

The respondent No. 1, a private limited company entered into a contract of lease with the Gwalior State Government for a period of one year in Samvat 1999. The lease was extended for a further period of ten years in Sampatram. When proceedings were initiated on 16.7.1952 to eject the Company, the Company filed Suit No. 14 of 1960 for declaration of title and perpetual injunction. The Trial Court held that the land admeasuring 495.05 acres was held by the Company in terms of the lease granted by the State and the Company was not a `pakka ' tenant and did not enjoy the status of a " Gair Maurusi" tenant. The High Court, however, held that since the Company had failed to pay the agreed rents and thus contravened the conditions of the leased land, proceedings were started against the Company and the company was not an occupancy tenant under section 185 of the Code as it had not become an ordinary tenant earlier in Madhya Bharat under Act No. 66 of 1950. The Company preferred an appeal before this Court by special leave. Allowing the Appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Section 182 of the M.P. Land Revenue Code, 1959 defines 'pakata tenant" as follows: "Section 54(vii). Pakka tenant means a tenant who has been or whose predecessor in interest had been lawfully recorded in respect of his holding as a `Ryot Pattedar ', `Mamuli Maurushi ' and `Pukhta Maur Through ' when this Act comes into force or who may in future be duly recognised as such by a competent authority. Explanation The term "Pukhtita Maulusi" included Istmurardar tenants, Malikana Haq holder tenants Malikana Khatoon holder tenants, Hakkiyat Mutafarrikat Sharahyana and Sakitul Mikiyat tenants". An `ordinary tenant ' is defined by Act No 66 of 1960 as a tenant other than a Pakkatenant and shall not include a sub tenant. [179E F] 1.2 The term `Pukukhta ' included Ist murusi tenant, Malikyanana Haq holders, Hakamyat Mutrikat Shah Sharahayana Muayana and Shakitul Kikiyat Tenants. An "ordinary tenant" is defined in section 2(i) of the Madhya Bharat Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, Samvat 2007 as a person holding land from the State Government under section 181, Section 181 of the code reads: "181. Government Lessees (1) Every person who holds land from a State Government or to whom a right to occupy land is granted by a State Govt or the Collector and who is not entitled to hold land as a Bhumiswami shall be called a Government lessee in respect thereof." The term 'Pukhukhta" included 1stmurusi tenants, Aliana Haqdar holder tenants. Malikana Shahava and Sakatul Mankiyat tenants. An `A 'ordinary tenant is defined under the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue & Tenancy Act Samvat 2008 as "a person holding the land from State Government". The term is defined to mean a tenant holding land other than the Pakka tenants and shall be not include any sub tenant." The position, therefore, was that in terms, of Act No 67 of 1950, the company is not a pakka tenant, as found by the High Court in the earlier judgment. [180F G] 1:3 In terms of section 2 (i) the Company is not an 'pukka tenant" and cannot be disputed that the original lease was obtained from the predecessor State and it continued to remain in possession of the land under the newly stipulated terms agreed upon between the Company & the Government to enable the company to remain In possession of land under newly stipulated term agreed upon.

The Orissa Land Reforms Act 16 of 1960 received the assent of the President on October 17, 1960. By section 1(3) of the principal Act it was provided that the Act shall come into force in whole or in part on such date or dates as the Government may from time to time by notification appoint and different dates may be appointed for different provisions of the Act. By a notification issued on September 25, 1968 certain provisions of Ch. IV were brought into force. By the said notification various provisions of that Act other than those contained in Ch. III and IV were inserted in the principal Acts. By Act 13 of 1965 amendments were made in the Principal Acts. The validity of these provisions was not challenged before the High Court on the ground that it is inconsistent with or takes away or abridges any of the fundamental rights conferred by Part III of the Constitution, It was urged on behalf of the landholders that when the principal enactment was enacted it became law in force and the ceiling limit prescribed thereby became effective even though Ch.IV was not extended by a notification under section 1 (3) Of the Act and since the subsequent legislation seeks to restrict the ceiling limits and vest the surplus land in the Government under section 45 as amended, there is compulsory acquisition of land which may be laid only if the law provides for payment to the landholder for extinction of his interest, the market value of that part of the surplus Land which is within the ceiling. HELD: (i) The right to compensation which is not less than the market price under any law providing for the acquisition by the State of any land in an estate in the personal cultivation of a person is guaranteed by the second proviso only where the land is within it the ceiling area applicable to him under anylaw for the time being in force. A law cannot be said to be in force unless it is brought into operation by legislative enactment, or by the exercise of authority by a delegate empowered to bring it into operation. The theory of a statute being "in operation in a constitutional sense" though it is not in fact in operation has, in our judgment, no validity. [901 D E] (ii) The law relating to the ceiling on the limit viz. IV of the Principal Act was never made operative by a Notification and was repealed by Act 15 of 1965. The ceiling limit under section 47 of the Amending Act was on that account inapplicable to the landholders who challenged the validity of section 45 of the amending Act. [991 F] (iii) The decision of this Court A. Thangal Kunju Mudaliar vs M. Venkatachalam Potti and Anr. ; , followed.

The appellants, who were the legal representatives of a Hindu widow, made an application to the District Judge for appointment of a guardian of the person and property of her minor son. The District judge held that there was severance of joint status by an informal partition between Mathurbhai and Kashibhai but he dismissed the suit on the ground that a suit of this character was not maintainable in law. On appeal, the High Court held that the widow had no interest left in her husband 's estate for more than the statutory period, and that the surrenderees could not claim possession so long as the widow was alive. Held, that the right to challenge it is no part of the widow 's property at all and, therefore, could not be surrendered to the reversioner. The fact that a surrender may and in the majority of cases does take the form of transfer, e.g., when the widow conveys the entire estate of her husband without consideration and not as a mere device to share the estate with the reversioners, in favour of the latter, is not an indefeasible life estate but an estate liable to be defeated on the happening of certain events which in Hindu law cause extinction of the widows 's estates. The true nature and effect of a surrender by a Hindu wife of her deceased husband ' 's properties have been thus summoned up and in our opinion quite correctly by a Division Bench of the Madras High Court (3) that an alienation, not for legal necessity, made by a stranger acquiring title against her interest created is to be deemed to be severed from the inheritance and if a surrender is made subsequently by the widow, the surrender must take it subject to such prior interest. Sulaiman J. in the Allahabad case laid down the law with perfect precision when he said that the effect of an alienation by a widow was not to spilt up the husband 'S estate into two parts or to give to the alienee an interest necessarily co extensive with her lifetime. The reversionary right to challenges it is not a part of a widow 'Susamu vs Kristamma, I.L.R. , referred to.

The respondent company, a company governed by the (U.P.) Cotton Mills Co. Ltd., was acquired by the Government of Uttar Pradesh under the U.P. Land Revenue Act, 1901. The Collector passed an order under section 128 A of the U .P. Act directing the holding of the meeting of the Company and that meeting shall be held in accordance with the order of the High Court notwithstanding any order of injunction etc. issued by any other court or authority in India or to be issued hereafter. The respondent company filed a writ petition in the High Courts challenging the validity of the said order on the ground that it had ceased to enjoy the privileges of a member of the Polytex Company by reason of the appointment of a Receiver by the Collector of Kanpur in respect of the ten lakhs shares in the Polyester Company held by the Cotton Mills Company. The writ petition was dismissed by the High court. In appeal to this Court, on behalf of the appellants it was contended that (i) the extraordinary general meeting had not been validly called since the Cotton Mill Company had ceased lo enjoy the privilege of a shareholder of a company by reason Of the appointment or of a receiver by the collector of Kanpur; and (ii) the Board of directors of a Company shall, on the requisition of such member or members of the company as is specified in sub section (4), forthwith proceed duty to call an extraordinary general meetings of the shareholders of the companies. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The attachment of the shares in question had not deprived the Cotton mills Company of its right to vote at the meeting or to issue a notice under section 169 of the Act. [867 D] 2. Section 187B of the Land Revenue (Development and Regulation) Act, 1951 provides that save as otherwise provided in section 153B but notwithstanding anything contained in any other provisions of the , or any other law or any contract, memorandum or articles, where any shares in a company are held in trust by any person, he shall within such time and in such form as may be prescribed make a declaration to the public trustee appointed under section 153A of the . [868 F] 3. The fact that 3,50,000 shares have been pledged in favour of the Government also would not make any difference Sections 172 to 178 A of deal with the contract of pledge. [889 G] 4. Section 184B provides that notwithstanding anything in any provision of the Indian Income tax Act or any law or anything, memorandum etc., where any share in a Company are held by a person as trustee, the rights and powers (including the right to trade, business and commerce) including the right of trade, commerce and intercourse with or under any other laws or any instrument, memorandum, or articles where any such shares in any company are holding in trust for any person. he shall, within such period and in the manner prescribed make an declaration to that effect. [879 G H] 5.

The petitioners were plaintiffs. They instituted a suit in a representative capacity under Order 1 Rule 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the Court of the Additional Senior Sub Judge, Barnala for a declaration that they were the owners in posses sion of the suit land along with some others, that the Gram Panchayat Mehal Kalan, Tehsil Barnala District Sangrur in the State of Punjab (the Panchayat) had no sort of right in the suit lands and that the suit property had been wrongly shown as belonging to the Panchayat by the entries made in the revenue records which were not binding on the plaintiffs and for an injunction restraining the Panchayat from interfering their possession. The Panchayat filed a revision petition before the High Court of Punjab and Haryana in Civil Revision Petition No. 571 of 1986, which came to be dismissed. In the special leave petition it was contended that since the question involved in the case was simply one of title to the suit Land and it was not necessary to decide whether the suitland was shamlat deh or not and whether the land had validly vested in the Panchayat or not being shamlatted, it had jurisdiction to try the suit. Dismissing the special Leave Petition, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court found that plaintiff in that case had only stated in the plaint that the land in question was 'Gali Sheh re aam ' or a throughfare belonging to a Gram Panchayat which was being used by the plaintiff as an approach to his house for about 30 years and had prayed for an injunc tion restraining the defendant from interfering with his right. The Gram Panchayat in question had not been impleaded as a defendant. [835E F] Bhagu & Ors., vs Ram Sarup and Ors., [1985] Punjab Law Journal Page 366, referred to. 2.1 In the instant case the suit had been filed against the Panchayat and the Panchayat had expressly claimed that the plaintiff had asserted his right was a street or not, and whether it belonged to the Gram Panchayats or not. Reliance was also placed by the counsel for the petitioners on a decision of the Punjab and Punjab High Court in Bhagu and Ors. vs Ram Swarup & Ors. [1985 ] Punjab Law journal Page 366 in which the suit has been held to be maintainable in a civil court even though the defendant had contended that the Land in question belonged to it as shamlat k deh. The question has to be decided by the Collector only under section 11 of the Act and not by the Civil Court. [863F G] 2.2 In the circumstances for the civil court to make a declaration in favour of the plaintiffs without deciding the question whether the property in question is shamlat mallat deh, it will not be possible in the circumstances of the civil suit to make such a declaration.

The Andhra Pradesh State Electricity Board is engaged in generation, distribution and supply of electricity in the State. The appellants belong to that category. Section 49 of the Act empowers the Board to notify the terms and conditions upon which it will supply electricity to a person. It is also empowered to frame uniform tariffs in that behalf. Sub section 2 specifies in fixing the uniform tariff, the Board shall have regard to all or any of the following factors namely: (a) the nature of the supply and the purposes for which it is required; b) the coordinated development of the electricity within the State in the most efficient and economical manner with particular reference to such development in areas not for the time being served or adequately served by the licensee; c) the simplification and standardisation of methods and rates of charges for such supplies; d) the extension and cheapening of supplies of electricity to sparsely developed areas. Sub sections 3, 4 and 5 empower the Board, on a written contract, has unilateral right to vary the term from time to time under clause 25.1.2 In all these cases, the appellants belong, to that class. Section 50 empowers the State Electricity Boards to notify terms and Conditions upon which they will supply electric electricity to consumers. The terms and condition were notified by the Board and the B.P.M.S. No. 690 dated 17th September, 1975. It was not necessary to refer in detail to the various terms and condi tions. However, what requires to be noticed is the terms & conditions oblige every consumer executing an agreement in the prescribed form, undertaking to abide by the term and conditions prevailing on the date of agreement and also agreed to be bound by the terms, and conditions as may be notified from time. It would be important to note under section 25, the board has unilateral rights to vary such terms from time and to time. The Board is clearly in the position of a trustee in respect of this money since the money is deposited by the consumers in trust with the Board. To secure the payment of consumption charges, the Electricity Board has to borrow and make payment of interest. This argument ignores the following important factors: i)This is not a security deposit but a consumption deposit; ii) It in the nature and character of an advance payment. iii)In the event of failure to pay, it could be proceeded against as seen from clause 28.1;2. Jagdamba Paper Industries case (supra), cannot be said to be a decision as to the rate of interest payable on fixed deposit because the nature & character of a security deposited is basically different from fixed deposit. The consumption deposit cannot be equated to the deposit in a bank and interest could be demanded as of right. The basis of supply of Electricity and the conditions on which it was supplied being statutory, the provisions under the conditions of supply that the Board should not pay interest on the security deposit has statutory basis and accordingly cannot be struck down as arbitrary on the basis of a commercial transaction governing a bank deposit. [278F G] Southern Steel Ltd. vs A P.

The petitioners, who were working as officers in the Telecommuni cation Research Centre, were recruited in four batches in 1965 and 1973. The Class I posts in the P & T Department consisted of the following posts: 1. Director (Senior Adminstrative Grade Level I) 2. Additional Director (Junior Administrative Grade) 4. Assistant Directors (Senior Class I). The Posts of Deputy Directors, Assistant Directors and S.T.Os Grade I were filled by the following methods: 1010 (a) by direct recruitment through the Union Public Service Commission, (the petitioners belong to this category; (b) by transfer of Group A Field Officers recruited through the P&T Board by written examination followed by an interview, (These officers belong to the Indian Telecommunications Service Group B), and (c) by transfers of Group B Field Officers who are Posts and Telegraphs departmental promotees belonging to the Telegraph Engineering Service, Group. The direct recruits to which category the petitioners belonged were not given any Special Pay in these grades and they were given only the pay at the pay scales prescribed for them. It was contended that the petition ers (direct recruits) who are specifically recruited to the P.T., were not entitled to any Special pay but the transferred officers from the Indian Telephone Service Group which is directly under the control of the P.& T Board of the Ministry of Communications, Government of India, and therefore, they were not enti tled to any special pay. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1(a) The petitioners have filed these petitions demanding payment of Special Pay to them also. [1010 F] (b)(i) It is seen from the answer that the Govern ment had virtually admitted that all relevant things such as qualifations, functions, duties and responsibilities are the same as between direct recruits and the transferred officials and that the transferred official officials had to be paid extra amount by way of Special pay in addition to their scale of pay which is the same. [1001 G] (ii) The Government had virtually admit ed that all rele vant things suchas those as quali cations, function duties and responsibility are thesame as those of the field officers transferred to TRC and what is the reason for not doing so. [ 1010 F H] (iii) There is no justification to deny the Special Pay at the same rates to the direct recruits working in the tele communication Research Centre. Denial of Special Leave in the above circumstances to thedirect recruits amounts to viola tion of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution of India.
