The appellant, who was employed as a munshi in the appellant 's Bidi factor at Bhandara, framed a charge sheet against him in respect of certain acts of misconduct, gross negligence of duty insubordination etc. on May 13, 1965. An enquiry held by the employer was held on May 15, after receipt of written statement from Nathu. Holding that the charges levelled against him were proved, the employer dismissed the third respondent with effect from August 1, 1965 and directed reinstatement of the third Respondent with all back wages. The appellant preferred an appeal to the State Industrial Court contending inter alia that the third respond ent had failed to comply with the provisions of law in that he did not make an application under section 42(4) of the Act which was a condition precedent to approaching the Labour Court and prayed that the order of the Labour court should be set aside on that ground alone. The State Industrial Tribunal confirmed the order. The High Court held that it was not necessary for an employee first to approach the employer or to follow the procedure laid down in section 42 (4) including the proviso before he could apply to the Labour Courts for relief under section 7(1) D. In appeal by certificate, HELD: (i) Under section 79(1), any employer intending to effect any change in respect Of an industrial matter specified in Schedule 11 of which item 3 reads "Employment including reinstatement and recruitment" must make an appli cation to the labour court. This sub section has a proviso which runs : "Provided that no such application shall lie unless the employee or a representative union has in the prescribed manner approached, the employers with a request for the change and no agreement has been arrived at in respect thereof. " The scheme of Chapter VIII seems to be that in regard to any "change" in an matter there must be compliance with the provi sions of that chapter. In other words, effort must first be made by the employers intending to affect any change or in respect o 'any order passed by the employee under standing orders which would of necessity include an order of dismissal, to see whether it was possible to come to any agreement and an application to the ' Labour Court could only be resorted to after efforts had been made to settle the dispute and no agree ment had been arrived. [737 C D] (ii) The scheme under Chapter VIII is that disputes should be settled as far as possible and primarily through conciliation and agreement, it does not stand to reason that an employee should be able to side step all this by a direct reference to the Industrial Court. A Labour Court is a creature of the statute and it can only exercise such jurisdiction as the statute confers on it : if there are certain pre conditions to the exercise of its jurisdiction, it must refuse to entertain any such application unless such pre conditions are first complied with. [ 737 E H] (iii) The Scheme of Chapter X seems to show that in respect to any 'change" there must have been compliance with section 42 of the .

The respondents, who were the successors in interest of the lessor company, filed a suit for eviction on the ground that they had become tenants under the lease after due attornment and were liable to eviction after the expiry of the lease period. The appellants ' application was allowed by the Munsif and an appeal therefrom filed by the respondents was dismissed by the Judicial Commissioner. The respondents then moved the Patna High Court in its revisional jurisdiction, inter alia, contending that the appellants ' applica tion under section 12 of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Evic tion) Control Act, 1947 before the Munsif was not maintain able. The plea was accepted by the High Court and the deci sion of the court below was set aside. According to the appellants their case in the notice a fresh tenancy had come into existence. The notice, therefore, was not one under section 10 of the Act at all. The question is whether the petition which was filed by them as an application under section12 should be treated as a plaint and the impugned proceeding as the one in a suit followed by an appeal and a second appeal. With the assistance of learned counsel for the par ties, it was contended that on the expiry Of such a tenancy the only remedy is to file a suit and in any event section 12 is wholly inapplicable in the facts of the case as the respondents by their notice did not seek an extension of the term of tenancy. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The jurisdiction of the Court is concerned. [975D] Madho Bibi vs Hazari Mal Marwari, AIR 1929 Patna 141; Lachhoo vs Munnilal Babu Lal Lal, AIR 1935 Allaha bad 183; Lachmu Bibi vs Hira Mal Marwar Ramchandra and others, AIR 1930 Pat. 472; Lach ener Prasad vs Munmilal Babu Lai Lal, ; , referred to. 2. The power is vested in the Controller. But as regards the question of dealing with eviction of tenants under section 11 and extension of period of lease under section 13, the civil court is the proper forum. In the present case it is the Civil Court, Ranchi which is the appropriate court either for filing a suit or for eviction under section ll or making an application u/s 12.

The appellant, a registered Society, filed the suit out of which this appeal arises in the court of the District Judge Jaipur City. The counsel engaged by the appellant were Sri Satya Narain Sharma and Sri Shyam Bihari Agarwal. The suit was later transferred to the Court of Additional Dis trict Judge No. 1 Jaipur City where it was renumbered as Suit No. 116 of 1974. After the institution of the suit, an election of the office bearers of the Society was held on 1.6.1973 and according to the appellant 's case one Sri Laxman Das Swami was elected as the Secretary. On 4.9.74 a prayer for withdrawing the suit was made by one Hari Narain Swami through another lawyer claiming to have been elected as Secretary of the society. In support of his claim, having been elected, none of them had any knowledge of the order passed by the Court. Later, in the next election, another Secretary named Jeeva Nand Swami was nominated and when he learnt about the fate of the case, an application was filed for recalling the order of withdrawal and restoring the suit to its file. The prayer was contested and the trial court rejected the application. The High Court agreed with the trial Court that the application under section 15 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure was not maintainable. While agreeing with the argument of the appellant that the trial com plaint had no jurisdiction to recall its order permitting the withdrawal of the plaintiff 's suit, the High Court observed that the mistake could not be corrected in the present situation. It has been contended by the learned counsel for the appel lant that the High court in C.W.P. No. 1406 of 1975 did not decide the dispute finally and left it to be settled by the civil court. The case was accordingly remanded to the trial Judge for reconsideration of the evidence on this point. The parties shall be allowed to lead further evi dence in support of their cases. The Trial Court, after holding that the appellant had filed an application under Section 15 1, Code of C.P., for recalling of the withdrawal order and restoring it to its filing. The trial court accepted his plea and ruled that it was the inherent power of every court to correct its own proceedings when it was satisfied that in passing a particular order it was misled by one of the parties. The appellant Society challenged the order before the High COurt by a petition under Section 1 15 of the C.C.P, which was also dismissed by the impugned judgment. The appel late Court held that the only remedy of the appellant is to file a fresh suit and accepted the case of Hari Narain Pandit. The appeal filed thereafter by Hari Narain Mahant before the Rajasthan High Court was dismissed. It was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Trial Court had no juris diction to recall the order permitting withdrawal of suit under its inherent power, and the High C.M.P No.1406 of 1976 did not decided the dispute provisionally and left the matter to be settle by the Civil Court. The respondent 's contention was that the suit filed under Section 2 1 1 1 of Code of Criminal Procedure, for restoration of the Suit was maintainable and the error committed by the trial candi date in favour of the respondent. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 A court has inherent power to correct Its own proceedings When it is satisfied that a party makes an application before the Court for setting aside the decree on the ground that he did not give his consent, the court has the power and duty to investigate the matter and to set aside the order if it is ultimately satisfied that the consent as a fact was lacking and the court was induced to pass the decree. [237E F] Sadho Saran Rai & Ors vs Anant Rai & Others, AIR 1923 Patna 483; Basangowda Hanmantgowda Patil & Ors. vs Churchigirigowda Yogangowda and Another, I.L.R.

The appellant was charged along with the co accused of having transferred by sale, High Denomination Bank Notes of Rs. 1,000 each to one Velji Lakhamshi Joshi for Rs. I,800 at the rate of Rs 180 per note and thus contravened the provisions of section 4 of the Ordinance read with section 109 Of the Indian Penal Code. The trial court acquitted the co appellant but convicted him under section 7 Of the Ordinance and sentenced him to pay a fine of Rs 8,000 and in default suffer six months rigorous imprisonment and the coaccused were awarded varying sentences of fine with which however he was not concerned. On appeal by the State of Bombay, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence passed against the appellant. Held, that the Ordinance in question having been promulgated during the period between June 27, 1940 and April 1, 1946, was perpetual in duration and continued in force until it was repealed. The Ordinance in respect of all Ordinances which were thus promulgated by the Governor General under section 72 Of the 9th Sch. of the Government of India Act, 1935, was a temporary one and continued operation even after April 1. The emergency under which the Governor was invested with the power to make and promulgate Ordinances for the peace and good government of British India or any part thereof under section 73 was the condition of the exercise of such power by the President and did not impose any limitation on the duration of the Ordinances thus promulgated. J. J., dissenting, that Ordinance in its present case continued in operation even though after April I, 1946 the Ordinance had ceased to be in force and was in operation on July 11, 1953, the date on which the offence in question was committed by the appellant and the appellant was rightly convicted by both the courts below.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to death by the Additional Sessions Judge, who confirmed the conviction and sentence of the appellants. The High Court in appeal upheld the convictions and sentences passed against them. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lants that (i) the deceased had not received reasonable consideration for the purpose of imposing the extreme penalty; (ii) the victim 's statement recorded under section 164 Cr. P.C., did not contain any indication as to what were the reasons for imposing the death sentence and (iii) the High Court was justified in confirming the death sentences passed under section 368(a) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The determination of public opinion on this difficult an(l complex question was essentially a legislative function not a judicial function. They concluded by stating that the death penalty and the judicial discretion vested in the Court regarding its imposition on an accused are constitutionally valid. [1069C D] 2.1 In the instant case, the High 'Court was justified by holding that the deceased 's conviction was neither 'erroneous in principle nor was 'arbitrary or excessive ' or 'indicative of an improper exercise of discretion '. Nor did the humanism of the Constitution holistically viewed subscribe to the hysterical assumption or facile illusion that a crime free society will dawn if hangman and firing squads were kept feversly busy. [ 1071E F] 2:2 The High ' Court was not justified in affirming the death convictions and sentence passed under sections 368(A) and 368(3) of I. P .C., 1973, on the ground that it had not considered the question of the appropriate sentence. [1172F G] 3.1 The assessment of public con siderations on this point is essentially a 'progressive ' stance which is out of place in a judicial pronouncement, which ought to be based on the facts and circumstances of the case and the law applicable. But the professed view does not stem from a firm belief in dignity of human life for they themselves advocate the death death penalty for certain classes of offenders, (I) R. On the facts before them they commuted the sentence of death to a sentence of imprisonment for life, and the decision cannot, therefore, be construed as laying down a ratio decidendi.

The appellant was compulsorily retired by the Commissioner of Income tax, U.P., on 2nd April 1956, and he was later promoted to the post of Income Tax Officer in 1945. His case was that he had worked to the entire satisfaction of his immediate superior officers and higher authorities and had earned a number of certificates highly appreciative of his work. He was confirmed early in 1952 as an Income tax Officer. The appellant also claimed arrears of salary, but he reduced this claim to Rs. 16,561.29. The Commissioner of Incometax, U P., by his order dated 2nd May 1956 reduced the appellant 's rank from the post. The appeal filed by him was dismissed by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and a second appeal before the High Court failed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the two authorities cited were not competent to initiate the departmental proceedings; (ii) the State of Assam & Anr. vs J. N. Roy Biswas, ; , referred to. HELD: (i). The question whether the appellant was given a reasonable opportunity to lead evidence and to be heard or not is largely a question of fact. It is only when an opportunity denied is of such a nature that the denial contravenes a mandatory provision of law or a rule of natural justice that it could vitiate the whole departmental trial; (iii) the plea that the appellant had been subjected to trial on allegations which had been the subject matter of previous enquiries overlooks that no charge was framed as a result of any previous enquiry. Therefore, the two Authorities cited: The State of Bihar & Anr., vs J N. Ray Biswas, and R. T. Rangachari vs Secretary of State do not help the appellant. If an inquiry is held at a particular stage, possibly to determine whether regular proceedings should be drawn up or started, it does not debar a departmental trial. That was the nature of the previous enquiries. It appears that it is only after the appellant his activities had become more than notorious that further enquiry was undertaken and regular charges framed. [586 H; 584 A B] (ii). The High Court had given its judgment eight months after it had heerad argumenst. He urged that the result was that the High court did not deal with a number other points which could be raised on behalf or of his client. It pointed out that one of the learned Judges who dismissed the application for a certificate of fitness of the case had also heard the arguments in the first appeal. There is no affidavit before this Court that any particular points argued before the Division Bench had not been referred to or dealt with by the Bench. Moreover, the Division bench had probably not dealt with all arguments on questions of fact because it did not consider it necessary to do so. After all, it was not hearing an appeal against the findings of the departmental authorities. It was for the appellant to satisfy the Departmental authorities which had looked into the case upto its final stages, that he suffered some injustice which could have affected the final decision.

The appellants who were the last purchasers of manganese ore within the State of Andhra Pradesh contended before the Sales Tax authorities that they were not the last purchaser but the M.M.T.C. was the last buyer within the state, and therefore, the M .M.M.,T. C. was liable to pay the tax. The High Court held that the contracts between the appellants and the M/M.S.T., were similar and, therefore, there should be examination of five other contracts. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the contracts were different; and (2) the contract of sale occasioned the export and that the contract between the Mec tee and the foreign buyers was integrally connected with the contract entered into by the M,M. T.C., which indicated that the appel lants ' contract of the sale occasioned export and therefore there should he examination of 5 other contracts; and that in any case, there were six contracts and it had been the case of the appe lants that the said contracts were similar, and, there was no privity of contract between them. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The judgment of the High Court is set aside. [444E] 2.1 In the instant case, the contracts entered into with the foreign buyer on F.O.B. basis indicated that they had been integrated F. O.B., contracts in the course of export. The appellants were required to bring the goods F.0.B to the ship named by the S.T .C.

The appellant was employed with the respondent M/s Bharat Electronics Limited as Salesman at its Delhi 521 Sales Depot on a salary of Rs. 520 per month from 8th December, 1973. His service was abruptly terminated by letter dated 12th October 1974 with effect from 19th October, 1974. Consequent upon this termination, an industrial dispute was raised and the Delhi Administration referred the following dispute to the Labour Court for adjudication: "Whether the termination of services of Shri Mohan Lal is illegal and/or unjustified and if so, to what relief is he entitled and what directions are necessary in this respect?" As the respondent management at one stage failed to participate in the proceedings, the reference was heard ex parte and the Labour court made an award on 2nd May, 1977 directing reinstatement of the appellant with continuity of service and full back wages at the rate of Rs 520 per mensem from the date of termination till reinstatement. Subsequently, respondent moved for setting aside the ex parte award and seeking permission to participate In the proceedings which motion was granted. The respondent contended that the appellant was a salesman appointed on probation for six months and subsequently on the expiry of the initial period, his service was terminated by letters dated 12st October 1974 and 12th Octo ber, 1974 with retrospective effect from August 19, 1974; and that he was not found suitable for the post to which he was appointed. The Labour Court held that the termination was neither illegal nor improper and the claim of the respondent was negatived. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The termination of service of the appel lant does not fall within any of the excepted categories or to be precise, excluded categories. Undoubtedly, the termination would constitute retrenchment and by a catena of decisions it is well settled that where pre requisite for valid retrenchment as laid down in section 25F has not been complied with, retrenchment bringing about termination of serv ice is ab initio void. In other words, it does not bring about a cessation of service. [522D E] 1:2 The termination would be a retrenchment and the workman continues to be in service. If he has, he would be deemed to be In continuous service for a period of one year and that if that service is continuous service within the meaning of sub section (1) his case would be governed by sub section 2(a) and his case need not be covered by sub s.(2). And sub section(2) provides for a fiction to treat a workman in continuous service, for a periods of one years despite the fact that he has not rendered uninterrupted service for 240 days within a period Of 12 calendar months. [525E F] 1 :3 The termination will constitute retrenchment. It is not necessary for the purpose of sub s(2)(a) that the workman should be in continuous serv ice for a continuous period of two years, but has rendered service for one year or six months, as the case may be, if the workman during the period of 12 calendar month just preceding the date with reference to which calculation is to be made has actually worked under that employer for not less than 240 days.

The appellant was appointed an Inspector of Consolidation by order dated October 5, 1953 of the Settlement Commissioner of Patiala and East Punjab States Union. The appointment was on temporary basis and terminable with one month 's notice. On February 5, 1955, the appellant was served with a charge sheet setting out his mis demeanour, an enquiry was held in respect of the alleged misdemeanour and his employment was terminated because in the view of the settlement officer with which view the Deputy Commissioner agreed. The Deputy Commissioner by order dt. March 17, 1955 ordered that the services of the appellant be terminated forthwith and that in lieu of notice he will get one month pay as required by the Rules. The appellant challenged the authority of the Deputy Commis sioner or the Settlement Officer to hold the enquiry and submitted his explanation to the charge sheet. On the report of the enquiry officer that the work and conduct of the public servant were unsatisfactory, an order of termination of employment was passed without affording him an opportunity of showing cause against the action proposed to be taken in regard to him. The High Court held that the appellant had no right to hold a post he was occupying and by the impugned order the appellant could not be dismissed or removed from service but his employment being terminated in exercise of authority reserved under the terms of employment, and no penalty was imposed upon the appellant, Held, that the protection of article 311 (2) of the Constitution applies as much to a temporary public servant. The protection of Article 311 (1) of 'the Constitution applies only to a permanent public servant and not to a probationer or a temporary employee. The question whether the order is by way of punishment in the light of the tests laid down in Parshotam Lal Dhingra case, and the enquiry against the respondent was for ascertaining whether he was fit to be confirmed. An order discharging a public servant even if a probationer in an enquiry on charges of misconduct. negligence, inefficiency or other disqualification may appropriately be regarded as one by way Of punishment but an order discharging such probationer following upon an enquiry to ascertain whether he should be confirmed is not of that nature x x x (x) The third proposition in the latter case was applicable only to temporary public servants and not a probationer nor to a probationary employee.

The appellant challenged the promotion of respondents Nos. 1 to 46 and others as Professors in supersession of their claims, contending that they were senior and more qualified for promotion, and contended that they had been senior and better qualified for being promoted, and that the High Court erred in taking a contrary view. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The State Government at first framed rules on November 15, 1968, for selections to be made to posts of Professors in the colleges. By Notification No. SRO 161 dated March 25, 1969 those rules were replaced by the rules made by the Governor specifically for the appointment of Professors which were called the "Jammu and Kashmir Professors of Colleges (Selection) Rules, 1969". The Commission set out the reasons for its decision and finally made its recommendation on merits. The Commission was therefore consulted on the suitability of the candidates for promotion as Professors and the second requirement of clause (b) of sub section (2) of section 133 was also complied with. [875 H; 873 A B] The State Govern ment at first framing rules on December 15, 1969 for selections made to the posts of Professor, names of four Lecturers strictly in order of seniority were sent to the Commission "at its direction" and they were interviewed and examined by the Selection Committee which was "formed" by the Commission. The Committee was presided over by a member of the Commission, the report of the Committee was formally submitted to the State Government under the Chairman 's note dated June 2, 1969, and the Commission then took its decision regarding the recommendation to be passed to the effect that the Committee would be presided over in favour of some committee composed of strangers to the commission. The State Govt. has stated in its reply that for every post of Professor names of 4 Lecturers strictlyin order of merit were sent by the Public Service Commission to "at their direction" which was communicated to the appellant under the chairman 's Note dated June 3, 1969.

The petitioner, a member of the Bihar Legislative Assembly made a speech in the Bihar Legislature when he was one of the oldest members of the Assembly. The speech was made on May 30, 1957 and the official authorised report was published and made available on January 2, 1958. The petitioner received a notice to show cause why appropriate action should not be taken against him for breach of privilege. This showed malice on the part of the Privileges Committee. The action of the privileges Committee raised constitutional points affecting the fundamental right of freedom of expression. The Legislature cannot have such a privilege as will deprive the citizens of their fundamental rights which are guaranteed by the Constitution, specially the right of free expression under article 19(1)(a). [812 H; 813 A B] The petitioner was not alleged to have done so and the Speaker had no power to take any action in respect of the said publication. The question whether the privilege conferred on the Legislature of a State is subject to the freedom conferred on a citizen under article19(1) (a) of the Constitution and the rules and standing orders regulating procedure of that Legislature. [813 E] The right to freedom of speech and expression includes the freedom of propagation of ideas and their publication and circulation, and the petitioner 's fundamental right under article 21 is not confined to the exercise of the privilege of free speech guaranteed by article 19 (1) of our Constitution. [889 F G] The question as to whether a privilege conferred upon the Legislature is subject only to the provisions of the constitution and the Rules and standing Orders regulating procedure in that Legislature, and it cannot be said that the powers, privileges and immunities enjoyed by the House of Commons are conferred by the latter part of article 105(3) on each House of Parliament and the members and committees thereof must be like the powers. privileges and immunity enjoyed by a House of the Legislature and the provisions thereof must also be like those of the House, but who, by virtue of the constitutional power, have the right to speak in, and otherwise to take part in the proceedings of the Houses or any committee thereof. [850 E] In the present case, the petitioner was alleged to be a member and an editor of a newspaper, which had been declared by the Speaker of the U. P. Legislative Assembly as run by Dr. section K. Sinha, Chief Minister of the State Dr. Section K. SINHA himself, has been the Chairman of the Committee. On May 30 1957, there was a debate in the House and it was decided that a portion of the speech was objectionable and ordered it to be struck off and expunged. It was a general statement. No specific 102 810 direction was given to the Press. The opposite party was claiming the right under Article 19( 1) (1), which includes freedom of views and their publications and circulation; and the Legislature had the privilege to prevent any citizen from publishing the proceedings or portion thereof, but never exercises it.

The respondents and two others, namely T.K. Satyanarayanan (No. 9) and V.S.R. Gupta (No . 10) in the list (Annexure 1), were all Readers in the private college, each having put in more than eight years of service there as a Lecturer. T. K. Satyanmurty was promoted as Reader on 4 1969 and was drawing Rs.600/ per month on the date of taking over. V. S.R Gupta was promoted to the post of Reader on April 5 1969 and he was drawing salary of less than Rs. 600/ . On July 30, 1970, the Government issued a circular superseding the earlier circulars on the subject. The respondents filed a writ petition in the High Court (S.C.) challenging the validity of the said circular. The High Court accepted the Writ Petition and held that the Respondents were entitled to consideration by the Public Service Commission for appointment as Readers under the Government in the manner laid down in the circular of March 23, 1971. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants (i) that since they had all the requisite qualifications for the appointment as Reader and they were all holding the posts of Reader before the take over, their names were not referred to the Public Services Commission for consid eration of their suitability for appointment; and (ii) that the High court erred in directing the Government to take into account, as experience, the service of the Respondents while they were in the Private College since, according to him, the necessary qualification was eight years experience in Class II, Orissa Education Serv ice (O.E.S.). Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The requirement of 8 years of teaching experience, as mentioned above, which is needed for appoint ment as a Reader is more than amply fulfilled by each of the respondents. [780C D] 2.1 In the instant case, the Respondents answered the test of educational qualifications, as well as, experience of teach ing in a recognised private college are discriminated amongst the very category of Readers on an irrational and illusory consideration. Denial of an opportunity to these Respondents even for being considered for the post is clearly violative of Article 16 of the Constitution.

The appellants applied for temporary permits under section 68 F(1) C.P.C. for plying the passenger vehicles on routes situated in Bulandshahr district, Uttar Pradesh. The U.P State Road Transport Corporation (Corporation for short) also made an application for grant of three temporary permits for the same purpose and the application was granted while the application made by each of the appellants was rejected on the ground that once a scheme had been published in view of the provision contained in section 68F(1 A) the Corporation alone to the exclusion of others is entitled to apply for temporary permit and if such an application is made by the Corporation and granted no one else is entitled, to obtain a temporary permit. This decision of the State Transport Authority was upheld both by the State Road Appellate Tribunal and the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that in view Of section 68(1A) the State transport Authority alone to exclusion of other operators is entitled for grant or renewal of any permit during the period intervening between the date of publication of the scheme and the date when the scheme had already been published, the Corporation would be entitled to all the temporary permits to the excluded of any other operator. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The State Transport Appellate Tribunal as well as the High court fell into an error by interpreting section 68 E(1 C) only to mean that even though there are 7 vacancies and the Corporation applied for only 3 temporary permits, once the Corporation made an applica tion for temporary licences not for the full strength but something short short of it there was no power left in the State Government to grant or renew any permit. [864 D] 2. The expression 'any person ' would comprehend any person even other than the Corporation. One has to read section 68 C(1 ) and section 68 A harmoniously. If the Corporation applies for all the permits but only for some, the inescapable conclusion is that for the remaining strength the Corporation has made no application for the temporary permit, once it made an appli cation for grant ing a temporary permits not for full strength But something short of the it there would be no application by the Corpora tion and section68 F(I C) would be squarely attracted. [986 E] 3.

The appellant, who was the son of a Hindu governed by the customary law prevailing in the Punjab, succeeded to his maternal grandfather 's estate. The respondents filed a suit for declaration that the two transactions of mortgage and sale in question did not bind their own reversionary rights because the impugned alienations were without consideration and were not supported by any legal necessity. The trial court held that the property in dispute was ancestral qua the appellant and that the impugned alienation was not effected for consideration or for legal necessity, but set aside the decree and remanded the suit for proceedings for substituting the legal representatives of the deceased defendant Ram Kala. After remand the legal represen tation of the appellant was brought on record and ultimately the original decree passed by the trial court was confirmed by the High Court. The High Court ordered that parties should bear their own costs throughout. Held, that the decision of the first Full Bench in Narotam Chand 's case must be taken to have been overruled. In the present case it is difficult to say that the doctrine of stare decisis really applies because the (1) VOL XXI P. 110 Correctness of the First Full Bench decision has been challenged in the High Courts from time to time and in fact the said decision had been reversed in appeal by this Court. It would not be correct to say, that these observations overrule the earlier Full Bench decisions of the Punjab High Court on the point of the relevant custom. The doctrine of law which has become settled by a series of decisions generally is binding on the courts and should be followed in similar cases. The rule of stare overruling is not so imperative or inflexible as to preclude a departure therefrom in any case, but its application must be determined in each case by the discretion of the court, and previous decisions should not be followed to the extent that error may be perpetuated and grievous wrong may result.

The appellants were tried by the Additional Sessions Judge, Birbhum, on charges under section 449 and section 307/34 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that on the night of 14th November 1950 when Haji Ebrar Ali was sleeping on the Verandah of his hut, these appellants came there and while one of them was sitting on the verandah of their hut, they attacked him with a dagger while the other three held him down. Fortunately, the injury inflicted on Ebrahim Ali did not prove fatal. The jury returned an unanimous verdict of guilt against all the appellants on both charges. The Sessions Judge accepted that verdict and convicted them under sections 449 and 307 read with section 34 of the Penal Code and sentenced them to rigorous imprisonment for four years under section 307 read and to rigorous imprison ment for two years under s.425 of the Act. He sentenced the other two appellants to rigorous fines, but the High Court dismissed their appeal. Held, that there was no substance in either of these contentions. Section 449 of the Code provides that whoever commits house trespass in order to the committing of any offence punishable with death shall be punished with imprisonment for life or with rigorous imprisonment and section 457 prescribes the punishment for house trespass if it is done "in order to" the committing 'of any offence, punishable with imprisonment. The words "inorder to" have been used by the legislature not only in section 449 but in two succeeding sections 450, 451 and 457 of the Criminal Procedure Code. Section 450 prescribes the punishments for house tax trespass if the purpose in committing the house trespass is the commission of an offence punishable under section 448 of the I.P.C. The Act did not result in death. So, he becomes punishable under s 307 of the IPC.

The appellant filed a suit for declaration of his title as collateral within four degrees of Gurdial, who was a Sarswat Brahmin. The respondent contested the suit mainly on the grounds (i) that the suit for a mere declaration was not maintainable; and (ii) that there was no custom whereunder the collaterals of the father who was the last male holder excluded the daughter from succession to the self acquired property of her father. Held, that the appellant had failed to discharge the onus that was initially on him and that being the position no burden was cast on the respondent which she need have discharged by adducing evidence of particular instances. The general custom of the Punjab being that a daughter excludes the collateral 's from succession even though they are within the fourth degree, the presumption will be considerably weakened. Consequently, in order to enable the appellant to displace the general custom recorded in Rattigan 's Digest of Customary Law, the respondent must produce a Riwaj i am which is a reliable and trustworthy document. The answer to question 16 as recorded in the 1913 Riwraj i am was wholly insufficient to discharge his onus that he had discharged by producing in evidence the Riwaz i am of the Gurdaspur district prepared in 1865 and 1893. Gopal Singh vs Ujagar Singh, A.I.R. 1935 Lah. 306, referred to. Held further, that even if the presumption as to the correctness of the Rwaj i m am was weak, the appellant must succeed.

The respondent was at the material time the Managing Director of a number of Companies registered under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. He applied to the Collector of Calcutta under section 31 of the Stamp Act for adjudication of duty payable on a power of attorney marked as exhibit A in the proceedings which he proposed to execute. By that power he empowered Messrs Douglas Chisholm Fairbairn and John James Brims Sutherland jointly and severally to act for him in his individual capacity and also as executor, administrator, trustee, managing agent, liquidator and all other capacities. The Collector referred the matter under section 56(2) of the Act to the High Court of Calcutta who differed in their opinion. The Board of Revenue, West Bengal has preferred this appeal by special leave. Held, that when two persons join in executing a power in respect of all the matters in which he could act, it should be held that there are distinct matters not only with reference to the capacity of the executant as trustee, executor and so forth, but in respect Of every transaction entered into by him in the personal capacity. The fact that the donor of the power of Attorney executes it in different capacities is not sufficient in his opinion to constitute the instrument one comprising distinct matters and thus requiring to be stamped with the aggregate amount of the duties with which separate instruments each comprising or relating to one of such matters would be chargeable under the Act, within the meaning of section 5. The words "distinct matters" used in section 5 are synonymous with the word "descriptions" occurring in section 6 and that they both refer to the several categories of instruments which are set out in the Schedule. The instrument in question cannot be split up into separate instruments Each comprising or dealing relating to a distinct matter in so far as the different capacities of the donor are concerned. A general power of power of an attorney comprises all acts which can be done by the donor himself, whatever be the capacity or capacities which he enjoys and cannot be divided up into individual acts which the donor is capable of performing whether in his personal capacity or in his representative capacity as trustee or as executor or administrator are also comprised within the instrument and are not distinct matters to be dealt with as such so as to attract the operation of section S.5. The position is the same when a person is executor or an administrator, because in that capacity he represents the estate of the deceased, whose persona is deemed to continue in him for purposes of administration. Chaudhury vs Chaudhury, , referred to.

The assessee, a company carrying on business in Bhavnagar, which was formerly an Indian State, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1949 50. In assessing the profits of its business by the two appellant companies for the year 194950 the Income tax Officer had deducted depreciation allowed under the Saurashtra Income tax Ordinance, 1949 and claimed deduction of depreciation allowance. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner as also the Income Tax Tribunal took a different view and held that this expression "or which would have been allowed to him if the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 was in force in the past" did not permit the Income 'tax Officer to make any deduction under this head. In appeal by the assessee to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Ordinance had not used the words "would have been allowable to him" nor the words would have allowed to be added to the words 'all depreciation actually allowed under any laws or rules of a Part B State relating to income Tax and super tax. HELD: (i) The words "any law relating to tax on profits of business" in paragraph 2 of the Removal of Difficulties Order must be applied according to its terms. [227 H] (ii) In view of the fact that in many cases where the Indian Incometax Act is in force, the assessee might find it to his interest not to make a claim for depreciation allowance and so no depreciation allowance would then be allowed to the assessee if the Income. tax Act had in fact been in force.

The petitioner, an instrumentality of the State of Karnataka in favour of the Mysore Construction Co. (M.C.) was a party to the contract. He invited tenders from registered contractors of appropriate class. Paragraph I of the notifi cation listed three "Minimum qualifying requirements" viz., that the intending tenderers should have executed civil and architectural works including insulation in a power plant/industrial complex, preferably in power plant; (2) should have an annual turnover of atleast 1 crore for each of the preceding three years. Paragraph V required the intending tenderer to furnish the following information "along with the application for issue of blank tender books", namely: (a) Audited balance sheet/Certificate from Chartered Ac countant for preceding three year; (b) Latest income tax clearance Certificate; (c) Copy of the Registration Certificate (d) annual output of the works of all the above nature at any site accompanied by a certificate from the organisation for whom the tenderer had carried out the works furnishing details such as rate of pouring of concrete. manufacturing of hollow concrete block, precast concrete block etc., and period of completion scheduled/envisaged, equipment and their deploy ment i.e., man months etc. The petitioner submitted his tender books on 6.2.1989. These were examined by the Chief Engineer as well as an independent firm of Engineering Consultants, namely, Tata Consulting Engineers (T.C.E.). Both the Chief Engi neer as well T.C., recommended acceptance of the tender of M.C .C. (which was the lowest tender in view of the fact that M. C.C had adequate experience in the construction of R.C,. works and they were capable of mobilising the work force required for the work. The principal argument advanced on behalf of the petitioner is that paragraphs I and V of the N.I.T. specified certain pre qualifying requirements viz., (a), (b), (c), (d), (e) and (f) specified certain conditions which, under the Notification Inviting Tenders (N.I.) had to be executed at any time before the final award of the contract; that subsequently this time frame was altered; and that the last date for receipt of application form for issue blank tender book remained as 17th January, 1989 but the other items were altered to read as follows: "1. Last date for submission of 10.2 .1989 clarification: 2. Period to issue blank tenders 10.02.1989 to books 16.2."89 3. The respondent submitted that after making necessary adjustments it was found that the tender was Rs. 15 lakhs less than the tender and that there was no adequate experience of mobilisation the workforce required for work. It may be mentioned that after taking necessary adjustments, it was noticed that the petitioner had already made a representation objecting to the consideration of the Tender Committee. The learned Single Judge rejected the peti tioner 's contention that this rule has been violated in the present case, even on the K.P.C, and that this is why the petitioner should not at all have entertained the tender forms.

The appellant, who was the owner of a house in Lahore, owned certain agricultural lands in Punjab. The appellant made an application to the Additional Custodian of Evacuee Property for confirmation of the transaction of exchange and consequent transfer to her of the property in agricultural land. The Additional Custodian recommended that possession may be given to the appellant and that the Patwari may be informed accordingly to take necessary action in the matter. But it did not appear from the record whether this was done or whether possession was delivered. At this stage a notice under section 27 of the East Punjab Evacuees ' (Administration of Property) Act, 1947, was issued to the appel lant calling upon him to show cause why the order of confirmation should not be set aside. The case was adjourned to 12th May 1953 at the request of counsel for the appellant but it did no appear from his record whether the said notice was done, or whether the possession was in fact delivered. On that date he passed an order confirming the exchange and further orders sanctioning mutation and other consequential orders made in connection therewith. The Custodian General passed an Order confirming the sale. In pursuance thereof a detailed allotment was made to twenty six individual allottees on the 27th October, 1949. There was a report of the Rehabilitation Patwari dated the 27st February 1950, showing that the allottees entered into possession of the land and cultivated their respective lands and settled down in the village. After the order confirming exchange was passed by the Additional Deputy Custodian on the 20th March, 1952, the appellant filed an application before the Additional Commissioner for confirmation under section 5 A of the Act stating that the transaction was not a bona fide one for valuable consideration and that it was open to him to file an appeal under the Act as persons aggrieved. The Assistant Commissioner rejected this application holding that the revision application was competent. On appeal, the Custodian General confirmed the order. Held, that the revisional power cannot be exercised when there was an appeal provided but no appeal was filed, that it is open to the Assistant Custodian who appeared before the Custodian in support of the notice for revision or to the allottees of the properties in whose interest the revisional order appears to have been passed, to file a appeal under section 8 of the Central Act as person aggrieved.

The appellant, a locality in the city of Bombay, was studded with small hardware businesses where pipes and fittings, nuts and bolts, tools and other small products were made and sold. The dispute arose as to whether the establishments (mentioned in the annexure) had been giving bonus to their workers till 1965. The Tribunal framed two issues which ran thus: "1. Whether the establishments are giving bonus or not? If so what should be the basis on which employers should make payment of bonus to its workmen for the years ending on any date in 1966, 1967 and 1969 ? 2. Whether payment of Bonus by the employers to their workmen has become custom or usage or condition of service in these establishments ? If so, what should he the basis upon which employers can make payment? of bonus based on profits and to recommend principles for computation of such bonus and methods of payment . The Tribunal rejected the demand for bonus. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) the claim put forward by the appellant before the Tribunal was, on the face of it unsustainable on the short ground that what was pleaded was profit based bonus only and therefore fell squarely within the Bonus Act; (2) the reference in respect also was not tenable and legal. HELD: (i) The Industrial Tribunal had no jurisdiction to try the dispute referred to it. [610 E] (ii) The claim put up by the workmen before the tribunal was, therefore, unsustainable on this short ground. [613 A] (iii) The reference in question was not maintainable because the claim for bonus was founded on tradition or custom or condition or of service and in that light, the Tribunal made short shrift of the workmen 's plea in these words: "In my opinion, the demand pertaining to the practice or custom prevailing in the establishments before 1965 is not such a matter as has to be adjudicated and it also did not fall under the provisions of Bonus Act. [514 F] (iv) The Tribunal had correctly considered the relevant provisions of the Bonus act and the surrounding circumstances and rendered its award dismissing the reference. [625 G] (v) The contention that the claim was based on a custom based bonus for the subsequent period was again irrelevant, because, as the claim is not based on the profits or the financial results of the employers but is based on custom ': was rejected by this Court in Churakulam vs State of Madras [1959] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 869, followed.

The petitioners in the Haryana Writ Petitions were appointed directly from the Bar to the Haryana Superior Judicial Service on July 28 and October 7, 1967 respectively. By Act 3 of 1966, the State of Haryana came into existence on November li 1966. Petitioners 1 and 2 were promoted to the Superior Judicial Services of Punjab and Haryana and Haryana. Respondents 3 to 11 were appointed direct recruits to the Punjab Superior Judicial service. Some of the more important grievances of the petitioners are that their seniority qua direct recruits is wrongly and unjustly made to depend upon the fortuitous circumstance of the date of confirmation, in the Superior judicial Service; that even if a substantive vacancy is available, the confirmation of a promotee in that vacancy is postponed arbitrarily and indefinitely, that promotees are treated with an unequal hand qua direct recruit for example, a promotee despite his satisfactory performance and the availability of a substantive post in which he can be confirmed, is continued in an officiating capacity until after a direct recruit completes his probation and is due for confirmation, and that, the High Court applied the principle of rotation as between promotees and direct recruits at the time of their confirmation when, in fact, that the relevant rules provide for is the application of a rule of quota at the date on which he completed the period of probation; and that even though a substantive vacancies are available, confirmation of an promotee in the vacancy is deferred arbitrarily and unreasonably, that promotions are treated as having been made without consulting the High court. The petitioners who were officiating continuously in the Higher Judicial Service of Punjab filed writ petitions in the High Courts challenging the seniority list on the ground that they had not been given a proper date of appointment to the higher judicial service; that the ratio of 2:1 between promotees & direct recruits has to be maintained at all stages, that is to say, not only at the stage of appointment but at the place of confirmation also.

The respondents Nos. 4 and 5, B. Kumara Swamy and G. Amarender, in this appeal filed R.P. No. 1615 of 1984 before the Andhra Pradesh Administrative Tribunal contending for promotion from Senior Assistant to Assistant Commercial Taxes Officer, Zonal seniority of Warangal local area comprising of Wardamagam, Karimnagar and Adila bad is the criteria. The Adilabad division consisting of Adilabad and Karimnagar Districts of the Commercial Taxes Division cannot be treated as a zone and the divisional seniority prepared by the department is bad in law. It was held by the Tribunal that in the im pugned order it gave rise to filing of W.P No. 998 of 1986 in this Court under Article 32 of the Constitution, the State Govern ment had no inherent power in creating a zone or organising local cadre within the zones except in accordance with the provisions made in the Andhra Pra desh Public Employment (Organisa tion of Local Cadres and Regulation of Direct Recruitment) Order 1975. Accordingly, it reiterated the original order dated April 29, 1988. The Constitution (Thirtysecond Amendment) Act, 1973 through Section 3 thereof brought into the Constitution Article 371 D with effect from July 1, 1974. This is a special provision in respect of the State of Andhra Pradesh empowers ing the President, having regard to the requirements of the state as a whole for equitable opportunities and facilities for the people belonging to different parts of the States, in the matter of public employment and in the matters of educa tion, and different provisions may be made for various parts of tho State to make an order, in particular (a) require the State Government to organise any class or classes of posts in a civil service of, or any class Or classes of civil posts under the State into different local cadres for different parts Of the State and allot in accord ance with such principles and procedure as may be specified in the order; (b) specify any part or parts of that State which shall be regarded as the local area (i) for direct recruitment to posts in any local cadre, (ii) for promotion to the post of Senior Assistants and Assistant Commercial Tax Officers, etc.

The appellant, who was the manager and Karta of a joint Hindu family, executed a simple mortgage of Gadi Sirampur in favour of the Chota Nagpur Banking Association Limited. In 1920 the Bank filed a suit against his son Wazir Narain Singh to enforce the mortgage security and obtained a mortgage decree. The suit was decreed by the trial court but Hiraman Ram died after the mortgage decree but Hiramen Ram continued in actual possession of the disputed villages and the plaintiff therefore filed the 16th November, 1939, the suit out of which this appeal arises. In spite of the fact that there was no allegation in the plaint that the defendant 's lease had the effect of rendering the security of the Bank insufficient, the High Court went into this question and a calculation of some figures came to the conclusion that the lease of the said disputed villages did not in any way render the security Of the bank insufficient. It therefore held that the suit was binding on the defendants and dismissed the plaintiff 's suit. Held, that the question whether the mortgagor in possession had power to lease the mortgaged property has got to be determined with reference to the authority of the mortgagor as the bailiff or agent for the mortgagee to deal with the property in the usual course of management. The true position has been stated in the following terms by this Court in Madan Mohan Singh vs Baj Kishore Kumar, (I.L.R. , and it is for the lessee if he wants to resist the claim of the mortgagee that the grant of the permanent lease was a dealing with the mortgaged land in the ordinary course of administration.

The petitioner, who was a contractor, sent bills on July 12, 1979 but payment was not made. For the first time he sent notice on Nov. 28, 1989 to the respondent for reference to arbitration. On receipt thereof, the respondent filed an arbitration suits in the Calcutta High Court under sections 5 and 12 of the . The Single Judge held that the claim was hopelessly barred by limitation. In appeal, the division bench set aside the order of the learned Single Judge and directed the parties to refer the case for arbitration. Hence these special leave petitions. Dismissing the Special Leave Petitions, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Clause 68 provides for appointment of an arbitrator and when the petitioner has legally invoked clause 68 and issued notice to the Respondent, the Respondent is duty bound to appoint an arbitrator or umpire and thereafter the same cannot be revoked except with the leave of the Court unless a contrary intention is expressed in the arbitration agreement. Therefore, by a conjoint reading of sections 5 & 12 (2) (b), it is clear that the court has been given power in given circumstances to grant leave to a contracting party to have the arbitrator or arbitrators removed and the arbitration agree entered into with other contracting part revoked. Where the Court grants such authority consequentially arbitration agreement shall cease to have effect with respect to the difference or dispute. It flows therefrom that there exist implied power vested in the court permitting a party to avail the remedy under sections5 & 12 to rescind the arbitration Agreement. [362G H; 363A B] 1.2 The provisions of the Limitation Act would apply to arbitrations and notwithstanding any term in the contract to the contrary, cause of arbitration for the purpose of limitation shall be deemed to have accrued to the party in respect of any such matter at the time when it should have accrued but for that term in an agreement. [363C] 1:3 The provisions relating to arbitration are essentially separate and they cannot be extended to arbitrations. They are not intended to be exhaustive so as to exclude them from the purview of limitation. [361E F] M/s Amarch & Lalit Kumar vs Shree Ambica Jute Mills Ltd., ; at 969; Pegler vs Railway Executive 1948 Appeal Cases 332 at 338, House of Lords held inapplicable. In the instant case, even assuming that the petitioner had put forward his claim in July, 1979 and the respondent had not acted thereon till November 28,1989 for long 10 years he did not move his little finger to approach the Engineer and later the Court. For this reason, it is an exceptional case and the courts below have justifiably exercised their discretionary power and jurisdiction under sections 4 and 12(2) of the Act to grant Leave to a party in exceptional circumstances to revoke the contract of arbitration. [365G H] 1 :4 The question whether the High Court was justified in permitting the respondent to rescind or the contract is whether the court would be justified to permit a contracting Party to rescind, the authority to refer disputes or differences to arbitration and decide the dispute or differences arising from the contract including the power of the arbitrator. They could also contract restricting the limitation for adjudication. [364G H, 365A] M.K. Industries Ltd. vs Union of India & Ors., ; , referred to.

The appellants obtained a preliminary decree on June 26, 1947 on the basis of a mortgage. The property mortgaged was an Estate within the meaning of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950. The Act came into force after the passing of the aforesaid preliminary decree. Thereafter the mortgagees applied under section 14 of the Act and got determined the compensation to which they were entitled under the Act. The appellants resisted that execution by filing an application under section 47 Civil Procedure Code (Misc. Case No. 94 of 1959) on the ground that the decree cannot be executed in view of the provisions of the . That application was dismissed for default of the judgment debtors on September 12, 1959. A second application raising the same ground of objection ( Misc. Case Nos. 94 and 110 of 1959), was filed by the judgment debtor on September 8, 1960. The application was rejected on January 4, 1962 after examining the contentions of the parties. Thereafter a third application raising it the same grounds of objection was dismissed on January 3,1962 after examining all the contentions raised by the appellants. The High Court in second appeal reversed the decision of the executing court and restored that of the trial court. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants: (i) that the objection as regards executability of the decree pleaded by the Judgment debtors is barred by the principles of res judicata; (ii) that it is not necessary for them to exclusively proceed under section 4(d); and (iii) that in construing the words of section 4 (d) it would be necessary to bear in mind the object of the , which was merely to provide for the transference to the State of the estates as specified. HELD: (1) The decision of this Court in Sidheshwar Prasad Singh vs Ram Saroop Singh, [1962] Supp. 3 S.C.R. 564, followed. (2) In construing section 4 it would not be right to assume that the interests of the debtors affected by the provisions Of the Act do not fall within the protection of the section. Section 4(a) provides that once an Estate vests in the State the various rights in respect of that estate enumerated therein shall also vest in the state absolutely free from all encumbrances. Among the rights enumerated therein undoubtedly includes the right of possession. In view of section 5 (1), there is hardly any doubt that the proprietor loses all his rights in the estate in question. After setting out the various interests lost by the proprietor, the section proceeds to say "such proprietoror tenure holder shall (i). XXXI, B.L.R., 400, followed and applied. (3) The provisions contained in section 16 in regard to the scaling down of the debts due by the proprietors and tenure holders clearly indicate that another object which the Act wanted to achieve was to give some redress to the debtors whose estates have been taken away from them by the notifications issued under section 3. Therefore, in construing section 5(1) it is difficult to say that what vested in the Government are only those interests not coming within section 6. Section 14 does not apply. [912 D E] (4) The contention of the appellants that the dismissal of a previous suit for default by the decree holder though by the time that petition came to be dismissed, the judgment creditor had resisted the execution on one or more grounds did not bar the further execution of the decrees in pursuance of fresh execution petition filed in accordance with law. [936 D] (5) The view of this court in Sidheswar Prasad vs Ram Narain Singh, ; , followed.

The respondents in Civil Appeal No. 5469 of 1990, who were all allocated to Group 'A ' Services (I.R.P.S.) in the year 1988 and who had appeared in Civil Services Main Examination of a subsequent year under the interim orders of the Tribunal for the Civil Services Examinations, 1988 or 1989, filed before the Benches of Administrative Tribu nal at Delhi were transferred to the Tribunal at Delhi since common questions of law arose for determination in all the O.As. The Tribunal rendered its main judgment in O.A. No. 206/89 Alok Kumar vs Union of India & Ors., and 61 other connected appeals, which are common. In the connected batch of Civil Appeals Nos. 206 of 89, this Court held that the impelling circumstances which led to the filing of these appeals and the common questions raised therein were so that the appellants could not be allowed to join the Probationary Training along with the candidates who would be appointed on the basis of the CSE 1988. The other judgment was passed on the ground that the Tribunal had set out only the facts in the case of Alok Kumar 's case so that it could not hold that the reasons given by the Government to justify the introduction of the impugned proviso have any rational nexus to the object of the scheme of recruitment to the All India Services or/and whether such reasons are arbitrary, unfair and unjust. The Court also held that in view of the power conferred by the second proviso to Rule 4 of the Civil Service Examination Rules (C.S.E. Rules) introduced by Notification No. 13016/4/86 AIS(1) dated 13 12 1986, the appellants were not entitled to appear in the C.S., or to sit for the main examination since the Tribunal has upheld the validity of the second Proviso to Rule4 of the Rules. The appeals filed against the said judgment and order were dismissed by this Court on 20 8 1990. In view of this decision, the Court directed that all those candidates who have been allocated to any of the Central Services, Group ' A ' or I.P., and who have appeared in civil services Main Examination, 1988/1989 under the Interim orders of Tribunal for Civil Services Examination, 1989 or 1989 under the admis sion of the Tribunal and are within the permissible age limit and have succeeded to be given benefit of their success subject to the provisions of Rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The appellants in C.A No. 5569/90, who had been allocated by the UPSC to the I.I.T.S, were given benefit under the said order. In all those cases, the respondents who have not been allocated, were directed to be permitted to appear again in the preliminary C.C. Examination, 1987 and they were given benefits of their successful success subject only to the provi sions of Rule17 of the CPC. The respondents filed appeals against the aforesaid judgment and orders before this Court. In C.P No. 1071/90 the appellants had preferred an application in December 1986 to sit at the next Civil Services examination, which was held by the Union Public Service Commission (UPSC for short) in June 1987 and the result was declared in July 1987. The C.M.C., who had earlier filed his application in Decem ber 1986 to appear for the preliminary exami nation in 1987, but this application was rejected on the grounds that the candidates were not eligible to sit in the next CSE and they had already appeared for the C SE 1988 even before he received the offer of appointment dated 2.1.1989. The appellant challenged his order of detention under section 3(1)(i) of the (COFEPOSA for short) by filing a writ petition before the High Court and that application, had been dismissed. The High Court held that on 25th November, 1986 while the detaining authority was assisted by a Deputy Collector and a Superintendent of Central Excise, the detenu was denied the assistance of a retired Assistant Collector of Customs and should the same had been refused. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that if Sundararajan had been permitted to assist the appellant his case would have been better placed before the Advisory Board. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The detaining authority had the assistance and the refusal of such assistance to the detenu, was not justified. [792B] 2.1 In the instant case, on 25.11.1986 while the detention order was confirmed, the appellant was denied his assistance in such circumstances. [788C D] 3.2 The detaining authorities had the benefit of the Advisory board and the rejection of such request to the appellant, was bad and continued detention of the appel lant became vitiated. [789E F] 4. In the facts of the case, it is clear that on 26th November 1986 while detaining authority is assisted by Deputy Collector, and a superintendent of Central excise, the detenue was denied assistance of the retired Assistant Collec tor of Customs. On the recommendation of the Board, the detention orders were confirmed. The appellant was a clearing and forwarding agent at Madras and was said to be a young man aged about 26 or 27 years. [781F G] 5. In view of the position of law and the facts in the case it is not possible to reject the contention that if the detaining authorities or the Government takes the aid of a legal practitioner or a legal adviser before the Board the detenu must be allowed the facility of appearing before the board through a legal Practitioner. [784E] 6. The rule in A. K. Roy etc. vs Union of India & Anr., ; referred to.

The Government of India, by a notification dated September 30, 1946, issued under r. 75 A(2) Of the Defence of India Rules (hereinafter called the Rules), framed under the Defence Of India Rules, 1939, directed that the goods should be requisitioned and acquired under the orders and notices already referred to. The Government of india, by an order dated September 20, 1946 made requisition of the said property for the purpose of securing the defence British India, public safety, the maintenance of public order or the efficient prosecution of war, or for maintaining supplies and services essential to the life of the community, that Government may by order in writing requisition any property movable or immovable and may make such further orders as appear to it to be expedient. The respondent challenged the validity of the requisition on the grounds (1) that the requisitioned goods were not served with the notices of acquisition; (2) that they were not properly served and therefore there was no acquisition of property on September 30. 1946, as provided by r. 74 A(3); and (4) that in view of the provisions of r. 76 A(5), the Government which was claiming ownership through the mills was also subject to a liability to pay compensation for the requisitioned articles. Held, that the notice of acquisition in this case was served on the respondent on September 20. 1946 and the notice dated September 15, 1946 issued by the Government of West Bengal under r, 75 A (2), Of the Rules was valid and binding on the respondents. The notice of the decision to acquire was given to the various managing agents of the mills as required by r, 74 A (1), and that the respondent was not entitled to any compensation for his requisitioned articles because the requisition order did not contain in so many words that it was being addressed " the managing agent of such and such mill, but the schedule attached made it clear that was addressed as managing agent. The word " service" used in r. 77 A (3) Of 0. XXIX, r. 2(a), means that provided in 0. XXI, r., 2(b), by effecting service on the principal officer of the Mills, namely, the managing agents. Held further, that as the notice was not served on him, there could be no valid and effective requisition. The words " service of such an order" in r, 77 A(1) (b) Of O.XXIX, R. 75A (2)(a), do not mean that the order of requisition must be brought to the knowledge of the person whose interests are being affected by it and that this was not done in this ease for neither the holders of delivery orders nor the mills were apprised of the orders of requisition on September thirty, 1946. Held also, that service of notice of requisition in this Case on the managing agency of the mill was effective service on April 30, 1947, and the respondent could not be said to have been served with a notice under r., 75 A of the Defence Rules.

The assessee, a Private Limited Company, was assessed to income tax for the assessment years 1963 64 and 1964 65. The Income Tax Officer did not agree and the matter was ultimately taken to the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal. The High Court answered the question in favour of Revenue and against the assessee following the decision of this Court in Metal Box Company of India Ltd. vs Their Workmen, ; , referred to. In Metal Box Co. Ltd. etc. vs Commissioner of Income tax, Andhra Pradesh etc., , the distinction between provision and reserve is stated in the following words: "The distinction between a provision and a reserve is in commercial accountancy fairly well known. Provisions made against anticipated losses and contingencies are charges against profits and therefore to be taken into account against gross receipts in the P & L accounts and the balance sheet. On the other hand, reserves are appropriations of profits, the assets by which they are rep resented being retained to form part of the capital employed in the business. Provisions are usually shown in the balance sheets by way of deductions from the assets in respect of which they were made whereas general reserves and reserve funds are shown as part of their proprietor 's interest. (See Spicer & Pegler 's Book keeping and Accounts, 15th Edn. p. 42). " While approving the said statement it was stated in Vazir Sultan Tobacco Co.Ltd. etc., that the assessee itself called it a provision. It did not call it a reserve nor was it set apart or appropriated as a reserve. The question referred to four items, namely, (i) amount set apart for contingent Rs. 4,50,000 liability (taxation) (ii) amount which is a reserve and should be included in its capital for the purposes of the Act. The assessee contended that inasmuch as no order levying additional tax under section 23A was made on or before the date relevant to the assessment year 1963 64, the said amount cannot be treated as a provision; and (iii) since no order imposing additional tax was passed with respect to the said assessment year, it could not be treated to be a provision, Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The expression "the distinction between "provision" and reserve" is stated to be used in the sense of "business". [113C] 2. In the circumstances of the case, there must be held that the High Court was right in holding it to be the a provision made towards a liability which had attached on account of the issuance of a notice. [114E F] 3. The distinction between the provisions and reserve was stated by the assessee in Vaz Nazir Sultan Tobacco Company Ltd. & Anr.

The petitioners in these writ petitions were direct recruits to the Indian Railway Service of Engineers (Class 1) (hereafter referred to as 'Engineers ' at places). While the President was the appointing authority of the Engineers, the Railway Board was the selecting authority of officers. The petitioners challenged the validity of the classification on the ground that they formed one class under the Indian Railways Establishment Board and supported their claim on diverse grounds so as to obtain the result that all Assistant Engineers formed one category under the I.P.C. and supported the claim on various diverse grounds, namely, (1) officers were appointed to temporary posts on the cadre of Engineers and that their seniority had to be reckoned on the basis of their length of continuous service, though they conceded that in any given year, the candidates appointed as Engineers on the date of selection by the Union Public Service Commission was placed above those appointed on the said basis of selection; (2) officers who were recruited by selection, but both by the Railways Board and the Railway Boards as respondents. Dismissing the writ petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The distinction between, the two services was well marked in Katyani Dayal 's case and the important question of equality was once for all settled. To find fault with it, at this juncture again on the touch stone of equality dimension would be to unsettle a settled position. That venture is neither in the interest of justice nor in the interests of service. When there has been complete absorption of the personnel of one service into the other, and the seniority of the absorbers is to be counted from their date of absorption as stipulated in their appointment matters and as held by this Court with weightage of half the length of service subject to a maximum of five years, it would otherwise be imprudent now, at that point of time to dig up old issues. The rule of weightage also appears to us to be reasonable and this is a pattern which has been noticed and approved in many a Service. Similarly when the dispute raised between the Officers in a representative capacity and Engineers not so represented, in Katakyani 's Case (supra), still it was a dispute raised before this Court which has already been decided finally. A dispute now sought to be raised under Article 32 of the Constitution between the officers in a Representative capacity and engineers not so representing, in the Katyni Dayal ' 's cases (supra). [1025E F] 2. The principle of constructive res judicata would bar the re agitation of the issues decided in Katalani Dayal vs Secretary, Home (Police) Department, Government of Bihar & Ors., ; and Direct Recruit Class II Engineering of officers Association vs State of Maharashtra & Ors. , ; and direct Recruit class II Engineering Officers Association vsState of Maharashtra and Ors., [1988] Supp. SCC 519, referred to.

The appellant was convicted and sentenced to various terms of imprisonment. The Ordinance provided that the Special Court shall try such offences or classes of offences as the State Government may, by general or special order in writing direct. Section 11 empowered the State Govern ment to constitute Special Courts for any area or for the whole of the State or any particular area, and section 12 empowered the Central Government to constitute a Special Court for such "areas" which was specified in the notification. The appellant challenged the validity of the Ordinance on the ground that it violated article 14 Of the Constitution as it had been passed by the State Legislature beyond the competence of a legislature and was therefore void. Held, that the Ordinance was not ultra vires section 11 of the Saurashtra Ordinance and was not intra vires. It was not correct to say that section 11 was not discriminatory in so far as it authorised the State Gov ernment to direct "offences" or classes or cases to be tried by the Special Courts constituted under the Act. The Legislature had left it to the State Govt. to classify offences or class of offences or categories of cases for the purpose of the ordinance, for the State was in a better position to judge the needs and exigencies of the state and the Court would not lightly interfere with the decision of the Government. Benoarilal 's case (1) L.R. 476 measure, referred to. The fact that the deviations from normal procedure were by no means calculated to imperil the chances of a fair and impartial trial was not so many or vital as in the Bengal case, did not affect the result, as the defect of absence of a reasonable or rational classification was still there. It is no answer to the charge by A of discrim inatory legislation to say, that B & C had also been placed in the same category as himself when he finds that D, E and F also liable for the same or kindred offences have been left untouched and are to be dealt with by ordinary courts under the normal procedure.

The appellants were charged with the offence of theft and murder. The prosecution case was that on the night of 16/17 February, 1968, the deceased had reported by Exh. Ka 7 dated 22.1.1968 that accused persons Om Prakash (A 1) and Sheo Gopal (A 3) had committed theft of timber belonging to the village school managed by him. A few days later on 26.1.,1968, the brother of Ram Shree (P.W.2) and his wife Ram Shree(P.Ws. 2 and 8) were sleeping in their house in Makhauli village Mauji Lal in the western kotha and PW 2 and her children in the eastern kothakha between which there was a barotha. There was a lighted lantern hanging from a peg at a height of 6 feet from the floor on the northern wall of the eastern Kotha of the house of the deceased.
