The deceased Mauji Lai and his two sons were sleeping near the cot of the western Kothaka. On hearing some commotion, the miscreants entered the eastern side of the northern kothara and PW 1 and his children in a tin shed situated west of the southern kotkha. There were about a month before this occurrence, Mauji lal (A 4) forcibly occupied Gaon Sabha land. In 1967 there was rioting in the village to which the prosecution party and accused belong. On 26.2.1968, PW 2 raised the wick of lantern material Exh. III, which had been lowered previously, and there was sufficient light in the kotcha for recognising the miscreants. The appellants were tried by the Sessions Judge, Kanpur in Sessions Trial No. 172 of 1969, in which all 18 accused persons were tried. The trial court acquitted nine accused, Bhoop Singh (A 5), Virendra (A 6) and Chandra Prakash ( A 7). The High Court dismissed the appeal filed by the State against the acquittal of the other nine accused. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. There is no reason whatsoever for not accepting the evidence of PW 2 who undoubtedly was in the northern Kotkha where the main part of the occurrence has taken place and must have had sufficient opportunity to indentify with the help of the lantern which was burning, the appellants who were previously known to her and not strangers and she has received as many as 19 injuries during the course of the incident which had gone on for about 15 20 minutes. The noise created during the occurrence had attracted the attention of the Sub Inspector of Police who belonged to some other police station and was in another village situate a couple of miles away from the one in which the scene of occurrence is situate. It is, therefore, not possible to agree with the learned Sessions Judge that no reliance could be placed on the evidence. [576F H] 2. The submission that PW 7 could have had a sufficient "glimpse" of the miscreants so as to be in a position to identify them.

The respondent, a bus operator, was terminated by the appellant Corporation on the ground of unsatisfactory service. The services of the respondent were terminated in accordance with section 25F of the . The respondent challenged the order of termination before the Labour Court which held that the discharge amounted to retrenchment as defined in section 2(oo) of the and those orders were bad for non compliance with the provisions of section 25 F of the Act. The appellant Corporation came before this Court by special leave. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the consensus of judicial opinion in later decisions of this Court is against the appellant 's stand. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. When a portion of the staff or labour force is discharged as surplusage in a continuing business, there are (a) termination of the service of a workman; and (b) by the employer. for any reason whatsoever, otherwise than as a punishment inflicted by way of disciplinary action. [787F] 2. The expression 'termination of service for any reasons whatsoever ' is understood to mean what they plainly say, it is difficult to escape the conclusion that the expression 'retrenchment ' must include every termination of service of the workman by an act of the employer.[787G H; 788A] 3. When the Act itself provides a dictionary for the words used in the statue, there is no doubt that when the Act themselves provides a precise dictionary for them, the words employed in the statute are understood to include what they clearly say, but this is not so in the instant case. [788B C] 4. The question of the correct interpretation of the definition of 'ret retrenchment ' in section2(oo)(d) of Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 has been left open. [789C D] 5. When an portion of staff or the labour force which is discharged by way Of disciplinary action, voluntary retirement of the workmen, retirement of a probationer would also amount to retrenchment. [781E F] 6. The definition expressly excludes termination of services as a 'punishment inflicted by means of disciplinary proceedings '. If such a position were adopted, the termination would be ab initio void for violation of principle of natural justice or for not following the procedure prescribed for imposing punishment. It is not necessary to dilate on the point nor to refer to the earlier decisions of the Supreme Court to both of which one of us was a party. [783E F; 784A] 7. The law has been subsequently amended as already indicated. In the series of cases that have come later, the Constitution Bench decision has been examined and the ratio indicated therein has been confined to its own facts. The view expressed by this Court in that case obviously did not meet with the approval of Parliament and, therefore, the law has now been subsequently revised as already stated.

The assessee, South Eastern Railway, disposing of unclaimed and unconnected goods for money consideration, applied to the Commercial Tax Officer for cancellation of the registration of the assessee as a "dealer" under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941. The Commercial Tax officer examined the case and did not accept the contention that the assessee was not a " dealer". On 6 June 1959 he made an order rejecting the application on the basis that the disposal of unclaimed goods for valuable consideration was a regular feature of the asses see 's activities, and that therefore a sale of goods took place. The revision application was rejected on 27 January 1960 on the finding that the sales effected by the assessee were sales under the Act and that the assesseee fell within the scope of the Act. The High Court held that a transfer of property was involved in the auction held by the assesses and that, therefore, a sale took place, and the Board further held that the systematic and organised charac ter of business carried on by the assesee clothed him with the status of a "business" under section 56 of the Indian Railways Act. Allowing the appeals to this Court, HELD: 1. The activity of so disposing of the goods was adjunctive to the principal activity of the carriage of goods by the Railway. It is an activity which may be regarded as necessarily incidental or ancillary to its business as carrier of the Goods. It seems to South Eastern Rail was a "manufacturer" for the purposes of the Bengal Reve nue (Sales tax) Act 1941. [781 E] 2. The activities of so disposed of were adjun tractive to their principal activity as carrier and of the t he goods. It appears to South Western Railway was a 'dealer" for purposes of section 2(c) of the said Bengal Finance Act, 1940. In the other case, the assessee Eastern Railway disposed of scrap and unserviceable material lying with it. The case is covered directly by the decision of this Court in the District Controller of Stores, Northern Railway, Jodhpur vs The Assistant Commercial Tax Offi cer & Anr., [1976] 37 S.T.C. 423. In these circumstances, the appeals are allowed, the judgment of the High Court in each case is set aside and the questions referred to the High court are answered in each ease in favour of the revenue and against the assessee.

The appellants were convicted of certain offences arising out of the overt acts committed by them. The main statement on which reliance was placed by the prosecution was that the moneys of the Bharat Insurance Company were diverted to Union Agencies by the transactions proved by the Prosecution, and that the proceeds of the sale and purchase of securities had not been credited in the books of the Union Agencies. Held, that the evidence showed that the money was received from the Insurance Company for nothing which was due to Bhagwati Trading Company from that company and that most of the money were being paid to the Union agencies for payment of which Bhagwati Trading Co. had no liability and that it could not have been possible for the prosecution to lead direct evidence about Gurha 's knowledge with respect to the full working of the scheme to provide for the losses of the union Agencies from the funds of the Insurance Companies. Dalmia vs The State of Bihar, ; , followed. In the circumstances of the case the reasonable conclusion can be that they mentioned Bhagwati Trading company as that represented the true state of affairs and Chokhani had to inform the Delhi Office of the Indian Union Agencies about the source of the moneys he was receiving for the Union Agency to meet its losses. The fact that the funds were diverted by the Insurance Co. in contravention of the manner in which he was to deal with that money did not make any effort to know what is required to be know by one earring on business for the purchase and sale of securities, and any attempt to have known this would have necessarily led him to know that securities were being purchased on behalf of the insurance Company and were not delivered to it and that Bhagwati Trading Companies purchased no securities from the Union Bank Agencies and that any payment by it to the latter was for something which B wait Trading Company was not liable to pay.

The appellants were allotted to serve in connection with the affairs of the former Saurashtra State. By virtue of section 8 of the States Reorganization Act 37 of 1956, the new State of Bombay was formed and by section 82 of the , the new state of Bombay which included the territories of the State of Saurashtra and Kutch was formed. Section 115 of the made provisions relating to services other than All India Services were made and by s.82 of the Act, the Government of Bombay sanctioned certain rules called "The Allocated Government Servants ' (Absorption, Seniority, Pay & Allowances) Rules 1957". The appellants were given notice of their appointment as clerks in the Secretariat Service of the erstwhile Saurashtra State of Gujarat. In exercise of the powers under article 309 of the Constitution, the Central Government issued a notification to the effect that the persons shown in the accompanying statement should be treated to have been regularly appointed in the posts shown against their names in column 4 of the statement with effect from the date shown in column 5 in the Departments mentioned in column 3 of the Statement. The appellants challenged the validity of the order on the grounds, inter alia, (1) that the order violated r. 138 of the Recruitment Rules framed by the Government in 1957; and (2) that it contravened the provisions of the Allocating Government Servants (Affees, Seniority Pay & Allowance) Rules, 1957. The High Court held that since the impugned order purported to amalgamate the former State and Kutch States personnel with the Gujarat Secretariat Service contrary to the terms of r.138 of the recruitment rules framed by it in 1957, and that the Government had no authority to vary the method of recruitment provided by the statutory rule 138 of Recruitment Rules which was mandatory, the orders of transfer to the Secretariat could not operate as absorption under the Allacated Government servants ' ( Absor absorption, Seniority or Pay & allowances) Rules. The State appealed to this Court. HELD: (i) The expression "absorption" has not been used in the order but that will not justify an inference that there was no intention to absorb the former and Kutch states personnel in the secretariat. [519 E] (ii) The Government of Gujarat had the authority to transfer, subject to the Constitution and the rules made under article 311 of the Constitu tion, any public servant to render service which by his training and aptitude he was competent to do. Transfer of the personnel from the States of Saurashtra & Kutch to the secretaries in the State cannot be challenged, and the that because they were posted between 1956 and 1960 in the Districts they will not be deprived of their statutory right under section 115(7) proviso. [525 E] N. Raghavendra Rao vs Deputy Commissioner, South Kanara, Mangalore ; , followed. (iii) The order dated August 19, 1966 was contrary to r. 13 of the Rules framed under article 310 of the Consti tution in 1957 and that it altered the conditions of service of the applicants; and that there had riot been any equivalence established between the posts in the Secretariats. of the states of Saurashtra, and Kutch and the posts In the new States and Kutch, after they were allotted duties to the State Government of Saurashtra were posted and assigned duties in various districts in Saurashtra and Saurashtra. But in the absence of evidence to show that the previous approval of the Central Govern ment was obtained, their right to be absorbed in equivalent posts in tho Secretariat and on terms not prejudiciallyvanta geous to those they were already entitled except with the previous, approval of Central Government.

The petitioners of the second category purchase oil seeds for use in manufacture of edible oils. The surplus oil seeds were sold to other dealers, registered or unregistered, inside and outside the State. The petitioners challenged the validity of the Punjab General Sales Tax (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1967 by which they amended section 15 of the Central Act. The contention was that section 2(ff), 5(1)(a)(vi) was in conflict with section 15 and was also unconstitutional being in violation of article 14 and 19. The State contended that there was a possibility of tax being levied at more than one stage, the provisions of the first proviso notwithstanding. The contentions were rejected by this Court on the ground that it was not necessary to refer to the Ordinances. HELD: (i) The question as to how far a party can ask for refund without the order of assessment being set aside by appropriate proceedings is highly doubtful; because at the time when the actual order of assess ment is passed, in certain eases, it may not be possible for a party to say whether he was entitled to exemption or not, under sub cl. (vi) of section 5(2)(a), negatives the assumption that the normal rule, under the Act, in respect of declared goods, is to levy the tax on the first purchaser. It will be absolutely difficult if not impossible for persons like the appellant, to collect materials in this behalf, because, there is no provision, contained either in the Act or the rules, on the basis of which it will be entitled to be supplied with all the material information, relevant for sustaining a request for refund. If the Central Sales Tax makes it mandatory that the tax can be collected only at one stage in our opinion, it is not enough for the State to say that a person, who is not liable to pay tax must nevertheless pay it in the first instance and then claim refund, at a later stage. [548 G H] (ii) The contention that section 5 (2)(A)(vi), was in inconsistent with section 5 of the Act was not correct. The question whether a party could ask for a refund without an order of Assessment being set down aside by proper proceedings is purely academic and it will depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case. [549 A B] (iii) The tax can, therefore, be collected at one point in time, in our view, be levied only at the one stage at which the tax was to be levied and because under section 15(1) of the , there could be no liability for payment of tax unless this stage was so stated in the statute or the Rules thereunder. [550 E] (iv) The levy of tax at one time is not discriminatory as it is against the equality clause and article 304 of the Constitution. [551 F G] (v) The word 'dealer ' in section 2 (ff), and in the proviso to section 1IAA, it was submitted that there could not be any discrimination between goods so imported and local goods. It was also contended that the levy of sales tax at different stages remained still and the Act continued to be in conflict With the Central Acts on the same reasons on which the State Legislature proceeded. [552 A B]. (vi). The question is now in the hands of the dealer himself and it is for him to decide whether he would not claim the benefit of section 11AA and ask for an refund or in future transactions delete the sales from his taxable turnover when he was not the last dealer liable to payment of the tax.

The appellants who were the representatives of three original plaintiffs instituted a suit against the respondent for enforcement of a mortgage, against the present respondent. The suit was contested by all the defendants except defendant No. 1 against whom it proceeded ex parte and there was a preliminary decree passed on May 15,1937, by which a sum of Rs. 1,08,098 was directed to be paid by defendant No 1 and defendants 3 to 7 in default of which the plaintiffs were declared entitled to apply for a final decree for sale of the mortgaged properties and the suit was dismissed against defendant No 2. Against this decree two appeals were taken to the High Court, one by defendants 3 and 4 to 7 being Appeal No. 48 of 1938 who contended that the mortgage debt was one and indivisible and even though different amounts were mentioned as payable by two groups of defendants in the decree, the decree holders were bound under the terms of the decree to release the entire mortgaged property even on payment of the amount directed to he paid by them under the decree. The High Court accepted this contention and held that defendant No . 1 was entitled to have the debt scaled down in favour of defendant No, 2 to 7 as scaled up by the High court in favour Of defendants 2 to7. Held, further, that the view taken by the District Judge was right and should not have been disturbed. The fact that in the working of the Madras Agriculturists ' Relief Act alongside the provisions of the Transfer of Property Act several curious and novel situations had arisen for which it was not possible always to find logical solu tions. They then proceeded to discuss the various decisions of the High Courts which had a bearing on this point and the conclusion which they reached may be summed up in their words as follows: "It is no doubt somewhat odd that when a person is declared liable to pay a larger amount he should on payment or tender of a smaller amount get his property exonerated from liability but this is inherent in and arises out of the proposition established by the decisions already dealt with, namely, that by the application of the principle of unity and unconsciency of a mort gagor decree a non agriculturist can indirectly get relief which he cannot directly get. The general law undoubtedly is that a mortgage decree is one and cum indivisible and exceptions to this rule are admitted in special circumstances where the integrity of the mortgage has been disrupted at the instance of the mortgagee himself; e.g., when there is severance of the interests of the mort gawalli with the consent of the mortgagor or a portion of the equity of redemption is vested in the latter. It is to be noted, however, that this principle does not apply to the case before us. The ratio decidendi in all these cases is not applicable to the present case.

The appellants filed a suit against the first respondent, who was the landlord of the premises in dispute under section 13 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 (Bombay Act VII of 1944) for eviction of the first respondents from the premises on the ground that they were trespassers and had no right to be on the premises. The City Civil Court held that it had jurisdiction to entertain the suit but dismissed the suit on the view that there was no lawful subletting by the first plaintiff of the said premises to the second and third plaintiffs as the provisions of section 10 of the Act had not been properly complied with. Against this decision, the appellants appealed to the Bombay High Court which was summarily dismissed. Thereafter, the present suit No. 2178 of 1954 was filed by the appellants in the City Civil court on September 20, 1954. In this suit the appellants prayed for a declaration that the first and third respondents were lawful sub tenants of the second respondent and were entitled to possession, use and occupation of the same as subtenants thereof. The Small Causes Court held against them. On appeal, the High Court dismissed the appeal holding that the City civil court had no jurisdiction to try the suit. It did not pronounce any opinion on the merits of the appellants ' case. Held, that the suit in substance was a denial of the right of the respondents as tenants and the premises had been lawfully sublet by them to the Second and third appellants. The suit related to possession of the Premises and the right to evict any of the plaintiffs was denied on the grounds that the second plaintiff was a tenant within the meaning of the provisions Of section 28 of the Rent Act and the Premises had been validly sublet by him to the first appellant and the latter was not entitled to remain in possession, that is to say, that none of the defendants to that suit were protected from eviction by any of them. The claim of the Respondents was one which arose out of the . Act or any of its provisions and only the courts specified in section 28 and no other could deal with it and decide the issue.

The respondent who was the managing director of a private company, filed a suit against the appellant and the appellants for the declaration that he had ceased to be a director on account of his failure to attend the directors ' meetings. The trial court accepted all the contentions of the respondent and made the declarations claimed. The High Court held that the appointment of the appellant was void in view of section 312 of the Indian Penal Code, and that section 312 did not prevent a managing director from appointing his successor, assuming assignment included appointment but it did not preclude a managing directors from assigning his office or appointing his successors which was what Dadoba had done. The appellants came to this Court by special leave. Held: (i) The High Courts were right in holding that the word "assign" in section 312 meant "appointment". The word "resign" is used in the sense of a term and not in the context of the Act. It does not mean "appointment." The word 'resignor ' in section 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, means "appointment", and includes appointment of his successor by a director. The word has been used in connection with the business of the company and it is not possible to hold that the appellant had any power under the articles to appoint a person as his successor. (ii)The section does not intend by section 317 to prevent that a managing Director cannot be appointed for a term exceeding five years at a time. The section was intended to protect the interests of the shareholders and the shareholders, and it would be an unwarranted extension of this principle to hold in regard to section 86B at the most that an appointment made outside the powers legally conferred by the articles is wholly ineffective and therefore is not an appointment at all and hence again does not result in an evasion of section 313.

The respondent filed an eviction petition against the appellants and one other partnership firm, carrying on business in the name and style of M/s. Adeshwar Glass Mart on the ground that they had unlawfully and without the consent of the respondent sublet the said shop let out to the respondent. The Trial Court held that the respondent was not entitled to any relief under section 10(2)(ii)(a) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and 419 Rent Control) Act, 1960. The Appellate Authority dismissed the appeal upholding the finding of unlawful subletting by the appellants. The appellants then preferred a Civil Revision Petition in the High Court which was dismissed holding that it is only by virtue of the provisions of order 30 of the Code of Civil Procedure 1908, that a firm can sue and be sued in its own name without the partners being impleaded. In appeal to this Court on behalf of the appel lants it was contended that the Code was not applicable to the proceedings under the Rent Act either and hence the ratio laid down in the aforesaid decision was directly applicable to them. Dismissing the Appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding that the provisions contained in section 10 (2)(iv) of Tamil Nadu Building (Lease & 419 Rent control) Act 1960 were not applicable. [420E] 2. In the instant case no such objection has been raised at all till the stage of Special Leave and it is certainly not open to the appellants to raise such an objection at a very late stage and thereby delay matters for a number of years. This contention must, therefore, be negatived. [421F G] Chhotelal Pyarelal, the partnership firm and others vs Shikharchand, , relied on by Mr. Nayar, the objection to the main tainability of the petition was raised at the earliest stage and was wrongly negatived by the Trial Court. In fact this Court observed as follows: "But we agree with the Division Bench of the High court that this cannot by itself result in the dismissal of the application. It would be merely a case of misdescription of the respondents to the application and this misde scription can be corrected at any stage of the proceedings. There can be no doubt that the partners of the firm are before the Court though in a wrong name. [416F G; 420A] Chhotal Pyarelal vs Shikherchand, ; , relied upon by Mr, Nayar, for the appellants it was not one which would have been fatal to the eviction petition. Had this contention been raised in the Trial court or even in the first Appel late Court, it would have be open to him to amend the eviction peti tion and join the partners as re spondents. [ 420F G]. Chhotelalsal Pyare Lal 's case, relied on.

The Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms (Ceiling on Agricultural Holdings) Act, 1 of 1973 was enacted by the Andhra Pradesh Legislature on January 1, 1973. The constitutional validity of the Andhra Act was challenged before the High Court in a writ petition which was dismissed by a Full Bench of the High court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that by reason of the enactment of the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act 1976 (the Andhra Pradesh Act) the Andhra State Act had become void and inoperative, and that by virtue of section 4(1) of the Act the Andhra Legislature had no competence to enact the Andhra P. Act which was enacted with retrospective effect from January 1 1975 and that the provisions of the said Act were repugnant to the provisions contained in the Central Act so far as the concerned land satisfying both the definition of "land" in the Andhra area Act and the definition "vacant land" in section 2(n) of that Act. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The Andhra Pradesh (Andhra Pradesh Land Reform) (Ceiling On Agricultural Holdings ) Act, 1973 was not an agrarian reform legislation and it is protected against challenge on the ground of infraction of Articles 14, 19 and 31 by the protective umbrella of Article 31A. [1156 C] 2.1 In view of the provisions in the amended Andhra Pradesh Acts, the Andhra Acts were those referred to in section 1(n)(A)(ii) and there can be no doubt that so far the urban agglomerations are concerned, it was not within the legislative competence of the State Legislature to provide for imposition of ceiling on land situate within these urban agglomeration. [1106 D] 2:2 The Andhra Act is an agrarian legislation and the provisions thereof have not reached the common man to any appreciable extent. It is no doubt true that if the AndhraP Act seeks to impose ceiling on lands falling within an urban aggltitute, it would be outside the area of its legislative competence, because it cannot provide for levy of ceiling thereon on land situated within these agglomerates. [1056 E] 2 :3 The Andhra P Pradesh Land Revenue Reforms ( Ceiling on Agricultural Holding) Amendment Act, 1977 was enacted to regulate the ceiling on urban immovable property and acquisition of such property in excess of the ceiling area and all matters connected therewith or ancillary and incidental thereto should be regulated in the State of Andhra Pradesh by Parliament by law. [1256 F] 2(a)(ii). The definition of 'family unit" in Section 2(f) is materially in the same terms as the definition definition of family unit in the Act. Therefore, any property which comes to the share of a divided minor son would in law belong to him and would not be liable to be required as part of joint family property. [1356 F G] 3:4 The AndhraP Pradesh Land Ceiling (Ceiling & Regulation) Ordinance, 1976 is an indirect legislation and does not fall within the purview of the definition in section 3(f).

The workmen of the Hot Mills section resorted to an illegal stoppage of work and on the next day all the three shifts of the hot mills section commenced a 'slow down strike. The workers of the factory were not included therein. The dispute was referred to the Industrial Tribunal which held that all the workmen who turned up on or before October 2, 1953, must be taken back in employment and the appeal on behalf of the workmen raised the question whether full compensation should be given to the work men who were directed to be taken to them back in service without condition and of the two men who came later. The Tribunal found that the decision of the Company to terminate his services was justified. Held, that the two Tribunals below have misdirected themselves as to the true scope and effect of the Standing Orders of the company and their decision with regard to the seven workmen mentioned above cannot be supported. It has been somewhat faintly suggested that if the notice dated August 23, 1953 terminated the services of the workman and the second notice, dated September 17, 1953 operated as a conditional revocation of the earlier notice, then there was no consideration for the condition imposed and the Company could change its mind and ignore the condition. The two Tribunals have mis direct ed themselves as regards the true meaning and effect Of the Standing Order in question and their decisions with regard thereto cannot be upheld. Held further, that when the words used in the notices sufficiently and clearly bring out the intention of the parties it is necessary to refer to other evidence in the record. It was not possible to proceed on the footing that the respondent workmen failed to produce satisfactory evidence of their absence, and that was the reason why they were not taken back by the Company. Held also, further, (per Das J., dissenting) that the Tribunal had misdirect ed themselves in as much as the two Tribunal had found that they were guilty of unauthorised absence and insubordination etc. The workmen were given continuity of service for the entire period of their forced unemployment consequent upon suspension.

The University of Rajas than invited applications for the post of Professor in the department of Botany. The Selection Committee constituted under Section 5 of the Rajasthan University Teachers and Offi cers (Selection for Appointment) Act, 1974 held interviews on 20th June, 1989 and selected Dr. G.S. Nathawat for the said post. Dr. Nhawat retired on 30th September, 1989. The appellant who was already selected and kept in the reserve list was appointed as Professor in a department of the Bot any. Dr., Bhikalal, Dr. Shiv Sharma, Dr, Sudhakar Mishra and Dr. T.N. Bhardwaj who were not selected filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the appointment of Dr. Uma Kant on the ground that the Selection Committee was not constituted in accordance with law and objection was also raised that once a selected person joins the post, the reserve List stood exhausted and the person named in the reserved list could not be appointed against a future vacancy. The writ petition was dismissed by the Single Judge holding that the constitution of the Selection Commit tee was valid but as regards the appointment to Dr. Urea Kant from the reserve lists it was held that once the person selected by the Selection committee had joined, that post was filled and some vacancy was caused thereafter a fresh and de novo selection committee had to be started because that will be a case of future vacancy after the post had been filled up on the recommendations of the selection Committee. The Division Bench also held that the Constitution of the Committee was valid and as regards appointment of Professor from the reserved List it was directed that Dr. Laxmi Kant should be removed from the said posts of Professor of Bt.Nathawat on 30.9.1989. In the appeal by grant of special leave, it was contended for the appellant that once there is a regular vacancy for a post, a Selection Committee has to be constituted and no appointment on such post could have been made from the Reserve List prepared by the selection Commit tionee on 20.6.89 and that even out of the petitioners who had filed the writ petition, Dr., Shiv Sharma himself was kept in reserve list and was there after appointed on the post. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court committed a clear error in restricting the scope of reserve list only against the post for which the selec tion was made and which according to the High court could only be available to the incumbent in the Reserve list if the person recommended in the main list did not join such post. Such interpretation is not borne out from any of the provisions of Section 3(1), Section 5 or sub section (4) of Section 6 of the Act of 1974.

The petitioners who were owners of plots of land in areas round about Bombay, commonly known as Greater Bombay, challenged the validity of certain sections of the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954. The petitioners contended that they had applied through their architect on January 2, 1962 for permission to change the existing user of their lands by putting them to industrial use and had written a letter to the Municipal Commissioner of Bombay for that purpose by which they proposed to construct on a portion of the land in section No. 70 Hissa No. 4 a shed for a factory and other necessary sheds. Along with the said letter, they gave a notice under section 33 of the Act to the effect that their lands were needed for the public purpose of a park in the Development Plan of 'P ' Ward of Greater Bombay. The respondents contended that the application was not made within two months from the date of publication of the development plan and that the power vested in the Town Planning Officer and other authorities under the Act were unguided, arbitrary and uncontrolled and as such infringed the fundamental rights of the petitioners under articles 14, 19(1)(f) and 31 of the Constitution. Held: (i) The provisions of sections 4 to 16(both inclusive) of the Municipal Act, 1922, regarding the levy of contribution towards the cost of the scheme and all other matters relating to the working of the Scheme were unauthorised and unreasonable and that they infringed the right under articles 19( 1)(f), 31 and 31. (ii) The power vested by section 13 was for a matter of no moment for the authority under section 13 is no less than the Municipal Commis sioner himself or the Chief Officer of the municipal Borough or a person exercising the power of an Executive Officer of any local authority. When the power had to be exercised by one of the highest officers of the local, authority intimately connected with the preparation of the Development plan in all its stages it was difficult to envisage what other authority could be entrusted with the work of appeal or revision. The preparation of a tentative development plan or the final development plan was not something which was left to the pleasure or discretion of the Local Authority. [284 D E] (iii)The provisions of section 13 were not ultra vires the Constitution as it was not covered by any of the entries in List 11 or List 111, Seventh Schedule to the Constitution; and even assuming that the State Legislature could pass the Act, nevertheless its provisions regarding the imposition of contribution from the cost to be paid for the scheme were unauthorised. [285 G H] (iv)The power vested under section 14 was not unguided, uncanalised and uncontrolled as such violated the fundamental right of the petitioner under articles14, 19 (1)(g), 31, 31 and 32 of the constitution.

The petitioners who were the petitioners in W.P. No. 234 of 1968, and three others, challenged the validity of the Constitution on the grounds that (i) the award merely fixes or demarcates the boundary between the State of Gujarat in India and West Pakistan regarding which there were disputes and much friction, and by the Award no cession of Indian territory was contemplated; (ii) the area is in different state at different seasons in the year for part of the year it is water and for the remaining part it is land; and (iii) the claim was supported by survey maps, correspondence between the officials of Kutch State and the British Adminis tration. HELD: (i). The dispute related to the boundary of Sind and Kutch as shown in the pre partition maps, which needs to be demarcated on the ground. The agreement between the two States was reached purely as an executive act, and no legislative sanction was obtained by the Government of India to its implementation. [301 D] (ii). The contention that the territory in this sector is contiguous to and in fact is an extension of the mainland of Sind, and apart from the survey maps there is no evidence of exercise of sovereign authority by the Maharao of Kutch at any point of time. Even granting that evidence the evidence about the exercise of the sovereign authority was inconclusive, the claim by Indian citizens to exercise fundamental rights in respect of the territory which formed part of that State before 1948 or was in de facto occupation and in respect thereof it cannot be implemented without the authority of an amendment modifying the boundary. [302 E F] (iii). The award merely fixed or demarcaates the boundaries between the States, is not a part of Indian territories. It is not evidence of the fact that it was territory over which the Maha Rao of Kutch exercised sovereign rights and which by merger of the State became Indian territory. The evidence on which reliance was mainly placed in support of the claim, was the conflicting alignments in the survey and other maps, the claims made by the petitioners. [303 G H] (iv). The argument that the area in this Sector belonged to the Kutch State is inconclusive because of the nature of the terrain, the shifting nature of what was called Rann, the highly discrepant and conflicting claims made from time to time by the British authorities as well as the Kutch state authorities before the State merged with the Dominion of India. [304 F G] (v). The reference to the petitioners and the petitioners urge that the award may be implemented only by an amendment amending modifying the relevant provisions in Schedule 1 to the Constitution, because in giving effect to the award of the Tribunal, cession of India is involved, and the executive is incompetent to cede Indian territory without the authori ty of a constitutional amend ment.

The mortgagor borrowed certain sums from one Rabindra Nath Chakravarty and executed a deed of mortgage whereby he agreed to repay the amount, and encum bered his share in Mauzas Bansjora and Simitanr and for repayment of the amount borrowed with interest at the rate of Rs. 1/8 per mensem. By another deed dated August 27, 192 the mortgagor created a mortgage in favour of Sasindranath Chakravartity and Indra Nath Chakrabartyto secure payment of Rs 5,500 advanced to him and interest thereon. The covenants of this mortgage deed were substantially the same as the covenants of the earlier mortgage deed dated June 14, 1922 and it was agreed that the mortgagees were to receive the instalment of royalty payable in Chaitra in respect of Mauza Bahaldih. Under these mortgages the due date for payment was April 14, 1925. On May 17, 1927, the mortgagor assigned his interest in Mauza Bansjorora to one Mahendra Nath Rai and on October 2, 1927 he assigned his share of the coal mines in Mauza Bahawih to one Moyee Devi. Thereafter in execution of a money decree obtained against the mortgagor, his right, title and interest in mauz Bahaldhih was sold on January 16, 1937 and after th sale was confirmed possession of Mauza Arrabham and Simannar and Bahaldhara. By two deeds dated June 18, 1946, Manimala Devi the plaintiff in the suit out of which this appeal arises obtained assignments of the rights of the mortgagees under the two deeds executed by Manimala Lal Chakravarties and Indranath Chakravarthy to secure payment Of Rs. 5,000 advanced to M and interest therein. The covenant of this deed was substantially the identical with that of the later mortgage deed. By paragraph 14 the mortgagor agreed that in the event of the tenants failing to pay the amount the mortgagor would compensate the mortgagee in respect thereof. By para 13 the mortgagor undertook not to transfer or assign MauzAs Bansjida and Simganr to any person, and had merely assured the mortgagee that he had not assigned the rights in Mauza Arrahldih till the date of mortgage by way of any encumberance to any other person. But that distinction would, for the purpose of ascertaining the true nature of the document, be immaterial, for even in the absence of a covenant not to assign the mortgagor 's interest, so long as the mortgage remained outstanding, the transfer made by the mortgagor of Mauzash Bansj Singh and Simranr Bahald Ranchi could not operate to extend the period of limitation for the suit. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that the mortgagor had lost all his interestin the mortgaged property on May 17 1927, in Mauza Surabyam and Simaminr Baha vs Ahmed. 646 by the two documents dated June 15, 1946 and August 27. 1922, and that the plaintiff 's claim to enforce the mortgage dated August 8, 1922 was at the date when the suit was filed within twelve years from April 14. The period of 12 years commencing from April 1, 1925 under article 132 of the Limitation Act had not expired.

The appellants employ as many as 7.000 workmen in those factories. In order to provide transport facilities to their employees to come to the factories from their respective villages, the appellants provided transport facilities which would pick up passengers from Pune or Khed or Vadgaon or places enroute to TELCO Factory at Pimpri and back. For this journey a nominal charge of Rs. 10 per month was realised by the appellants from the employees. Similarly, for the transport facilities provided to the employees from Pimpri Railway Crossing and onwards to TILCO factory, they were charged at the rate of Rs 5 per month. A charge of RS. 2 per month for the Transport of employees from Chinchvad Village to TLWCO factory at Pimgra and back was levied for the transported of employees of the company from Chinchevad Village, Pune or Lhed or Lhalgaon or Alandi or places in enroutes to TTELCO factory. The appellants contended that these amounts were realised by them only from a particular category of employees and no charges were levied in respect of those employees who were in supervisory grades. In the course of arguments it was pointed out that when the company was prepared to grant free transport facilities, there was no reason why the same amenities should not be extended to the other employees and Mr. Nariman contended that even if a nominal charges is realised from the appellants that would not make the transport a public service vehicle carrying passenger; so as to attract the provisions of section 3 which is the charging section of the Act, the tax could be levied only on passengers who are carried by stage carriage which is of the nature of a public services vehicle. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The Bombay Motor Vehicles (Taxation on Passengers) Act, 1958 has been amended several times right from the year 1960 to 1975. Before analysing the relevant provisions of the Bombay Motor Vehicle Rules 1959, it may be necessary to extract the Preamble to the Act which runs thus: "Whereas it is expedient lo provide for the levy of a tax on passengers, carried in certain classes of public service vehicles. . vehicles in the State of Bombay are not included within the ambit of the taxing provisions of that Act. [361E F] 2(i) The dominant object of the impugned Act was to impose tax on certain classes Of public services vehicles. In other words, the preamble indicates that vehicles which could not be termed as public service Vehicles fell beyond the ambit o the taxing provision of the said Act. Therefore, the transport service in the present case which was registered as private service vehicle falls squarely within the purview of the definition of the expression "public service vehicle" under section 2(7) of the . [361F G] 3(ii) The word "public" has got a well known connotation and means a carriage to which any member of the public can have free access on payment of the usual charges. It cannot by any process of reasoning or stretch of imagination be deemed to include employees of a private company who are given facilities not as members of the Public but as holding a special status, namely, the employees of that Company. Thus, qua public the employees form a separate class and cannot be said to be public as contemplated by rule 2(1).

The appellants, who were residents of the locality and had objected to the grant of a licence for a temporary cinema, applied for a quasi permanent cinema to respondent No. 3 Prem Narayan son of Ganpatlal Chouksey, proprietor Chitra Talkies, Lalbagh, Burhanpur (M.P.) against which a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution by the appellants was dismissed in limine by a speaking order dated 6th March 1978. The second respondent made an application on 5th December 1975 for grant of licence for the temporary cinema and the District Magistrate having jurisdiction issued a no objection certificate vide his order dated 10th February 1976 for a period of six months. This licence was renewed upto 30th June 1976 and there was a further renewal up to 30th September 1976. A subsequent application for renewal was turned down by the Distt. Magistrate on 29th June 1977 on the ground that Paras Talkia with permanent cinema licence which was closed, has now been functioning in the locality, and therefore a renewal of the licence for such a temporary Cinema would not be proper. The appellants filed a writ petition under article 226 questioning the validity of the order dated 27th December 1977 contending that they were residents within the locality as there was no impediment to the granting of such a licence, and that it being a matter left to the subjective satisfaction of the State Government, the State Govt. on being satisfied that there was an impediment to grant of such licence, was perfectly justified in granting the same and therefore it was not a fit case for interference of the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that District Magistrate was not influenced by the fact that there is a mosque, and a temple in the vicinity of the place where the proposed cinema house was to be constructed but he was influenced by an extraneous consideration that a cinema having a permanent cinema license having been re opened in the area there wasno need for a cinema house with a "temporary" licence and that the order granting the no objection Certificate was violative of the principles of natural justice. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that if before the grant or refusal of a permit, the applicant is entitled to notice of hearing of the appeal, and, therefore, the grievance of the appellant without merits because initially when no objection certificates were applied for they did not object and one who has not objected cannot subsequently make a grievance. Dismissing the appeal ^ HELD: 1. The rules envisage issuance of a license for a permanent Cinema and as a first step, selection of a site where the cinema house is to be located. Selection of the site and its clearance by the licensing authority by the issuance of no objection certifi cate is an important step to be taken in the direction of finally constructing a cinema building and obtaining a licence. When any person desires to erect a cinema meaning thereby a place where an exhibition by means of cinematograph is to he given, he must apply for a no objections certificate in respect of the sites where the Cinema house is To be advertised in the manner prescribed inviting the public to file objections. After considering the objections, the licensing author has to decide whether to grant or refuse the noobjection certificate.

The plaintiff instituted a suit against the defendant alleging that by a contract dated September 2, 1957, the defendant agreed to assign to the plaintiffs his leasehold interest under a mining lease in respect of 184 acres of land in Kudrekanave Kaval, Hosadurga Taluk and claiming specific performance of the contract. The Trial Court decreed the suit but the High Court allowed the appeal holding that there was no concluded contract between the parties. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the plaintiff had failed to establish the new case; (2) the suit was not an acceptance of the offer, and (3) the mere filing of a bill in a suit to enforce specific performance was regarded as sufficient acceptance of his offer unless the offer had been withdrawn before the filing of the suit. HELD: (i) The plaint in O.S. No. 46 of 1957 was not a suit for specific performance. [584 D] (ii) In the peculiar facts of Bloxam 's case a contract to take shares was concluded by an oral application for shares followed by allotment though no notice of allotment was given to the applicant.

The appellants were office bearers of M/s. S.K.G. Sugar Ltd., (Lauriya). A complaint was registered against them under sub rule (3) of Rule 3 of the Sugarcane (Control) Order, 1955 read with section 7 of the , on the ground that they had failed to pay to the sellers the price of sugarcane purchased by them within the time prescribed. The appellants contended that the investigation was being carried on against them and that investigation on various grounds was not in accordance with law. The High Court held that there was no merit in this contention. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the regulation of price of sugar is expressly dealt with by the Bihar Sugar Factories Control Act, 1937; (2) the Regulation of the price at which any essential commodity may be bought or sold and in addition to the Sugar Control Order 1955 which was issued by the Central Government on 27th August, 1955, it also issued the Sugarcane Control Order,1955, on the same date investing it with the power to fix the price; (3 ) the regulation is a valid one and does not infringe article 19(1) of the Constitution. HELD: (i) The question whether the cultivation and sale of sugarcane can be regulated under section 3 of 'the Act came up for consideration for this Court in Ch. Tika Ramji & Ors. vs The State of U.P., [1966] 1 S.C.R. 491, followed. (ii) The power conferred on the Government under section 2 of the Act cannot be challenged as invalid. There is no substance in the contention that the impugned order contravenes the fundamental right guaranteed to the citizens under article 19 (1 ). No fundamental right is conferred on a buyer not to pay the price or to pay it whenever he pleases. The contention that in view of section 11 of the . Act no cognizance could have been taken of the offence alleged was premature. [677 D E] Ch.Tika Ramji and Ors.v The State Of U. P., ; , referred to.

The Government of Karnataka decided to adopt a policy to encourage rapid industrialisation. An order dated 12th January, 1977 was issued which recited that the Government had on 30th November 1966, issued directions indicating the incentives that would be given to entrepreneurs starting new industries in the Mysore State. The said order stated that the scheme of concessions adopted by the Government earlier had given room for many types of misuse and the earlier orders had not prescribed any ceiling limits or restrictions on the quantum of refund of sales tax or concession to be granted. The High Court held that the concession granted by the said order dated 30th June, 1969 was being misused and undue advantage was being taken of the same. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the doctrine of Promissory Estoppel was not applicable in the present case because it was found by the Govern ment of Karnataka that the concessions granted under the said orders were being misused, and undue hardship was being enjoyed by the same; and that the grant of concession constituted a promissory estoppel against the Government on the basis of which they had acted by starting new industrial units requiring investment of considerable funds and the Government was not entitled to go back or that promise as it had sought to do by the order dated December 12, 1977. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The Government had, therefore, failed to establish the requisite ground or the basis for which it might be allowed to go on its promise. [948D] 2.1 In order to test the validity of the order of 30th May, 1969 one has to see the substance of the concession given under the order and not merely certain words used out of context. Although the benefit regarding sales tax granted to the new industries is by way of refunds of sales Tax paid to the extent stated in the Order, it is clear that in effect, the benefit granted is in the nature of an exemption from the payment of the sales tax and reduction in the sales Tax liability to the amount stated in tho order. [947E F] 2:2 The Government has, therefore failed to prove the requisite grounds or the foundation of which it may be allowed. [946G H] 3.

The appellants were tried for the offences under Sections 147, 148, 302 and 302 read with Section 149 I.P.C. on the allegations that they caused the death of Madda Laksha mandas of village Ramaraogudem on November 1, 1980 near the Tobacco garden of A 1. The Trial Court acquitted A 7 of all the charges. A 1 to A 6 were however found guilty for the offence punishable under Sections 148 and 302 I. P.C., but convicted them under Section 148 and sentenced them to imprisonment for life. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of A 4 to A 5. The appellants contended that after the acquittal of four accused persons by the courts below the conviction of the appellants under Section 149 and on applying 149 I P. C. cannot be sustained. It was argued that the appellants being three in number, could not have formed an unlawful assembly within the definition of Section 141 I.p.C.; that apart from the seven accused persons there were some other unidentified persons who were involved in the crime; that the High court clearly fell into error in confirming the conviction under Sections 302 and 149 IP. C., on the ground that they formed an assembly alongwith some unidentified person; that as the appellants formed an unarmed assembly along some un unknown persons, there was no question of their forming an unlawful unlawful assembly with the common object of killing the deceased; that there was force in the contention of the learned counsel for the appel lants that after acquittal of 4 accused persons, by the Courts below the sentence of death could not be sustained; and that the conviction was bad. On behalf of the respondent it was contended that the appellant being three persons in number could not had formed an incor pation within the meaning of Section 2(1)(a) of the Act. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. There is force in this contention of PW 1, the wife of the deceased, PW 2, the daughter of the de ceased. The evidence that the complainant and the accused belonged to opposite factions and there was long standing enmity between the parties. During the last 30 years, there had been murders and rioting between the two factions. The deceased Madda Padshamandas was undergoing life imprisonment for the murder of one of the persons belonging to the group of the accused. He had come on parole. On the day of occurrence at about 7.00 A.M., when he was passing near the field of A I he was attacked by the accused party. According to the eye witness, PW 1 and the deceased belonged to the opposite factors and there were long standing rivalry between the ac cused and the parties; during the last thirty years, There had been fences and riling between the said two fares. The appellant acted in the forefront of their common intention of murdering the de cease. [8H; 9A] 2. It is in evidence that PW 1 was attacked along with some un unnamed persons. The prosecution case from the very beginning was that A1 to A7, the named persons formed the Unlawful assembly.

The assessee was the owner of a house situated in Ernakulam which he had purchased in 1958 for the price of Rs. 16,500. On 25th December 1965 the assessee sold the house for the same price of RS. 16500 to his daughter in law and five of his children. The assessment of the assessee for the assessment year 1966 67 was completed on 4th April 1968 but no amount was included by way of capital gains in respect of the transfer of the house since the house was sold by the assessee at the same prices at which it was purchased and no capital gains accrued or arose to him as a result of the sale. On 4th March 1969, however, the Income tax officer issued a notice under section 148 of the Income Tax Act seeking to reopen the assessment of assessee for that year. The notice did not state what was the income alleged to have escaped assessment but by his subsequent letter dated 4th3 1969 intimated to the assessee that he proposed to fix the fair market value of the property sold by him on 25th Decem ber 1965 at Rs. 65,000 as against the consideration of Rs 16, 500 for which the house sold and assess the difference of Rs 48,500 as capital gains. The assessee raised objections against the reassessment proposed to be made by the Income ' tax officer but the objections were over ruled and an order of reassessment was passed by the Incometax Officer including the sum of Rs, 48, 500 as capital gain and bringing it to tax. The appeal filed by the Revenue was dismissed by a Division Bench of the High Court. In this appeal by certificate, on behalf of the appellant it was contended that : (1) The object and purpose of sub section (2), as explicated from the speech of the Finance Minister, was not to strike at honest and bonafide transactions where the consideration in respect thereof was correctly disclosed or declared by him; (2) the transfer was effected with the object of avoidance or reduction of his liability under section 45; and (3) the transaction was a perfectly bonafide transaction. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The object of sub s.(2), is to avoid or reduce the liability of the assesses to tax on capital gains.[637F] 2.1 In view of these conditions, this provision has a limited operation and does not apply to other cases where the tax liability on capital gain arising on transfer of capital A assets between parties not connected with each other, is sought to be avoided or reduced by an under statement of the consideration paid for the transfer. [637G] 2:2 The object underlying sub section(2), namely, to extend the coverage of the provision in sub section 1 to other case of under statement Of consideration. It would therefore be legitimate in interpreting sub s (2). [638C D] 3:1 The object & purpose of subsection (2); as expresated from speech of Finance Minister was not intended to strike At honest and bona fide transactions where consideration for the transferred is under stated or in other words, the assessee has actually received a larger consideration for transfer than what is declared or disclosed by him, sub s(1) provides that the fair Market value of capital asset transferred by the assesee as on the date of the Transfer shall be taken to be the full value of consideration for such transfer and the assessee shall be taxed on capital loss on that basis.

The appellant was charged with the offence of selling adulterated food. The prosecution case was that the Til seeds sold were unfit for human consumption and thereby committed an offence under section 16(1)(a)(i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954. The Trial Court held that the purpose for which the Tileds were kept was quite immaterial. It further held that mens rea in the ordinary or usual sense of this term is not required for proving an offence defined by section 7 of the Act. On appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the whole object of the impugned Act was to prevent adulteration of "food" meant for human use and that it was part of the prosecution case that the entire object of that the Act was 'to prevent adulteration ' meant for Human consumption. HELD: Dismissing the appeal, (i) The use of the article sold by the appellant was not entirely irrelevant. It is more correct to say that it is presumed from the nature of the Article itself or the circumstances and manner of offering it for sale. Where circumstances raise a genuine doubt on the question whether what was kept by a seller was "fruit" at all, this must be resolved (1) A. 1. R. , referred to. (ii) The appellant must get the benefit of that doubt. As already indicated above, the appellant must have got the benefit thereof. [331 D E] Bhagwan Das vs Delhi Administration ; , followed. Bhagwan Das & Anr. vs Delhi Adminis tration ; , distinguished.

The appellant, a Government servant of Madhya Pradesh was dismissed from service by the Collector on 13th January 1966. He preferred an appeal to the Divisional Commissioner and that appeal was dismissed on 31st August 1966. The order of dismissal was communicated to the plaintiff on 19th September, 1960. The plaintiff gave notice under section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure on 17 6 1969 asking for a declaration that the order of dismiss ing was inoperative and he continued to be in service. This suit was dismissed in the Courts below on acceptance of the defence plea that it had not been filed within three years from the date when cause of action first arose, as required under Article 58 of the First Schedule of the . When this appeal came up for hearing before a Division Bench, reliance was placed on the decision of this Court in Sita Ram Goel vs The Municipal Board, Kanpur & Ors., ; and it was contended that the suit was barred by limitation. The Division Bench rejected the contention of the appellant relying on the decisions of this court in Sitaram Goel 's case which had been decided by a Bench of five Judges. In appeal to this Court, it was submitted on behalf of the appel lant that the judgment of this case was distinguishable from those cases where the order passed by the Collec tor did merge into the order dated May 7, 1949 merged in the appellate order of the State Government and the High Court was right in its view that it would not be correct to say that the Order of dismissal merged in that order. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The cause of actions shall be taken to arise when the remedies available to the public servant under the relevant service rules as to re spect are disposed of.

The appellant filed a suit in forma pauperis in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Chittoor for his half share in the properties which once belonged to the joint family consisting of himself and his father and to this suit he impleaded his father as his son and several alienees from him. His case was that the alienations effected by his father were not binding on him and so his share in all the said properties was not affected by them. The trial court rejected his contention that the alienation did not bind him, upheld all the alienations and dismissed his suit. On appeal the High Court reversed the trial court 's decree in respect of alienations which covered items 2, 10 and 14 in Schedule A as well as item 5 in Schedule B. Held, that the decision of the High Courts was correct. The word "decision" in article 133(1) should mean not a part of the decision or the grounds given for it but the decision on that part of tho controversy between the parties which is brought to this Court in appeal must be considered as a whole and enquire whether it is a decree of affirmance or not. In determining the question as to whether the appellate decree passed by the High court affirmed the decision, the appellate court must be consider as a part in relation to the decision Of the trial Court similarly considered as the whole. If there is a variation made in the appellate award in the decisionof the trial judge it is not a decree but merely makes a variation in regard to the order as to costs such a variation would not confer a right of appeal as regards matters unconnected with the matter in respect thereof which there has been a variation. The principle of affirmation on which the provision rests postulates either affirmance, affirmance and variation by the appeal court as an act of adjudication and that necessarily means the decision. of the appeal Court on the merits.

The High Court in exercise of its revisional jurisdiction under section 115, Code of Civil Procedure, read with section 115 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, held that no such revision petition was maintainable before the High Court. The District Judge had exclusive jurisdiction under Section 115 in a case arising out of original suits of the value of Rs. 20,000 and above, including such suits instituted before 20th September 1972. In consequence, the High court possessed exclusive jurisdiction to entertain a revision petition filed on and after that date, irrespective of the valuation of the suit out of which the case arose: (i) A revision petition under section 5 of the U.P. Civil Laws (Amendment) Act, 1973 was admitted, after preliminary hearing, before 1st February 1977; (ii) The District Court possessed exclusive juris diction under Section 116 in cases arising out o f original suits or other proceedings of any valuation, decided by the District Court; and (iii) A Revision proceeding pending immediately before 1 8 1978 of the nature in which a District Court would exercise revisional power under section 25. Dismissing the appeal and Special Leave Petitions, ^ HELD: The High Court was not vested with revisional jurisdiction in respect of a revisional order under Section 25, Provincial Small Cause Courts Act. [39E] Har Parasad Singh & Ors. vs Ram Swarup & Ors., ; , followed. In the instant case, the entire sphere of revisional jurisdiction was restored to the High 977 Court, no such power being now vested in the District Judge. The State amendments now divided it between the High Courts and the District Judges.

The respondents, who were the owners of certain lands in a town planning department, filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity of a notification dated February 8 , 1984 issued by the State Government under section 52(1) of the Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act, 1959 for the acquisi tion of certain land belonging to them required by the Urban Improvement Trust, Jaipur for a public purpose namely, for implementation of a development scheme. The Special Officer held that the alleged need of the respondents was just a pretence and he was satisfied on the material on record that the land was really not needed by them bona fide and their real object was just to get the land released from acquisition. The State Government in its special leave petition have explained that the notification under section52(1 ) of the Act could not be issued till February 8, 1984 because the Government were primarily thinking of making the land available for construction of residential houses before making provisions for construction and construction of a Three Star Hotel on an area of 6,000 square yards as their real objects was to get it released from the acquisition. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court had no territorial jurisdiction to issue a rule nisi on the petition filed by the respondents under article 227 of the constitution or to make the ad interim exparte prohibitory order restraining the appellants from taking any steps to take possession of the land acquired. [605C D] 2.1 In the instant case, the cause of action neither wholly nor in part arose within the territorial limits of the Calcutta High Court and therefore the learned Single Judge had no jurisdiction to issued a rule on the Petition filed by them under article226 of the Constitu tion or to pass the ad hoc prohibitory order against the appellants. [065D E] 2:2 The question whether service of notice is an integral part of the cause or of action within the meaning of article 226(2) of Constitution must depend upon the nature of the impugned order giving rise to a cause of Action. The notification dated Feb 8,1984 issued by State Government u/s 52(i) of Rajasthan Urban improvement Act, 1976 became effective the moment it was published in the official Gazette as thereupon the notified land became vested in the State Govern ment free from all encumbrances.

The respondent filed a suit for eviction and arrears of rent and damages for use and occupation pendent lite. The appellant contended that the building in question was constructed substantially out of funds obtained from the sources mentioned in the proviso to section 2(2) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of letting, Rent and Eviction) Act 1972 and that it was covered by the new Rent Act. The trial court negatived the defence and decreed the suit for ejectment as also for recovery of arrears of rents and damages. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the findings of the trial court on all other points except the finding about the arrears of the rent. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that since the building had become more than ten years old on the date of the suit and was exempted from the operation of the new Act, the new rent Act had no application to the building. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The question in the present case is whether by seeking the benefit of section 39 of the Act there is a change in the cause of action. [338E] 2.1 In order to appreciate the contention of the parties it will be relevant at this stage to refer to section 20 of the old Rent Act which provides that nothing in this Act shall apply to a building during a period of ten years from the date on which its construction is completed.

The appellant company entered into three contracts for the construction of aerodrome, hangarettes, buildings and stores. After the works were completed, disputes arose between the parties over the bills and eventually by an agreement dated February 6, 1948 they were referred to arbitration of one Col. A. W. section Smith. The arbitrator made his award on June 4, 1948, and sent a copy thereof to the parties. The respondents thereupon filed a petition under sections 17 and 20 Of the Indian , for a decree in terms of the award. The appellant contended that the agreement was not one relating to execution of works as that had been completed and the dispute related only to payment of the bills, and that further the essential feature of an arbitration agreement was the constitution of a private Tribunal and it could not therefore be brought within item 2 and that accordingly it fell within item 12. Held, that the copy of the Award which was sent to the Government would appear to have been insufficiently stamped. The document in court which is a copy cannot be validated: That was held in The Rajah of Bobbili vs Inuganti China Sitaramasani Garu, A.I.R. 1948 P.C. 829 and in the present case the Secretary who had signed the award sent to him the Government could have been validated on payment of deficiency and penalty under section 35 Of the Stamp Act and had it validated. The law is no doubt well settled that the copies of an instrument cannot be validation: That is held in the instant case, irresistible that Y. K. Lall, the Executive Engineer had been authorised to execute the agreement dated Feb 6,1948. It was suggested that the Secretary was possibly labouring under a mistaken notion that the contract should refer to arbitration was covered by item 2 of the original contract so as to include an arbitration shows that the intention of the parties was to treat the agreement for arbitration as part and parcel of that contract. Even after the agreement it was executed, the Secretary made corrections and modifications in the agreement on the basis that it was the Government that was a party thereto. The subject matter of the arbitration was a claim which concerned the Government. The proposal at the earlier stages to amend cl. 23 of the Original contract so that as regards the execution of the works, it would have become part of the contract and there would have been no occasion for the present contention.

The respondent, a Superintending Engineer in the Public Works Department, was working as Executive Engineer in Public Works department in the State of Punjab in the year 1979. On various dates in that year, he placed orders for purchase of sign boards which were required by the Department to avoid accidents on roads and for traffic safety. The requisite sign boards were purchased in pursuance of the aforesaid orders. In the year 1980 some complaints were received against the respondent pertaining to the purchase of the sign boards. vigilance enquiry was instituted by the Vigilance Bureau to enquire into the complaints and ultimately a First Information Report was lodged against the Respondent under sub sections (1) and (2) of Section 5 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. In that meantime, the respondent retired from the post of Executive Engineer with effect from October 31, 1982. The aforesaid First Information Reports were challenged by the Respondent in the High Court of Punjab and Haryana in Criminal Miscellaneous No. 5837 M/85 on the ground that the same having been lodged about three years after his retirement and about six years after the event of purchase of signed boards in 1979 was in the teeth of Rule 2.2 of the Punjab Civil Service Rules, Volume II and consequently was liable to be quashed. The High Court allowed the petition holding that the said rule placed an embargo on initiating judicial proceedings for prosecution of a government servant on the expiry of four years of the cause of action or the event referred to in the said Rule and the High court committed an error of law in taking the view that it would be a futile exercise to consider the question of law involved in the appeal for the reason that the Respondent had retired as long as on December 13, 1979. The State of Haryana filed appeals against the aforesaid order before this Court. On behalf of the appellant it was contended that keeping in view the scope of Article 309 as also the purpose of Rule2, the said Rules cannot be interpreted to be a rule placing an embargo upon prosecution of government servant if the conditions stated therein are satisfied. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The object of framing the said rules is to get the interpretation made by the High Courts of Rule ' 2.3 In view of what has been said above and keeping in mind the scope and interpretation of Rule (2), there is no doubt with regard to the interpretation of the said r.2. [918G H] 1.4 The purpose of the third proviso thereto is, as the scope for a proviso, to carve out an exception to the right conferred on the government by the substantive clause if the condition mentioned therein are fulfilled. This purpose can be achieved if the said proviso by adopting the rule of reading down is interpreted to mean that even if a Government servant is prosecuted and punished in judicial proceedings instituted in respect of cause of actions which arose or an event which took place more than four years before such institution, the government will not be entitled to exercise the right of withholding or withdrawing a pension or any part of it, whether permanently or for a specified period and the right PG NO 918 recovery from a pension of the whole or part of any pecuniary loss caused to Government, if, in a departmental or judicial proceeding, the pensioner is found guilty of grave misconduct or negligence which constitutes an offence punishable either under the Penal Code or Prevention of corruption Act or an analogous law should be granted immunity from such prosecution after the lapse of a particular period so as to provide incentive for efficient work would not only be against public policy but would also be counter productive.

The respondent company was floated as a public limited company under the Indian Companies Act 1913, to acquire and carry on the business of manufacture and sale of "Amrutanjan". The authorised capital of the company was 7,000 ordinary shares and 3,000 preference shares. Under the Articles of Association of the Company, both preference and ordinary shareholders were entitled to vote at the meeting of the general meetings. In the course of assessment proceedings of the respondent company, the Income tax Officer found that for the three years ending March 31, 1947, March 31. 1948 and March 31 1949 the company had declared each year a total dividend of Rs. 38,750/ . The Income tax officer served a notice on the respondent under section 23 A Of the Income Tax Act, 1922, to show cause why an order under section 22A Of the Act should not be passed against the company and after considering the objections raised by the company ordered on March 31 1953 that the undistributed portion of the assessable income of the appellant as computed for income tax purposes and reduced by the amount of income tax and super tax payable by the respondent in respect thereof, shall be deemed to have been distributed as dividend amongst the shareholders as at the date of the respective general meetings, and that this order was confirmed in appeal by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Income. tax Appellate Tribunal. The High Court held that the respondent Company was one in which the public were substantially interested and there fore the Income ' tax Officer had no jurisdiction to pass the order under s.23 A Of Act for any of the three year and on that footing answered the question in the negative. In appeal by certificate, Held: (i) The Explanation to section 23A of the Indian Income tax Act, is not in reality a clause which defines what a company, in which a public are substantially interested, has to be regarded as one in whom the public are not substantially interested; (ii) Where a shareholder holds or a group of shareholders acting in concert holding fifty one per cent or more of the voting power, which controls the working of a company it is from its very nature a company in which there is no controlling member or group and therefore the public is substantially interested.
