But the Legislature by the Explanation has raised a conclusive presumption in those cases where shares of the companies carrying not less than twenty five per cent of the share voting power are held by persons other than the controlling group, the shares yielding a fixed rate of dividend have to be excluded; (iii) Where there is an individual member or a groups of shareholders who acting in association in concert hold fifty one percent or more or more Of the voting powers, which control controls the functioning of a Company, it isfrom its very character a company In which there was no controlling members or group, and therefore, the public have substantially interested in the matter of exercise, of voting rights. The total voting power was 5,500 one vote, for each share, ordinary and preference alike and twenty five percent of that voting power is 1,375, but to invite the presumption under the Explanation this power must be exercisable only by the or dinary shareholders, and not by shareholders entitleci to a fixed percentage of dividend. The rule which excludes from the computation of voting power holders of shares entitled to a specified rate of dividends is that section 23 Of the Indian Incometax Act is directed primarily against the accumulation of undistributed dividends to avoid payment of non corporate rates of super tax. But shareholders who are entitled to share a fixed amount of dividend are not directly interested in such accumulation: it matters little to them whether the dividend is immediately distributed to the ordi nary shareholders or is accumulated, and, therefore, in assessing whether the twenty five% of the shares are vested in persons other not substantially con tained. But even that argument is of no value, for twenty five cent of shares of a share of the ordinary shares.

The first appellant was a registered joint stock company. The first appellant 's selling procedure was this. When goods were ready for sale, it sends Dwarkadas Khetan & Company in duplicate a " ready sale note ". These notes contain particulars about the bales and the persons to whom they are to be delivered. Upon receipt of this advice slip the first appellant sent a " advise slip " telling it that the money had been received and asking it to prepare a delivery order. The second appellant then made an " advice slip " informing it that he had effected a sale, (2) the selling agent had paid the first appel lant for the goods, (3) specific bales had been set aside and appropriated to the sale and consequently the property in the goods had passed, (4) the goods were actually left the Mills ' premises, and (5) they were in the Dady Seth godown under the control of Dwarkadash Khetan. The appellant was convicted by the Presidency Magistrate on two counts. Held, that the first count relating to the 6 bales was a similar one and the facts follow the same pattern. They had been detailed in the High Court 's judgment and it could not be accepted. Dwarkadadas Khetan vs Emperor (A.I.R. , followed. The words "physical possession" in section 2(1) of the Essential Supplies Act, 1946, are wide enough to include physical possession or possession in fact and (2). legal possession which need not coincide with possession in law is called custody rather than possession. If a man lives abroad over a period of years and leaves his house and furniture in charge of an agent who has the keys of the house and immedi ate access to and physical control over the furniture, it would be difficult to say that the agent was not in physical possession. Dwarkeshwardas vs Emperor ([1952] S.C.R., referred to.

The respondent was a Senior Lecturer in a Government College. He was charged with offences under section 161, Indian Penal Code and section 5(2) read with section 5 (1) (d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 read with s 114 of the Indian Penal code. The Special Judge who tried both these cases found him guilty of the offence with which they were charged. He imposed a sentence of 2 years ' rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 1,000/ . Both the convicted persons filed appeals to the High Court. The High Court held that the prosecution case had been proved against both Dwivedi and Thakkar on merits but on the view that even an Examiner was a public servant it was necessary that the person committing that offence must be a public Servant. Allowing the appeal by certificate, HELD: (1)(a) The word "otherwise" refers to other than corrupt or illegal by which a public officer may abuse his position. There are two ways of looking at the clause on is that the words "corrupt or illegal means" stand by themselves and as soon as it is established that a public person has by such means obtained any valuable thing or pecuniary advantage he will be guilty of offence. But the abuse of position as a public employee would be essential whether the means are corrupt or unlawful or are of the nature covered by the word " otherwise". [327 D E] (b) The words "obtains" in section 161 of the Code indicate that the word 'Otherwise ' refers to any other than incor pation or illegal or are or of the type covered by it. If that is so, the abuse by corrupt or wrongful means or by other means of the character mentioned in section161 of the Penal Code, if it is habitual, falls within clause (a). Bribery of the kind specified in section 1 65, if the meaning to be given to the word otherwise ' is, as earlier stated, the words 'by corrupt or lawful means" or "by otherwise" form a single clause and do not form two clauses. If this is so the abuse would be the necessary ingredient of the offences; the abuse being either by corrupt and illegal means or illegal mean by other mean of the category mentioned in the section. [329 H] Dhaneshwar Narain Saxena vs Delhi Administration, ; , referred to. (c) The use of the word `other wise ' refers not to corrupt or improper means but to other words which a Public servant may abuse the position. [328 D E; 328 A B] (d). The word 'corrupt ' is used in the sense of giving it a wide meaning and does not include any act done by a public authority for obtaining valuable thing etc. [330 C] Dhaneswar Narain Saxena v Delhi Administration ; , applied.

The petitioners, who were engaged on terms of casual labour for periods ranging varying between 10 140 and 16 years in the Construction Department of the Signal Unit in Northern Railway, filed writ petitions under Article 32 of the Constitution challenging the claim of the petitioners. The Senior Signal & Telecom Engineer (Power Signalling) has filed a counter affidavit on behalf of the respondents challenging the claims of the petitioner. According to them five out of forty four petitioners in this group of writ petitions had undergone medical examination and were granted temporary status as Khallasisis. One of them has been directed to be absorbed against a permanent vacancy in the open line; five others have refused to go to the open Line for permanent absorption. He further averred that though prior to the issue of the Railway Board 's directions on January 1, 1984, project casual labourers were not entitled to all the privileges like House Rent Allowance, City Compensatory Allowance, Casual Leave, increment etc., they are now entitled to be treated at par with maintenance workers and to declare that they are entitled to equal pay for equal work and have asked for their absorption in the regular cadre in the permanent category as per the circulars issued by the respondents. A number of documents and circulars issued on January1, 1984 have been produced in support of their claim. The senior Signal and Telecom Engineer, (Powerignalling) filed a Counter affidavit on his behalf challenging the said claims. According ly the respondents five out four petitioners had undergone Medical examination and they were granted Temporary status as khallasamis. Another Senior Signary & Telecom Engineers, who had been directed by the Administration to be absorption against permanent vacancy, has filed an additional counter affidavit. At the hearing of the applications, counsel for the petitioners as also the learned Additional Solicitor General were given full opportunity of placing their arguments and documents. In addition, they have also furnished written submissions. 141 It is stated on behalf that out of Forty four petitioners sixteen have now been empanelled and of them five have been given temporary appointments; eleven are said to have refused not to join and seventeen are still continuing with temporary status. The respondents filed a rejoinder affidavit contending that the Administration was requiring continuous service for purpose of eligibility, learned Additional Advocate General on instructions obtained from the Railway officers present in Court during arguments has clarified that continuity is not insisted upon and though there is break in such continuity the previous service is also taken into account. On behalf of respondent it was contended that the allegation of discrimination does not exist. The petitioners have filed a Rejoinder affidavit contending inter alia that the allegations of discrimination do not exist, and that by the time these writ petitions were filed, the Railway, Board ' 's order of 1st of June, 1984 had not been given but with those directions now holding the field, the ambit of grievances has been very much reduced. The Additional SolicitorGeneral contended that no pensionary benefits are admissible even to temporary railway servants and, therefore, that retiral advantage is not available to casual labour acquiring temporary status, and, that the retiral advantage was not available in the case of casual labourers acquiring temporary Status. On the other hand it was submitted on behalf respondent Administration that there is perhaps slackness in enforcing them. The Railway Establishment Manual has made provisions for their protection but implementation is not P effective. Several instructions issued by Railway Board and the Northern Railway Headquarters were placed before us to show that the Adminis tration is anxious to take appropriate steps to remove difficulties faced by the casual labour but there is indeed slackfulness in implementing them. It was also contended that on eventual absorption in regular employment half the service rendered with temporary Status is counted as qualifying service for pensionary benefits. The Railways Administration to take prompt steps to screen such of the Petitioners who have not yet been tested for the purpose of regularising their service. On these facts, it was prayed that the petitioners be directed to consider the claims and make appropriate orders for regularisation. Disposing of the writ petitions, this Court, HELD: 1.

The appellants entered into contracts with the respondent for settlement of their business in cotton through a notification issued by Forward Markets Commission. The terms and conditions of forward contracts in cotton including "hedge contracts" were governed by the provisions contained in certain bye laws of the Association and of these that relevant to the consideration of the matters in this appeal was bye law 52AA which on the date when the appellants entered the contracts ran as follows: "52 A.A. (1) whether or not the prices at which the cotton may be bought or sold are at any time controlled under the provisions of the , if the Textile Commissioner with the concurrence of the Forward Markets Commis sion and after consultation with the Chairman, permits resumption." The appellants entered on December 16, 1955, a notice to show cause why action should not be taken against them for contravening the bye laws. They contended that the Forward Market Commission could not, having regard to the terms of the statute under which it was created, be a proper recipient of the power with which it purported to do under the amended bye law and secondly that the Association was in law incapable of conferring that power on the Forward Marketing Commission or on any other body. Held, that the notification dated January 24, 1956, by the Forward markets Commission was illegal and the appellants would be entitled to issue a writ of mandamus in the terms prayed for. The words "by or under this Act" in section 12(1) of the Act include a rule made in exercise of the powers conferred on the Central Government by section 12 of the .

The assessee, a shareholder of a company, was assessed to tax under section 16(2) of the Income tax Act, 1922. The income tax Officer brought the entire amount to tax declared as dividend for each of the three years in question and grossed up the amounts under section 17(2), of the Act. In appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the entire sum for each year was income in the hands of the assessee but only a part of it being dividend, within the meaning of section 2(6A) of Income tax 'Act, 1922, was liable to be grosated up. The High Court also observed that it was agreed between the parties that the answers in the negative on all questions were subject to the final decision in appeals filed against the orders made in Income tax References Nos. 131 of 1961 and 3 of 1964 and pending in this Court. In these appeals, by special leave, the assessee contended that distribution to the assessee of the amount attributable to salami received by it for the grant of long term leases after 31st March 1948 was not taxable as dividend but as income of the assesseee from other sources. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The High court had to decide on the facts of each case whether any amount of salami was capital gain and whether any part of the compensation received for compulsory acquisition of land was capital gains. Prima facie, receipt of compensation for land compulsorily acquired which forms part of its fixed assets is of a capital nature. Senairam Doongarmall vs Commissioner of Income Tax, Assam, ; , referred to. (2) The assumption made that the whole amount of compensation was deemed to be capital gain cannot therefore be sustained.

The respondents, who were engaged in the manufacture of timber, challenged the jurisdiction of the court in C.C. Nos. 145 and 148 of 1988 to quash the complaint holding that Sandal Wood Oil is not 'wood oil ' as defined in Section 2(f) (1) of the Kerala Forest Act, 1961 for short, the Act '. The High Court quashed the complaint on the ground that Sandariwood oil is a wood oil and held that bamboo oil being the bye product derived commercially manufacturing process is not wood oil. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The expression 'wood Oil ' used in the Act will require purposive interpretation drawing the context in which the words are used and its meaning will have to be discovered having regard to the intention and object which legislature seeks to subserve. [503C] 1.2 In the instant case, the High Court was right in holding that the definition of 'public servant ' is incorporated in the definition it would only mean natural bye product directly drawn from the trees. The expression wood oil being a technical and part of inclusive definition has to be construed in its technical sense and in an exhaustive manner. It cannot be restricted in a narrow circumference as was done by the learned Single Judge so as to defeat the object and purpose of the Act. [403E F] 1:3 In the context this Court laid that cardinal principle of statutory construction referred to hereinbefore would apply. Narasimhan; , the definition under Section 2 (f) would show that it did 506 not intened to exclude what was ordinarily and in common parlance be spoken of wood oil.[503F G] 1 :4 The expression "wood oil" is generally used as a word of extension. When used in an interpretation clause, it seeks to enlarge the meaning of the words or pharases occuring in the body of the Statute. [506G H] 1;505 2. The literal interpretation would aid conservation of sandle wood, a valuable forest wealth, prevent illicit failing and transportation of them and makes the manufacturers of sandley accountable to the possession of sandwood trees or chips or roots etc. Incorporation of sandlingwood oil abundentecatela in Karnataka Act and and and absence thereof in sister Acts operating in South India does not detract from giving its due meaning. The expert opinion is only an opinion evidence on either side and does not aid us in interpretation. This Court in Adity Mills vs Union of India, ; did not adopt the dictionary meaning as it may be to some extent delussive guide to interpret entries in Central Excise and Salt Act.

The prosecution case was that there was no evidence against the appellants sufficient to warrant a conviction and (2) there were no compelling reasons for reversal of the judgment of acquittal. Held, that the High Court should not set aside an order of conviction unless there are " substantial and compelling reasons" for doing so. Surajpal Singh vs State, Aher Raja Khima vs The State of Saurastra, ; , referred to. In the present case the evidence in the present ease was of such quality and no legitimate inference could be drawn. The High Court was therefore right in accepting the testimony of these witnesses in support of the correctness of the two dying declarations nor could the statement of the deceased alleged to have been made in the circumstances of this case be considered sufficient to support the conviction of the accused. Sundarlal vs The state of Madhya Pradesh, A.I.R. 1954 S.C. 28 and Ram Pratap, Ahar Raja Khuma vs The King, Aheher Raja khima vs State of Sikkim, ; referred to, Held, further, that in view of the infirmities which the testimony was given in regard to circumstances exactly similar to those which arose in the case now before this Court no legitimate conclusion could be arrived at. The evidence in this case was of a circumstantial nature and no reasonable inference of guilt of the appellants could properly be drawn; the second point on which the judgment Of the High court was assailed was the lack of compelling reasons justifying interference with the findings of the trial court.

The appellant company was an all India complex having establishments in different parts of the country. In Bihar alone, it had two factories one at Jamshedpur and the other at Ranchi and its depots at Patna and other towns. The factory at Jamshedpur was an establishment under the Bihar Shops and Establishments Act. Certain disputes having arisen between the appellant company and its workmen employed in the factory at the com pany and the said workmen represented by their union, the Indoxco Labour Union, Jamshedpur, regarding the matters specified in their joint applications dated 7 9 1963 annexed hereto. The dispute was referred to the Tribunal for adjudication. The Tribunal held that the constitution of the said Indox Co Labour Union came to be amended as from January 6, 1963 and that as the said reference was made in October 1963 i.e., after the purported amendment, "the mention in it of the dispute as a dispute between the company and the workmen of all the establishments of the appellant Company in Bihar eligible for its membership. The appellant company challenged the award on the ground that the Tribunal was in error in making its award operative not only to the said workman at its Jamshedpur factory but also to workmen at its other establishments and that in doing so it acted beyond jurisdiction. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The Tribunal 's conclusion, therefore, that the union 's constitution was duly amended on either January 6 1963 or that, therefore the/ndian Oxygen Workers Union represented the workmen concerned was mentioned in the said agreement and the statement and no other dispu sion of the Indian Oxygen Workers ' Union is erroneous and cannot be sustained. [526 F] (2) The appellant Company had been allowing those of its workmen who are the tmion 's representatives to attend without loss of pay 'proceedings before conciliation officers and industrial tribunals. This is fair because conciliation proceedings are likely to get thwarte if the workmen 's representative are not there to discuss the disputes and put forward their point of view before conciliation officer and wherever possible to arrive at a settlement or compromise. Over and above this facility, the workmen get various types of paid leave. As the figures of such leave are not correctly 'stated in the award, it is impossible to say that the tribunal erred in doing or acted unjustly. [561 F G] (3) The company would in that case be indirectly increasing the hours of work and consequently altering its conditions of service. If after taking into consideration the fact of comparatively higher scale of wages prevailing in the appellant 's Company the Tribunal fixed the rate for overtime work at 1 1/4 times the ordinary rate of wages, it was impossible to contend that the award was justified as the Tribunal has observed, in the interest of a proper growth of trade union movement and the promotion of harmony in industrial relations inasmuch as if facilities are given to the workmen to conduct the administration of the union themselves, there would be less possibility of outside elements establishing their hold on the union. [562 F G; 564 A B] (4) The contention that an obligation to grant special leave to attend the meetings of the executive committee of the Union cannot be accepted.

The assessee was assessed to tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1918 in respect of income from business inter alia in timber at Abdullapur. In assessment proceedings for 1943 44 the assessee contended that the firm had come into force and the first succession to the business after April 1, 1939 was in March 1943 when the assessee was dissolved and on that account the assessee 's business in timber which was carried on by that firm was taken over by the assessee. The Income tax Officer completed the assessment without giving to the assessee the benefit of sub sections (3) or (4) of section 25 of the Indian Incometax Act, 1922. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order holding that succession to a family firm was not admissible. On appeal by the Revenue, the High Court held that in the facts and circumstances of the case the Tribunal was correct in law in holding that the assessee firm was entitled on dissolution of that firm in March 1944 to the benefit under section 25(4) or 25 (4). The question for determination in this appeal was whether in the circumstances of this case, the Tribunal is correct in holding. HELD: The instrument recites : "We, R. B. Jodha Mal Kuthiala son of Lala Gopi Mal Sahib Sud of the one part and Gajjan Mal Kshiala, of the other part, residents of Haroli District Hoshiarpur and presently of Simla." Whereas the said oral (agreement) is being reduced to writing and we agree that : "the instrument of partnership in the first instance recites that the accounts were settled upto March 31, 1939. It is then recited that all the partners had become separate from April 1 1939 i.e., the business had continued for the whole or a part of the day on April 1. 1939. The partnership therefore came into being at the precise point of time at which the Indian income tax (Amendment) Act 7 of 1939 came into force. It could not be said that the assesse was carrying on business at the commencement of the Income tax ( Amendment) Act, 7 of1939.

The appellant was granted a stage carriage permit under section 48 of the (briefly the Act) for the route Devenagere to Shimoga via Honnali by the Regional Transport Authority, Shimandhar, by its order dated May 3/4, 1963. The said order was challenged in a writ petition filed by him before the High Court and obtained stay of the operation of the order. The appeal was dismissed on September 27, 1963, but the Secretary to the Regional transport Authority called upon the appellant to produce the relevant documents and the certificate of registration for making necessary entry in the permit. The appellant produced the same on April 26, 1967 and the permit was issued on the same day. Against the order of the State Transport Appellate Tribunal, the Secretary of the Regional Road Transport Authority called for a fresh permit from the appellant. The Secretary to Regional Transport authority called upon him to produce relevant documents, and the appellant produced them on April 27, 1967. On April 25, 1967, the secretary to the Transport Authority asked the appellant as to whether he had no jurisdiction to issue a permit under rule 119 of the Mysore Motor Vehicles Rules, 1963 after a lapse of such a long time from the date of the grant of the permit and that the Secretary should produce the necessary documents and certificate of Registration for making requisite entry in his permit. On May 3, 1967 the Secretary asked the Secretary as to the appellant whether he was entitled to issue the permit under Rule 119 of Mysore Motor vehicles Rules, 1945 after a period of nearly six months from the grant. The secretary produced the relevant document on April 25. 1967 and issued the permit on the said date. Against this order of refusal, the appellant filed an appeal to the State Government which was dismissed by majority on January 29, 1969. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that there was no period of limitation under rule 151 of the old Rules which was applicable to his case, for the issue of a permit; and that there had been no period Of limitation under Rule 151 of that Rules which had been applicable to him, for issue of the said permit. HELD: The appeal must be allowed. The order granting the permit to the Appellant stands restored There will be no order as to costs.

The appellant was a sitting member of Parliament. The election symbol of the appellant was elephant and the election symbol was elephants and the appellant challenged the election on grounds of corrupt practices as mentioned in sub sections (2), (3A) and (4) of section 123 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that there was no discussion of the oral evidence of P.W. 11, impleaded the appellant as a party to the election. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent that the appellant 's witnesses were not allowed to cast their votes and they also said that it was announced by beat of drums that no Chamar or Bhangi should cast a vote. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The publication in the newspaper 'Vir Arjun ' Exhibit 22 is to the effect that differences between Hindus and Harijans were being spread by the supporters of the Republican candidate meaning thereby the appellant and if students from Muslim University were brought in by them then students from Ghaziabad would be brought into the field. [899 D] Badat & Company vs E. I. Trading, ; , followed. (2) The appellant 'short was not shown to have been made by respondent Shastri 's workers and supporters. The statements in exhibit 22 do not make any reflection on the moral or mental nature of the appel lant and they do not touch the personal character of the appellants nor do they promote enmity or hatred on grounds Of religion. [900 E] Badarath & Company, vs E .I. Trading; , followed, (3) The statements made in exhibit 23 did not make a reflection on moral or physical nature of respondent Prakash Vir Shastri on 7 February 1967 at the Town Hall Maidan. Even if it were proved the slogans do not offend the provisions of either sub sections(3A), and ( 4) of s 123 of Act. [901 F] Badratat & Co. vs E, I.T.R. , referred to.

The respondent mortgagor filed an application under Order XXI Rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the sale. Two other petitions of objections were filed by one Chiranji Lal and by another judgment debtor, Mst. Abhey Kanwar. All these objections including the applica tion of Ganpat Singh under Order 21 Rule 90 CPC were dismissed for default and, consequently, the sale was confirmed by the District Judge on January 2, 1979. On July 17, 1980, that is more than one year after the sale, was confirmed, the decree holder auction purchaser filed an appli cation under Order XXII Rule 95 of the C.P.C. for setting it aside the auction sale. The said application was opposed by the judgment debtor on the ground that as the application was filed more than two years after the confirmation of sale, it was barred by limitation under Article 134 of the . 360 It was held by the learned District Judge that in view of the provision of Explanation I1 of Section 47 which was inserted in the Code by section 20 of the code of Civil Proce dure (Amendment) Act, 1974, Article 136 prescribing a period of limitation of 12 years for the execution of the decree and not Article 134 would apply. The learned Single Judge held that after the amendment of the Civil Procedure Code, Article 134 stood impliedly repealed by Section 47 read with Article 136 of the Limitation Act and Article 136 was thus impliedly repealed. Hence this appeal by certificate. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In view of clause (a) of Explanation II to section 47 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908, an application for delivery of possession can be filed within three years from the date on which sale became absolute as prescribed by Article 180 of that Act, but under Article 136, such an application can be made within one year from the day on which the sale becomes absolute.

The appellant was the candidate of a political party. The first respondent filed an elec tion petition claiming a declaration that he 's election was void on the ground that he had committed two corrupt practices within the meaning of Section 123(4) of the Representation of People Act, 1951. The High Court negatived all the said corrupt practices except two, viz., (i) printing and publication on March 22, 1987, a day prior to the election; (ii) publication of a wall poster both maligning the personal character and conduct of the first respondent; and (iii) publication on the date of election. The appellant 's appeal was rejected by the High Court holding that both these acts amounted to corrupt practices. In this appeal, it was contended for the appellant that: (i ) the first respond ents had not stated as to why it would create such an impression among the electorate; and that in any case, the statement in the pamphlet that "the Marxist leader arrested is also known" were a clear and direct reference to the first Respondent, be cause it was an admitted fact that the first re spondent was arrested for an offence of harbouring the accused in that murder case. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The publication was intended to create an impression and did create an intention that the incident of murders had taken place a day previous to the Election. However, whereas in a libel action it may further be necessary to prove that those with special knowledge of the candidate 's Election agent or any other person with the consent of the election agent, and in his interest, and the corrupt practice by such agent has materially affected the result of his election, the High court may decide that the election of the returned candidate is not void. [776F] 2. The words "anything done by him" used no imputa tion could be read in the words as against him. [771C D] 3.

The respondent No. 5, who proposed to construct a five star hotel on a tract of land admeasuring 44,820.49 square yards at Bandra, Bombay, filed an application for permission to develop the disputed land in favour of respondent No 5, which was rejected by the Municipal Corporation on the sole ground that it was proposed to earmark the said land under reference as a recreational ground with suitable internal network of roads during the revision of the development plan. The respondent No 2, however, filed a writ petition challenging the legality and validity of the resolution dated 14.3.1974 and also the provisions of section 20 of the Urban Land Ceiling Act, 1966, which were dismissed by a Single Judge of the High Court. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the whole of the land should be kept reserved for a green belt or recreational ground in the interest of general public; and (ii) the entire land should not be kept open for a Green belt or recreation ground in view of the clear provisions of sections 46 and 31(6) of the Act and having regard to the position that in the sanctioned plan of 1966, the said lands was included in the residential zone and no proposal to exclude it therefrom in the draft revised development plan had been published, the Municipal Commissioner was not justified in rejecting the application for approval of the plan submitted by respondent No 4. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The ground for exemption is that 75,000 sq. of vacant land is available for the development of gardens. As a matter of fact, Counsel submits, it is not a vacant land, but contains 350 houses. It is, therefore, apparent that in granting sanction to the plan, the respondent No . 5 was quite alive to public interest. At this stage, there is no merit in this appeal challenging the order of the respondent sanctioning the development Plan of the Respondent No. 2 sanctioning the Development Plan of 1966. [922D E] Life Insurance Corporation of India and Another vs Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay and Others, Writ Petition No. 2944 of 1932 disposed of on 6.3 .1984; Life Insurance Corpn. of India & Anr. vs Municipal Corpora tion of GreaterBombay and Ors., Writ Petition (Civil) No. 282776 of 1985 dated 6.1.1985; Life insurance Corporation of lndia and Another v Municipal Corporation, Greater Bombay & Ors., writ petition No. 1406 of 1978 dated 6th March, 1984; and Life Insurance Corpora tive of India vs Municipal Corpo ration of Greater ' Bombay and Ors. Writ Petition Nos. 1408 of 1978 and 1606 of 1979 dated 6 3.1984. [936E F] 2.

The appellant, a manufacturer of cloth, filed two complaints against the employers alleging that they had closed their industrial undertakings and were not guilty of any unfair labour practice. The Industrial Court dismissed them. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the industrial undertakings of the employers had never been closed or at any rate have resumed working in full and that the old workmen were not being re employed. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. When it is claimed that the employer has resorted to closure of industrial activity, the Industrial Court in order to determine whether the employer is guilty of unfair labour practices must ascertain on evidence produced before it whether the closure was a device or pretence to determine the services of the workmen. The duration of the closure may be a significant fact to determine its intention and bonafides of the employer at the time of closure but is not decisive of the matter. [69H; 70A] 2. When the Industrial Tribunal rejected the complaints filed by the appellant union which did not command to this court, and to avoid any such error being repeated in future, it would lead to a startling result in that an employer who has resorted under closure bonafide wants to re open, revive and re start the industrial activity he can not do so on the pain that the closure would be adjudged a deviceor or pretence. [70B C] 3. When once it is alleged that the appellant had resorted to the closure of the industrial undertaking, the industrial court in order that the action of the respondent was questioned must keep in view all the relevant circumstances at the stage of closure decide and determine whether it was bona fide and for reasons beyond the control of the employee. [71F G] 4. The term " closing of a place of business" is gradually expanding and that till all the old workman are re inducted in service no new hand will be recruited. [72G H; 72A] 5. In case of a lockout there is only closure of a business itself permanent and irrevocable, whether the termination is brought about malafide and whether it could have been avoided were matters irrelevant and what is to be seen is whether in fact and in effect there is a closure or not. [73B C; 73A] 6. The question whether the closing down of the Industrial activity was a mere device or a pretence to decide the services or whether it is bonafide and for reason beyond the Control of the management. [74F G; 74C] 7. In examining this aspect, the Tribunal observed as under: "During that the undertaking is carried out in letter and spirit, the appellant company refused to continue to employ the workmen employed by him even though the business activity was not closed down". The essence of lock out is the refusal of the Respondent employer to continue. There is no intention to close the industrial activities. Even if the suspension of work is ordered it would constitute lock out. On the other hand closure implies closing of the industry as a consequence of which workmen are rendered jobless.

The assessee company, which was incorporated on July 29, 1924 as an investment company, the objects of which are set out in cl. III of the Memorandum of association and more particularly in sub cls. 1, 2, 15 and 16 of that clause. The assessment years in question were 1943 44 to 1948 49 excepting the year 1947 48. According to its petition made in the High Court, the assessee company dealt with its assets as follows: "The petitioner company purchased during the period 1st July, 1925 to 30th June, 1928, shares of the value of Rs. 1.33,930 included shares of Loyal Mills Ltd., sold to the members of the staff and shares of that value were handed over to the creditors in payment of the loan granted by them. From the year ended 30th September, 1943, reconstruction scheme of the Appollo Mills Ltd. 48 took place under which debentures held by the petitioner company in the Apptto Mills were redeemed and the proceeds were reinvested in the new issue of shares made by the Apptls. The Income tax Officer accepted the plea of the assessee and treated it as a dealer in shares, securities and immovable properties and assessed it on that basis. For these years and for the assessment year 1943 44, the appellant company made its return in that basis but after the return had been filed for the year 194344, the Income tax department accepted the contention of the appellant and treated the same as a 'dealer ' in shares securities and immoveable properties and taxed it on the basis of being an investor. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissed the appeal and upheld the order of the Income Tax Officer. In reference to this Court, HELD: (i) The question whether the profits and losses arising from the sale of shares, security etc. cannot be taxed as business profits involves the application of law to the facts found in the setting of the particular case. [52 D] (ii) The High Court was right in holding that the question as to what were the characteristics of the business in shares or that of an investor is a mixed question of fact and law and what was the legal effect of the facts finding of the Tribunal on the primary questions of fact; but it is open to the High court to examine whether the Tribunal had applied the relevant legal principles correctly or not in reaching its final conclusion. [53 E] G. On the last occasion it was pointed out by this Court that the questions actually framed by this court on the last occasions are not appropriate and (1) 54 do not reflect the real controversy between the parties.

The appellant was recruited to the Madras Provincial Judicial Service as District Munsif in 1935. In 1949 he was promoted to the office of Subordinate Judge, and on June 19, 1950, he was posted as Subordinate Judge of Masulipatnam, Krishna District. On August 22, 1950 when judgment was still pending, the Government passed an order placing the appellant on suspension until further orders. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court for quashing the order of suspension dated January 28, 1954, on the grounds that under the Andhra Civil Services (Disciplinary Proceedings Tribunal) Rules, 1953, which had been published by the Andhra Government on October 22, 1953 with effect from October 1, 1953 and which was published by it on October 20, 1953. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) Rule 4 of the Andhra civil Services (Classification, Control and Appeal) Rules provides that enquiries against subordinate judicial officers could not be referred to a Tribunal under r. 4(1)(a). [422 D] (ii) The order passed by the High court on January 28 was merely one of suspension pending final orders by the Government, and such an order is neither one of dismissal nor removal from service within article 311 of the Constitution. It was also not correct to say that the conclusion of the High Courts that having regard to its setting, the proviso should more properly be read as qualifying sub rule (2) was correct.

The respondent, a registered holder of 2674 shares of Gannon Dunkerley & Co. was a registered shareholder of the appellant company and its registered office in Bombay died on May 13, 1945, having made and published a will disposing of his extensive estate in the United Kingdom and in British India. The National Bank of India Ltd. obtained probate of Gannon 's will in theUnited Kingdom and appointed the respondent as the executor to administer the estate in British country. The respondent filed an application under section 23A of the Income tax Act, 1922, for the assessment years 1946 47 and 1947 48 on the ground that it was barred by limitation. The Income tax Officer included dividends deemed to be distributed and after processing the amount under section 18(5) included it in the total income of Anderson and levied tax thereon at the appropriate rate. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the respondent had reason to believe that Anderson 's income assessable to income tax for the year ending 31st March 1949 had escaped assessment and that he proposed to re assess the escaped income and for that purpose called upon Anderson to make a return of his total income and the total world income assessable for the years ending March 31, 1949. The Tribunal held that in view of section 24B(1) of the Act, the respondent was not liable to pay tax on receipt of income due to the deceased, notwithstanding that he died while assessment proceedings were pending because the proceedings could not be continued and the assessment could not therefore be made after the tax payer 's death. The High Court answered the first question in the negative and declined to answer the second question. With special leave, Held: (i) The legal personality of a deceased person cannot vote on behalf of the shareholder and may not become a director of the company on the strength of the representation alone. A shareholder in place of the person whose estate is vested in him, but because as a representative it is his duty to discharge the obligations enforceable against the estate. Under an order made by the Income Tax Officer under section23A of Income tax, 1922 dividend is deemed to have been received by such deceased person, is to be regarded for the purpose of assessment as the personal income of the legal representative is to charge tax not in accordance with the provisions of the statute. (ii) The expression "assessee" in section 2(2) as substituted by the Indian Income tax (Amendment) Act, 25 of 1953 with effect from April 1, 1952, means a person by whom income tax or any other tax which would have been payable by him under this Act if he had not died". In view of the express provision contained in section 35 of the Indian Companies Act, 1913, a transfer of the share or other interest of a dead member by his legal representative though he is himself not a member is as valid as if he were a member at the time of the execution of the transfer. The expression 'assessee ' in section 23 A does not warrant the application of two different interpretations in the matter of extension of the statutory legal personality according as the income is actual or notional.

The appellant was the Ruler of a State. After the passing of the Indian Independence Act, 1947, the appellant executed an Instrument of Accession to the Dominion of India popularly known as "The Stand Still Agreement". On December 15, 1947 he entered into an agreement with the Government of India whereby he ceded the State of Baster to the Government and to make provisions for other matters connected therewith. Under section 3 of the Act vesting of proprietary rights in the State Government takes place on certain conditions mentioned in that section being complied with, the definition of 'proprietor ' is stated in section 2 cl. (m) and it is "mahal" in relation to merged territories means any area other than land in possession of a raiyat which has been separately assessed to land revenue. The appellant was not only an ex Ruler but a maufidar appears to be clear. The ordinary dictionary meaning of the expression 'maufidar ' is that one who, or that which, exercises rule especially of a supreme or sovereign kind. One who has control, management, or head ship within some limited sphere". The High Court rejected the contention on behalf of the appellant that as he was a "Ruler" within the meaning of article 366(22) of the Constitution he did not come within the expression "a Ruler" as contained in the definition. Held, that the appellant was an ex ruler and that article 366 (22) did not make him a Ruler for the purposes of the , and as such he was within the class of persons who were by name specifically included in the definitions of ' jagirs and jagirs.

The respondent, a Garden Curator in the Office of the Scientist SE, Botanical Survey of India, Eastern Circle, Shillong, was transferred from Shillong to Pauri (Uttar Pradesh) by the Senior Administrative Officer, office of the Director, B.P.S.E., Botanyanical survey of India (Ministry of Environment and Forests, Government of India). As many as 19 persons were transferred under the said order including the respondent. The respondent approached the Gauhati Bench of the Central Administrative Tribunal (Original Application No. 33 of 1991) questioning the order of his transfer. He submitted that his wife is also employed at Shillong in and off ice of the central Government, that his children are studying at Shillong and further that he himself had suffered back bone fracture injuries some time ago. He also submitted that the guidelines contained in Government of india O.M. dated 3.4.1986 have not been kept in mind while ordering his transfer, tie complained that some other officials who have been serving at Shillong for a longer period, have been allowed to continue at Shillong. The learned Single Member of the Tribunal recorded the following finding: "In view of the above facts and circumstances and findings it is held unhesitatingly that the transfer order No. BSI. 80/5/80 Estt. dated 29.1.1991 in respect of applicant S.L.Abbas was malafide and liable to be quashed". The Union of India preferred this appeal. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The guidelines issued by the Government on the subject are applicable to the case of the respondent, and that as far as possible, husband and wife must be posted at the same place even if their employers be different. [455G] 1.2 In the instant case, the guidelines do not have statutory force. Who should be transferred where, is a matter for the appropriate authority to decide. Unless the order transferring is vitiated by mala fides or is made in violation of any statutory provisions, the Court cannot interfere with it. While ordering the transfer, there is no doubt, the authority must keep in mind the guidelines issued on the Subject. Similarly if a person makes any representation with respect to his transfer he the appropriate Authority must consider the same having regard to the exigencies of administration and enable the two spouses to live together at one station if it is possible without any detriment to the administrative needs and the claim of other employees." [456H; 432A B] Bank of India vs Jagjit Singh Mehta, [1992] 1 S.C.C., 306 rendered by a Bench of which one of us (J.S Verma J.) was a member. On a perusal of the judgment, it is clear that the learned Single Judge who passed the impugned order is a former Judge of the High Court and is thus aware of the norms and constraints of the writ jurisdiction.) The Administrative Tribunal is not an Appellate Authority sitting in judgment over the orders of transfer. It cannot substitute its own judgment for that of the authority competent to transfer. [ 432E F] Bank Of India vs Jagir Singh Mehta [1992 ] 1 S .C.R. 306, followed.

The appellants were tried for the murder of one Jawahar. Three charges were framed against them. A7 was charged under Section 302 read with Section 109, I.P.C. for instigating A1 to 6 to commit the murder. The second charge related to rioting wherein A1, A2, A4, A5 and A6 armed with sticks, A3 armed with aruval (bill hook) and A4 armed with lathis, attacked Jawahar at about 8.30 A.M. on January 2, 1977 and caused him multiple injuries as a result of which he died on the same day. All the ac cused persons were acquitted by the Trial Judge. On appeal the High Court maintained the acquittal of A4 to A7 but reversed the findings in respect of A1to A3. Allowing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1. The participation of the appellants in the occurrence which resulted in the death of Jawahar has been proved beyond doubt. [334E] 2. The presence of the appel lants in the incident which resulted into the death was proved beyond doubts. [433F G] 3. Taking in view the nature of injuries on the person of the deceased and the facts and circumstances of this case, the 3 offence committed by them came within the parameters of Section 325 read with 34, I P.C., and instead convict them under Section 325, IP. C.

The appellant Bank filed a suit against the respondents including the respondent firm and its partners to recover a sum of Rs.18,14,817.91 being the balance (inclusive of interest) of three principal amounts of Rs,3.00 lakhs, Rs.7,00,000 and Rs.80,000 respectively advanced by the Bank to the firm under cash credit account on 28 11 1967, 3 4 1968 and 17 2 1972 respectively. It may be noticed that the Bank was nationalised on July 7, 1969 under the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act V of 1970, which came into force on July 19, 1969. The respondent firm owned certain motor vehicles which were mentioned in A and Schedules to the plaint of the suit. The firm had two partners, namely, one section Doranna Choudhury, since deceased, the father of the respondent No. 3 and the respondent Nos. 4 to 12, the alienees, who were alienees of the mortgaged properties. In addition to the hypothecation of the A and Schedule properties made in its favour to secure repayment of the aforesaid amounts of loan, the other partner, the respondent, created an equitable mortgage in favour of the Bank on December 22, 1969 in respect of E schedule properties of the plaint. Section Doranna Choudhary, since the deceased also created an equity mortgage in respect thereof, the appellant Bank was not, therefore, formed or created under any special Indian law. The respondents contested the suit by filing written statements denying the creation of any equitable mortgage by the deceased partner and the respondents Nos. 2 & 3 in favour and of the bank. The appellants denied the creation or creation of the mortgages by the respondent. The Bank also contended that they were bona fide purchasers for valuable consideration and the Bank had been nationalised or formed under the Ordinance VIII of 1969 promulgated on July 18, 1969 and the present Banking Companies Act only ratifies the already created Bank under the said Ordinance, the appellants Bank was therefore not formed in pursuance of any `special Indian law '. The trial court decreed the suit against both the respondents. The High Court also held that no equitable mortgage was created in favour by the bank and, accordingly, dismissed the suit filed by the appellant. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 The Banking Companies Acts are quite legal and valid. No other point has been urged by either party in this appeal. In view of the definition, the expression `special ' must be an enactment of the British Parliament. If, on the date the Act was passed, there was no Indian Legislature, such an interpretation might be justified, but when there were existence of Indian Legislatures including a legislature at the Centre, it would be quite unreasonable to think that `specialIndian Law ' must he a law enacted by the British parliament. [966C D] 1.2 The intention of the Legislature is very clear in that the provision of section 4(e) would apply to a corporation which is the creature of a special Indian Law, whether it is created in pursuance or by or under the special Indian laws. There is no difference or distinction whatsoever between the corporation formed in pursuant of a `special I ' and a corporation formed by orunder a special law. It will be highly unreasonable and illogical to think, that as a corporation has been formed by an intermediary third party acting under a law as different from an activity of formation carried on by that law itself. [970E F] 1:3 The intention is very clearly clear in the provision.

The Central Government issued a notification fixing the ex factory price per maund of sugar produced in Punjab, Uttar Pradesh and North Bihar. The petitioners challenged the validity of the notification on the grounds (1) that the impugned notification was beyond the authority conferred on the Central Government under section 3 of the Act and clause 5 of the Order which empowered the Central Govern ment to fix the retail price, i.e., the price for the consumer, (2) that it compels factories to sell sugar at a loss, (3) that there is no reasonable safeguard against abuse of power and no provision for a check by way of appeal or otherwise was provided against the order of the Central Govt. The contention was rejected by the High Court on the ground that the Act did not authorise the Central Gov ernment to fix ex factory prices, and (4) that in any case it was discriminatory because it fixes ex factory rates only for factories in Punjab. Held, that the object of the impugned Notification was to provide for control of production, supply and distribution of trade and commerce in essential commodities in the interests of general public so that the 17 130 supplies of such commodities may be maintained or increased, their equitable distribution secured and they may be available to the general public at fair prices. The Act did no warrant for holding that under section 2 (c) of the , the Government must not only fix exfactory prices but also wholesale and retail prices. It was well known that the wholesale and wholesale prices depend upon ex factory Price, in the case of a commodity like sugar. Therefore if fixation of price at the ex factories level is enough to ensure a fair price for it, there is nothing to do with the cost of production; nor were the Government bound to fix prices separately so far as factories in other parts of India and there was no reasonable basis for such clasification. The impugned notification did not subserve the purposes of the section and the Order. There was no reason to cut down the generality of the words used in clause (c). The object of section 3 is undoubtedly to secure essential commodities at fair price, but it does not follow from this that this object can only be achieved if retail prices are fixed and that there was discrimination. In fact there is a discrimination after the control of sugar prices in these three regions and the contention that the factories in the other areas were left uncontrolled with the result that there would be discrimination.

The Government of West Bengal by its order dated September 13, 1956 transferred the dispute between the parties to the Second Industrial Tribunal under section 10 of the , and directed that the award be modified in accordance with law. The Fifth Industrial Tribunal made an award on August 26,1957, and it was duly notified in the Calcutta Gazette on September 26, 1957. As a mistake had crept in, the award was modified by the Tribunal by its Order dated August 30, 1951. Under the award the Tribunal held that there was rise in the cost of living index and that to neutralise the said rise the employees should get an increase of Rs. 7 in dearness allowance on the pay scale up to Rs. 50 and Rs. 5 on the Pay Scale above Rs.50. On that basis the dearness allowance payable to the employees was worked out and awarded. The correctness of the award is questioned in these appeals by special leave. Held, that the Tribunal had rightly relied upon Exhibit 3, corrected on the basis of the information given by the State Statistical Bureau, West Bengal for ascertaining the working class cost of working index since August 1954 up to March 1957. The Tribunal was right in holding that there could be no justification for interfering with it in view of the fact that the dispute was referred to the Industrial Tribunal and the Government acted well within its powers in transferring the dispute pending before the Second Tribunal, to the Fifth Industrial Tribu nal. The Act did not provide for any special or exceptional circumstances which would justify making up its mind and the Tribunal could not have relied upon a technical point but had chosen to get a decision of the Tribunal on merits, or it might be that there were no basis for the contention, as the company might have received notice under the said section. The Government made the order of transfer on April 9, 1957, i.e., after section 2 of the Amending Act 18 of 1957 was deemed to have come into force. It must therefore be held that the Government acting well within Its powers in transferred the disputes pending before it and transferring the same to another Tribunal constituted under the Act before the Amending Acts came into force and directed the Tribunal to give an award in accordance therewith.

The appellant, a religious institution dedicated to the propagation and promotion of the tenets of the Veera Saiva cult of Hinduism, was appointed as an Executive Officer under the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1927. The predecessor in office of the appellant filed a suit challenging the scheme on the ground that it contravened the appellant 's fundamental rights guaranteed by article 19(1)(f) and so, it could not be enforced. The District Judge held that some provisions of the scheme contravened the petitioner 's right under article 19 (1) (f ), and so he directed the Board to hand over possession to the Executive Officer on the grounds that the scheme under which possession was sought to be taken over from him was invalid inasmuch as it contravened his fundamental rights under article 1 9(1) of the Constitution. The appellant came up in appeal by special leave: Held, that the provisions of section 103 (a) and (b) clearly bring out the fact that where the legislature wanted the conti nuance of the action taken under the provisions Of the earlier Act only if the said action was consistent with the relevant provisions of that Act, it has so provided. The scheme of section 105(a) & (b), clearly brings out the facts that where a legislature wanted to the conclu sion of the act taken under those provisions only if that action was inconsistent with the provisions or of the latter Act, there is no scope for refusing to apply the test for which he contends. The said provision clearly brings the fact in that if a scheme governed by section 103(d) is deemed to have been made or sanctioned under the pro visions of the former Act and thus continued modifications in it can be effected by adopting the procedure prescribed by section 62(3).

The appellant was appointed as Hindi Teacher in Bani gochha, M.E. School (Orrisa) for a period of 89 days or till a candidate selected by the State Selection Board was made available. He joined the school on July 12, 1982 and continued to serve the school with repeated spells of 89 day appointments and one day break in between the spells till May 25, 1986. The appellant continued to work as Hindi teacher in Bani wentchha M. E. School for a short period of time. Although the period of summer vacation during all these years was not approved by the educational authorities, the appellant continued till 18th July 1986. He was not paid salary for the period he had remained absent from duty and his appointment after 1986 had not been approved by educational authorities. The managing committee even passed a resolution on July 6,1987 requesting the educational Authorities of the State to approve the continuous appointment of the appellant as Hindi Teachers with effect from July 12 1982. The High Court rejected the prayer for regularisation holding that the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of the Validation Act on the following reasoning: "Admittedly, the petitioner was appointed on December 12, 782 and continued till June 18, 1986 with breaks in between and the petitioner 's appointment was conditioned by the stipulation that he would continue until replaced by a candidate from the Select List. His case, therefore will not come within the preview of the validation Act and, therefore, the question of issuing any direction to regularise his service in a substantive vacancy because of the validate Validation Act does not arise. " The appellant filed a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the Orissa High Court claiming regularisation as Hindi teachers with effect on July12, 1982. It was contended that the appointment was made otherwise than in accordance with procedure laid down in the Education Act and the Rules framed thereunder; that he was entitled to be regularised in terms of the provisions of Section 3 of the Orissa Aided Educational Institutions (Appointment of Teachers Validation) Act, 1989 (the Validation Act). The High court rejected the writ petition holding that since the appellant had been appointed on 12.7.1982 and continued upto 18th June 1986 with break breaks in the between and respondent 's appointments was conditioned, by the stipulations that he should continue until replacement by a candidates from the select list; his case would not come under the pre review of the validating Act and therefore, he was not enti to the benefits of the Validating Act. The appeallant filed an appeal before this Court contending that on the plain reading of Section 2 of the Amending Act the appellant is entitled to regularisation as he was appointed regularly in accordance With procedure laid by the Education Authorities for a long period has led to the breach of Article 14 of the constitution. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The validation Act covers the field upto December 31, 1984. The State Government of Orissa will do well to consider the cases of all those who have completed one year or more as ad hoc teachers after December 31.1984 and come out with a scheme or any other appropriate measure to regularise their services. [994C D] Rattan Lal vs State of Haryana, ; followed. Rattan Lal V. State of Delhi, A.I.R. 1987 S.C. 478 speaking through Venkataramaiah, J. (as the learned Judge then was) observed as under: 994 The State Govern ment is expected to function as a model employer". "We strongly deprecate the policy of the state Government under which `ad hoc ' teachers are denied the salary and allowances or the period Of the summer vacation by resorting to the fictional breaks of the type referred to above. These `ad adhoc ' teachers shall be paid salary and allowance for the periods of the summer vacations as long as they hold the office under this order. Those who are entitled to maternity or medical leave shall also be granted such leave in accordancewith the rules.

The appellant was the Chairman of a Panchayat Samiti and the ground that he was disqualified from being chosen as a member of the Assembly. The respondent challenged the election of the appellant in an election petition inter alia on the ground, (1) that the office of Chairman of the Panchayat Samiti was an office under the State Government of Punjab and that the allowances paid under these rules made that office an office of profit; (2) that r. 3 did not convert the office as a part of the duties of the Chairman and (3) that in any case, the payment of travelling allowance and daily allowance under r. 4 to 7 was in addition to the payment under r . 3 and payment of two sets of aLlowances must necessarily result in profit to the payee. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the various questions involved were of considerable importance and should be settled by a larger Bench, referred the matter to a Full Bench. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent that (1 ) r. 7 did not authorise the Chairman to draw travelling allowance, and daily allowances while performing duties within the district and should only be entitled to theseallowances when required to travel outside the district; (ii) that under r, 3 of the Punjab Panchayat Samitis and Zila Parishads Non Official Ministerial Members ( Payment of Allowances) Rules, 1965, the Chairman was entitled to draw Travelling allowance and Daily Allowance even when travelling within the District. HELD : (i) The daily allowance is invariably fixed after estimating what extra expenditure in a day the person concerned would have to incur. A Chairman, it appears, was expected to incur more expenditure per day than a Member and that seems to be the reason why a higher rate of daily allowance was prescribed for him. [427 D] (ii). The appellant had failed to establish that the allowance payable under r 3 to 7 of the Rules result in any pecuniary gain to a Chairman of Panchayat Samiti or Zila Parishad was in excess of the amount of expenditure which he would have incurred for the purpose of performing the journeys in order to discharge his official duties. [446 E] Ravanna Subanna vs G.S. Kaggeerappa, A.I.R. 1954 S.C. 653 at p. 656, followed.

The appellant was the tenant of Kothi No. 196 situated in Dholki Mohalla, Sadar Bazar, Meerut ever since 1961 on a rent of Rs. 93 per mensem. The tenanted premises was let out to the appellant for running a Dal and Oil Mill. The respondents purchased the building from the erstwhile owners in 1963 a year later, they filed a suit for eviction on the ground that the appellant had made constructions materially altering the accommodation without their consent causing substantial damages to it. It was not necessary to refer to other grounds as the sole ground which survived for the decree of eviction relates to the material alterations made in the tenanted premises without obtaining the consent of the landlord. The disputed constructions include a partition wall in a hail converting the same into two portions and tin sheds shown by letters ABHG and CDGH. The trial court held that the partition wall did not constitute material alteration, it further held that there was no material alteration in the accommodation. On second appeal, the Additional Civil Judge set aside the trial Court 's order and dismissed the respondents suit on the findings that none of the construc tions constituted material alteration justifying appellant 's eviction under section 14(c) of the U.P. Cantonment Rent Control Act 10 of 1952. The High Court also held that since two sides of the tin shed were resting on the pucca wall it constituted a material alteration and that the construction was permanent or temporary in nature, did not attract any of the provisions of the Act. Allowing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The finding recorded by the trial court and the relevant evidence placed before the parties clearly show that the Partition wall did neither actual ly partition the hall converting the two portions for its convenient use, it could be removed without causing any damage to the building. [975D] 2.1 In the absence of any legislative defi nition of the aforesaid words it would be useful to refer ted to the meaning given to these words in dictionaries. Concise Oxford Dictionary defines the word 'alter ' as change in character, position 'Materially ' as an adverbim means 'a substantial change in the character, form and the structure of the building without destroying its identity.

The appellant company filed a suit against the respondent firm for setting aside an ex parte decree for Rs. 28,479/ passed in favour of the respondent. The trial court held that summons in the suit was not duly served on the company and it came to know about the decree on 29 7 1975. Hence he set aside the ex parte judgment. The respondent firm filed a revision petition before the High Court under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, which allowed the revision, set aside its judgment and upheld the passing of the exparte decree. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 In view of the provisions contained in Order 5 Rule 17 of the C.P.C., it is not necessary for the High Courts to interfere with it. [1031E] 1.2 The words "Principal Officer" in clause (a) of Rule 2 would include managing agents and it can, under this rule, be on a juristic person. Accordingly service on managing agents who are a corporation is valid under clause (A). [1032F G] 1:3 In the instant case nothing of the kind was done. It was not the case of the Respondent in its rejoinder filed in the Miscellaneous case that the service of summons as effected in accordance with the first part of clause (b) of Order 29 of the Civil Procedure Code. Annexure A to the counter affidavit filed by the respondent is the petition filed by him under Order 9 Rule 13 of the code.

The appellant filed a complaint against the respondents on the basis of a police report. After passing a preliminary order on the 29th July, 1976 (wherein the Magistrate had recorded reasons for his being satisfied that a breach of the peace existed, the Magistrate called upon the parties to file their written statements and then after a full enquiry as provided by section 145 the Magistrate passed the final order declaring the appellant to be in possession of the land. Against this order, the respondents moved the High Court under section 482 Cr. P.C. for quashing the order of the Magistrate. The High Court allowed the petition and remitted the case to the Magistrate for a fresh enquiry. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) there was no clear finding by the Magistrate in the final orders that there was an apprehension of breach of peace; (ii) there is no evidence to show that any prejudice was caused to any of the parties who had the full opportunity to produce their evidence before the Court. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1(i) The High court erred in holding that the final decision of the magistrate was vitiated in absence of a finding that breach of law existed at the time the order was passed. [95 D] (ii). The Magistrate had given a finding to the effect that there is apprehension of the breach of ' peace and once he records his satisfaction in the preliminary order, he can continue the proceedings. It is not necessary that at each stage he should be satisfied that there exists an imminent apprehension of such breach. [96 F] Hari Ram & Ors. vs Banwari Lal & Ors., ; , referred to. (iii) The Magistrate must be satisfied regarding the existence of a breach on the date of preliminary order irrespective of the rights of the party. [97 E F] R. H. Bhutani vs Shri Brij Lal & ors. ; , followed.

The appellant, a public company registered under the Indian Companies Act, and its Managing Agents are the firm of Messrs. K. R. Thyagaraja Chettiar and Co., whose partners are Mr. Thoyagarajasam Chettiar and his two sons. The company is resident and ordinarily resident in British India its head office being at Madurai in Madras State. It carries on business in the manufacture and sale of yarn, and for the purpose of that business it purchases cotton and occasionally sells it. Its profits arise for the most part from the sale of the yarn and to some extent from the re sale of cotton. According to the account books of the company, its profits from business for the account year 1941 42 were Rs. 9,25,364, for 1942 43 Rs. 2409,832 and for 1943 44 Rs. 29,1388 1. In its returns, the appellant showed these amounts as its income chargeable to tax for the respective years. The Department did not accept the correctness of the figures shown in the accounts. It contended that the company had earned more profits than were disclosed in its accounts and that it had contrived to suppress them by resort to certain devices. Held, (per curiam), that the finding of the Commissioner was correct and must be affirmed. The question whether the sales entered in the books of a public body constituted under the Income tax Act or not was one of mixed law and fact. The decision in Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay vs Ahmedbhai Umarbhai and Co. (1910) L.R. 70 I.A. 222, referred to.

The appellant, a former employee of the respondent company, was appointed as a General Manager in the respondent 's mill at Dehra Dun and later on he was converted into a company. The firm suffered a loss. In the next year the profit being less than Rs. 1 lakh, the commission payable to the General Manager was 25%. The Income tax Officer disallowed the claim on the ground that it was excessive and quite unreasonable looking to the salary paid to Shri Vaish. He also found that no general practice of giving commission at the rate of 25 % existed in the assessee 's line of business. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner reduced the amount of Rs. 5,000 as a reasonable amount payable as commission. The Tribunal held that the post of General Manager carried the responsibility equal to that of the Director who was given the charge of the conduct of business after the death of Shri Vaish and the General manager. In reference under section 66(2) of the Income tax Act, 1922, the High Court answered the question against the assessee. The appellant contended before this Court that in the circumstances of the case, the amount claimed as expenditure was laid out wholly and exclusively for the purpose of the business of the assessee within the meaning of section 10(2)(xv) of Income tax, 1922. HELD: (i) In the present case, both the Appellate Tribunal and the Appellate Tribu nal rejected the view of the Appellate Asstt. Commissioner that the rate was reasonable and the allowance was therefore restricted to half of the amount claim claimed by the assessee.[530 D] Swadeshi Cotton Mills Co. Ltd. vs C.I.T., U.P. ; , followed. (ii) The principle of this decision applies to the present ease and it must accordingly be held that in view of section 5(2), (xv) and 10( 2)(xv), the entire amount of commission paid to the general Manager was an amount laid out or expended wholly and solely for the purpose of business, profession or vocation as required under section 10 (2)(Xv). [530 E] Swadehi Cotton Mill Co. vsC.I., U P. ; followed.

The appellant was a workman employed in the Digha factory of Bata Shoo Company. On January 13, 1954, the management served him with a charge sheet alleging that he had been doing anti union activities inside the factory during the working hours and so was guilty under section 12B(1) of the Standing Orders and Rules of the company. The appellant submitted his reply denying the charge and asking to be excused. On March 7, 1957, the appellant filed a fresh petition stating that he did not want his case to be represented by Fateh Singh as he had no faith in him. This application was dismissed by the Tribunal on February 26, 1957. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the Tribunal committed a serious error in rejecting his application for separate representation and (ii) the award of the Tribunal was not made in accordance with law. Held:(i) The scheme of the Industrial Disputes Act does appear to contemplate that the machinery provided therein should be set in motion to settle only disputes which involve the rights of workmen as a class and that a dispute touching the individual rights of a workman was not intended to be the subject of adjudication under the Act, when the same had not been taken up by the Union or a number of workmen. (ii)(a) The appellant was the Secretary of the Union. If were the Union had not taken up his cause, there would not have been any reference. In view of all the circumstances, it cannot be said that the Tribunal acted improperly in refusing the appellant 's prayer for representation through representatives of his own choice in preference to Fateh Singh, the Secretary, of the union. (b) The statement by the counsel will be honoured by the company and the company agreed without prejudice to pay an ex gratia amount of Rs. 1,000/ .

The appellants instituted a suit for ejectment and recovery of rent against the respondents on the allegation that the respondents were the tenants in the house. The suit was decreed by the trial court but the High Court set aside the decree for ejectment against the appellants. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) Rule 4 of O. XLI of the Code of Civil Procedure does not apply to an appeal filed by some of the plaintiffs against the whole decree in pursuance of the provisions of r. 4 of 0. XLI. The two deal with different stages of the appeal and provide for different contingencies. There is nothing common in their provisions which make the provisions Of one interfere in any way with those of the other. [553 D E] (ii) Rule 33 really provides as to what the Appellate Court can find the appellant entitled to. It empowers the Appellate court to pass any decree and make any order which ought to have been passed or made in the proceedings before it and thus could have reference only to the nature of the decree or Order in so far as it affects the rights of the appellants.[553 E] State of Punjab vs Nathu Ram, [1962] 2 S.C.R. 636 applied. (iii) The High Court could not have heard the appeal of the surviving appellants when the appeal by the kedar Nath had abated and the decree in favour of the respondents had become final against his legal representatives. [554 D E; 556 C] State Of Punjab vs Budh Prakash, A.I.R., 1959 Orissa 148, approved.

The appellant tenant of a building in Delhi having been inducted into possession by the respondent landlord under a letting of May 19, 1954 evidenced by a deed which fixed the term merely as less than a year. The landlord had been receiving rent from the tenant until the time he filed a petition for eviction under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act on the ground that no notice to quit had been given nor notice of forfeiture as prescribed by those sections. There was no dispute that neither notice to terminate the tenancy under section 111(g) nor notice to forfeiture of determining the tenancy had been issued, nor notice thereof. The appellant tenant fell back on certain defences grounded on ss.106 and 111 of the TP Act on account of which no notice could be given. The Rent Controller ordered eviction and the Appellate Tribunal affirmed it.
