In appeal by certificate under article 133 of the Constitution, the appellant tenant contended that the lease had expired by efflux of time limited thereby under section III(g), and no notice terminating the tenancy was needed and further that the forfeiture of the tenancy caused by sub letting contrary to the terms of the deed could be availed of by the landlord even in the absence of a notice as contemplated by section 111 (g) because the TP act, as amended by the Amending Act of 1929 did not, in terms, apply to the present lease and the principles of justice, equity and good conscience. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The requirement of a valid notice under section 11(1)(b) is intrinsic evidence of the fact that the formality is merely statutory and it cannot trace its origin to any rule of equity. [919D] 2. The mere institution of the legal proceeding for eviction fulfils the requirement of law for determination of the lease. Once a certificate of fitness has been granted under article 134, the appeal in all its amplitude, is before this Court and every point may be urged by the appellant provided this court permits it, having regard to the circumstances. Even so, it is argued that only where a lease has been duly determined giving rise to a right to present possession under the or the contract of lease he cannot evict the tenant unless he satisfied any one of the grounds set out in section 3. Firstly, the lease is one where the time is not limited and therefore section 111 will not apply and is terminable on the part of the lessor only in the manner provided by section 106, i.e., by 15 days ' notice expiring with the end of the month of the right. The counter contention of the landlord apart from the plea of statutory tenancy requiring no further notice to determine, is that the lessee has reasonable notice of termination even though it does not expire with the expiry of the stipulated period. [ 909D E] 3. In the instant case, there was some confusion in this order about the determination of lease being under section 112(g). The Tribunal applied what he considered to be the principles governing the situation as could be held to be consistent with the rules of equity, justice and good justice. [900G H] 4. The High Court was right in its view.

The Governor of Assam was satisfied that the appellant, who had been dismissed from service, was unfit to be retained in public service and that he ought to be dismissed from serv ice. The Governor made these two orders on April 1, 1965, which were later amended by the Amending Act, 1963, which came into force on October 6, 1963. The amended Article 311(2) had been reproduced in the judgment of this Court in Khem Chand vs Union of India and Others ; , followed. In order to enable the Governor to pass an order of dismissal without holding an inquiry, it is necessary that the Government servant should have the opportunity, to say, if that be his case, that he has not been guilty of any misconduct to merit any punishment at all and also that the particular punishment proposed to be given is much more drastic and severe than he deserves. The satisfaction recorded by the Governor, therefore, related to the third step to be taken under clause (2) of article 311 as enumerated above. In the present case, in the impugned order dated April 1. 1965, the satisfaction of the Governor was recorded in the following words: "It is not expedient to give the said Shri P. K. Hore an opportunity to show cause against the action proposed to he taken in regard to him. . ". The satisfaction of this Governor under sub clause (c) of the proviso to cl.(2) was recorded by him in the language in which the provision in article 311(1) stood prior to its amendment by the Constitution (Fifteenth Amendment) Act, 1964, and which was as follows: " Provided that this clause shall not apply (a) where a person is dismissed or removed or reduced in rank on the ground of conduct which has led to his conviction on a criminal charge; or (b) where the authority empowered to dismiss or remove a person or to reduce him in rank is satisfied that for some reason, to be recorded by that authority in writing it is not reasonably practicable to hold such inquiry. " The satisfaction under the unamended provision, therefore that the Governor had to arrive at was that it was not expedient in the interest of the security of the State and that the satisfaction did not extend to the inexpediency of giving P.K. Kahore an an opportunity of showing cause against his action proposed. The appellant challenged these orders by a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution on the grounds (1) that the order of the Government did not satisfy the requirements of sub clause(c) Of cl.(ii) of Article 31 1; (2)(a) that it is too much to hold that the High Court was in error in holding that the opinion of the Chief Secretary was recorded as required by the amended article 311. HELD: The satisfaction, recorded by this Governor, was not a mere formality and was based on an extraneous considerations. [488 F] Khem Chand V Union of lndia, ; , referred to. (1)(a). It is not obligatory that the President or the Governor should have given a reasonable opportunity of show cause for showing cause. The consultation with the Public Service Commission in such cases cannot be dispensed with. It is only under article 320(3) (c), that consultation with, the Commission is necessary on all disciplinary matters affecting a person serving under the Government of a State. [489 G] Khemchand vs Union Of India and Ors., ; , applied. (b). The consultation was not prescribed either by the Rules or by the Regulations. The consult was only under Article 320(2)(c) which lays down when the Public Services Commission shall be consulted.

The Shia community of Mohalla Doshipura, Varanasi is a Shia Muslim and the members of his sect numbering about 4000 constitute a religious denomination having a common faith and they observe MOHARRAM for two months and eight days in a year in memory of Hazrat Imam Hussain who alongwith his 72 followers attained martyrdom at Karbala in Iraq. The said religious belief is practised by the men folk and the women fol kah of the Shia Community by holding Majlises (religious discourses), Recitations, Marsia and doing other performances. Plot No. 246/1130 on which there is a Zanana Imambara structure of white stone having 12 pillars) constructed by Shias in 1893 used for holding Maj lises, Recitations etc. when it over flows the Baradari. Particulars of the religious rites, practices and functions performed by the members thereof on the occasion of the observance of MOHAR RE: (a) The Tazia (representing and signifying the dead body of Hazarat Imam Hussain) is kept in the Wakfs on plot No. 247/11 30 on which it stands apted ground, belongs to both the sects as it was constructed out of general subscription from members of both the religious sects and every Mohammedan is entitled to go in and perform his devotions according to the ritual of his own sect or school; (b) The members of their sect numbering over 4000 constitute an religious denomination. Plot Nos. 245, 246, 247, 248/23/72, 602, 603, 602/1133, 246/2634 and 247/2630 in the said Mohalla and buildings and structures thereon belong to the Shias community of that Mohalla have a right to perform their religious functions and practices on the said plots and structures as also an appropriate writ, direction or order in the nature of mandamus commanding respondents 1 to 4 not to prohibit or restrain the Shiras of the Mohalla from performing their religious duties and practices thereon. The Shia Muslims of Mohalla Mohalla Dhaloshippura are founded by the followers folks and the Women fol lk of Shia sect of MohallaDoshipcha, Police Station Jaitpura (formerly Adampur) in the city of Varanasi and in particular are seeking a declaration that the 9 plots of land bearing plot Nos. 248, 246 and 247 in the aforesaid Mohalla and building structures thereon belonged to the Sunni community of village Doswara and that the members and Shia communities of Shias have a rights to perform religious functions, practices, observances and functions on the property in question as claimed; it is contended that a clear and sharp distinction must be made between title and ownership of the concerned plots of lands, title and/or ownership of structures on those plots and the rights exercisable by the Shiana community over the concerned plot and structures on these plots and structure thereon and there are considerable gaps and inadequacies in the documents and material before the Court in that behalf which can only be filled in by trial and by recording evidence and in the absence of adequate material no declaration as to the title to the plots or structures or even as to rights in or over the plots and buildings could be granted in favour of the Sunni Community. Allowing the writ petition, ^ HELD: 1. The Notification dated 26th February, 1944 issued under section 5(1) of the 1936 Act by the Sunni Board is of no avail to the Sunnis for the purpose of defeating the customary rights of Shiadas to perform his religious ceremonies and functions over the plot and structure on the other plots and constructions thereon which had been listed as Shia Wakfs under the Notification dated 15th January, 1954. [1135C] 2.

The assessee, a limited company, disclosed capital gains of Rs.3.10 lakhs but claimed set off of capital loss of Rs 3.17,500 sustained by it during the assessment year 1957 58 over sale of shares to three associate concerns. The Income tax Officer disallowed the claim for set off on the footing that when in the assessment years 1957 58 and 1957 58 the loss was claimed it was excluded in the computa tion of income as capital loss and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner while disposing of the assessee 's appeal had stated that it was a notional capital loss. As no further appeal was carried by the assessee with the first appellate order, the matter had become final. The assessee challenged the rejection of its claim before the Appellate Tribunal and reiterated its claim. The Tribunal came to the conclusion that the assessee was entitled to the benefit of set off provided it satisfied that its capital loss was computed under the old Act. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that: (1) the benefit conferred under section 24 of 1922 Act continued to be given effect to under the 1961 Act and notwithstanding the wordings of section 80 of the latter Act, the High Court was Fight in holding that the claim of setoff was admissible in its view. (2) The benefit conferred by section 24 continued to he given effect from under the 1922 Act and not under the Income tax Act; (3) the loss claimed for the assessment period 1957 58 could be set off against the income determined for the assess ment year 1965 66, which could be carried forward to subsequent years; and (4) the claim was not admissible. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court reached the correct conclusion and there is no merit in the appeal. [1165B] 2.1 In view of the provisions of section 74(1)(b), and section 80 together, it is necessary to turn attention to the relevant provisions thereof and they are in sections 74 and 80. For convenience they are extract ed: "Section 74(I)(a) Where in respect of any assessment year. the net result of the compu tation under the head "capital gains" is a loss such loss shall. subject to the other provisions of this Chapter.

The respondent was recruited as a Senior Scientific Officer on October 12, 1966 in the Defence Science Service. He was posted in the Directorate of Technical Development and Production (Air) (DTD & P). The recruitment when made was always to the Defence Engineering Service, and after the recruitment, the recruits were posted according to the exigency of the service, in any of the three units. Their 22 services were inter changeable and inter transferable be tween the three Units. All, the service conditions of the persons working in the three establishments including scales of pay, superannuation age etc. were the same and were regulated by the same set of Rules, viz. Defence Science Services Rules. In the year 1979, the Defence Scientific Service was trifurcated and reconstituted as Defence Research and Development Serv ice (DRDO) was reconstituted as defence Research and development Serv ice. The respondent approached the Administrative Tribunal, who held that the respondent was not liable to be retired at the age of 58 years his superannuation being deemed to have been increased to 60 years in view of the OM dated 24.12.85 read with OM dated 10.2.86 referred to above. It was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Government had a right to prescribe different conditions of service for the members belonging to the different units, and merely because the superannuation age of the members of theDRDS was increased, it could not be held that he belonged to another unit, viz DAQAS, was entitled to the said benefit. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The decision of the Tribunal is both proper and valid, and there is no substance in the present appeal. [22D] 2. In spite of the decision of this Court in Union of India vs R.S. Gupta, ; , it was not necessary to decide whether the Government has such power.

The appellant was elected to the Sangli City Municipality. The election of councillors to the said Municipality was held under the Maharashtra Municipalities Act, 1965. The counting of votes took place with regard to Ward No. 25 on June 4, 1967. According to the election petition, the results were published in the Official Gazette on June 15, 1967 and the petition was filed on June 24, 1967, i.e., within time prescribed by the Act. The appellant contended that the procedure adopted by the trial court was wrong in that the two witnesses who were examined as Court witnesses had been cited by the election petitioner earlier and the learned Judge had in the exercise of jurisdiction vested in him refused to issue summonses to them when he was asked to do so on August 21, 1968. Held, that the High Court was not right in refusing to quash the order. The provisions of section 21(1) (a) of the Act clearly show that the powers of the court in this respect are wide amplitude and specially when investigation is being made into allegations about the commission of a corrupt practice. It may be that in the instant case, if the two persons had not been examined, the Judge might well have decided the issue the other way. But the Act certainly gave him the power to do such thing and no exception can be taken to the course adopted by tho Judge although it must be recorded that his earlier order refusing to issue summones to him in the first instance when asked to does so on the 21st August was hardly justifiable.

The U. P. Sales Tax (Validation) Act, 1958, was passed by the Governor of Uttar Pradesh on March 31, 1956, validating the said notification as from March 31. 1956. The validity of this Act was challenged in a petition under article 32 of the Constitution on the ground that it contravened articles 14 and 19(1)(f), (g) and (g). Held, that the Validation Act was not ultra vires the powers of the legislature under entry 54, List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution. The impugned notification was intra vires the power of the Legislature under Entry 54, for the reason that it operates retrospectively. It was not a tax on the occasion of sale and there was no other entry in List II or List III of the VII Schedule to tile Constitution. Firm Bangali Mal vs Sales Tax Officer, ; , followed. The State of Madras vs Boddu Paidanna & Sons, ; and Firm Bangli Mal vs sales tax Officer, , referred to. Held further, that a sale for the purpose of the entry must be what in law is recognised as sale. In the present case there was a sale of goods as known to law, and the impugned notification did not contravene article 14 or 19(6)(g) of the constitution. The sales tax sought to be taxed took place between April 1, 1956 and July 31, 1957 whereas the Validation Acts by force of which the tax became payable came into force in 1958. It is therefore not a sale on the date when the impugned Act was passed.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to death by the Sessions Court, and the High Court affirmed it in appeal. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The special circumstances of this case constrain us to relent a little on principle because the restorative approach to sentencing has been jettisoned by the courts below. [592 D] 2. In prison treatment must, therefore, be geared to psychic healing, release of stresses, restoration of self respect and cultural normalisation apart from training to adapt oneself to the life outside. The functional failure of our pachydermic prison projects, exacerbated by its tension and trauma on the one hand and the reverse ethos inside on the other, deserves judicial cognizance. [593 E F] Sunil Batra 's case and later that, constitutionally viewed punitive deprivation of personal freedom must be goal oriented and humanely restorative, apart from being deterrent. The insulated years behind the insensitive bars must possess a hospital setting if correction is a social purpose, as Gandhiji often insisted. In jail treatment must therefore be geired to psychologistaling, released of stressers, restoration or cultural normalization apart from experience to adapt molester to life outside; and in this perspective, we bl deterrence with correction and reduce the sentence to rigorous imprisonment for two years. [595 G H] Sunil Kumar Batra vs Delhi Administration, ; , referred to. 3. The Special circumstances of the case constracted us to re ferred a little more on principle since the restatory approach to sentence has been shuttisoned. [566 F] 4. The task is not done by a negative reduction in the prison term. What is more important is a set of positive prescriptions which will ensure his turning a new leaf. One major method in securing this goal is to keep alive the family tie of the person in prison so that he may not deteriorate into a non person. Within limits of the Prison Act and Rules thereunder, the State Government or the Inspector General of Prisons will ensure that on parole, furlough or orders, the young appellant turns a newlic leaf of normal life. [591 G H; 592 A B] 5. The Court must restore the man. A hyper sexed homo sapiens cannot be occupilitated by humiliating or harsh treatment but that is precisely the perversion of unreformed Jail Justice which some criminologists have described as the crime of punishment. This Court has held, in Sunil Batra vs State of Delhi, ; and later followed.

The respondent, a limited company dealing in land, maintained its accounts on mercantile system. By an order dated June 21, 1946 under rule 75A(1) of the Defence of India Rules read with section 19 of the Act certain plots of land measuring about 19.17 acres in village Kankulia in the District of 24 Parganas and belonging to the assessee were requisitioned by the Government of West Bengal. Subsequently the land was acquired permanently in the State Government under s.5, Requisition of Land (Continuance of Powers) Act, 1951 by a notice of acquisition dated December 27, 1952. The Land Acquisition Officer awarded a sum of Rs.24,97,249 as compensation payable to the respondent. The assessee preferred an appeal before the Arbitrator and the Arbitrator made an award on July 29, 1955 whereby he fixed the amount of compensation at Rs.30,10,873 on account of the permanent acquisition of the land, thus enhancing the original amount of the compensation by Rs.513,624 on which he directed interest at 5 per cent per annum from January 8, 1953, the date of acquisition to the date when payment till the date was made till the day of the acquisition. The State Government then appealed to the High Court and during the pendency of the appeal on April 25, 1956 it deposited Rs.736,691 which the assessee was permitted to withdraw on May 9, 1956 on furnishing security. On receipt of the amount credited it in its suspense account on the same date. During the assessment proceedings for the assessment year 1956 57, the relevant accounting period being the year ended March 31, 1956 the Income Tax Officer brought to tax a sum which had already been assessed to tax. The Appellate Tribunal accepted the other contention and held that the compensation received by the assessee related to the acquisition of land which was the stock in trade of the assessee and was, therefore, a trading receipt of business carried on by the respondent, and therefore, was a trading income. On appeal by the Revenue before the Income tax Appellate Tribunal two contentions were raised by it. The High Court answered the question in favour of the respondent and against the Revenue. Dismissing the appeal by certificate, ^ HELD: 1. The view taken by the High Courts is correct. [395F] 2.1 In the majority judgment delivered by N.H. Bhagwati, J. it was explained that the words "arising or accruing" describe a right to receive profits and that there must be a debt owed by some body. Unless and until there is created in favour by the assesses a debt due by somebody", it was observed that the right to such income in the nature of compensation would arise or accrue and till then there was no liability in praesenti in respect of the additional amount of compensated damages or additional compensation which are claimed by the owner of the Land.

The appellants filed a suit against the respondents for eviction of the appellant from the suit premises and for certain other reliefs. The appellants contended that the compromise decree was void as being against the provisions of the Act. The trial court accepted the appellants ' objection to the execution on the ground that the decree was not a nullity and was executable. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that paragraph 1 of the compromise petition was an admission in respect of only the first part, namely, the positive aspect of clause (f) and not of the second part, viz., that the landlord has no other reasonably suitable nonresidential accommodation. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The suit was clearly valid and executable. [882 F] In order to get a decree or order for eviction against a tenant whose tenancy is governed by any Rent Restriction or Eviction Control Act, the suitor must make out a case for eviction in accordance with the provisions Of the Act.[883 A] In the instant case, on facts of the case, the compromise was clearly legal and executable and it was not necessary to refer to any piece of evidence adduced at the inconclusive trial. [888 C D] The object of the Delhi and Ajmer Rent Control Act is to protect the tenants from protracted litigation. It does not find much difficulty in bringing the section at par with other similar State statutes and holding as a matter of construction that no decree for eviction can be passed except on one or more of the grounds enumerated in Section 12(1). A Bench of the Madhya Pradesh High Court in Smt. Chandan Bai vs Surja, ; , relied on.

The assessee company, doing business as selling agents of a Textile Mill. For the assessment year 1955 56, the assessee was assessed on a total income of Rs. 1,61,089/ and taxes paid were Rs. 69,973/ leaving a distributable balance of Rs 60,761/ . In this year also the company did not declare any dividend because of the loss referred to earlier. The Income tax Officer however, again invoked the provisions of section 23A(1) and levied additional super tax @ 4/ per rupee on the surplus of Rs 61,898,000/ . The Appellate Assistant Commissioner took the view that the loss incurred by the company was a capital loss. But all the same as there was no commercial profits in the relevant accounting years it was not reasonable to expect the assessee company to declare any dividends in respect of those years in view of the capital loss incurred and he, therefore, cancelled the orders of the Income tax officer under section 23 A(1). The Tribunal agreed with the conclusions reached by the Appellate Assistant. Commissioner and held that the losses incurred by it were a capital gain. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The question is not whether the value of the shares may go up in future but whether the Directors were justified in not declaring dividends in view Of the loss suffered. [851 D] Commissioner of Income tax, West Bengal vs Gangadliar Bannerjee and Co. , referred to. (ii) The assessee had suffered a capital losses of Rs 12,00,000 and it was due to the loss of Rs, 12,000 on account of depreciation in the value. [864 E] Commissioner Of Income tax West Bengal, vs Gangadhar Das Gupta, ; , followed.

The appellants filed objections before the Civil Judge, Aligarh. The Civil Judge modified the award and the award announced by the appellant was accepted. The appellant filed a petition under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure for modifying the award on the ground that no appeal lay against the order of the Civil judge. The District Judge allowed the petition and set aside the order passed by the Civil Court. On appeal to the District Judge, a preliminary objection was raised that no appeals lay (1) I.L.R. [1959] 1 All. 65, referred to in section 37 of the Act. Held, that the effect of section 37 is that all the provisions of the except sub section (1), of section 6, sections 7, 12, 36 and 37 apply to arbitrations under the Consolidation of Holdings Act. Section 37 of ' the Act does not make any distinction between provisions like section 39 and section 15 of the . Further, the effect Of section 46 and section 47 is that every provision of the , except sub sections (1 ) of section 8, 6, Sections 7,12, 36, and 37, apply to arbitration proceedings under the Act, and it is not necessary to rely (1)[1959] Supp. 1 All E. 354, referred only to arbitration under the consolidation of Holdings Rules, 1954 but there is thus discrimination which offends article 14 of the Constitution. Attar Singh vs The State of U.P., [1959]. Supp. I S.C.R 928, approved.

The petitioner was diploma holder in Engineering and holds the post of Executive Engineer in the respondent Corporation. Till 1974, the promotion post of the superintending Engineer was available both for diploma holders and degree holders according to merit cum seniority. This was so according to the practice followed by the Corporation without making any rules or regulation in that behalf. In 1974, a corporation made regulations by passing a resolution and continued the same practice. The petitioner challenged the validity of the said resolution before the High Court which dismissed the petition. Hence this special leave petition. Dismissing the Special Leave Petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The proposition that in the absence of rule or regulation the authority can prescribe service conditions by executive instructions and this is what was done till the year 1988 and is also sought to be done since 1988 by the impugned resolution. [Emphasis supplied]. 1.2 In the absence o r. or regulation, the authority cannot prescribe service condition by executive instruction and this has been made without noticing the decision in Khosa 's case. Hence, the observation are per incuriam as regards the next contention, admittedly neither the practice adopted till 1988 nor the resolution passed by the respondent corporation in 1988 nor resolution passed in accordance with section 64 of the Act. [795C D] 1.3 The proposition in the instant case that in view of the above, the petitioner could be given a higher scale than non matriculate Tracers thought their duties were identical, is not justified. It was a case where no separate quota for promotion to the post was kept for degree holder Junior Engineers and diploma holder Junior Engineer. The degree holders Junior Engineers had sought a relief that such a quota be kept. It is while dealing with this relief claimed, that this Court had observed that it could not be don e except by carving out two classes in the same category of junior Engineers o the basis merely of their qualification which is not permissible in law though the creation of selection grade in the said category on the basis of merit and on seniority is well known and permissible. The principle that in a State of Mysore & Anr. vs P. Narasing Rao, ; , relied upon by the Court is afraid, not correct. It has been a case of direct recruits and promotees integrated into one cadre. Once they were integrated they lost their birth marks, viz., the different sources from which they were recruited. [769E F] State of Jummu & Kashmir vs Triloki Nath Khosa & Ors., ; , referred to Roshan Lal Tandon vs Union of India, ; and distinguished.

The petitioners in the writ petition were members of the Bar Association. The first petition was by an advocate practising in this Court; the second by the Supreme Court Advocates on Record Association and the last by the Honorary Secretary of the Bombay Bar Association, which was a public interest litigation, sought relief for one for mandamus to the Union of India to fill up the vacancies of Judges in the Supreme court and the several High Courts of the country and ancilary orders of directions in regard to the same. The petitioners contended that the petitions were not maintainable and the filling up of the vacancies in the superior courts was not a justiciable matter, and that the filing of the writ petitions by the petitioners was not justiciable matter. Reliance was placed on the decision of this Court in S.P. Gupta vs Union of lndia, [1982] 2 SCR 365, which held that while the ratio in S P. Gupta 's case left the matter of fixing up of a Judge strength to the President of India under the constitutional scheme, and the choice of Judges to the prescribed procedure once the sanctioned strength was determined it was the obligation of the Union to maintain the sanctioned cadre in the Superior Courts and these cases were allowed to proceed. Dismissing the writ Petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The primacy of the Chief Justice of India in the process of selection would improve the quality of selection. [438C] 2.1 In view of what we have already stated and the assurance held out by the learned Attorney General, it is clear that further monitoring for the time being is not necessary. As already pointed out, the petition from Bombay was confined to filling up vacancies in this High Court. Excepting two, the remaining vacancies have been filled up and the number of unfilled posts has been reduced to around 22. The total posts to be filled up were 30 in number 19 being permanent and 11 additional vacancies. [414E F] 2:2 It is clear on a plain reading of clause (2) of Article 124 that it is the President, which in effect and substance means the Central Government, which is empowered by the Constitution to appoint Judges of the Supreme Courts.

The respondent, a Head Cashier in the K.G. Road Branch availed of 15 days leave from April 17, 1978 to May 1, 1978 and was allowed an advance of Rs.2,500 on April 4, 1978 under LFC to be adjusted later on his submitting the LFC Bill. He submitted a bill for Rs. 2,800 on May 5, 1978 along with a stamped cash receipt purported to have been issued by him. The said bill was passed by the Bank on May 15, 1978 but subsequent investigations revealed that the firm of M/s. Shri Manju Travels was a spurious one which indulged in issuing fake travel receipts. Thereupon the respondent was served with a charge sheet dated October 12, 1978 followed by a departmental enquiry. A letter was also addressed on the same day to M/S. Shri Manu Travels, Bangalore requesting them to furnish the details of the persons who traveled and the amounts received by the said firm. No reply was received from the said Firm but the respondent sent a reply on August 10, 1978 which was not found to be satisfactory. Some correspondence ensued between the respondent and the appellant in this connection but finally the respondent 's was served alongwith a charge sheeted sheet dated November 12,1978 followed by another departmental enquiry wherein he was retired from service on January 31, 1979. The respondent filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of discharge in the High court. A Single Judge of the High COurt held that such an enquiry is incompetent and without jurisdiction and therefore null and void. The Division Bench of the said High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that since the impugned order of dismissal got merged in the appellate order, the initial defect, if any, stood removed, was repelled by the learned Single Judge on the ground that 'as the original order was without jurisdiction or competence, there was nothing for the Appellate Authority to confirm '. The appellant preferred a Letters Patent Appeal against the said order of the Single Judge. A Division Bench dismissed the appeal holding that the de facto doctrine can have no application. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in quashing the impugned orde rs of punishment but having regard to the special facts and circumstances pointed out earlier, it should not have ordered payment of 'all consequential benefits flowing from the declaration that the impugned Order was bad in law. [205E] 1.2 In the instant case, the respondent did not attribute any bias or mala fides to the Enquiry Officer nor did he com plain that he was in any manner prejudiced on account of the alleged misconduct committed by him and therefore his actions and decisions were saved. The de facto concept envisages that acts performed de facto by officers within the scope of their assumed official authority are to be regarded as binding as if they were performed by officers de jure. While the de f facto doctrine saves official acts done by an officer whose appointment is found to he defective the private parties to a litigation are precluded from challenging the appointment in any collateral proceedings. But the doctrine does not come to the rescue of an intruder or usurper or a total stranger to the office. Obviously the doctrine can be invoked in cases where there is an appointment to office which is defective; but notwithstanding the defect to the title of the office, the decisions made by such a de facto officer clothed with the powers and functions of the Office would be as efficacious as those made by a de jure officer. The same would, however, not be true of a total intrud er or usulper of office. [206F G] 1:3 In the facts and circum stances of this case, it is clear that the respondent had admittedly retired from serv ice in 1986 and if the order imposing punishment is quashed he would ordinarily have to be paid his wages etc., upto the date of his retirement.

The respondents submitted to the appellant plans for its sanction for execution of work consisting of repairs, additions as well as alterations to the said building. The Commissioner of the appellant Corporation by letter informed the respondents that their application for execution had been refused on the grounds "that the proposal was under acquisition and also effected in the ROW and the land was residential against proposal of commercial". A dispute arose between the parties regarding the construction of a new road which was to be constructed. The respondents submitted their applications for execution and the Commissioner of Delhi by letter dated February 4, 1966 informed the respondent that their applications were quite legal and that there was no violation of any law or rules having failed, they filed a writ petition in the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution praying for the issue of an order or direction in the nature of mandamus directing the appellant to accord sanction to the plan. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Commissioner could decline the sanction only if there was a contravention of sub section (2) of section 336 or section 340 or any other provision of the Corporation Act or of any other Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Master Plan prepared by the Authority for Delhi which has statutory force, had come into operation under the Development Act and therefore the Master plan prepared by him did not contravene any of the provisions of sub sections (2), (3) and (4) of Section 336 or any provision of any of other law. HELD: The Master Plan is prepared under section 7 of the Delhi Development Act, 1957 and it has come into force on September 1, 1962. [172 E] Under section 8(1) of the Development act, the Commissioner is entitled to refuse sanction of a building or work if the building or works or use of the site for the building would contravene any other law '. If the proposed building or use is indicated in a Master Plan, a different use of that land cannot be permitted. Similarly, if a Zonal Development Plan provides for a particular use of any land or building in that zone it cannot be put to a different user. If neither of the plans provide for the particular use or of the land in the area or Zone section 14 will have no application whatsoever. [173 E F] The Master plan and the two maps relied on by the appellant do not give any indication that any part of the proposed road shown in the Master plans will pass through any of its properties. The provisions of section 7 clearly indicate and that is borne out by the various matters mentioned in the master Plan that the master plan will only give a very broad outline of DeLhi as it will look in future. Though there is an obligation on the Authority to prepare the Zonal Development plans simultaneously with the preparation of the Master Planning Plan, or as soon as there may be thereafter, no such Zonal Development plan has been prepared. That assumes considerable importance in this case because it is the Zonal development Plan, under section 8 (2)(a) which will show the approximate location and extents of land uses proposed in a zone for roads; further, under sub cl. (d) of sub s.(2) Of section 8, the said Zonal Development Plans will also contain provision regarding the allotment or reservation of land for roads. If such an indication is made available by the Zonal Planning Plan then section 14 would quite naturally stand attracted, because any user of a land or buildings otherwise than in conformity with the Zonal Master Plan will be hit by that section.

The appellant No. 1 was the Minister of Industries and the appellant No, 2 was the Secretary to the Government of the Commerce and Industries Department of the State of Vindhya Pradesh. The period of lease expired on 30th October, 1951 but there was an option reserved to the lessee to have a renewal of the lease for a further period of 15 years from the date of such expiration. There were disputes between the syndicate on the one hand and the Panna Durbar on the other and by his order dated the 31st October, 1946, the Political Minister of Panna stopped mining operations of the sy Syndicate. The appellant No 1 was asked to see the appellant 's name in the list of documents seized from him and handed over the sum to the appellant. The appellants were asked to come to the said dressing table opened by the police. The appel lant No. 2 told the appellant that he would go to Rewa and see the appellants at the time and the appellants demanded from them a bribe for the purpose. The case of the prosecution was as follows: By an agreement executed on the 1st August, 1936 between the Panna Ganbar of the one part and the Madan Durbar of Madhya Pradesh, the appellant Nos. 1 and 2 were appointed as Field Manager to get the said order of the Political Department stopping the working of the mines rescinded. Pannalal made several applications for procuring the cancellation of the said orders and on the 13th January, 1949, the Personal Assistant to appellant No., 1. The Special Judge acquitted both of them but convicted the appellants of the various offences with which they were charged. On appeal by the State, the Judicial Commissioner reversed the order of acquittal passed by the Special judge and convicted both the appellants. The High Court held that the appeal to the Judicial Com missioner from the acquittal by the special judge was competent and that there was no infringement of the fundamental rights of the appellants under articles 14 and 20 of the Constitution. Held, that the statement made by the appellant to him was not recorded under the provisions of section 164 of the Criminal Procedure Code and was therefore inadmissible in evidence and could not be proved orally by him. The statements made by him were admissible in evidence as there was nothing to show that he had anything to do with the appellants ' case.

The respondent was serving the State Police as a constable when an incident took place on 17.2.1971, which led to the prosecution of the respondent along with Head Constable Kahan Singh and the Sub Inspector Baldev Singh. The charge made against the respondent was that he physically assaulted and detained one Gurdial Singh. He was acquitted by the trial court. The High Court dismissed the second appeal in limine. In this appeal it was contended on behalf of the appellant that Rule 16.2(2) of the Punjab Police Rules, 1934 mandatorily directs that a police officer judicially sentenced to rigorous imprisonment exceeding one month shall be dismissed and this mandate of law cannot be ignored on the ground that in the case of another member of the police force a mistake was committed. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The question involved in this suit should not have been lightly brushed aside by the High Court in the manner it has been done. [825 D] 2. Rule 16 is mandatory and prescribes a maximum punishment for a person who has been convicted under section 325 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. The respondent was given the benefit of probation by the criminal court and his case, therefore, was distinguishable. Even in the concluding paragraph of the judgment of the Additional District Judge, the possibility that "the other police officials convicted with him" (that is, the plaintiff) might have been later punished, is recognised. It has been further urged on behalf o the appellants that the finding of the Addl. District Judge on the question of limitation is patently illegal inasmuch as the judgment assumes that no law of limitation was applicable to suits where an order is impugned as being void. The view taken by the first appellate court permitting the competent authority to inflict only minor punishment on the respondent in certain conditions, and the direction about the payment of salary and other emoluments. After heat ing the learned counsel for the parties, we agree with the appellants ' contention that the question involved should not be lightly brushed t aside by it has rightly been done [825 E F] 3. The appeal is accordingly allowed. There will be no order as to costs.

The appellant, a private limited company carrying on business in tea garden tools and requisites and also acting as agents for selling tea. In fact the bulk of its income was from selling commission on tea. The assessment year in question is 1959 60 in the relevant previous year which ended on June 30,1958, the assessee entered into certain transactions in jute. On April 17, 1958 the assessee had contracted to purchase 1100 bales of B Twill and 2500 bales of corn sacks: the contract for B T will was with two parties M/s. Raghunath & Sons (P) Ltd., for 500 bales and M/S. Mahadeo Ramkumar for 600 bales. The transactions thus resulted in a loss of Rs. 98,534 to the assessee and the assessee claimed adjustment of this loss in the computation of its Income for the assessment year 1959 60. The Income tax Officer held that the transactions were not speculative and the loss should be treated as business loss relying on two decisions of this Court: Bayana Bhimayya and Sukhdevi Rathi vs The Govt. of Andhra Pradesh, ; , D. M. Wadhwana vs Commissioner of Income tax, West Bengal, ; and D.M. Wadhwani vs Commissioner Of Income tax (supra), overruled. In appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner the Tribunal referred to the High Court the following question of law: "Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case the Tribunal was right in holding that the transaction described above entered into by the assessee were speculative transactions within the meaning of explanation 2 to section 24(1) read with Explanation 2 and restored the order of the Income tax officer. " The High Court answered the question in the affirmative and against the assessee. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the transaction was not speculative in nature; (ii) the transactions described above were speculative and consequently the losses suffered by the asses see could not be set off against the profits made by the assssee 's non speculative business High Court on reference following its earlier decisions in D. P. Wadhvani vs Commissioner, Income tax ; , followed.

The first respondent was a candidate for the general seat and the appellant in Civil Appeal No. 213 A of 1953 for the General seat. The nomination paper was rejected by the Returning Officer at the scrutiny stage and so he was unable to contest the election. The appellant filed an appeal against the order declaring the whole election void. The Election Tribunal decided in favour of the first respondent but declared the whole ' election void, holding that the appellant was right in rejecting the first contention and declared the entire election void and dismissed the second appeal. Held, that the nomination papers were not signed by the proposers and seconders in the usual way by writing their names, and as their marks were not attested it was evident that they had not been " subscribed" because " subscribing " imports a "signature" and as the Act sets out only kinds of "signatures" which it will recognise as II signing", for the purposes of the Act, the words "subscribe" in section 36(4) must be construed in the sense set out above. The word "subscribes" is not defined but it is equally clear, when the Act is read as " a whole along with the form in the second schedule that "subscribing" can only be used in the manner prescribed by the Rules and where the signature cannot be written it must be authorised in the way prescribed by them. The words " subscribing to the word " sign " in the Representation of the People Act, 1951, show that the writing of a signature and the making of a mark are to be treated differently. The Returning Officer was therefore bound to reject any nomination paper on the ground of any technical defect which is not of a substantial character but he cannot remedy the defect.

The appellants, who were employees of the respondent company, went on an indefinite peaceful strike with effect from August 30, 1972 pursuant to a strike notice given by the Company. The appellants ' union made a formal demand calling upon them to report for duty on or before September 18, 1972 failing which their absence would be construed as voluntary abandonment of service and their names would be struck off from the muster rolls of the company. On September 19, 1972, the appellant wrote to the respondent stating that it did not wish to revise its earlier decision under which their names had been struck off the rolls. The respondent replied that the appellants ' Union had neither voluntarily abandoned the service of the Company and did they wish to do so. Thereupon, the appellants made a written demand calling on them to re instate the appellants and others who had been removed from service on the ground that they had abandoned their service. On October 23, 1972 the respondent wrote to them acknowledging their letter dated September 26, 1972 but stating therein that it was not wish either to revise the earlier decision or to withdraw its earlier decisions under which the names had already been struck out by letters dated September 21, 1972 and September 26. 1972. The appellant replied that it had not abandoned the Company 's service. The Industrial Tribunal rejected the appellants contention on the view that the action of the appellant in removing the names of the appellants from its rolls was illegal and invalid. In appeal to this Court, it was contended for the appellants that (1) what is the true meaning of the expression 'abandonment of Service '; and (2) whether in the circumstances of the case it could be said that the appellant had voluntarily abandoned their services of the Respondent company. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The intention may be inferred from the acts and conduct of the party, and is a question of fact. Temporary absence is not ordinarily sufficient to constitute an abandonment of office '. From the connotations reproduced above it clearly follows that to constitute abandonment there must be total or complete giving up of duties so as to indicate an intention not to resume the same. In Buckingham Co. vs Venkatiah & Ors., , this Court held that under common law an inference that an employee has abandoned or relinquished service is not a question Of fact which has to be determined in the light of the surrounding circumstances of each case. [616C D] 2. The failure to perform the duties pertaining to the office must be with actual or imputed intention, on the part of the officer to abandon and relinquish the office. The words 'abbutonment of service ' are not ordinarily enough to constitute a abandonment of an office '.[617E F] 3. In the instant case, there was nothing in the surrounding circumstance or the conduct of appellants indicating or suggesting an intention on their part to abandon service which in view of the ratio of Gopal Chandra Misra 's case, can be legitimately said to mean to detach, unfasten, undo or untie the binding knot or link which holds one to the Office and the obligations and privileges that go with it Their absence from duty was purely temporary and could by no stretch of imagination be construed to as voluntary relinquishment by them of the Appellant 's services. [625F G] 4. The fact that the respondent had along with other workmen gone on indefinite strike which ended on October 22, 1972 in response to the strike notice issued by the union to the Company to press its demand for re instating the appellants, and others, who had not only returned the cheques sent to them by the company on account of their leave salary gratuity etc. The respondents stand that the letter of the petitioner dated September 7, 1972 was received by them on September 20, 1972 is a receipt by them and not earlier was never denied or refuted by the appellant.

The respondents, who were trustees of a public trust, mortgaged a house belonging to the trust. The trustees did not pay the instalments due under the decree and in an application for execution by the mortgage, the mortgaged property was put up for sale and the bid of the appellant was accepted for Rs. 5,000 by the executing court. The respondents applied under 0. 21 r. 89 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the sale and deposited Rs. 250 being 5 % of the purchase money for payment to the appellant and Rs. 6 for payment of the mortgage amount. The Subordinate Judge passed an order disposing of the execution application and directed that Rs.250 out of the amount deposit, by the trustees be paid over to the respondents. In appeal against that order by the appellant, the District Court reversed the order holding that since the trustees had failed to comply with the requirements of r. 88 of 0.21 C.P.C., the executing Court had no jurisdiction to set aside the auction sale and directed the execution proceedings to be disposed of in accordance with law. The High Court held that sale of the mortgaged properties which belonged to a public Trust without the sanction of the Charity Commissioner being prohibited by section 36 of the Bombay Public Trusts Act, was invalid and on that view remanded the case to the District Judge for decision on all the points correctly arising out of it. Against this order, the appellant came up in appeal to this Court. HELD: (i) The High Courts were not right in holding that the requirements Of 0. XXI r.89 were complied with and the Subordinate Judge had no power to set it obligatory upon the court to issue notice to the Charity commissioner and if that officer desires to be joined as a party, to implied him in a proceeding to enforce a mortgage by sale of immovable property. [459 D] (ii) The Legislature did not intend to put any restriction upon the power of the Civil Court executing a decree for recovery of money due from the trust, by sale, of the property of the trust and the section imposes a fetter on the power to the trustees: it is not intended thereby to confer upon the Charity Commissioners an overriding authority upon actions of the civil court in execution of decrees. The section imposes an embargo on the powers of the trustees. It imposes a restriction upon their power of sale, by auction sale of property of a trust. [461 F] (iii) The legislature did not want to put restrictions upon the powers conferred on the Charity Commission under 0 . 21 r 89 of C. P.C. in respect of the territory of Gujarat. When pressed with the observations made in the two cases cited at the Bar, Raju. J., held that a single Judge of a High Court was ordinarily bound to follow that precedent. because by following the precedent the judge would act contrary to section 165 of the Indian Evidence Act and would also violate the oath of office taken by him when entering upon his duties as a Judge under the Constitution; and (iv) that a judgment of a Full Bench of the High Court may be ignored by a Single Judge, if the Full Bench judgment is given on a reference made on a question of law arising in a matter before a single judge or a Division Bench. Such a judgment according to Raju J. would "Dot be a judgment at all" and "has no existence in law". [459 E] (v) The decision of Bhagwati, J. in Pijare Karimbhai 's case was binding upon the High Courts.

The Government of India, by an order dated April 21, 1970, retired a Government servant from service under Rule 2(2) of the Liberalised Pension Rules, 1950. The Government had also the power under Rule 56(j) to retire a Government serv ant at any time after he has completed 30 years of qualifying service. The appellant challenged the said order by means of a writ petition before the High Court which was accepted and rule 2(1)(j) of Pension Rules was declared invalid. The Union of India appealed against the judgment of the High court. The Division Bench allowed the appeal holding that there was no in firmity in Rule 2 (2) and that there is no vice of arbitrariness in the Rule. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The object of Rule 2 of Pension Rule 2 is to chop off the dead wood. Rule 2 provides no guide line and gives absolute discretion to the Government. There is thus no force in the argument and it is rejected. [800G] 1.2 The object underlying Rule 2 has been to chull off the unwood wood. Rules 2(ii) of pension Rules are not inconsistent with Rule 2. There was thus no substance in the contention that there has been discrimination between the Government servants who have out lived their utility but there is a rational basis for the argument that it gives unguided power to the Railway authorities to pick and choose railway employees for the purpose of pre mature retirement. [899H; 899A] 1:3 The object is to Chop off dead wood, Rule 2 gives unguided discretion to Government to retire an officer who has completed thirty years ' qualifying service though he has a right to continue till the age of superannuation which is 58 years. Any Government servant who has attained the age Of 55 years can be retired prematurely under F.R. 56(J) only on the ground of 'Public Interest ' whereas another Government servant, who is only 51 and has completed 20 years of qualify service can be picked up for premature retirement under the Rule.[899A B] 1 :4 The object and purpose of Rule 2046 of the Indian Railway Establishment Code and para 620 of the Manual are different from that of clause (h) and (k) of Rule 2946 of Pension. A Division Bench of the Madras High Court came to the conclusion that Rule 2045 having been framed under Article 309 of the Constitution and being a compendious rule, the railway employees are only govered by the said rule and para 621 was void and inoperative. This Court while setting aside the judgment and order of the Single Judge of the Andhra Pradesh High Court held as under: "Thus the areas of operation of Para 620 of Railway Pension Manual is different from the clause (g) and para 623 of the Railway Pension Scheme should be treated as supplementary to Rule 2047 of the Rules. The said para which has been framed by the Union Government in exer cise of its executive powers under Article 73 of the Constitu tion and being an unified rule, is identical to Fundamental Rule 56 (j). Para 620 is in the nature of executive instructions but is similarly worded as Rule 2.(2)

The assessee was an unregistered firm carrying on business of manufacture and sale of katechu. The chargeable account period was 1 4 1943 to 31st March, 1944. There were two partners of the assessee firm, namely L. Phoolchand and M/s Biharilal Balkishan each having profits in proportion of 11 annas and 5 annas respectively. The work in connection with the extraction of Katechu was carried on in Nepal by 1.4.1943 to 31th March, 1943. The sales in this case were effected between 26th July, 1943 to 4th April, 1944, while the business was dis continued. Therefore, while there was manufacturing activity there was no sale during the financial years ending 31st December, 1941 and 31st Maru ber, 1943, sales took place from 5th May, 1941 to 31rd March, 1945. The dispute in this appeal is with regard to the set off of deficiency of profit relating to the periods 20th October, 1940 to 17th October 1941 and 23rd November 1942 to 31 st March, 1948. The Excess Profit Tax Officer held that the business carried on during 10th October 1940 to October 2941 was completely differ ent from the business carrying on during the chargeable accounting period under consideration. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner also found that the constitution of the firm during the relevant chargeable accounting periods was the same as in 1940 41 and the same business of manufacturing Katechin in Nepal and selling the finished products at kanpur was carried out by M/S BiharilalBalkishan in the account styled "Kalyanmal Phoolchand". The Appellate Assist ant Commissioner also held that there could be no profit or loss during the said two chargeable accounting years although there were no sales effected, yet profits accrued to the assessee. In appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commis sioner held that no profits accrued unless sale was effected and, therefore, there was a no merit in the submission made on behalf of the asses see that during the two chargeable relevant accounting periods, though there were sales effected yet profits accrue to the assesse. The Tribunal also found (i) that there was profit arising during the accounting period ending 31th December, 1942 to 3rd March 1943 and (ii) that the manufacturing operations were carried on at the said periods and as such there could not be any profit or gain during the provi sions of section 13 of the Income Tax Act, 1922. The High Court held that it was necessary to determine what part of the profits realised upon the sales from 30th May 1941 to 29th September, 1941, should similarly be apportioned between the manufacturing activity during the rele vant accounting period and the sales during the taxable accounting period ended 31st Decu ber 1944. In the appeal by the assessee, it was contended on behalf Of the Revenue that as provided in the Act, the provisions of the Act would apply to every business of which any part of profits was made during the com pensation period, is chargeable to income tax. It was further urged that no part of profit could be said to have been suffered any deficiency of profits during those periods. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The concept of "accounting period" in the background of the 'chargeable accounting period ' can thus be harmo nised. [610E] 2.1 In order to work out the scheme of the E.P.T.

The Kerala Public Service Commission invited applications for filling up 130 expected vacancies in the posts of Junior Engineers in the Public Works Department, as per notification published in the Kerala Gazette dated 16th May 1978. The qualifications specified for the posts were B.Sc. in Civil Engineering or Mechanical Engineering of the Kerala University or its equivalent as prescribed by the special rules of the said Kerala Engineering Subordinate Service (General Branch). The applicants had to appear in the written test conducted by the KPSC and there after in an interview held by it. There was a common question paper which contained, in category I, questions in Civil engineering and in Category II, questions were in Civil nature, questions of civil Engineering and in category II, question in Mechanical Engineering. The applicants who had qualified in Civil Engineers challenged the judgment of the High Court on the ground that they had qualified for Civil Engineering question paper and answered the questions in Category I on the one hand and those who had appeared in the viva voce test held by them. It was contended in the applications that the applicants who were qualified in civil engineering question paper could not rationally be included in a common rank list after the interview. The learned Single Judge of the K PSC allowed the Writ Petitions and directed the Government to prepare "two lists, namely, one for the Civil Bench and the other for the Mechanical Branch on the basis of examination already conducted". He proceeded: "With respect to it the Service Commission has not yet published the rank list. On receiving information from the Government on the above lines, the Public Service Commis sioner & R will implement the orders forthwith. " The Kerala Public Services Commission filed a petition before this Court for clarification of the position and directions particularly praying that the expression "the common list prepared by the Public Services Com mission should be deleted". This Court dismissed the S.L.P. filed by Shri section Gopa Kumar against the judgment dated 23rd March, 1979. The petitioner challenged the order of the Division Bench of the Madras High Court dismissing a number of writ appeals. The contentions raised in the Special Leave Petitions were: (i) that the applicant who had been advised 239 candidates according to the separate lists for Civil and Mechanical Engineering prepared on the strength of directions given by the learned Single judge and that these candidates had already been appointed, and (ii) that they have already been appoint ed. Dismissing the special leave petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in dismissing the writ appeals, having regard to the developments which have taken place. Accordingly, the special Leave Petitions are dismissed. [749E] 2. In pursuance of the directions given in his judgment dated 3rd April 1980 quoted above, the Government and the Public service Commission of Kerala proceeded to prepare separate lists. But facing difficulties, in view of the observation of this Court in its order dated 23th April 1980 extracted above, it is necessary to clarify the position. [750G] 3. The KP.SC has stated in its counter affidavit that there were directions to the K.PSC to prepare two separate rank lists one for Civil Engineers and the others for the Electrical Engineering graduates. The name of Gopa k Kumar appears in the latter list. The rank list for Engineering (Civil) contains names of 152 candidates and the Other (Mechanical) contains 202 candidates. All the Civil Engineering selected have already be appointed. Shri Gopa Chandra Kumar 's lank was 138 in the rank List of Engineers (Mechanical). He will be appointed when his turn comes. [751B C] 4.

The respondent filed a suit for dissolution of partnership and accounts valuing at Rs.150 as being the sum of Rs.50 for rendition of accounts and another sum of over Rs. 50 for profit to the share of the plaintiff arising out of the business. The trial court passed an order on 26th December 1981 on the basis of the false allegations made by the defendant. The respondent challenged the valuation given by the plaintiff as grossly undervalued and arbitrary. The issues relating to the correct valuation and pecuniary jurisdiction of the Court to enter the suit were taken up as preliminary issues and decided in favour of the respondent. The defendants challenged the order by a civil revision application before the Calcutta High Court which was dis missed. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In a suit of accounts the plaintiff is not obliged to state the exact amount which would result after taking all the accounts and he may, therefore put a tentative valuation upon the suit, but he is not permitted to choose an unreasonable and arbitrary figure for that purpose. At page 392 of the judgment in Meenakshisundaram Chettiar vs Venkatachalam Chettiar, [1945] ILR XXIV Patna 334, the plaintiff non applicant before the High Court filed a civil suit praying for accounts from appellant No. 1. Rejecting his claim to put any valuation under section 7(iv)(f) of the court Fees Act, the High court observed that when a plaintiff is required to place the valuation on his claim he must state a valuation which need only be approximately correct but qualified it by saying that, "it must not be arbitrary or manifestly inadequate. It is true that in a suit where for accounts the correct amount payable by one party to the other can be ascertained only when the accounts are examined and it is not possible to give an accurate valuation of the claim at the inception of the suit. The plaintiff is, therefore, allowed to give his own tentative valuation. Ordinarily the Court shall not examine the correctness of the valuation chosen, but the plaintiff cannot act arbitrarily in this matter. If a plaintiff chooses whimsically a ridiculous figure it is tantamount to not exercising his right in this regard. In such a case it is no longer open to the court but its duty to reject such a valuation. [511F H] Smt. Tara Devi vs Sri Thakur Radha Krishna Maharaj, ; , referred to. 1:2 The interpretation put by the learned counsel on the decisions of this Court is not correct and cannot be accepted. None of the two cited judgments relied upon by Mr. Chatterjee helps him. It was true that when the valuation put by plaintiff appears to be arbitrary and unreasonable the court may reject it and leave the plaintiff to correct the valuation or have the suit rejected. Similar was the view of the Patna High Court in suits covered by section 7 (iv)(c) in Salahuddinhyder vs Dhanoolal, [1946] ILR XIV Patna 334 and Shama Pershad Shahi Shahi vs Sheopershad Singh XLI, I.C.

Dismissing the appeals, this Court HELD: 1.1 The State intended the exemption to be confined only to the cases covered by the subsidy/loan schemes prevalent earlier.
