The Delhi Higher Judicial Service Rules, 1970 which were framed by the Lieutenant Governor of Delhi in consultation with the Delhi High Court, were published in the Delhi Gazette on August 27, 1970. These rules were framed under Article 309 of the Constitution. Rule 2(b) provides that `Cadre Post ' means any post specified in the Schedule and includes a temporary post carrying the same designation as that of any of the posts specified in Schedule. Part III of the said Rules deals with method of recruitment to the service. Recruitment of promotees is dealt with by Rule 5(1), according to which, recruitment of persons to the Service from the Delhi Judicial Service shall be made by the Administrator on the recommendation of the High Court. In other words, promotees are appointed to the Delhi Higher judicial Service. A person who is appointed to that Service from Delhi HigherJudicial Service is called `direct recruit '. By Rule 4, the authorised permanent strength of the service and the posts included therein shall be as specified in that Schedule. The petitioners who were working on deputation as members of one or the other of the Tribunals in Delhi, like the Industrial Tribunal or Sales Tax Tribunal. In that capacity some of them are working on a deputation as member of one of the Tribunal in Delhi. like the industrial tribunal or the Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal. The Union of India, the Delhi Administration, the High court of Delhi and direct recruits to the said Delhi Higherjudicial Service were impleaded as respondents to the petitions. The Delhi Higher Administrative Service was constituted on May 15, 1971 with a complement of 12 posts. The Rules were framed in consultation With the High Courts from amongst the members of the Delhi judicial Service, which were then created by the Delhi Adminis tration in the cadre of Additional District and Sessions Judges. In the meantime, the Lt. Governor of the State of Delhi made an order on August 26, 1970 appointing a person to the post of Additional Distt. & Sessions Judge. The petitioner who was working as a member of the Haryana Higher Judicial Services was appointed as a direct recruit. By Notification dated August 27. 1970, he was appointed to be the `direct recruits '. He challenged the validity of these Rules on the ground that seniority between promotees and direct recruit must be determined in accordance with the respective dates of their continuous officiation as Additional District & Sessions Judges and that direct recruits who were appointed as Additional Distt., and Sessions judges after the promotees are so appointed, cannot rank higher in seniority over the promotees. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the seniority between direct recruits and promotees must be fixed in accordance of the respective date of their actual officiation in the Cadre post i.e. a direct recruitment and not according to the dates on which direct recruits were appointed to their respective posts and the dates from which the promotees have been officiating continuously either in temporary posts created in the Service or in substantive vacancies to which were appointed in a temporary capacity. The respondents filed writ petitions before this Court under Article 32 of the Consti tution praying for a direction that the petitioners be treated as senior to the promotees who are appointed on the basis of their respective continuous officiation in Delhi Higher Courts and direct them to be treated senior to them. Allowing the writ petitions, ^ HELD: 1.

The appellant, who was a partner in a trading venture, conducted an action for dissolution and for account of the partnership business. The Income tax Officer assessed the Ambala Flour Mills in the three years of assessment in the status of an association of persons. In appeals by Debi Parshad, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner set aside the order of assessment and directed that the direction for assessing the income should be deleted. The Tribunal referred the questions at the instance of the Commissioner of Income tax. The High Court answered the first question in the negative. The second question was whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case, the appeals were maintainable in law. Held, that where the income tax Officer assesses the income of an Association of persons under section 31(3)(b) the Appellate Tribunal is competent to set aside such assessment and to direct the Income tax officer to do what he has failed to do. The expression "any person" in the setting in which it appears must be confined to a person intimately connected in the said sense with the assessments of the year under appeal. Commissioner of lncome tax, U.P., vs Kanpur Coal Syndi cate, , referred to. Commissioner off Income tax, Uttar Pradesh vs Kanpur coal Syndia, ; and Commissioner of income tax, Kanpur Coal Co. Ltd. vs Kanpur Chandra Mohan Das, , distinguished. Held further, that the expression " any person" used in section 34 sub section (3) proviso 2 at p. 346, must be restricted to a persons intimately linked in the aforesaid sense with those assessments of that year under Appeal. Commissioner Of Income tax U. P., vs Lucknow Coal Sythi cation, , applied.

The appellant filed a suit for partition of his share and obtained a decree in the trial court. The respondent contended that the compromise and release deed executed by the appellant 's father and the decree that was subsequently passed between the parties were fair and bona fide transactions and since they amounted to a settlement of the disputed claim by the appel lant 's mother, the plaintiff was bound by them. Held, that the suit was not barred by article 17 B of Schedule II of the Act as it applied only to suits filed on the Original Side of the High Court. The plaint did not strictly attract the provisions of article 17 A of Schedule 11 and that the court fee had to be paid either under section 7(iv)(b) or under section 8 of the Suits Valuation Act. The suit was therefore governed by section 3 of the Madras Act and it could not be reopened at this stage. It was not correct to say that in cases falling under section 6, sub section (iv)(c), a departure has been made and liberty has been given to the plaintiff to value his claim for the purpose of court fees and the valuation for jurisdiction alone is mentioned. The Court fee had therefore to be levied either under sections 7(v) and 7(vi)(b). Held, further, that in suits falling under sub section(iv), a distinction has been drawn between cases falling within sub section 2 of section 7 of the Indian Suits Valuation act and those falling under subsection (iv) of section 8. The valuation for court fees is not the same in such cases; but it is the value for court fee stated by the plaintiff that is of primary importance. The result is that it is, the amount at which the plaintiff has valued the relief sought for the purposes of Court fees that determines the value of jurisdiction in the suit and not vice versa.

The New Delhi Municipal Committee (NDMC) sought special leave to appeal against the decision of the NDMC dated 18.2.1987, declining to sanction the Revised Plans for the construction of "Statesman House" a high rise building on plot No. 148, Barakhamba Road New Delhi of which the first respondent is the lessee. The High Court allowed the writ petition and directed the NDMC to convey its formal sanction of the building plans on or before 5th May, 1989. Aggrieved by the decision, the appellant filed an appeal in this Court. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the permissions for the multi storeyed high rise buildings were not in accordance with the Bye laws and that the clearance of the Chief Fire Officer did not prevent the NDMC from enforcing the applicable bye laws. On behalf of Respondent No. 1 it was submitted that the refuge areas were not located on the "external" walls, as interpreted by the NDMC and the lack of a provision for the pedestrian walk way. Disposing of the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The clearance from the Chief fire Officer envisaged by Bye law 17.1 is an additional condition and not a limitation on the power of the Respondent to satisfy itself that the building plan provide for adequate fire safety precaution in accordance wi th its bye laws or in a better measure. The clearance by the Chief Pro duct Fire Officer, which is expected to involve and follow a technical assessment and evaluation, obliges the NDMC, to give due weight to it but, having regard to the scheme and language of the Bye law 16.4.8 are not inflexible and that in appropriate cases, where the plans and designs incorporate fire safety measures which, in judgment of the Delhi High Court, are considered to provide for the safety in a measure better than those envisaged by the bye laws 16. 4.1. The primacy to the Chief Levi sion Officer 's implicit in the approach of the High Court is erroneous and virtually renders the clearance o fication of theChief Fire Officer binding on the NDMC. A reasonable construction bye laws 6.2.[615E F] 1.2 In regard to tho divera cy and acceptability of fire safety Measures in the build ing design, it was urged that the sanction given by the Respondent No 1 distributing 'Refuge Areas ' in each floor provide such a better and more reliable fire safety measure than those contemplated by the Bye Laws and the Chief Educa tion preferred to accept them. As to the requirement of bye law 16 4.8.1 that the exemption area shall be provided on the external walls, it is not correct to say that the rigid interpretation sought to be placed by the appellant on the bye law16.8 and 16.8 was not justified.

The plaintiff filed a suit for partition against the plaintiff of all joint family properties including the accounts of all the businesses. The plaintiff was running the liquor shops, defendants Nos. I and 2 who were the appellants, were carrying on the motor bus business while defendant No. 4 was running a grocery shop. The parties tried to have partition effected between them through arbitrators but the attempt failed. On June 29, 1945, all the five brothers filed a Suit for partition impleading the plaintiff as a minor and the Court finding the compromise to be for the benefit of the minor accepted it and passed a decree in terms of the compromise on July 25, 1947. The defendants Nos., I and II who continued to run the business, were jointly or in partnership with their brothers after the 1st April, 1946, and the plaintiff was bound by the terms of compromise and the consent decree following upon it. Held, that the compromise closed once for all the controversy about taking any account of the joint family businesses including the motor business after the 31st March 1946, but the plaintiff is not barred from reaping the fruits of that business. The compromise having been found not to be vitiated by fraud, misrepresentation, mistake or mistake, the decree passed thereon has the binding force of res judicata. Held further, that a consent decree is as binding upon the parties thereto as a decree passed by invitum. The agreement having been held not to have been vitiated by any fraud, mis misrepresentation, misunderstanding or mistake and the decree was therefore not binding on the parties.

The appellant was a factory manufacturing salt. The Salt Works were extended over an area of about two hundred and fifty acres. Some of the other salt works, however, had even larger areas. The only buildings on this land consisted of temporary shelters constructed for the resident labour and for an office. At a few places pucca platforms exist for fixing water pump when required to pump water from the sea. When not required, this pump was kept in the office. With the exception of the constructions already mentioned, the entire area of Salt Works was open. On the sea side, it had bunds in order to prevent sea water flooding the salt pans. Clause (m) of section 2 of the Act provided that " premises shall not be excluded from the definition of a factory by reason only that they were open air premises ". The appellant contended that the process of converting sea water into salt did not amount to manufacture of salt as no process for making, altering, packing, cleaning or otherwise treating or adapting any article or substance with a view to its use, sale, transport, delivery or disposal was carried on. Held, (per Sarkar and Raghubar Dayal, JJ.) that the appellant 's Salt Works did come within the definition Of the word " factory" in cl. (k) of s 2 of tile Act. The process of conversion of sea water from salt into salt carried on the appellant Salt Works comes within the expression " premises " in the definition section 2(k) and would be a factory if the work carried on there comes within that definition of the word ' factory " and would therefore be a " factory if it had a building and unless the Factory Act clearly provided for the application of the Factories to it. The appellant was rightly convicted of the offence of working the factory without obtaining a licence.

The respondent entered the service of the Princely State of Mysore in 1935 as Instructor in Tailoring and joined duty there on December 1, 1949. He was promoted to the post of Instructor in tailoring and he joined duty thereafter on December 11, 1949, but no order was passed in the case of the respondent despite repeated representations made by the latter. In 1953, the then State of Madras set up the Department of Technical Education and the Polytechnic at Devangere became part of that Department. The respondent continued to make representations to the effect that like other employees who were taken on deputation from other Departments, he should also be absorbed in the Department. On June 11, 1956, the State Government referred the respondent 's case to the Public Service Commission who examined it and by a communication dated February 2, 1960 made these recommendations in favour of the Respondent: "It is stated in the Government letter dated 26 10 1959 that the Director who was the Unit officer for both the departments ordered the transfer of Sri Srinivasa Murthy who was fully qualified as Tailoring Instructor in the Technical Education Department and there was no need to classify the vacancy post to which he was transferred under the then existing rules. Along with him, Sri K. Narayanaswamy Chetty, who was junior to him in the parent department and came on deputation to the Polytechnics and joined duties there on 12th December 1949. This decision was challenged by the respondent before the High Court. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the State had evolved a principle "that if a person was deputed to the Department from another department and he stayed on in that other department for a reasonable long time his absorption in that department should be made to relate back to the date on which he Was initially sent". Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High court was fully justified in granting the relief. [259 F] (2) In the special circumstances of this case, the High court had rightly held that his "impermissible reversion" for a short while in 1955 to the parent Department was no ground to hold that he was not similarly situated as K. N. Chetty. [260 D E] (3) The acceptance of the respondents ' contentions would have unsettled pre Constitution matters, and it would have been directly productive of results going against section 115(7) of the States Reorganization Act. Moreover, the petitioners in that case claimed to be promoted with effect from past dates. There was no principle of policy or service rule on the basis of which they could claim such promotions as of right. [261 F G] (4) The respondent ' 's contention that this principle whereby the absorption in the department of Technical education was related back to his date on Which a person initially came on a deputation, was never departed from except in the cases of the petitioner. This being the case, he was in all material respects, in the same situation as K N. N Chetty. very rightly, the appellant 's writ petition should not be granted.

The petitioner, an advocate practising in this Court, complained of malpractices indulged in by social organisations and voluntary agencies engaged in the work of offering Indian children in adoption to foreign parents. The letter referred to a press report based on "empirical investigation carried out by the staff of a reputed foreign magazine" called "The Mail", and alleged that not only Indian children of tender age were under the guise of adoption "exposed to the long horrendous journey to distant foreign countries at great risk to their lives but in cases where they survive and where these children are not placed in the Shelter and Relief Homes, they in course of time become beggars or prostitutes for want of proper care from their alleged foreign foster parents. " The petitioner accordingly sought relief restraining Indian based private agencies "from carrying out further activity of routing children for adoption abroad" and directing the Government of India to carry out their obligations in the matter of adoption of Indian children by foreign parents, and directing that the Indian Council of Social Welfare and S.O.S., Children 's Villages of India be carried out within their respective jurisdictions in accordance with law of their country. The petitioner contended that (i) the letter was treated as a writ petition and by an order dated 1st September, 1982 the Court issued notice to the Union of India the Indian Councils of Social welfare and S,O. S, Children 'S Villages for India and the Indian Association of Social Secrets and the said Indian Council should be directed to appear in answer to the writ petition; (ii) the adoption of foreign parents by foreign parent was a well thought out document dealing comprehensively with various aspects of the problem in its manifold dimensions, and (iii) the Court had in most cases where an application is made by a foreign parent for being appointed guardian of a child in the courts in Bombay, Delhi and Gujarat, the child study report as well as the home study report together with other relevant material in order to enable it to decide whether it will be for the welfare of the child to be allowed to be adopted by the foreign parents and if on a consideration of these reports and materials, the court comes to the conclusion that it will for the Welfare of the children, the Court makes an order appointing the foreign parent as guardian of the minor child with liberty to him to take the child in adoption any amount in respect of maintenance of the said child or its medical expenses. Allowing the writ Petition, ^ HELD: 1. The adoption of children by Foreign parents need not wait until social or child welfare agencies are recognised by the Government as directed in this order, but pending recognition of social or Child welfare agencies for the purpose of inter country adoptions, which interregnum, we hope will not last for a period of more than two months, any social or family agency having the care and custody of a children may be permitted to process an application of a foreigner, but barring this departure the rest of the procedure laid down by us shall be followed wholly and the principles and norms enunciated by this Court in this judgment shall be observed in giving a child In inter country Adoption. Social status and family background. Accommodation for the child. [804C D] 2. The recognised social or children agency sponsoring the application of the foreigner must also undertake while forwarding the application to the social or Children welfare agency in India, that it would ensure adoption of the Child by the foreigner according to the law of his country within a period not exceeding two years and as soon as the adoption is effected, it will send two certified copies of the adoption order to the Social or child Welfare agency in Indian family. [853D E] 3.

The appellant company employed workmen numbering over 5000. The gross effective salaries and wages of its employees for the relevant accounting year amounts to Rs. 1,05,32,880. Its accounting year is from 1st April to 31st March of the succeeding year. For the accounting year 1964 65, the Company declared and paid bonus at 20% to all employes in accordance with the provisions of the . The appellant company claimed that this amount should be deducted from its gross profits for calculation of direct tax or alternatively rebate for bonus found payable by it. The Central Government by order dated June 23, 1967 referred for adjudication to the National Industrial Tribunal, Calcutta, the following dispute " What should be the quantum of bonus payable to the workmen of the Indian Cable Company Limited Calcutta for the accounting years 1965 66" and the Unions contended before the Tribunal that the computa tion of allocable surplus by the company has not been properly made in accordance. The Tribunal accepted the evidence of the appellant with regard to certain items, but held that a sum of Rs. 21,06,576 being bonus at20% of the gross effective salary and wages was payable for the year in question and it directed the payment of the balance 6.49% within the period mentioned 109 in the Award. The appellant appealed to this Court by special leave against the award of the Tribunal. It was contended on behalf of the Union that (1) the method of computation of notional direct tax under the Act adopted by the Tribunal is contrary to the decisions of this Court; and (2) the Tribunal committed an error when it added back the sum of RS. 2.65 lakhs to the gross profits as per profit and loss account, and therefore, the award in the Indian Oxygen Ltd. was not justified in adding back the said amount to gross profits. HELD: The claim of the Unions that after distribution of bonus at 15% for the years 1964 65 there must have been a surplus and it should have been set on for the next year, namely, 1965 66. This assertion made on behalf 's behalf was controverted by the appellant on the ground that there was no surplus left after paying, the maximum 20% bonus for the assessment year 1965 66 could not have been declared for the period 1964 65 and in order to honour the declaration made by the Company, bonus was paid at that percentage. This evidence of Mr. Gupta has been rightly accepted by the tribunal. Once the evidence is of Mr . Gupta, this plea of the union also has to be rejected.

The appellant, who was working as a Commercial Tax officer in 1953, was promoted as an Assistant Commercial Tax Officer in 1954. On promotion as Deputy Commissioner of Commercial Taxes he was posted as Member of the Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal in the same cadre. On September 28, 1975 he was retired under Fundamental Rule 56(d) of the Tamil Nadu General Rules for the State and Subordinate Services. His service book showed that he had an excellent record of service. He earned several encomiums, commendations and appreciations. The various promotions gained by him react his good record of Service. But there was one dark spot. In 1969 when he was working in as Commercial Tax officers it was noted in his Confidential file by the Deputy Commissioner that the charges should be dropped. The Government accepted the report of the Directorate and dropped the charges making the following order on 29 11 1974: "As the preliminary enquiry disclosed a prima facie case of corruption, a detailed enquiry was taken up by the Directorate of Vigilance and Anti Corruption. The Board of Revenue (CT) was requested to frame charges straightaway as for a major penalty against Thiru D. Ramaswami on the basis of allegations levelled against him. The Full Board of revenue then reported that the charge framed against ThiruD. Ramaswami in consequence of the detailed enquiry conducted by the Vigilance Department cannot be pursued and proved. The appellant filed an appeal before the Government which was rejected. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Government was entitled to take into consideration the entire history of the petitioner including that part of it which was prior to his promotion, 80 Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The previous history of a Government servant should be completely ignored, once he is promoted. Sometimes, past events may help to assess present conduct. But when there is nothing in the present conduct casting any doubt on the wisdom of the promotion, we see no justification for needless digging into the past. [80 E] 1.2 The previous History of a government servant should not be completely overlooked, once the appellant was promoted. Ordinarily, past event events may assist to assess future conduct. However when there are nothing in this case casting any doubts on the fairness of the promotions, it is impossible to sustain the order of the Government retiring the appellant from service. [81 G H] 1:3 The previous long history of Government servant would be completely ignore once he was promoted and Sometimes, future events may aid to assess conduct. [82 E F] Swami Saran Saksena vs State of U.P., ; , followed.

The appellants who were the operators of a motor transport operators whose permits were liable to be modified or cancelled under the provisions of the Schemes on their coming into force, challenged the validity of the schemes framed by the Corporation. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions filed before it and held that the Regional Transport Authority which was specifically mentioned in section 68 F(1) was empowered to issue the permit to the transport undertaking " notwithstanding anything contained in Ch. IV A of the . Held: (i) The scheme is vitiated by non compliance with the requirements of section 68 C and the Rules made thereunder, and it is not necessary that the materials placed before the Court estab lish that the Corporation gave effect to it as a direction which they were expected to and did obey. It was not correct to say that such authority is deprived of the power to issue a permit by reason of section 64F(1). The Regional Transport Authori ties, which is specifically mentioned therein in section68 F(I) is empowered to grant permits to the Transport Undertaking " notwithstanding any anything contained therein in Ch . IV A. (ii) Assuming that the Chief Minister directed the order in which districts were to be taken up for nationalisation, still the scheme framed by it could not be assailed as not in conformity with the requirement of section 66 C. The Regional transport Authority which is expressly mentioned in Ch.(I) was competent to issue permits to a transport undertaking notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in Chapter IV A and that the section rendered the provisions Of Rule 141 of the Motor Vehicles Rules inapplicable to cases covered by section 68F( I).

The appellant, a public limited company registered as a dealer under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941, having its registered place of business at Calcutta, claimed exemption under section 5(2)(a)(ii) of the Bengal Sales Tax Act, 1940. The Commercial Tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that the declaration forms received from its dealers in respect of the goods received from it was missing and that the return filed by the appellant did not contain any particulars as to the fact that they had issued the declarations to it but only stated that the officer did not issue the requisite summons to the parties concerned. The appellant then flied a petition under article 226 of the Constitution in the High Court for issuing an order directing the respondents, i.e., the Commercial Tax officer and the Commissioner of Commercial Taxes to implement the assessment order. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the furnishing of the declaration form was not obligatory but only to be made if a demand is made by the authority concerned. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the words "on demand" in r. 27A which, according to the learned counsel, indicates that the production of the prescribed declaration forms is not obligatory and only to he made if the demand is not made by a authority concerned; (ii) the production must be made before the authority; (iii) the expression "on demanded" only fixes the point of time when the declaration Form forms are to be produced; otherwise the rule would be inconsistent with the section. HELD: Dismissing the appeal, (i)(a) The object of section 5 (2)(b)(ii), is to give exemption to a dealer in respect Of sales to registered dealers of specified classes of goods, it seeks also to prevent fraud and collusion in an attempt to evade tax. In the nature of things, in view of innumerable transactions that may be entered into between dealers. it will well nigh be impossible for the taxing authorities to ascertain in each case whether a dealer has sold the specified goods to another for the purposes mentioned in the section; but that does not enable him to ignore a statutory condition to claim exemption. Sub rules (3) and (4) of r.27A are not helpful to the appellant. They provide only safeguards against abuse of the declarations forms by the purchasing dealers; they do not enable the selling dealer to either directly apply or to compel the purchasing dealer to apply for duplicate forms; nor do they enjoin on the appropriate authority to give the selling dealers a duplicate form to replace lost one. [629 G H] (b) The expression "for the purpose of section 3(2) (a)(iii) of tho Act and the rules made thereunder is self evident. While they are obviously intended to give an exemption to the dealer in regard of sales to unregistered dealers of certain specified classes, it sought also to avoid fraud and ' collusion in a attempt to evading tax.

The petitioners were convicted under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to life imprisonment by the Sessions Judge, Patna in connection with a trial of certain undertrial prisoners in 17 jails in Bihar. The State Government directed that necessary steps for transferring women under "protective custody" should be taken and directions issued by the Government. The petitioners challenged the validity of the said orders on the grounds: (1) that the provisions of section 167(2), were not complied with; (2) that there was no compliance with the direction given by the Court in the earlier case, and (3) that no reasons had been given by it for the State Government as to why there has been such enormous delay in bringing the under trial prisoners to trial. Dismissing the writ petition, ^ HELD: 1. The requirement of the proviso to section 167 was complied with in their case. [529 F] 2. The Court should have the requisite information bearing on the problem. It is not uncommon to find that under trial prisoner who are produced before the Magistrates are unaware of their right to obtain release on bail and on account of their poverty they are unable to engage a lawyer who would apprise them of his right to apply for bail and help them to secure release on jail by making a proper application to the Magistrate in that behalf. [540 A B] 3. The right of one charged with crime to counsel may not be deemed fundamental and essential to fair trials in some countries but it is in ours. These, of course would be the most difficult to anticipate. Equal justice and free legal aid: The State shall secure that the operation of the legal system promotes justice on a basis of equal opportunity, and shall, in particular, provide free legal assistance, by suitable legislation or schemes or in any other way, to ensure that opportunities for securing justice are not denied to any citizen by reason of economic or other disabilities. [541 C] 4. The Constitution is an organic document which has been evolved by the Courts in India. It does not permit any Government to deprive its citizens of constitutional rights on a plea of poverty. [543 D E] 5.

The appellant, who was the landlord and the respondent, gave notice of termination of tenancy to the respondent on December 31, 1951 under section 34(1) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948. The respondent thereupon made an application for possession of the land to the Mamlatdar. In the meantime, an amendment was made to the Act by the insertion of sub section (2 A) to section 34 by the Amending Act XXXIII of 1952 which came into force on January 12, 1953. By this amendment certain restrictions were placed on the right of the landlord to terminate the tenancy of a protected tenant. The appellant contended that the right to terminate a tenancy having arisen when the notice was given, the law to be applied, in case of notices given before the Amending Acts came into operation and therefore the respondent could not claim relief from the court. Held, that the view taken by the High Court is correct and sub section(2 A), which provides for a notice of ejectment but does not provide that the notice should be for one year, is also applicable to all cases where notices might have been given but where the tenancy had not actually terminated before the coming into force of the Amending act. The words "the date on which the right is to terminate" in sub section 2 A are used in the sense of giving a right to the landlord 's intention to terminate tenancy and does not speak of any notice at all. Therefore, when the legislature has to look to the application of sub s.(2A) it is the date on Which the tenancy terminates which determines its application. The restriction by sub section A(2) is on the rights to terminate, but flubs. (2A), imposer, restrictions on the landlord right to terminating the tenancy and do not speak or of any notices at all; therefore, when a notice under section 14(1), is merely a declaration to the tenant of the intention to terminated the tenancy, the crucial date is not the date of notice but the date fixed for termination of the tenancy.

The petitioners, who were evacuees and the houses of one Khadim Ali, filed a petition raising a question of violation of the fundamental right to hold property guaranteed by article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution. The petition was dismissed on the sole ground that it had been filed beyond the time prescribed for it. Held, that no appeal lay to the claim made in the petition. The order dismissing the appeal did not affect the petitioners ' rights under the will if any, and say nothing about them. In the result, the petition must be allowed and set aside the order of January 10, 1952, in so far as it affected the rights of the petitioners in the properties concerned. There was no judicial determination by the Custodian General of any fact affecting Zafar Ali 's right in the houses. If, as was conceded, Zafar Ali had filed an appeal to the Custodian against the order dismissing his appeal, he personally at least, is bound by the order dismiss the appeal. The acts of the Custodian in so much as they deprive the petitioners of their property cannot be upheld. It was well established and not disputed that no property of any person can be declared to be evacuee property unless that person had first been given a notice under section 7 of the Act: Held, further, that the order passed by the High Court did not infringe the fundamental rights of an evacuee which the petitioners on the admitted facts were not entitled to hold. The orders of January 1, 1952 and January 10 were without jurisdiction so far they deprive them of their properties.

The assessee company had two Departments (1) for spinning of yarn from raw and waste wool, and (2) for weaving of yarn. The second Department carried on the operations of spinning of spinning yarn from imported wool tops by raising a loan of Rs. 7 lakhs from the Industrial Finance Corporation. The plant went into production in September 1952. The assessee Company appointed M/s. Murlidhar Chiranjilal as the sole selling agents for the worsted yarn on payment of 2% commission. Subsequently on December 15, 1953 the assessee company entered into an agreement with Mis Saligram Premnath under which the latter were appointed as the principal selling agents on certain specified conditions, the important of which being that the agents were to finance the assessee Company to the extent of Rs 2,50,000 and the assessee agreed to pay 6% interest on the advances to be made by the agents and further agreed to make payment of 6% commission on net profits of the worstned plant in the course of two years. The selling agents M/S. Salig Ram Premnath advanced a sum of Rs 6,26,847 and Rs. 73,787/ for the assessment year 1957 58 as a deduction under section 10(2)(xv) of the Income tax Act, 1922. The case of the assessee was that the two amounts mentioned above being in the nature of commission paid to the selling agents would be deemed expenses incurred by the company in order to earn profits and would therefore fall within the ambit of section 10 (2)(XV) of Income tax, 1922, as it was not incurred for the purpose of the business or for earning profits. The Income tax Officer disallowed the deduction claimed but held that the deduction was actually a division of profits after the profits had come into existence and had been ascertained therefore could not be claimed as a valid deduction under the provisions of section I10 (2). The Appellate Assistant Commissioner also rejected the contention of the Revenue and held that in order that the sums in question were not legal deductions as contemplated by section 10, (2), (xv) and section 10 of the Act but amounted to application of profits for after they were earned. The Tribunal further held that it was a permissible deduction under s.10(2) (XV) Of the Income Tax Act, 1961, in the assessment years 1956 57 and 1957 58 respectively. On reference by the High Court, the High court answered both the questions in favour of the appellant company and held against the Revenue. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the view taken by the Tribunal that the amounts in question amounted to a legitimate deduction under i.

The assessee, a private limited company, maintained an accounts pertaining to him in its books. The Income Tax Officer rejected the contention of the assessee and determined a sum of Rs. 25,107 as dividend under section 2(6A)(e) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. He arrived at this figure by including the current profits of the company for the account year ending March 31, 1959. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissed an appeal filed by the assessee. The Tribunal in second appeal upheld the claim of the appellant that the words "accumulated profits" in section 2 (6A) (e) could not be construed as including current profits but it rejected the contentions of the Revenue and determined the accumulated profits at Rs. 18,950. The Revenue applied for a reference to the High Court of Kerala, and at its instance the Tribunal referred the following question to the high court: "Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of this case, the Appellate Tribunal was legally correct in holding that the accumulated profit will not include current profits for the purpose of section 2.(6A), of the Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1939 ?" 947 The High Court answered the first question in favour of the respondent. Hence the appeal by the Revenue. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High court was right in answering the first two questions in favour. [949 A] 2.1 The expression "accuumulated profit" occurs in section 3(6 A)(e). It is clear that the statute expressly contemplates an application in that behalf by a party desiring a reference, to the Income Tax Tribunal. The application has to be filed within a prescribed period of limitation. If the application is rejected by the Appellate Assistant Tribunal, it is the applicant thus refused who is entitled to apply to the Appellate Court. [948 G] 2:2 In the instant case, there are cases where it has been held that there is an absolute bar against a non applicant seeking a reference of questions of law on a reference application made by the other party. They include : Commissioner of Income Tax, Madras vs section K. Srinivasan and Commissioner of Wealth tax, Gujarat II, Ahmedabad and Commissioner for Income tax, Madras v A. M. V. Murugappan & Ors., [1963] Supp. 1 S.C.R. 952; Commissioner of income tax, West Bengal vs A. K. Das.

The appellant was the Mahant of a religious institution known as Rajgunj Asthal in Burdwan, and the suits out of which the present appeals arose were instituted by him to recover possession of various plots of land in the occupation of the defendants or in the alternative for assessment of fair and equitable rent. The respondents contested the suits and pleaded that the lands were not Mal lands comprised within Mouza Nala forming part of the permanently settled estate of Burdwan, that neither the Maharaja nor the plaintiff claiming under him had any title to them, and that the entry in the record of rights was correct. The District Judge held that the documents on which the defendants claimed to have dealt with the properties as owners under assertion of an adverse title were not proved to relate to the suit lands and that they must therefore be excluded. On appeal by the respondents, the High Court held that there was no proof that the respondents set up any adverse title prior to 1931, much less that the plaintiff had knowledge of the same. Held, that a presumption of lost grant could not be founded on the entry of the record in rights. There are also other difficulties in the way of presuming a lost grant in favour of the predecessors of the respondents. The suit properties formed part of one Mauza Nala within the Zamindari of Burdwan and if a grant had been made in favour Of the predecessors in title of the parties, it must have been made by the Maharaja or by the Rajgun jhar Asthal. But the defendants have in their written statements denied the title of both the Maharaja and the Asthal, and having failed in that plea, cannot fall back on a presumption Of lost grant by the very persons, whose title they have repudiated. This does not exhaust all the difficulties of the defendant. The suits properties formed parts of one Village Mauza Naka within the zamindari of Burdwan within the estate of Alipore within the estates of Alipur and if the grant had be made in respect of a portion of it must be held to have been by the Raja or by Rajgun Jhar Astha.

The appellant filed a suit for specific performance of a contract dated 15th December 1965 for sale of agricultural land. The plaintiff sought to repel the contention that the land which was the subject matter of the contract was covered by the provisions of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948 ( 'Tenancy Act ' for short) and as the intending purchaser, the plaintiff was not an agriculturist within the meaning of the Act, section 63 of the Tenancy Act prohibited him from purchasing the land and, therefore, as the agreement was contrary to the provisions contained in section 70(a) read with sections 85 and 85A of the said Act, the same cannot be specifically enforced. The trial court held that the certificate had no evidentiary value and was not valid. On appeal by the plaintiff, the High Court agreed with the trial court observing that Civil Court has undoubtedly jurisdiction to entertain a suit in a civil suit for Specific performance of contract for sale and while considering the main issue whether specific performance should be granted or not, civil court will have to consider whether there are prima facie any facts on account of which granting of specific performance would result into a transaction forbidden by law and, consequently, civil Court will have jurisdiction to decide the incidental or subsidiary issue and recorded a finding that the plaintiff is not an agricultural labourer. In appeal by certificate, it was contended for the appellant that if the court does not take note of Ext 78, an issue on the pleadings would arise whether the plaintiff be an agriculturist and in view of the provisions under section 70 (a) of the Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961, the issue would have to be referred to the Mamlatdar for decision and the Civil Court would have no jurisdiction to try the issue. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The jurisdiction of the civil court to settle, decide or deal with any question which arises under the Tenancy and Agriculture Lands Act is totally ousted. Therefore, it an issue arises in a Civil Court whether a person is an agriculturist or not and, if section 85A provides for suitable machinery for reference of the issue to the competent authority under the Land Revenue Act, then notwithstanding the fact that such an issue arose in a properly constituted civil suit cognizable by the Civil court, it would have been referred to, the competent authorities under the Act to get the question decided by the authority and on such decision being brought before the Civil Courts, it will be binding on the civil Court and the civil courts will have exclusive jurisdiction to settle. decide or dealt with any issue which is required to be settled, decided or dealt by the competent Authority under the said Tenancy Act. [591 D] 2.

The assessee, a heavy engineer manufacturing boilers, machinery parts, wagons etc. for the assessment years 1958 59 and 1959 60 claimed exemption of tax under section 15C of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922 in respect of the profits and gains derived from its Jute Mill Division for the year 1959 60. The assessee had previously in the earlier years bought from outside the castings manufactured in the steel Foundry Division which was started in the assessment year 1958 59, and continued thereafter. Again in the year '1959 60, in addition to the manufacturing of cast ings in the Steel Foundry division, the Income tax Officer found that out of the total sales of Rs.1303,509/ sales to the Boiler Division totalled only a sum of Rs,1,13,6971/ . The Income tax officer and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner on the above facts held that the machinery was new, was housed in a separate building and that industrial licences had to be obtained, for manufactur ing the parts in question. On appeal by the assessee, the High Court held that even though the manufactured products of the new industrial undertakings were mostly used in the assessee 's other business of manu facturing boilers, wagons, etc., the element of profit was there and the extent of the same could be ascertained as the assessee was maintaining separate books of account. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that setting up of a separate unit to do something in the course of pre existing manufacturing process to aid the production of the said article as was being produced by the pre existing industrial undertaking would not amount to starting of a new industrial undertaking and that production of articles yielding additional profit attributable to the new outlay of capital in a different and distinct unit is the heart of the matter, to earn benefit from the exemption of Tax liability under section15C. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in answering the two questions in the negative and against the assessee. [764E] 2.1 In order that the new undertaking can be said to be not formed out of tho already existing business, there must be a new emergence of a physically separate industrial unit which may exist on its own as a viable unit. This has not happened here in the case of the two undertakings which are separate and distinct. It is clear that the principal business of the assessee is heavy engineering in the Course of which it manufactures boilers, trucks etc.

The inam lands were granted to the appellants for performance of services connected therewith. The inams were confirmed by the British Government. For over 80 years, the inams were in the enjoyment of alienees from inamdars. By an order passed on April 10, 1947 under section 44 B of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1926, the Revenue Divisional Officer resumed the inam lands and regranted them to the temple. On October 17, 1947, this order was confirmed by his order dated October 17. 1947. The appellants instituted a suit in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Madurai under the proviso to section 44B(2)(d)(ii) asking for a decree declaring that the inam grants consisted of the melwaram only. The suit was withdrawn to the Court and registered as O.S. No. 3 of 1954. They instituted another suit in which they prayed for a declaration that the order of the Collector dated October 16, 1947 was a nullity. This suit was transferred to the court of the District Judge and registered in O. S. No, 4 of 1954 and the District judge dismissed the suit as O 'S. 3 Of 1954. The High Court allowed the appeal holding that the inams comprised both melwarams and kudiwaram rights in the land. On this last point, the High Court did not express any opinion. It may be noted that O.s. 3 and 4 of the 1954 Act were tried along with O. 'S Nos. I and 2 of 1954, and disposed of by the District Judges by a common judgment. The State appealed to this Court by special leave. HELD : (i) The inam title deeds, the entries in the Inam fair register prepared at the time of the confirmation of the inams by the Inams Commissioner in 1863 and the contemporaneous statement made by the inamdars are of the same pattern in respect of all the inams. It is sufficient to refer to Ex. B 4, B 5 and B 6 relating to the inam for the service of Sree Padarn Thangi (palanquin bearers). The statements exhibit B 4 show that the lands were being enjoyed by the Inamdars and were granted as inams. The amount of the assessment or melwar was very low and could not be an ade quate remuneration. for the services to be rendered, the inam is a grant of both the melaram and the kudiwara rights are rightly resumed under section44 B(2) (a)(i). [547 D E] (ii) The inams in the present case were not personal inams. They were inams granted to office holders as remuneration for services to being rendered by them in connection with the temple; there was a well recognised distinction between the grant of the land burdened with a condition of service and the grant Of land as remunerationfor an office, see, Noor Mohammad vs Noor Muhammad Tuquee, [1870] 13 H.I.A.438,464. (2) The lands were not Personal inams. they were inam inams granted by the inamsdars and are within the purview of section 44 A B(1)(a)(ii).

The appellant Corporation was governed by the Indore City Municipal Act, 1909. By virtue of the power conferred on it by that Act the Municipality used to levy and collect house tax 127 at the rate of 7% of their gross annual letting value less 10% statutory allowance in lieu of costs of repairs or on any other account whatsoever. The appellant Corporation challenged the validity of the tax imposed on the basis of gross annual rent. Held, that the appellant Corporation had to prepare a fresh assessment list every year and need prepare such list once in every 4 years and can adopt an earlier assessment list such an adopted list becomes the assessment list for that particular official year as if it was a new list and 'to which sections 75 and 76 apply. The tax levied under the old Act and the rules framed thereunder on the ground of gross rent was inconsistent with section 73(2) of the Act. The saving and deeming provisions in section 2(c) can only apply if the tax is assessed in the manner consistent with the provisions of section 73, that is, if it is assessed on the net and not the gross annual rental value after deducting 10% of the gross letting value. The word 'if ' appearing in sub sec. 2 of section 79 is obviously a mistake and must be read as "as if" because the word 'is ' standing by itself makes no sense at all. 79 therefore has to be construed to mean that though a Municipality need not prepare a new assessment list once again in every four years and could adopt an another earlier assessment List such an adoption list becomes its assessment list, for that specific year as when it was adopted it became the list for such subsequent year subject to the procedure laid down in section 75 and76.

The respondent company was incorporated in 1937 primarily with the object of acquiring and working the rights, title and interest in a match factory belonging to one A. V. Thomas at Medical. The Memorandum of Association empowered the Company to manufacture and deal in acids, alkalis and other chemicals. The assessee company carried on its business of manufacturing matches till the account year ending April 30, 1941. Thereafter, the profits from the business became less and less due to War conditions. In a confidential report made on August 1, 1944, to the shareholders, the 963 Directors stated that the price obtained had shown a capital appreciation of about six times the cost price, and the sale included chemicals and paper for manufacture which had not been sold in the first instance. The Deputy Commissioner of Income tax, however, held that the assessee company was liable to income tax on a profit of Rs. 2 lakhs arising from this sale. The High Court held that by the sale no business was done, and that the amount obtained was only by way of realisation sale and was not, therefore, liable to tax. On appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the transaction of sale of the raw materials along with the business, including machinery, plant and premises was a revenue sale; (ii) the amount of Rs 1,15,259 was properly brought to tax as a trading profit; (iii) the decision that the sale of match, machinery and premises, was a distinct from the sale price of chemicals by the assessee Company was not a capital holding but a profit on the sale. Held:(i) The transaction was not during the carrying on of the business or even for the purpose of carrying on the business but was for the purposes of putting an end to the business and that thus the excess represented a capital investment and not a trading profits; (iv) the assessee was carrying on a trading busi ness. The fact that the clause in the Memorandum gave power to the Company, to Bell chemicals cannot be used in this connection because the evidence clearly showed that clause was never used and the two sales of chemicals through the years were too petty in themselves to afford evidence of a continued or sustained trading business in wines and spirits till his existing stocks were exhausted, and, therefore the excess obtained by him represented profit. The transaction in question was not one of purely buying and selling, but was a sale in the course of business operations which alone would have attracted tax if profit resulted. In the present case, there was no identifiable price for the chemicals and raw materials except by comparing the two prices offered to be paid by the buyer, that is to say, the price without the chemicals, and raw material and the price with them; (v) the sale was of the entire assets including goodwill, and not in a reali sation sale, not with a view to trading in chemicals and the raw material but to close down the business; and (vi) the sales were of the whole stock. The distinction between a sale of an entire stock as a part of trading and a sale or of the same stock as the winding up sale was one with which the New Zealand Courts would be familiar, and which it would be more easy for the New Yealand Judges than for their Lordships to appreciate.
